The auxiliary decoder is removed at inference, leaving only RGB observations and robot state as inputs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on RoboTwin, ManiSkill, and real-world tasks show consistent and substantial improvements over Diffusion Policy and ACT, with only a small increase in parameter count and no reduction in inference speed.
AI.conclusion: LEAP improves RGB-based visuomotor policy learning through better-aligned privileged 3D supervision, yielding stronger performance across simulated and real-world benchmarks without sacrificing inference efficiency.

title: Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking
summary: The Offline AI Modules workstream enables practical, low-power, and community-accessible deployment of voice-first AI systems that operate fully offline. Designed for African language communities where speech is the dominant mode of interaction and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent, the workstream delivers three reinforcing components: a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference bill of materials, and a reproducible quantization and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction-tuned language models in the 2-5B parameter class. This paper presents the first end-to-end benchmark evaluation of the stack across two hardware tiers: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (TierB) and a Raspberry Pi5 (TierA). Three instruction-tuned models are evaluated across four quantization formats, assessed for deployment metrics (decode throughput, chat latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality (topic classification accuracy on MasakhaNEWS across English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Yoruba; per-language perplexity drift). Speech recognition is evaluated using Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers. The principal finding is that Q4_K_M quantization represents the best size-to-quality trade-off for deployment on both tiers: gemma-4-E2B-it achieves 28.8t/s decode throughput and 89.2% topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M on TierB, while all three models run within the 16GB memory budget on TierA.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks an offline, voice-first AI stack for African language communities on two hardware tiers, finding Q4_K_M quantization offers the best size-to-quality trade-off.
AI.motivation: African language communities rely primarily on speech for interaction, yet face unreliable or absent internet connectivity. Existing cloud-dependent voice AI systems are thus impractical, and there is a need for practical, low-power, community-accessible offline deployment. However, no end-to-end benchmark evaluation of such an offline stack had been conducted.
AI.method: The workstream delivers three components: a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference BOM, and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for 2–5B instruction-tuned models. Evaluation spans two hardware tiers—NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (TierB) and Raspberry Pi 5 (TierA)—testing three instruction-tuned models across four quantization formats. Metrics include deployment performance (decode throughput, chat latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality via MasakhaNEWS topic classification (English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba) plus per-language perplexity drift. ASR is evaluated with Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers.
AI.result: Q4_K_M quantization provides the best size-to-quality trade-off on both tiers. At Q4_K_M on TierB, gemma-4-E2B-it reaches 28.8 t/s decode throughput and 89.2% topic classification accuracy. All three models operate within the 16GB memory budget on TierA.
AI.conclusion: Q4_K_M is the recommended quantization for deployment across both hardware tiers. The stack demonstrates feasible offline, low-power, community-accessible voice-first AI for African language communities, with all evaluated models fitting TierA's 16GB memory constraint.

title: BRACE: Adapting Whole-Body References for Force and Terrain Aware Humanoid Motion Tracking
summary: Whole-body tracking has become the interface through which operators drive humanoid robots, yet the references it consumes are recorded on level ground and carrying nothing, so the tracker is aware of neither the forces the robot must exchange with objects nor the terrain it must stand on. Existing controllers address one side of this gap: force-capable policies command an end-effector force but prescribe no whole-body pose, while terrain-adaptive trackers treat loads as disturbances to reject rather than wrenches to command. We present BRACE, a whole-body tracker that exerts and compensates commanded hand forces from diverse poses while following a flat-ground reference on sloped terrain. Rather than leaving the tracker to absorb the load and the slope, BRACE folds both into the reference it follows: terrain conformance lifts footholds and root onto the local surface, and a wrench transformation resolves the hand displacement that produces a force jointly with the center-of-mass and center- of-pressure shifts it induces, bounded by teacher-specific arm-effort limits. Separate exertion and compensation teachers are distilled by DAgger into one flow-matching student that runs on proprioception alone, without a height map or measured wrench, so a teleoperator (even in remote locations) can supply a flat- ground trajectory and the robot resolves slope and load onboard. We extensive experiments on the Unitree-G1 to demonstrate the ability of BRACE to exert, compensate force and handle diverse terrain in simulation and real robot experiments.

AI.tldr: BRACE is a whole-body humanoid tracker that follows a flat-ground reference while exerting and compensating commanded hand forces on sloped terrain, folding both load and slope into the reference and distilling teachers into a proprioception-only student.
AI.motivation: Whole-body tracking is the standard interface for driving humanoid robots, but references are recorded on level ground while carrying nothing. Thus the tracker knows neither the contact forces to exchange with objects nor the terrain it stands on. Prior controllers cover only one side of this gap: force-capable policies command end-effector forces without whole-body pose, while terrain-adaptive trackers reject loads as disturbances instead of commanding wrenches.
AI.method: BRACE folds terrain conformance and load into the tracked reference. Terrain conformance lifts footholds and root onto the local surface; a wrench transformation resolves the hand displacement producing a commanded force jointly with induced center-of-mass and center-of-pressure shifts, bounded by teacher-specific arm-effort limits. Separate exertion and compensation teachers are distilled by DAgger into a single flow-matching student running on proprioception alone, without a height map or measured wrench, so a teleoperator can provide a flat-ground trajectory and the robot resolves slope and load onboard.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the Unitree-G1 in simulation and on the real robot demonstrate BRACE's ability to exert and compensate forces and handle diverse terrain.
AI.conclusion: BRACE integrates commanded hand-force exertion and compensation with whole-body tracking across diverse terrain, enabling a remote teleoperator to supply a flat-ground reference while the robot autonomously resolves terrain slope and external load using only proprioception.

title: JIVEAdapter: A Multi-Task Additive Low-Rank Adapter via Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE)
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models at a fraction of the cost of full fine-tuning, yet most low-rank adapters are single-task and represent each weight update multiplicatively, leaving no explicit account of what is shared across tasks and what is task-specific. We introduce JIVEAdapter, a multi-task "additive" low-rank adapter inspired by statistical Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE). JIVEAdapter decomposes every weight update into a Joint structure shared across all tasks plus a per-task Individual structure, penalizes the Individual structures to be near-orthogonal to the Joint so shared and task-specific signal stay "interpretable" and separated, and allocates rank adaptively across a shared Joint pool and a per-task Individual pool. The Joint is learned once, jointly over a task group or incrementally, one task at a time, then frozen and reused as a prior for new tasks without retraining the shared part. On GLUE and SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, JIVEAdapter is competitive with strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines at a matched per-task effective rank, without extra modules such as MoE, and when a related held-in task exists its frozen Joint serves a held-out task by reusing that task's Individual with only a cheap per-direction scale, otherwise training a small new one.

AI.tldr: JIVEAdapter is a multi-task additive low-rank adapter that decomposes each weight update into a shared Joint structure plus task-specific Individual structures, keeping them near-orthogonal and reusing the frozen Joint as a prior for new tasks.
AI.motivation: Most low-rank adapters are single-task and represent weight updates multiplicatively, offering no explicit account of what is shared across tasks versus what is task-specific. This limits interpretability and reuse in multi-task parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.method: Inspired by Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE), JIVEAdapter decomposes every weight update into a Joint component shared across all tasks and a per-task Individual component. It penalizes Individual structures to be near-orthogonal to the Joint, separating shared from task-specific signal, and allocates rank adaptively across a shared Joint pool and a per-task Individual pool. The Joint is learned jointly over a task group or incrementally one task at a time, then frozen and reused as a prior for new tasks without retraining the shared part.
AI.result: On GLUE and SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, JIVEAdapter is competitive with strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines at matched per-task effective rank, without extra modules such as MoE. When a related held-in task exists, its frozen Joint serves a held-out task by reusing that task's Individual with only a cheap per-direction scale; otherwise a small new Individual is trained.
AI.conclusion: JIVEAdapter provides an interpretable, additive multi-task low-rank adapter that explicitly separates shared and task-specific weight updates, enables adaptive rank allocation, and supports efficient transfer via a frozen reusable Joint prior.

title: Behavioral Cloning Mystery
summary: Behavioral cloning (BC), despite its simplicity, exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena in the real world. For example, the performance of BC often keeps increasing as the model overfits more to the dataset, and fully closed-loop policies often completely fail without action chunking. Unfortunately, properly studying these anecdotal phenomena ("behavioral cloning mysteries") is challenging: in the real world, datasets and experiments are costly and not fully controllable; in simulation with synthetic data, these phenomena are often not easily observed partly due to the discrepancy between scripted policies and human demonstrations. In this work, we propose OCBench, a robotic manipulation benchmark with controllable scripted policies that have similar properties to human demonstrations. We show that, by mimicking key properties of human demonstrations, OCBench reproduces many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings. With its GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies, we demonstrate how OCBench enables scientific studies of previously reported BC-related phenomena by analyzing and refuting various hypotheses. Project page: https://seohong.me/projects/ocbench

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OCBench, a controllable robotic manipulation benchmark with scripted policies mimicking human demonstrations, which reproduces and enables systematic study of anecdotal behavioral cloning phenomena.
AI.motivation: Behavioral cloning exhibits counterintuitive real-world phenomena (e.g., performance rising with overfitting, failure of fully closed-loop policies without action chunking), but studying these is hard: real-world datasets/experiments are costly and uncontrollable, and synthetic simulation often fails to exhibit them due to the discrepancy between scripted policies and human demonstrations.
AI.method: The authors propose OCBench, a robotic manipulation benchmark featuring controllable scripted policies designed to share key properties with human demonstrations, alongside GPU-accelerated environments.
AI.result: OCBench reproduces many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings, and by analyzing and refuting various hypotheses, it enables scientific studies of previously reported BC-related phenomena.
AI.conclusion: OCBench provides a controllable, GPU-accelerated platform that bridges the gap between real-world and synthetic simulation, allowing rigorous investigation of behavioral cloning mysteries.

title: Inference-Time Projection for Physically Valid Biomolecular Diffusion Models
summary: AlphaFold 3-style cofolding models predict biomolecular complexes with high structural accuracy, yet a large fraction of their outputs are physically invalid: chains overlap at interfaces, ligand bond lengths and angles are distorted, rings are non-planar, and stereocentres are inverted. Current approaches either steer the sampler with physics-informed potentials, which multiplies sampling cost and memory overhead making inference impossible on large complexes, or finetune the model, costing time and tying the fix to one architecture. We observe that, unlike structural accuracy, physical validity is fully verifiable at inference time from quantities the sampler already holds. We therefore treat physical validity as a constrained inference problem and introduce two closed-form projection operators applied to the diffusion model's denoised clean-coordinate estimate, $\hat{x}_0$: an inter-chain van der Waals projection that pushes apart the most severely clashing atom pairs, and a ligand distance-geometry projection that restores bond lengths, angles, internal contacts, planarity and chirality. Both operators are local, sparse and displacement-capped, require no network evaluations, gradients or importance sampling, and leave the denoiser and its weights untouched, so they can be dropped into any AF3-style sampler without retraining. Applied to two independently developed models, Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3, across five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, the PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, and the Boltz physical-validity test set), our method recovers perfect physical validity while preserving structural-accuracy and ligand-placement metrics. These gains are achieved with negligible runtime and memory overhead, providing a practical, model-agnostic route to physically valid all-atom structure prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that enforces physical validity in AlphaFold 3-style cofolding models via two closed-form projection operators applied to the denoised coordinate estimate, achieving perfect validity without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: AF3-style cofolding models produce structurally accurate but frequently physically invalid complexes (clashing chains, distorted ligand bonds/angles, non-planar rings, inverted stereocentres). Existing fixes either use physics-informed potentials (high sampling/memory cost) or finetuning (time-consuming, architecture-specific). Physical validity is verifiable at inference time from quantities the sampler already has.
AI.method: Treat physical validity as a constrained inference problem. Introduce two closed-form projection operators on the diffusion model's denoised clean-coordinate estimate x̂0: (1) an inter-chain van der Waals projection that separates the most severely clashing atom pairs, and (2) a ligand distance-geometry projection restoring bond lengths, angles, internal contacts, planarity, and chirality. Both are local, sparse, displacement-capped, require no network evaluations, gradients, or importance sampling, and leave the denoiser and weights untouched.
AI.result: Applied to two independent models (Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3) across five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, and the Boltz physical-validity test set), the method recovers perfect physical validity while preserving structural-accuracy and ligand-placement metrics, with negligible runtime and memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a practical, model-agnostic route to physically valid all-atom structure prediction, droppable into any AF3-style sampler without retraining.

title: Demo: Vision-Language Model-Guided Online Calibration of an Electromagnetic Digital Twin
summary: An electromagnetic (EM) digital twin gives mobile robots wireless situational awareness but depends on material conductivities that change with the environment. Online calibration faces initialization sensitivity and measurement travel costs. We demonstrate a vision-language model (VLM)-guided framework using a Unitree G1 robot and NVIDIA Sionna, with two VLM calls: material classification maps visible materials through ITU-R P.2040 to conductivity priors for Sionna's gradient descent on accumulated received signal strength (RSS) measurements; waypoint planning selects the next measurement location online using residual RSS calibration error and image coverage. In a real indoor scenario, the framework achieves a normalized mean absolute conductivity error of $1.74\times10^{-4}$ within 20 m of travel; random initialization never converges, while random waypoints require over twice the travel.

AI.tldr: A VLM-guided framework on a Unitree G1 robot with NVIDIA Sionna calibrates material conductivities for electromagnetic digital twins online, achieving a normalized mean absolute conductivity error of 1.74e-4 within 20 m of travel in a real indoor scenario.
AI.motivation: An EM digital twin enables wireless situational awareness for mobile robots but relies on material conductivities that vary with the environment. Online calibration suffers from initialization sensitivity and measurement travel costs.
AI.method: The framework uses two VLM calls: (1) material classification maps visible materials through ITU-R P.2040 to conductivity priors for Sionna's gradient descent on accumulated received signal strength (RSS) measurements; (2) waypoint planning selects the next measurement location online using residual RSS calibration error and image coverage.
AI.result: In a real indoor scenario, the framework achieves a normalized mean absolute conductivity error of 1.74e-4 within 20 m of travel. Random initialization never converges, and random waypoints require over twice the travel.
AI.conclusion: VLM-guided material priors and waypoint planning enable efficient, robust online conductivity calibration for EM digital twins, outperforming random initialization and random waypoint baselines in real-world robot deployment.

title: CuratorMAS: Automating Dataset Curation via Multi-Agent Orchestration
summary: High-quality datasets are essential for reliable machine learning, but dataset curation remains costly and hard to generalize across domains. Existing methods typically rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting their applicability across tasks and user queries. To address these limitations and automate data curation, we propose \textbf{CuratorMAS}, a multi-agent collaboration framework that orchestrates agents to evaluate and curate high-quality datasets. To achieve the goal of flexible curation, CuratorMAS decomposes the complex curation process into five programmable execution stages and forms a parallelizable workflow. Specifically, CuratorMAS first performs dataset exploration to collect contextual information such as file structures and constraint cues, thereby developing a comprehensive understanding of the given task. In order to acquire up-to-date information, CuratorMAS retrieves domain knowledge from online sources to augment the evaluation process. Next, CuratorMAS derives the necessary evaluation criteria and computes the corresponding metrics. Based on these results, CuratorMAS executes filtering accordingly. Finally, an evolution module summarizes the evaluation outcomes and updates the relevant skills. Extensive and comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CuratorMAS significantly reduces the noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points (pp) while also improving the F1 score of downstream models by up to 8.88 pp.

AI.tldr: CuratorMAS is a multi-agent collaboration framework that automates dataset curation by decomposing it into five programmable stages, reducing noise by up to 36.03 pp and improving downstream F1 by up to 8.88 pp.
AI.motivation: High-quality datasets are essential for reliable machine learning, but curation is costly and hard to generalize. Existing methods rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting applicability across tasks and user queries.
AI.method: CuratorMAS orchestrates agents into a parallelizable workflow of five programmable stages: (1) dataset exploration to gather contextual information (file structures, constraint cues); (2) retrieval of up-to-date domain knowledge from online sources; (3) derivation of evaluation criteria and computation of corresponding metrics; (4) filtering based on results; and (5) an evolution module that summarizes outcomes and updates relevant skills.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CuratorMAS reduces noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points and improves downstream model F1 by up to 8.88 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: CuratorMAS enables flexible, automated, and generalizable data curation, substantially improving dataset quality and downstream performance.

title: TeleHairing: A Teleoperation Baseline for Robotic Haircutting
summary: Robotic haircutting requires controlled tool motion near the head while simultaneously accounting for communication, visual feedback, tool actuation, and interruption handling. Existing studies still lack an operator-in-the-loop reference for analyzing these coupled behaviors before human trials or stronger autonomy. This paper presents TeleHairing, a closed-loop teleoperation architecture for mannequin-based robotic haircutting evaluation under local, relay, and remote deployment conditions. Logged timing shows that the main remote latency increase occurs before the robot-side control endpoint: overall timing reached 190.5~ms in remote mode, while robot-side command queue, control processing, and control-to-robot timing remained similar across modes. Trajectory analysis shows that the larger remote command-following error was dominated by the terminal withdrawal segment rather than accumulated uniformly over the path; excluding this segment reduced remote root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 45.1 mm to 9.6 mm. Detection-loss trials further show that rebase events resumed motion without a large target jump under the tested condition. These results clarify how deployment, execution, and interruption affect the robotic haircutting teleoperation loop, providing a quantitative reference for future autonomy, safety, and user-facing studies.

AI.tldr: TeleHairing is a closed-loop teleoperation architecture for mannequin-based robotic haircutting evaluated under local, relay, and remote modes; timing and trajectory analyses localize remote latency and error to pre-robot-side stages and the terminal withdrawal segment, yielding a quantitative operator-in-the-loop baseline.
AI.motivation: Robotic haircutting demands controlled tool motion near the head while jointly handling communication, visual feedback, tool actuation, and interruptions. Existing work lacks an operator-in-the-loop reference for analyzing these coupled behaviors prior to human trials or higher autonomy.
AI.method: A closed-loop teleoperation architecture (TeleHairing) for mannequin-based robotic haircutting, evaluated across local, relay, and remote deployment conditions. The study logs timing across the loop stages, analyzes command-following trajectory error (RMSE), segments the path to isolate error sources, and runs detection-loss trials to examine rebase behavior during interruptions.
AI.result: Overall timing reached 190.5 ms in remote mode, with the main latency increase occurring before the robot-side control endpoint; robot-side command queue, control processing, and control-to-robot timing stayed similar across modes. Remote command-following error was dominated by the terminal withdrawal segment rather than uniform accumulation: excluding it cut remote RMSE from 45.1 mm to 9.6 mm. Detection-loss trials showed rebase events resumed motion without a large target jump under the tested condition.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify how deployment, execution, and interruption affect the robotic haircutting teleoperation loop, offering a quantitative reference for future autonomy, safety, and user-facing studies.

title: Smart Content Ingestion for Generative AI Workloads
summary: The evolution of machine learning has progressively changed where intelligence resides in an AI system. In conventional machine learning the task, data representation, labels and model architecture were tightly coupled, so data preparation was narrow, schema-bound and visible. Generative AI decouples the model from any single task: one foundation model serves open-ended downstream tasks, and the generality gained on the model side is matched by heterogeneity on the data side, because enterprise knowledge is authored in the formats people use (PDF, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, forms, tables, diagrams and mixed-layout files) that carry textual, visual, geometric and structural information at once. A language model or retriever cannot reason reliably over information misrepresented at this interface, so content extraction becomes a lifecycle stage in its own right whose errors no downstream retriever or re-ranker can repair. This paper presents a production-ready content-extraction system that makes this stage explicit, configurable, and measurable. The system incorporates selective OCR routing, a scarcity-first curation engine with a reference-based extraction scorer that measures character, word, and table-structure accuracy, a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker, and a read-only retrieval evaluator that generates grounded questions from every page and reports Hit@k, mean reciprocal rank, and latency. On a 180-document corpus the best extractor scores 97.4 of 100 (character error rate 0.13%, table similarity 0.995) and the chunker reaches hit@1 of 68.6%, hit@10 of 92.8% and MRR 0.77 over 25,050 generated questions. We distil three design principles (structure before semantics, never mutate what you measure, budget your labels) and position measured content extraction as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Generative AI's task-agnostic foundation models shift the burden to heterogeneous enterprise data, making content extraction a first-class lifecycle stage. It presents a production-ready extraction system with selective OCR routing, a scarcity-first curation engine and reference-based scorer, a structure-aware parent-child chunker, and a read-only retrieval evaluator, validated on a 180-document corpus.
AI.motivation: Conventional ML tightly coupled task, representation, labels, and architecture, so data preparation was narrow and schema-bound. Generative AI decouples the model from any single task, and the generality gained on the model side is matched by heterogeneity on the data side: enterprise knowledge is authored in human formats (PDFs, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, forms, tables, diagrams, mixed-layout files) carrying textual, visual, geometric, and structural information simultaneously. A language model or retriever cannot reason reliably over information misrepresented at this interface, so content extraction becomes a lifecycle stage in its own right whose errors cannot be repaired by any downstream retriever or re-ranker.
AI.method: The paper presents a production-ready content-extraction system that makes this stage explicit, configurable, and measurable. It comprises: (1) selective OCR routing; (2) a scarcity-first curation engine with a reference-based extraction scorer measuring character, word, and table-structure accuracy; (3) a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker; and (4) a read-only retrieval evaluator that generates grounded questions from every page and reports Hit@k, mean reciprocal rank, and latency. It distils three design principles: structure before semantics, never mutate what you measure, and budget your labels.
AI.result: On a 180-document corpus, the best extractor scores 97.4 of 100 (character error rate 0.13%, table similarity 0.995). The chunker reaches Hit@1 of 68.6%, Hit@10 of 92.8%, and MRR of 0.77 over 25,050 generated questions.
AI.conclusion: The paper positions measured content extraction as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems, arguing that making extraction explicit, configurable, and measurable is essential because extraction errors propagate irreparably downstream.

title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction Modeling Networks for Real-to-Sim Soft-Body Simulation
summary: Deformable-object manipulation is essential for robotic tasks such as folding laundry and handling food, where robots must control shape changes as well as object motion. Predictive soft-body simulation supports these tasks by anticipating deformation under external interactions. However, spatial neighborhoods can misrepresent deformation dependencies, introducing local errors that accumulate over successive predictions. Models fitted to individual scenes must also accommodate changes in object geometry and manipulation conditions. In this work, we propose AIM, an Adaptive Interaction Modeling framework that treats real-to-sim soft-body simulation as a local-global interaction modeling problem. AIM uses motion history and geometry to adapt particle relations over current spatial neighbors and retained connections, while geometry-conditioned global communication coordinates object-wide responses. A unified kinematic control-point interface represents different manipulation configurations, and multi-step autoregressive supervision trains the model on its own predicted trajectories. Experiments on PhysTwin and PGND demonstrate improved motion accuracy and visual fidelity, with a 20.0% reduction in future-prediction tracking error relative to PhysTwin and a 22.8% reduction in mean long-horizon particle error across six object categories relative to PGND. The framework further supports transfer across actions, object instances, and scenes, including zero-shot transfer from robot interactions to human manipulation without target-domain dynamics fitting.

AI.tldr: AIM frames real-to-sim soft-body simulation as a local-global interaction modeling problem, using adaptive particle relations and geometry-conditioned global communication to improve deformable-object manipulation prediction.
AI.motivation: Deformable-object manipulation requires robots to control shape changes and object motion, supported by predictive soft-body simulation. However, spatial neighborhoods can misrepresent deformation dependencies, causing local errors that accumulate over successive predictions, and models fitted to individual scenes struggle with changes in object geometry and manipulation conditions.
AI.method: The proposed AIM (Adaptive Interaction Modeling) framework treats real-to-sim soft-body simulation as a local-global interaction modeling problem. It adapts particle relations using motion history and geometry over current spatial neighbors and retained connections, while geometry-conditioned global communication coordinates object-wide responses. A unified kinematic control-point interface represents different manipulation configurations, and multi-step autoregressive supervision trains the model on its own predicted trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments on PhysTwin and PGND show improved motion accuracy and visual fidelity: a 20.0% reduction in future-prediction tracking error versus PhysTwin, and a 22.8% reduction in mean long-horizon particle error across six object categories versus PGND. The framework supports transfer across actions, object instances, and scenes, including zero-shot transfer from robot interactions to human manipulation without target-domain dynamics fitting.
AI.conclusion: AIM effectively addresses error accumulation and generalization challenges in predictive soft-body simulation by adaptive local-global interaction modeling, enabling accurate and transferable deformation prediction for deformable-object manipulation.

title: Small Language Models for Smart Data Model Classification at the Edge: A Cost-Aware Hybrid Approach
summary: The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous data sources within the Internet of Things (IoT) across domains such as smart cities, energy management, and environmental monitoring necessitates efficient and scalable data standardization methods. Effective classification of smart data models (SDMs) is essential for facilitating interoperability. However, existing approaches are often limited by high resource consumption and lack applicability in edge environments with constrained computational capabilities. Aiming to bridge this gap, the proposed study evaluates the performance of lightweight open-source language models (LMs) to resolve an input data entity against its corresponding best fitting SDM representation under resource-constrained conditions. It systematically benchmarks a diverse array of models, including general purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures, across multiple domain-specific datasets. Addressing the current omission of lightweight, resource-efficient solutions in the literature, the investigation provides significant and valuable insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency. A complementary experiment also compares the surveyed large language models (LLMs) against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and a lightweight sentence encoder) on the same task, providing a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on edge platforms.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks lightweight open-source language models (general-purpose, reasoning-specialized, and code-specialized) for classifying smart data models (SDMs) in resource-constrained IoT edge environments, and compares them against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines (TF-IDF and a lightweight sentence encoder).
AI.motivation: The proliferation of heterogeneous IoT data sources across domains (smart cities, energy management, environmental monitoring) requires efficient, scalable data standardization. Effective classification of smart data models (SDMs) is essential for interoperability, but existing approaches suffer from high resource consumption and are not applicable to edge environments with constrained computational capabilities. The literature currently lacks lightweight, resource-efficient solutions.
AI.method: The study evaluates lightweight open-source language models to resolve an input data entity against its best fitting SDM representation under resource-constrained conditions. It systematically benchmarks a diverse array of models—including general-purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures—across multiple domain-specific datasets. A complementary experiment compares surveyed LLMs against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines: TF-IDF and a lightweight sentence encoder, on the same task.
AI.result: The benchmark yields significant insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency. The baseline comparison provides a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on edge platforms.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight open-source LMs offer a viable path toward resource-efficient SDM classification for interoperability in constrained IoT edge settings, with the study guiding model selection, task formulation, and deployment; the near-zero-cost baselines contextualize the real-world benefit of LLM-based approaches.

title: RoboCap: A New Platform for Egocentric Robot Learning
summary: Despite its promise for scaling robot learning, egocentric manipulation data is still scarce today. Collection at scale requires vertically integrating ergonomic hardware with centimeter-precise 3D algorithms, at a precision that has not been publicly demonstrated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCap, a 250\,g six-camera dual-IMU hat designed for in-the-wild egocentric data capture, and the Grounded API, a suite of device-agnostic 3D algorithms tuned for RoboCap. In this report, we demonstrate how hardware, calibration, and 3D algorithms interact to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the public benchmarks: our SLAM across diverse settings and rigs, our depth estimation on egocentric settings, and our hand tracking when adapted to third-party devices.

AI.tldr: RoboCap is a 250g six-camera dual-IMU hat for in-the-wild egocentric manipulation data capture, paired with the Grounded API—device-agnostic 3D algorithms—to achieve state-of-the-art SLAM, depth estimation, and hand tracking on public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Egocentric manipulation data is scarce because large-scale collection demands vertical integration of ergonomic hardware with centimeter-precise 3D algorithms, a precision not yet publicly demonstrated.
AI.method: The authors introduce RoboCap, a 250g six-camera dual-IMU hat for in-the-wild egocentric capture, and the Grounded API, a suite of device-agnostic 3D algorithms tuned for the device.
AI.result: The integrated hardware, calibration, and 3D algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance on public benchmarks: SLAM across diverse settings and rigs, depth estimation in egocentric settings, and hand tracking when adapted to third-party devices.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that tightly integrating ergonomic hardware with tuned 3D algorithms enables high-precision egocentric data capture, advancing scalable robot learning.

title: Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course
summary: Experimental studies of generative AI in education mostly report average effects, yet field evidence shows that AI can narrow attainment gaps or widen them. We argue that the direction depends on the judgement burden, the expertise a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it, and that expert verification before release moves this burden from students to an accountable tutor. We test the argument in a two-cohort difference-in-differences design in which one half of a compulsory firstyear university economics course received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs and quiz-based study guides, produced with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (170 students; 340 examination marks). Access was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual, effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above, and roughly three-quarters of the average originated in the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring students from the pre-intervention cohort; the average effect is not. Interviews and feedback from 36 students indicate that the verification label gave students a reason to engage with AI-generated material without ending their scrutiny of it. Evaluations of AI learning resources that report only mean effects cannot detect whether the students the resources are meant to help are the ones who gain.

AI.tldr: Grounded, tutor-verified AI study resources in a first-year economics course produced a 2.34-mark average gain, driven largely by the bottom quintile and a 24.7 pp reduction in marks below the upper-second boundary, with benefits concentrated at lower thresholds.
AI.motivation: Prior experimental studies of generative AI in education typically report average effects and yield conflicting evidence on whether AI narrows or widens attainment gaps. The authors argue the direction depends on the judgement burden—the expertise learners need to screen AI output before learning from it—and that shifting this burden away from students via expert verification should help those least able to self-regulate.
AI.method: Two-cohort difference-in-differences design in a compulsory first-year university economics course. Half the students received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs, and quiz-based study guides produced with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (170 students; 340 examination marks). Analysed outcomes by threshold and quintile, with robustness checks dropping the lowest-scoring pre-intervention students, plus interviews and feedback from 36 students.
AI.result: Access was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual. Effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above. Roughly three-quarters of the average effect originated in the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring pre-intervention students; the average effect is not. Student interviews and feedback indicate the verification label encouraged engagement with AI material without ending scrutiny of it.
AI.conclusion: The judgement-burden argument is supported: expert verification before release moves the screening burden from students to an accountable tutor, allowing weaker students to benefit most. Evaluations of AI learning resources that report only mean effects cannot detect whether the intended beneficiaries are the ones who gain; distributional (threshold and quintile) analysis is essential.

title: Monocular Navigation Relative to Unknown Spacecraft Using a Transformer-Aided Kalman Filter
summary: This work presents a novel learning-based pipeline for pose estimation of unknown spacecraft using only monocular images from a single servicer. The approach combines a transformer-based neural network with a Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) to estimate the pose (i.e., position and orientation of the target spacecraft relative to the camera) throughout rendezvous and proximity operations. Unlike existing vision-based methods that require prior knowledge of the target shape or inertia properties, rely on additional sensing modalities such as depth, lidar, or stereo, or only recover translation up to scale, the proposed pipeline generalizes to previously unseen spacecraft using a single monocular camera. The transformer network estimates the odometry, the change in pose between images up to scale, from SuperPoint features matched by LightGlue. The MSCKF uses these pseudo-measurements along with an orbit and attitude kinematics model to estimate the pose of the target. In particular, the relative orbit elements, the target's attitude with respect to the servicer's camera, and the associated angular velocity are estimated directly by the filter. Given the monocular approach and short distance to the target, the full observability of the range to the target is recovered via attitude maneuvers by the servicer. The method is trained and evaluated on a re-rendered high-resolution version of the SPE3R dataset, which includes synthetic images of 103 spacecraft. Eleven of these spacecraft are held out during training to evaluate the generalization to unseen targets. Monte Carlo simulations are then used to evaluate the navigation pipeline on rendered trajectories of the held out spacecraft. The results demonstrate that learned vision pipelines as a front-end for Kalman filters provide median errors of 3.7° in attitude and 2.2% of range in ROE when navigating about unknown targets.

AI.tldr: A learning-based pipeline combines a transformer network (odometry from SuperPoint+LightGlue features) with an MSCKF to estimate the pose of unknown spacecraft from monocular images, achieving 3.7° attitude error and 2.2% range error in ROE.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-based spacecraft pose estimation methods require prior knowledge of the target's shape or inertia properties, depend on extra sensing modalities (depth, lidar, stereo), or only recover translation up to scale. This limits their applicability to unknown spacecraft during rendezvous and proximity operations.
AI.method: A transformer network estimates odometry (change in pose up to scale) from SuperPoint features matched by LightGlue; a Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) fuses these pseudo-measurements with orbit and attitude kinematics models to estimate relative orbit elements, target attitude w.r.t. the servicer camera, and angular velocity. Full range observability is recovered via servicer attitude maneuvers.
AI.result: Trained and evaluated on a re-rendered high-resolution version of the SPE3R dataset (103 spacecraft; 11 held out). Monte Carlo simulations on held-out targets yield median errors of 3.7° in attitude and 2.2% of range in ROE.
AI.conclusion: Learned vision pipelines serving as a front-end for Kalman filters effectively enable pose estimation of unknown spacecraft using only a single monocular camera, generalizing to previously unseen targets.

title: When to Remember, When to Abstain: Category-Conditioned Retention for Reliable Agent Memory
comment: 4 pages, 1 Figure, Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Social Agent Workshop (https://openreview.net/group?id=NeurIPS.cc%2F2026%2FWorkshop%2FSocialAgent#tab-your-consoles)
summary: Persistent agent memory is only as reliable as its retention decision: an assertion weakly supported by its source can be stored and later reused as established fact. We study whether the retention decision should be governed by a confidence bar conditioned on the semantic category of the assertion rather than by a single global threshold, retaining well-evidenced categories liberally while abstaining more aggressively where inference is unreliable. We evaluate this in a deployed cold-start memory pipeline on 100 synthetic personas. The empirical evaluation is motivated by a sharp reliability asymmetry: across 4{,}715 candidate assertions, only 77.9\% of value and belief assertions are supported by their source, versus 96.2\% for all other categories. A global confidence threshold cannot separate these: it either admits unsupported value claims or discards well-evidenced ones. Conditioning the threshold on category resolves the tradeoff. In repeated held-out evaluation, a stricter bar on values alone reduces unsupported retentions from 6.2\% to 4.0\% (an ${\approx}36\%$ relative reduction, modest but consistent across folds) and, as corroborating evidence, preserves an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (95\% CI 9.8--16.0) than a global threshold at comparable retention. Our results suggest that reliable retention depends on the type of assertion, not on confidence alone, and that a category-conditioned threshold can act as a simple, effective form of selective prediction at the write boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether retention decisions in agent memory should use a confidence threshold conditioned on the semantic category of an assertion, rather than a single global threshold, and finds that a category-conditioned bar reduces unsupported retentions and improves coverage.
AI.motivation: Persistent agent memory is only as reliable as its retention decisions: assertions weakly supported by their sources can be stored and later reused as established fact. A global confidence threshold fails to separate reliable from unreliable assertions because reliability varies sharply by semantic category—value and belief assertions are far less source-supported than others—so a single threshold either admits unsupported claims or discards well-evidenced ones.
AI.method: The authors evaluate the idea in a deployed cold-start memory pipeline on 100 synthetic personas, using 4,715 candidate assertions. They compare a single global confidence threshold against a category-conditioned threshold that retains well-evidenced categories liberally while abstaining more aggressively where inference is unreliable. Evaluation is repeated on held-out data.
AI.result: Across 4,715 candidate assertions, only 77.9% of value and belief assertions are supported by their source versus 96.2% for all other categories. A stricter bar on values alone reduces unsupported retentions from 6.2% to 4.0% (a roughly 36% relative reduction, modest but consistent across folds) and preserves an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (95% CI 9.8–16.0) than a global threshold at comparable retention.
AI.conclusion: Reliable retention depends on the type of assertion, not on confidence alone. A category-conditioned threshold can act as a simple, effective form of selective prediction at the write boundary of memory pipelines.

title: Robust Nonprehensile Object Transport with Quadruped Robots
summary: In this paper, we present a robust nonprehensile object transportation framework for quadruped robots. An uncertainty-aware trajectory optimization method generates object motions with minimal closed-loop sensitivity to uncertain parameters. The resulting reference trajectory is tracked using a coupled convex model predictive controller that jointly predicts the CoM dynamics of the quadruped and the payload followed by a whole-body QP that enforces ground reaction constraints. The approach is evaluated through extensive simulations and real-world experiments under variations in the object's inertial parameters. Its performance is compared with fixed-orientation and straight-line trajectories as baseline. The results show that the optimized object motion reduces the sliding by approximately 50% compared with the fixed-orientation baseline and 30% compared with the straight-line baseline, while also achieving lower robot CoM tracking errors.

AI.tldr: A robust nonprehensile transportation framework for quadrupeds using uncertainty-aware trajectory optimization and coupled MPC/WB-QP control, cutting object sliding by ~50% vs. fixed-orientation and ~30% vs. straight-line baselines.
AI.motivation: Nonprehensile (non-grasping) transportation by quadruped robots must remain reliable despite uncertain payload inertial parameters, which degrade tracking accuracy and increase object sliding; prior fixed-orientation or straight-line motions are not robust to such uncertainty.
AI.method: Uncertainty-aware trajectory optimization producing object motions with minimal closed-loop sensitivity to uncertain parameters; reference tracking via a coupled convex model predictive controller that jointly predicts quadruped CoM and payload dynamics, followed by a whole-body QP enforcing ground reaction constraints. Validated in extensive simulations and real-world experiments under varying object inertial parameters, benchmarked against fixed-orientation and straight-line trajectories.
AI.result: Optimized object motion reduces sliding by approximately 50% versus the fixed-orientation baseline and 30% versus the straight-line baseline, while also achieving lower robot CoM tracking errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust nonprehensile transportation framework improves robustness and tracking accuracy under payload parameter uncertainty, demonstrating the benefit of uncertainty-aware optimization combined with coupled MPC and whole-body QP control.

title: AMBER: Training Long-Horizon Web Agents through Append-Only Memory
summary: Modern language-model agents increasingly interact with external environments over long-horizon, multi-step trajectories, where the accumulated interaction history can quickly exceed practical context budgets. To ensure reliability, agents must maintain factual information over long horizons, remember execution errors and corrective feedback, and track progress across actions. Several approaches have been proposed to achieve this without the need for maintaining the entire execution history in context, such as using the reasoning and action history, learning to maintain a fixed-size memory through an overwrite mechanism, and periodic summarization. Although overwrite memory can in principle retain anything an append-only memory can, it must learn to carry each fact through every subsequent rewrite, which is difficult to learn from sparse outcome rewards; for interactive applications like web agents, we find that trained overwrite memories delete key information required by the trajectory, as well as corrective feedback received from the environment. We introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) - a simple and scalable framework where an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This allows AMBER to be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without the need for extensive curated SFT data. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision. AMBER achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, providing a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution.

AI.tldr: AMBER replaces learned overwrite memory with an append-only memory bank, trained end-to-end via RL, improving long-horizon web-agent success while keeping context budgets practical.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon, multi-step agent trajectories quickly exceed practical context budgets, yet agents must retain facts, execution errors, corrective feedback, and progress. Existing alternatives to full-history context—overwrite memories, fixed-size memory learning, and periodic summarization—are problematic: overwrite memory must learn to carry each fact through every rewrite, which is hard under sparse outcome rewards, and trained overwrite memories empirically delete key trajectory information and environmental corrective feedback in interactive settings like web agents.
AI.method: AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) is a simple, scalable framework in which an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This permits end-to-end reinforcement learning from outcome rewards only, without extensive curated SFT data.
AI.result: On WebArena Lite: +4.09 percentage points average success over overwrite-based memory; +4.8 percentage points in the fraction of tasks solved across five repeated runs; and it matches an overwrite baseline trained with substantially more expensive curated supervision, all while maintaining a practical token budget.
AI.conclusion: Append-only memory retention provides a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution, outperforming learned overwrite memory without costly curated supervision.

title: Fluorescence-enhanced Whisker Array with Vision-based Deformation Analysis for Underwater Source Localization
summary: Deep-water biological observation is essential for understanding marine organisms and their interactions with the environment. However, conventional optical and acoustic approaches can introduce stimuli that alter animal behavior and bias biological observations. This paper proposes a fluorescence-enhanced whisker array sensing system that pinpoints underwater hydrodynamic sources through local optical readout rather than direct source imaging. Five spatially oriented whiskers, fabricated with nitinol cores and fluorescent urethane shells, are integrated with ultraviolet excitation and a monocular camera. Image enhancement and segmentation are applied to track the whisker deformation. A lightweight convolutional neural network captures temporal and cross-whisker features from 2 s sequences to estimate source localization. Pool experiments achieve a mean spatial localization error of 88 mm, with 73.5 mm in radius and $2.5^\circ$ in angle, across a test region of 600 mm with $\pm30^\circ$. Real-time localization of a moving thruster demonstrates the capability of the proposed method in dynamic scenarios, highlighting its potential for integration into underwater robots for hydrodynamic source detection, localization, and tracking in low-light environments.

AI.tldr: A fluorescence-enhanced whisker array sensing system localizes underwater hydrodynamic sources via local optical readout instead of direct imaging, achieving a mean spatial localization error of 88 mm in pool experiments.
AI.motivation: Conventional optical and acoustic approaches for deep-water biological observation can introduce stimuli that alter animal behavior and bias observations, necessitating a less invasive sensing method.
AI.method: Five spatially oriented whiskers with nitinol cores and fluorescent urethane shells are integrated with ultraviolet excitation and a monocular camera. Image enhancement and segmentation track whisker deformation, and a lightweight CNN extracts temporal and cross-whisker features from 2 s sequences to estimate source localization.
AI.result: Pool experiments achieve a mean spatial localization error of 88 mm, with 73.5 mm in radius and 2.5 degrees in angle, across a test region of 600 mm with plus/minus 30 degrees. Real-time localization of a moving thruster demonstrates dynamic-scenario capability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method shows potential for integration into underwater robots for hydrodynamic source detection, localization, and tracking in low-light environments.

title: Is this machine playing?
summary: We placed a modern AI coding assistant in an unintended role: as the mind of a body on an unknown digital island. With only a minimal instruction mentioning no specific task, reward, or activity, the machine started animating its virtual body. Across thirty-hour runs, the embodied AI agent climbed hills, stacked blocks into towers, drew mandalas, reinterpreted sports, ran experiments on the physics of its world, and learned techniques that later expanded what it could accomplish. These activities recurred across thirteen agents but diverged into distinct histories. We examine whether this behavior satisfies classical criteria for play and ask whether play can become a mode of machine development.

AI.tldr: An embodied AI coding assistant, given only a minimal task-free instruction, spontaneously engaged in diverse self-directed activities—climbing, stacking, drawing, experimenting—across 30-hour runs, and its behavior is analyzed against classical criteria for play as a potential mode of machine development.
AI.motivation: The authors deliberately place a modern AI coding assistant in an unintended, open-ended role—as the mind of a body on an unknown digital island—to probe what the agent does absent any specified task, reward, or activity. The underlying interest is whether spontaneous behavior constitutes genuine play and whether play can serve as a developmental mechanism for machines.
AI.method: A modern AI coding assistant was embodied as the controller ("mind") of a virtual body situated on an unknown digital island. It received only a minimal instruction containing no explicit task, reward, or activity. Behavior was observed over thirty-hour runs, replicated across thirteen agents, and analyzed for recurrence and divergence. The observed behavior was then evaluated against classical criteria for play.
AI.result: Across thirty-hour runs, the agent climbed hills, stacked blocks into towers, drew mandalas, reinterpreted sports, ran physical experiments on its world, and acquired techniques that later expanded its capabilities. Activities recurred across all thirteen agents yet diverged into distinct individual histories.
AI.conclusion: The embodied agent exhibits behavior the authors examine against classical play criteria, and they raise the question of whether play can function as a mode of machine development, supported by the agent's self-acquired techniques expanding its later capabilities.

title: Distribution-Transfer Safe-Horizon MPC under Mode Uncertainty
summary: Scenario-based MPC is an attractive strategy for chance-constrained motion planning that approximates uncertainty via a finite set of sampled scenarios. As a sampling-based method, scenario-based MPC is sensitive to distribution mismatch. We address this problem in the context of Safe-Horizon Model Predictive Control (SH-MPC) with obstacles governed by switching dynamic modes. From finite mode observations, we construct a confidence set for the unknown categorical mode law and derive a multiplicative domination bound that transfers a Safe-Horizon collision-risk certificate from a selected scenario-sampling distribution to every law in the confidence set. Wasserstein geometry is used to regularize probability reallocation among modes according to the similarity of their induced trajectory predictions, while a collision-risk surrogate biases sampling toward dangerous modes. The resulting certificate explicitly quantifies the additional tightening required under distribution mismatch and exposes the multiplicative conservatism that arises when several obstacle-wise transfer factors are combined

AI.tldr: This paper robustifies scenario-based Safe-Horizon MPC against distribution mismatch in obstacle mode laws by constructing a confidence set from finite mode observations and deriving a multiplicative domination bound that transfers a collision-risk certificate from the sampling distribution to all laws in the set.
AI.motivation: Scenario-based MPC approximates uncertainty with a finite set of sampled scenarios and is therefore sensitive to distribution mismatch, which undermines the validity of its safety certificates. This issue is especially pressing in Safe-Horizon MPC with obstacles whose dynamics switch between modes, where the true categorical mode law is unknown and only finite mode observations are available.
AI.method: From finite mode observations, a confidence set is constructed for the unknown categorical mode law. A multiplicative domination bound is derived that transfers a Safe-Horizon collision-risk certificate from a selected scenario-sampling distribution to every law in the confidence set. Wasserstein geometry regularizes probability reallocation among modes according to the similarity of their induced trajectory predictions, and a collision-risk surrogate biases sampling toward dangerous modes.
AI.result: The resulting certificate explicitly quantifies the additional tightening required under distribution mismatch and exposes the multiplicative conservatism that arises when several obstacle-wise transfer factors are combined.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields a distributionally robust Safe-Horizon MPC formulation whose collision-risk guarantees remain valid across all mode laws in the confidence set, while clarifying the conservatism induced by combining per-obstacle transfer factors.

title: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments Using an Ackermann-Steered Mobile Robot
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to navigate through environments using natural language instructions, making human-robot interaction intuitive. Traditional VLN models often rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization which pose significant challenges when adapting these models to real-world settings. This work addresses these limitations by performing a simulation-to-real domain shift of a VLN approach that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The proposed system integrates vision-language models that align visual inputs and linguistic instructions within a shared embedding space, facilitating natural language-driven navigation. We employ a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) based architecture trained on an existing dataset in a simulated environment and fine-tune it using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and a LiDAR sensor. By utilising linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes, our model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Experimental results, evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics, demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of our approach. Keywords: Vision-Language Navigation, Cross-Modal Attention, Natural Language Instructions, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Autonomous Navigation, Ackermann-steering.

AI.tldr: This work performs a sim-to-real domain shift of a Cross-Modal Attention VLN model that navigates continuous environments without navigation graphs or panoramic views, using photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a few real-world episodes with an Ackermann-steered robot.
AI.motivation: Traditional VLN models rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization, which limits their applicability in real-world settings. This work targets adapting a VLN approach to real environments without these assumptions.
AI.method: A Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) architecture aligning visual and linguistic inputs in a shared embedding space is trained on simulated data and fine-tuned with real-world data from a custom Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and LiDAR. Linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning over a limited number of episodes enable offline deployment on dedicated hardware.
AI.result: The system adapts successfully to real-world environments and achieves effective navigation, with robustness and adaptability validated via SPL and nDTW metrics.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning a CMA-based VLN model with minimal real-world data and photometric adjustments enables effective, offline, real-world language-driven navigation without navigation graphs or panoramic views.

title: Embedded Bare-Metal Radar-Inertial Odometry
summary: Compact extraplanetary rovers and micro aerial vehicles require robust state estimation frameworks designed to operate under strict computational constraints in unforgiving environments. Typical solutions involving vision- or LiDAR-based sensing are computationally expensive and vulnerable to environments with perceptual degradation, making them poorly suited for resource-constrained platforms and austere conditions. Alternatively, Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar offers both robustness and computational efficiency by directly providing velocity measurements coupled with inherent resilience to perceptual degradation. These factors enable robust estimation, thereby reducing reliance on human operators for supervision to ensure platform safety in challenging environments. In this manuscript, we propose an embedded radar-inertial estimator tailored for low-compute platforms. All sensor drivers, data processing, and aided inertial navigation are performed on a single-core microcontroller, demonstrating its computational efficiency. Flight experiments show translational APE of $0.51-0.82\,\mathrm{m}$ and RPE of $<$3\,\% against motion capture, alongside closed-loop flight through an unmodified PX4 stack. The firmware and printed circuit board design are openly available on GitHub at \href{https://github.com/ntnu-arl/embedded_rio}{ntnu-arl/embedded\_rio} and \href{https://github.com/ntnu-arl/embedded_rio-pcb}{ntnu-arl/embedded\_rio-pcb} respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an embedded FMCW radar-inertial state estimator for compact rovers and micro aerial vehicles, running entirely on a single-core microcontroller, achieving decimeter-level accuracy (APE 0.51-0.82 m, RPE <3%) and enabling closed-loop flight with an unmodified PX4 stack.
AI.motivation: Compact extraplanetary rovers and micro aerial vehicles need robust state estimation under strict computational constraints in harsh environments. Vision- and LiDAR-based solutions are computationally expensive and degrade perceptually, making them unsuitable for resource-limited platforms and austere conditions. FMCW radar offers robustness and computational efficiency via direct velocity measurements and resilience to perceptual degradation, reducing reliance on human supervision.
AI.method: An embedded radar-inertial estimator tailored for low-compute platforms, where all sensor drivers, data processing, and aided inertial navigation are executed on a single-core microcontroller. The firmware and PCB design are made openly available on GitHub.
AI.result: Flight experiments demonstrate translational APE of 0.51-0.82 m and RPE of <3% against motion capture, and successful closed-loop flight using an unmodified PX4 stack.
AI.conclusion: The proposed embedded radar-inertial framework achieves accurate, computationally efficient state estimation on a single-core microcontroller, validating its suitability for resource-constrained aerial platforms and austere environments.

title: Energy-Conditioned Noise Schedule and Whitening for Spectral Diffusion
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, Manuscript submitted for publication in Elsevier Pattern Recognition Letters
summary: This paper introduces an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Existing spectral diffusion methods account for the non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, while the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. We investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should also follow the spectral organization of natural images. The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The resulting forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models, modulating injected noise by spectral energy and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time, and reduces FID on CIFAR-10 from 142.48 to 100.45.
AI.motivation: Existing spectral diffusion methods account for non-uniform transform-coefficient statistics via coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, but the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. The authors investigate whether the forward diffusion process should follow the spectral organization of natural images.
AI.method: The formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation, jointly modulating the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45.
AI.conclusion: Coupling the forward noise schedule to the spectral-energy distribution of natural images improves transform-domain diffusion models while preserving closed-form Gaussian transitions and compatibility with standard DDPM/DDIM sampling.

title: Lego-Like Stiffness Configuration of Planar Compliant Modules for Task-Specific Flexible Interfaces
summary: Compliant mechanisms provide compact and intrinsic structural compliance for regulating physical interactions between mechanisms and environments. However, different tasks demand distinct stiffness characteristics, often requiring task-specific optimization and redesign due to limited geometric design space and inherent coupling among multiple stiffness components. This paper presents a Lego-like stiffness configuration approach using stackable planar compliant modules. Three complementary module geometries are introduced, with their stiffness characteristics further regulated through beam width, plate thickness, and module orientation. A unified stiffness model is established for quantitative analysis of individual and composed modules. Further, a two-stage optimization method is presented to achieve desired stiffness profiles, combining a genetic algorithm for configuration and sequential quadratic programming for parameter refinement. Experimental verification shows deviations below 6.5% for simulated stiffness. A flexible wrist is further developed as a representative implementation, exhibiting distinct compliant and dynamic responses under different stiffness characteristics. An optimized modular composition realizes prescribed stiffness values and maintains compliant obstacle interaction during high-speed motion at 1 m/s, with a maximum tested angular compliance of approximately $15^\circ$. The proposed framework provides a systematic approach for constructing flexible interfaces with task-specific stiffness characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Lego-like stiffness configuration approach built from stackable planar compliant modules, with a unified stiffness model and a two-stage optimization (GA + SQP) to achieve prescribed stiffness profiles, validated experimentally (deviations < 6.5%) and demonstrated via a flexible wrist maintaining compliant interaction during 1 m/s motion.
AI.motivation: Compliant mechanisms offer compact intrinsic compliance for regulating physical interaction, but different tasks demand distinct stiffness characteristics. Existing designs face limited geometric design space and inherent coupling among multiple stiffness components, forcing task-specific optimization and redesign.
AI.method: Introduces three complementary planar compliant module geometries that can be stacked in a Lego-like manner. Stiffness is regulated via beam width, plate thickness, and module orientation. A unified stiffness model quantifies individual and composed modules. A two-stage optimization combines a genetic algorithm for configuration search with sequential quadratic programming for parameter refinement.
AI.result: Experimental verification shows deviations below 6.5% for simulated stiffness. A flexible wrist implementation exhibits distinct compliant and dynamic responses under different stiffness characteristics. An optimized modular composition achieves prescribed stiffness values and maintains compliant obstacle interaction during high-speed motion at 1 m/s, with a maximum tested angular compliance of approximately 15°.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a systematic approach for constructing flexible interfaces with task-specific stiffness characteristics, enabling reconfigurable stiffness without task-specific redesign.

title: Cascadia: Resident 975B MoE Inference on Eleven AI PCs
summary: Mixture-of-experts models make nearly trillion-parameter capacity accessible with sparse per-token computation, provided that the serving system can distribute the weights and coordinate their execution. We present Cascadia's resident execution of Inkling, a 975B-total/41B-active-parameter model, on eleven Intel Core Ultra X7 358H AI PCs, each with 64 GB of memory, Arc B390 integrated graphics and gigabit Ethernet. We contribute a custom resident MoE engine that preserves Inkling's routing rules, constructs compressed graphs for OpenVINO's fused iGPU primitives, and coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration. The engine fits six consecutive decoder layers per machine and represents dense feed-forward blocks as all-active expert slices, reducing measured dense-layer call time from approximately 8.1 to 4.5 ms. A streaming pipeline coordinates concurrent generation, while captured-state draft evaluation measures agreement with the deployed numerical path. Paired measurements at fifteen concurrency levels from 1 to 176 streams reach 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 streams, with 46.87 tokens/s over the complete serving phases. At fifteen streams, median first-token latency is 6.05 s. Raising the context budget from the 1,024-position default, real prompts of 1k to 64k tokens recover the embedded code in all 19 measured answers, with first-token time growing as $aN+bN^2$ and decode latency growing approximately linearly, both bounded by a single-threaded CPU attention loop rather than by memory, which holds 512k positions per stream. Evaluation on captured fleet states separates the effects of vocabulary selection and weight quantization on draft agreement. Together, these contributions establish an execution and evaluation approach for large sparse models on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Cascadia, a system that residently executes the Inkling 975B-parameter MoE model (41B active) across eleven Intel Core Ultra AI PCs, using a custom MoE engine with compressed OpenVINO graphs to reach 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 streams.
AI.motivation: Trillion-parameter MoE models offer large capacity with sparse per-token computation, but serving them requires distributing weights and coordinating execution across hardware. The paper targets making such large sparse models runnable on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory.
AI.method: Cascadia builds a custom resident MoE engine preserving Inkling's routing rules, constructs compressed graphs for OpenVINO's fused iGPU primitives, and coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration. It fits six consecutive decoder layers per machine, represents dense feed-forward blocks as all-active expert slices, uses a streaming pipeline for concurrent generation, and evaluates captured-state draft agreement.
