AI.result: Measured across fifteen concurrency levels (1-176 streams): 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 streams, 46.87 tokens/s over complete serving phases; median first-token latency 6.05 s at fifteen streams. Dense-layer call time drops from ~8.1 to 4.5 ms. With context budgets from 1k-64k tokens, all 19 answers recover embedded code; first-token time scales as aN+bN^2 and decode latency grows roughly linearly, both CPU-bound by a single-threaded attention loop while memory holds 512k positions per stream.
AI.conclusion: The contributions establish an execution and evaluation approach for large sparse models on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory. Captured fleet-state evaluation isolates the effects of vocabulary selection and weight quantization on draft agreement.

title: Towards Decentralized Formation of Minimum-Length Communication Networks Using Robot Swarms
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Multi-robot missions in infrastructure-denied environments frequently rely on reliable communication links between spatially separated locations. We propose a fully decentralized framework for constructing and dynamically maintaining communication networks without centralized topology planning or global positioning infrastructure. Driven strictly by local interactions, robots reconfigure local network topologies and adjust their physical positions to minimize overall network length while adhering to communication constraints. Formal analysis shows that our local reconfiguration operations guarantee continuous network connectivity, strictly decrease network length with every branch transfer, and bound worst-case performance to the shortest starlike tree. Embodied simulations and physical multi-robot experiments confirm that our approach forms networks near the length of centrally computed Euclidean Steiner trees. Additionally, the system dynamically adapts to moving targets and optimizes deployment by utilizing only necessary connectors, preserving excess robots for auxiliary tasks. This work enables autonomous swarms to self-organize adaptive ad hoc communication infrastructure in communication-denied environments, which could support applications varying from subterranean exploration to planetary missions.

AI.tldr: A fully decentralized framework lets robot swarms self-organize and dynamically maintain communication networks using only local interactions, achieving near-optimal (Euclidean Steiner-like) network lengths while guaranteeing connectivity and adapting to moving targets.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot missions in infrastructure-denied environments need reliable communication between spatially separated locations, but existing approaches typically require centralized topology planning or global positioning infrastructure, which may be unavailable. The paper aims to enable robots to build and maintain communication links autonomously without such centralized or global resources.
AI.method: Robots are driven strictly by local interactions to reconfigure local network topologies and adjust their physical positions, minimizing overall network length while satisfying communication constraints. The framework is fully decentralized, requiring neither centralized topology planning nor global positioning. Local reconfiguration operations (e.g., branch transfer) are used to reduce network length.
AI.result: Formal analysis shows the local operations guarantee continuous network connectivity, strictly decrease network length with every branch transfer, and bound worst-case performance to the shortest starlike tree. Embodied simulations and physical multi-robot experiments confirm the approach forms networks near the length of centrally computed Euclidean Steiner trees. The system also dynamically adapts to moving targets and uses only necessary connectors, preserving excess robots for auxiliary tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work enables autonomous swarms to self-organize adaptive ad hoc communication infrastructure in communication-denied environments, with potential applications ranging from subterranean exploration to planetary missions.

title: SPECTRUM: Proximal Spectral Modulation for Looped Self-Distillation
summary: A model that learns from its own outputs inherits more than their correctness: it inherits which solutions it produces. We formulate Looped Self-Distillation, a self-evolution framework for code generation in which a model repeatedly generates and learns from its own raw outputs, under a fixed information budget, without ongoing external assessment or test-based selection of the generated samples. We identify a consequential separation: correctness can improve while the breadth of correct implementations contracts. We introduce SPECTRUM, which re-estimates loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor at each round and converts it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. All generated completions train a single student, whose subsequent inference requires no intervention. After five rounds of experiments on MBPP, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the initial model's 64-sample correct AST richness, compared with 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation and 65.5% for a subspace-projection control. The advantage persists at matched correct-sample counts. Without further training or recalibration, the resulting student also achieves higher matched-correct richness than Vanilla SD on HumanEval+ and APPS Intro, demonstrating transfer of the diversity benefit. These findings establish correct-solution retention as a complementary objective of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and show that generation-time intervention can improve the solution repertoire retained by subsequent students.

AI.tldr: Looped Self-Distillation shows correctness can improve while correct-solution breadth contracts; SPECTRUM, a spectral modulation method, preserves solution diversity across recursive self-training rounds.
AI.motivation: Models that learn from their own outputs inherit not only correctness but also *which* solutions they produce. The authors observe a consequential separation in recursive self-improvement (RSI): correctness can improve while the breadth of correct implementations contracts, an aspect previously overlooked.
AI.method: The authors formulate Looped Self-Distillation, a self-evolution framework for code generation where a model repeatedly generates and learns from its own raw outputs under a fixed information budget, without external assessment or test-based sample selection. They introduce SPECTRUM, which re-estimates loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor each round and converts it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. All generated completions train a single student, and inference requires no intervention.
AI.result: After five rounds on MBPP, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the initial model's 64-sample correct AST richness, versus 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation and 65.5% for a subspace-projection control. The advantage persists at matched correct-sample counts. Without further training or recalibration, the student also achieves higher matched-correct richness than Vanilla SD on HumanEval+ and APPS Intro, demonstrating transfer of the diversity benefit.
AI.conclusion: Correct-solution retention is established as a complementary objective of recursive self-improvement, and generation-time intervention can improve the solution repertoire retained by subsequent students. This reframes diversity preservation as a first-class concern in self-evolving code models.

title: SharedKV-BT: Node-Local Typed Decisions for Behavior-Tree Agents
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Last updated on October 5th, 2026
summary: Agent tasks require sequences of interdependent decisions. Autoregressive models support more flexible decision interfaces than conventional classifiers but incur the latency of token-by-token generation. Recent shared-prefix methods reduce this cost by reusing encoded context and scoring multiple decisions in parallel, but do not model decision dependencies or verify execution. We propose SharedKV-BT, where each active node of a behavior tree (BT) exposes stage-local fields and candidates, and Shared-KV scores the candidates in parallel and passes the selected decision to a separate execution system. We tested SharedKV-BT on robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks. Across three tasks, SharedKV-BT made typed decisions 2.36-4.15 times faster than prompt-matched autoregressive decoding. On the manipulation task, node-local Shared-KV improved joint decision accuracy from 75% to 94% and closed-loop success from 0% to 60%. Fixed-score policy replay showed that stage gating prevented out-of-order actions and external postconditions prevented premature completion.

AI.tldr: SharedKV-BT combines behavior trees with shared-prefix parallel scoring (Shared-KV) to make typed, stage-local decisions 2.36-4.15x faster than autoregressive decoding, while improving joint decision accuracy (75%->94%) and closed-loop success (0%->60%) on manipulation, navigation, and computer-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Agent tasks require sequences of interdependent decisions. Autoregressive models offer flexible decision interfaces but suffer from token-by-token generation latency. Existing shared-prefix methods reduce cost via encoded-context reuse and parallel scoring of multiple decisions, yet they neither model decision dependencies nor verify execution.
AI.method: SharedKV-BT: each active node of a behavior tree exposes stage-local fields and candidates; Shared-KV scores candidates in parallel; the selected decision is passed to a separate execution system. Stage gating enforces ordering and external postconditions gate completion.
AI.result: On robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks, typed decisions were made 2.36-4.15x faster than prompt-matched autoregressive decoding. On manipulation, node-local Shared-KV raised joint decision accuracy from 75% to 94% and closed-loop success from 0% to 60%. Fixed-score policy replay showed stage gating prevented out-of-order actions and external postconditions prevented premature completion.
AI.conclusion: Coupling behavior-tree structure with shared-KV parallel scoring yields faster, more accurate, and order-correct decision-making, with execution verification handled by external postconditions.

title: Can Semantic Geometry Teach an AI Judgement?
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Four bounded studies of semantic measurements for pre-action judgment; consequence-graph hypothesis remains untested
summary:
How can an AI agent determine what rules to follow? One rule permits an action. Another imposes a condition, exception, or conflicting obligation. Deterministic systems can resolve those relationships when they have been specified. When they remain implicit in language, an agent can follow one rule while missing another that should stop it. Refusing every unresolved action avoids that risk, but also blocks permissible actions.
  We wanted the agent to make the distinction and still act. Our initial hypothesis was that geometric measurements could supply a basis for judgment. We represented actions and policies as vectors, then tested whether their geometry could identify governing policies and interpret the action's relation to them.
  Across four studies, the tested approaches did not establish reliable pre-action judgment. In the final synthetic study, a lexical router recovered every governing and blocking policy while reducing median policy checks by 97.7%. The composed pipeline nevertheless escalated all 2,304 test actions, including those it should have allowed. Supplying every policy to the same downstream mechanism changed no decision. Finding the policies had not solved the problem of interpreting them.
  This result led us to revise our hypothesis: judgment in AI agents requires developing a consequence graph. Such a graph would connect the actor and authority to policy conditions, exceptions, and the changes an action would produce. Follow-on studies will ask whether making those relationships explicit helps the agent distinguish when to act, stop, or seek review.

AI.tldr: Geometric/vector representations of actions and policies failed to yield reliable pre-action judgment in AI agents; even perfect policy retrieval (97.7% fewer checks) did not fix interpretation failures — all 2,304 test actions were wrongly escalated. The authors revise their hypothesis toward a "consequence graph" linking actor, authority, conditions, exceptions, and action effects.
AI.motivation: AI agents struggle to determine which rules govern an action when rule relationships (permissions, conditions, exceptions, conflicting obligations) remain implicit in language. Deterministic resolution only works when relationships are explicitly specified; otherwise an agent may follow one rule while missing another that should constrain it. Refusing all unresolved actions is safe but over-blocks permissible actions, so the goal is to enable the agent to distinguish correctly and still act.
AI.method: Initial hypothesis: geometric measurements could ground judgment. Actions and policies were represented as vectors, and their geometry was tested for its ability to identify governing policies and interpret the action's relation to them. Across four studies, including a final synthetic study using a lexical router for policy retrieval, the pipeline's pre-action judgment was evaluated. A condition was also tested where all policies were supplied directly to the same downstream decision mechanism.
AI.result: The geometry-based approaches did not establish reliable pre-action judgment across four studies. In the final synthetic study, the lexical router recovered every governing and blocking policy while cutting median policy checks by 97.7%, yet the composed pipeline escalated all 2,304 test actions, including those that should have been allowed. Providing every policy to the same downstream mechanism produced no change in decisions.
AI.conclusion: Policy retrieval is not the bottleneck; interpreting retrieved policies is. The authors revise their hypothesis: agent judgment requires a consequence graph connecting the actor and authority to policy conditions, exceptions, and the changes an action would produce. Follow-on studies will test whether making these relationships explicit helps an agent decide when to act, stop, or seek review.

title: ScanSTL: Parallel Robustness Evaluation for Signal Temporal Logic
summary: Repeated evaluation and differentiation of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness can become a computational bottleneck in robot planning and control. Sequential temporal recurrences limit parallelism, while dense masking increases memory requirements. We propose ScanSTL, which combines associative temporal aggregation with parallel scans and ordered block reductions. Eventually and Always use range extrema, while inclusive strong Until composes compact segment representations. A common range engine handles bounded and shifted intervals, including the guards required before delayed Until witnesses. Each exact temporal operator computes complete robustness traces with linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth on uniformly sampled finite signals. An open source JAX implementation supports automatic differentiation, batching, and compilation. We compare ScanSTL with STLCG and STLCG++ using CPU and GPU operator benchmarks and nine composed specifications. Across these nine specifications at 512 samples, ScanSTL achieves geometric mean speedups of 243 times for forward evaluation and 104 times for gradient computation over STLCG++ in JAX on the CPU. On an RTX~5090 GPU, ScanSTL evaluates unbounded Until over more than two million samples with median times below 0.1 ms for forward evaluation and 0.25 ms for gradient computation. Simulated escort and patrol experiments with a robot dog further demonstrate faster repair of violating plans and greater solver capacity in model predictive control.

AI.tldr: ScanSTL reformulates STL robustness evaluation as associative temporal aggregation using parallel scans, achieving exact temporally-complete robustness traces in linear work/storage and logarithmic parallel depth, with large speedups over STLCG++ and efficient GPU scaling.
AI.motivation: Repeated evaluation and differentiation of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness is a computational bottleneck in robot planning and control. Existing sequential temporal recurrences constrain parallelism, and dense masking inflates memory usage, limiting scalability and performance.
AI.method: The method combines associative temporal aggregation with parallel scans and ordered block reductions. Eventually and Always are computed via range extrema; inclusive strong Until composes compact segment representations. A common range engine handles bounded and shifted intervals, including guards required before delayed Until witnesses. Each exact temporal operator computes complete robustness traces with linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth on uniformly sampled finite signals. An open-source JAX implementation supports automatic differentiation, batching, and compilation.
AI.result: In CPU and GPU operator benchmarks and nine composed specifications, at 512 samples ScanSTL achieves geometric-mean speedups of 243x for forward evaluation and 104x for gradients over STLCG++ in JAX on CPU. On an RTX 5090 GPU, it evaluates unbounded Until over more than two million samples with median times below 0.1 ms forward and 0.25 ms for gradients. Simulated escort and patrol experiments with a robot dog show faster repair of violating plans and greater solver capacity in MPC.
AI.conclusion: ScanSTL provides exact, temporally-complete STL robustness traces with efficient parallel, differentiable computation, delivering substantial speedups and enabling scalable planning and control applications such as plan repair and model predictive control.

title: Internalizing Agent Experience into Diffusion Model Weights via On-Policy Context Distillation
summary: Wrapping an image generation model in an agentic harness can effectively boost Text-to-Image task performance: the harness can leverage memory, skills, workflow orchestration, result verification, and iterative refinement to continually construct and revise prompts, thereby eliciting better images. These gains, however, remain external to the diffusion model and are realized only while the full harness runs. We propose Diffusion On-Policy Context Distillation (D-OPCD), which treats the agent-improved prompt as privileged context and distills the knowledge encoded in the agent harness into the weights of the diffusion model, so that the model retains part of the harness's benefit when conditioned on the original query alone. Using a Text-to-Image agent equipped with our proposed Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), we show that D-OPCD can internalize harness capabilities into the generator's weights, raising the average direct-generation score from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks. With this knowledge absorbed into the weights, the harness can shed its saturated skills and resume evolving: a second ASE round on the updated generator improves on a skill-free harness by additional 1.83 points, pointing toward text-to-image systems in which harness and model keep improving each other through continual co-evolution.

AI.tldr: D-OPCD distills agent-harness knowledge (privileged improved prompts) into diffusion model weights, boosting direct Text-to-Image generation from 60.52 to 65.09 and enabling harness-model co-evolution for a further +1.83.
AI.motivation: Agentic harnesses (memory, skills, orchestration, verification, iterative refinement) improve Text-to-Image performance by constructing and revising prompts, but these gains are external to the diffusion model and only manifest while the full harness is running. The authors aim to internalize harness benefits into model weights so that the generator retains part of the improvement when conditioned on the original query alone.
AI.method: Diffusion On-Policy Context Distillation (D-OPCD) treats the agent-improved prompt as privileged context and distills knowledge encoded in the agent harness into the diffusion model's weights. The approach uses a Text-to-Image agent equipped with a proposed Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), performing on-policy context distillation so the generator absorbs harness capabilities.
AI.result: D-OPCD raises the average direct-generation score from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks. After knowledge absorption, a second ASE round on the updated generator improves over a skill-free harness by an additional 1.83 points.
AI.conclusion: Harness capabilities can be internalized into generator weights; once absorbed, the harness can shed saturated skills and resume evolving, pointing toward Text-to-Image systems where harness and model continually co-evolve and improve each other.

title: Expressiveness, Equivalence, and Uncertainty in Velocity Obstacles and Closest Point of Approach Metrics
summary: Time to Closest Point of Approach (TCPA), Distance to Closest Point of Approach (DCPA), and Velocity Obstacles (VOs), are widely used to assess and mitigate collision risk in autonomous navigation, yet their relationship and behavior under uncertainty remain largely unexplored. Assuming perfect state information, we establish a relationship between these representations over finite and infinite prediction horizons and derive conditions under which they provide equivalent characterizations of collision risk. Under bounded uncertainty, we extend the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) metrics and VO to convex relative-state sets. We show that in this setting, independently computed TCPA and DCPA bounds lose the joint relationship required for VO membership, while uncertainty-aware VOs preserve this relationship through a set-valued representation of collision-inducing velocities.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the relationship between CPA metrics (TCPA, DCPA) and Velocity Obstacles, showing equivalence under perfect information and demonstrating that uncertainty breaks this relationship unless set-valued, uncertainty-aware VOs are used.
AI.motivation: TCPA, DCPA, and VOs are widely used for collision risk assessment in autonomous navigation, but their mutual relationship and behavior under uncertainty have not been systematically explored. This gap limits principled use and combination of these tools.
AI.method: The authors first assume perfect state information and establish a formal relationship between the representations over finite and infinite prediction horizons, deriving conditions for equivalence in characterizing collision risk. They then extend CPA metrics and VOs to convex relative-state sets under bounded uncertainty.
AI.result: Under perfect information, conditions are derived under which TCPA, DCPA, and VOs equivalently characterize collision risk. Under bounded uncertainty, independently computed TCPA and DCPA bounds lose the joint relationship needed for VO membership, whereas uncertainty-aware VOs retain this relationship via a set-valued representation of collision-inducing velocities.
AI.conclusion: Equivalence between CPA metrics and VOs holds only under perfect information. Under uncertainty, preserving the joint relationship requires uncertainty-aware, set-valued VOs rather than separate TCPA/DCPA bounds.

title: MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
summary: Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. The tools they reach for, terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers, were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an OOM kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: an agent-hosting substrate should continuously emit observable signals an operator or auditor can check while agents run. We present MemMux, a local runtime that turns resource governance into checkable signals (per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead), with a claims-disciplined benchmark against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux keeps the fleet under budget (7.5 GiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it, and it alone surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). We report the cost: the 1 Hz attribution scan runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and a one-command reproducer.

AI.tldr: MemMux is a local runtime that turns OS-level resource governance for fleets of coding agents into continuously checkable signals—per-agent memory attribution, complete subtree reclamation, escaped-process visibility, and bounded footprint—outperforming tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline.
AI.motivation: Developers run many coding agents concurrently on one workstation, each spawning language servers, test runners, and browsers. Existing tools (tmux, agent managers) are built for window arrangement, not memory governance. Consequently, no standard tool can attribute memory to a specific agent, confirm a terminated agent's descendants are gone, detect an escaped child process, or prevent swap/OOM kills from silently discarding uncommitted work.
AI.method: The authors frame resource governance as a runtime-verification problem: an agent-hosting substrate should continuously emit observable signals an operator or auditor can verify at runtime. They build MemMux, a local runtime providing five checkable signals: per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead. Evaluation uses a claims-disciplined benchmark on identical workloads against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline, under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, plus validation on real Claude Code sessions.
AI.result: Under a binding memory budget, MemMux keeps the fleet within 7.5 GiB with zero swap by admitting a subset of agents and reclaiming under pressure, while ungoverned tools run every agent, pin RAM at its ceiling (2x over budget), and spill ~2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree vs. the raw baseline stranding half, and it alone detects escaped children (10 of 10). Cost: the 1 Hz attribution scan runs ~0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten—above the 2% target. Real Claude Code sessions show 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees.
AI.conclusion: Treating multi-agent resource governance as runtime verification yields a practical, auditable substrate: MemMux delivers bounded memory, complete reclamation, and escaped-process detection that ungoverned tools lack, though its attribution-scan overhead exceeds the target at ten agents. The engine, benchmark, and one-command reproducer are released.

title: Toward Trustworthy Physical AI for Human Interaction
summary: Robots are entering human spaces faster than we can establish when they deserve trust. We propose a framework for trustworthy physical AI that integrates Safety, Behavioral Intelligibility, and Perceptual Alignment across embodiment, control, cognition, and design. Trustworthiness emerges from aligning physical capabilities, observable behavior, and expectations people form during interaction.

AI.tldr: A framework for trustworthy physical AI that unifies Safety, Behavioral Intelligibility, and Perceptual Alignment across embodiment, control, cognition, and design layers.
AI.motivation: Robots are being deployed into human environments faster than criteria for warranted trust can be established, creating a gap between deployment speed and trust assessment.
AI.method: Proposes a conceptual framework organizing trustworthiness around three pillars—Safety, Behavioral Intelligibility, and Perceptual Alignment—spanning four levels: embodiment, control, cognition, and design.
AI.result: Trustworthiness is framed as emerging from the alignment of three elements: physical capabilities, observable behavior, and the expectations people form during interaction.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy physical AI requires cross-layer integration rather than isolated safety or performance guarantees, with trust treated as an emergent property of aligned capability, behavior, and human expectation.

title: Verifying Coordination in Parallel Coding Agents: NP-Bench and a Scheduling Planner
summary: A team of coding agents can look fine agent by agent yet fail as a team: each passes its own tests while the merged result is broken, and single-agent evaluation never catches it. As teams run several LLM coding agents in parallel on one codebase, the agents collide: two rewrite the same function, one codes against a contract a teammate just changed, and integration fails after the work is done. Most coordination tools react (watch for a conflict, then warn), but at agent speed the warning arrives after the wasted edit. We recast the problem as scheduling: take each work item's declared scope, partition the work into disjoint scopes, and order merges along the producer->consumer graph, all up front. We build this planner into Nerveplane and evaluate it with NP-Bench, an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark (no coordination; reactive detection; proactive planning) that verifies integration off a real git merge, both in a deterministic simulation and with live agents. The planner lifts clean-integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and cuts merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with a gap that grows in the number of agents. On a live breaking contract change it rescues an outcome both baselines miss on every seed: the clean-integration rate rises from 0 (no coordination and reactive detection) to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small one, while agents respect assigned scopes (0/5 leakage). A cross-session memory drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on strong and weak models alike. We also report a negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales; its value is cost and capacity, not attention. Across two capability tiers and two vendors, the benefit did not shrink as models got stronger, because it comes from how work is allocated, not model reasoning.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM coding teams fail at integration even when each agent passes its own tests. Nerveplane recasts coordination as up-front scheduling: partition work items into disjoint scopes and order merges along the producer→consumer graph. On NP-Bench (no coordination / reactive detection / proactive planning), planning lifts clean integration from 1/9 to 9/9 and cuts conflicts from 13 to 0, with the gap widening with team size, and remains robust on live breaking contract changes and across capability tiers.
AI.motivation: Parallel LLM coding agents working on one codebase collide: two rewrite the same function, one codes against a contract a teammate just changed, and integration fails after the work is done. Existing coordination tools are reactive (detect a conflict, then warn), but at agent speed the warning arrives only after the wasted edit. Single-agent evaluation cannot catch team-level integration failures, since each agent passes its own tests while the merged result is broken.
AI.method: The paper reframes coordination as a scheduling problem solved up front: take each work item's declared scope, partition the work into disjoint scopes, and order merges along the producer→consumer dependency graph. This planner is implemented in Nerveplane. It is evaluated with NP-Bench, an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark (no coordination; reactive detection; proactive planning) that verifies integration off a real git merge, both in deterministic simulation and with live agents. The paper also tests a cross-session memory module and an experiment routing facts to agents under long-context, window-fitting scales.
AI.result: The planner raises clean integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and reduces merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with the gap growing as the number of agents increases. On a live breaking contract change, clean-integration rises from 0 (no coordination and reactive detection) to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small model, with 0/5 scope leakage. Cross-session memory drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on both strong and weak models. A negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales. Across two capability tiers and two vendors, the benefit did not shrink as models got stronger.
AI.conclusion: Proactive, scope-partitioned scheduling solves agent team integration failures that reactive coordination and no coordination both miss. The benefit stems from how work is allocated rather than from model reasoning, so it holds across capability tiers and vendors and grows with team size. Routing facts to agents offers value in cost and capacity, not in attention.

title: AeroBuoy: A Drone Deployable, 3D Printed, Autonomous Robotic Buoy for Environmental Inspection in Remote and Hazardous River Systems
comment: 7 pages. Accepted version. Published in the 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Winner of the IROS 2025 Best Paper Award on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics in memory of Motohiro Kisoi. Reuben O'Brien and Angus Lynch contributed equally
summary: Monitoring of waterways such as remote and hazardous rivers and streams is important so as to assess the impact of external factors including construction runoff or climate change. Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can offer excellent environmental inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, or access protected water bodies but they have several shortcomings in terms of maneuverability. This paper proposes an environmental inspection system consisting of an autonomous data collection buoy which is designed to be deployed to inaccessible river systems using a drone. The system can perform a drop off and pickup of the buoy depending on the requirements of a particular location and monitoring task. Utilising the natural flow of the river the buoy autonomously steers down, using GPS and magnetometers so as to maintain the desired trajectory. The buoy is capable of measuring water temperature but it can also be equipped with a range of sensors such as water oxygen meter, sonar for river bed inspection, or turbidity for water clarity. This paper describes the system design, presents an analysis of the self-righting capabilities of the buoy, and shows a full system demonstration at the Ōrewa River in Auckland, New Zealand.

AI.tldr: An autonomous, drone-deployable data collection buoy is proposed for monitoring remote and hazardous rivers, using GPS and magnetometers to steer along the natural flow, demonstrated on the Ōrewa River, New Zealand.
AI.motivation: Monitoring remote and hazardous rivers is important for assessing impacts of factors such as construction runoff or climate change, but versatile autonomous robotic boats have shortcomings in maneuverability, and inaccessible water bodies are difficult to reach.
AI.method: Design of an environmental inspection system comprising an autonomous data collection buoy deployed and retrieved by a drone; the buoy exploits the natural river flow to steer autonomously downstream, using GPS and magnetometers to maintain a desired trajectory, and carries a water temperature sensor plus optional sensors (oxygen meter, sonar for river bed inspection, turbidity sensor). The paper also analyzes the buoy's self-righting capability.
AI.result: The system design is described, an analysis of the buoy's self-righting capabilities is presented, and a full system demonstration is shown at the Ōrewa River in Auckland, New Zealand.
AI.conclusion: The drone-deployed autonomous buoy offers a viable environmental inspection and monitoring solution for remote, dangerous, or access-restricted water bodies, with demonstrated deployment and operation in a real river setting.

title: Does the Model Use the Feature? Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs
summary: Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. Yet steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model's own computation. We examine this inference and propose an empirical contract whose tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs. One test copies a feature's value from an input that shows a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal); the other restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it. Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known--unknown abstention contrast. Dense known--unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama, and how fully a released subject--verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model. Tracking a concept and steering a behavior therefore do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature, and each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested.

AI.tldr: Steering a feature far outside its natural range can produce effects that don't reflect the model's own computation. The authors propose an empirical contract testing features at naturally observed values, finding that feature-behavior tracking and steering alone do not prove the model actually uses a feature.
AI.motivation: Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. However, steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model's own computation. The authors question this inference and aim to evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs.
AI.method: The authors propose an empirical contract with two tests that evaluate features at naturally observed values. The first test copies a feature's value from an input showing a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal). The second restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it.
AI.result: Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known-unknown abstention contrast. Dense known-unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama. How fully a released subject-verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model.
AI.conclusion: Tracking a concept and steering a behavior do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature. Each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested.

title: What the Elevation Map Cannot See: Semantic-Aware Locomotion and Execution-Aware Navigation for Humanoid Robot
summary: Navigation for humanoid robots is critical, yet large-scale evaluation on physical hardware is often impractical due to cost and safety concerns, making simulation benchmarks essential. Existing VLN benchmarks achieve physically executable navigation, but still assume (1) all hazards are observable from elevation maps; (2) realized motions closely match desired motions. In real environments, however, fallen bottles may be ambiguous in elevation maps, while phones and water spills may be difficult to differentiate; hazard avoidance by the locomotion policy can cause the robot's actual trajectory to deviate from the path intended by the VLN policy. Such command-execution mismatch can accumulate and lead the robot toward unintended locations. To expose these failure modes, we introduce a benchmark that models both elevation-subtle hazards and execution deviations, together with a closed-loop VLN + locomotion control framework that continuously realigns high-level navigation with the robot's actual state. We evaluate navigation in simulation and further validate the locomotion policy on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Results show that semantic input reduces contact with hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, while anti-deviation improves navigation success. These findings highlight the need to evaluate humanoid navigation jointly in terms of route completion and hazard avoidance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a simulation benchmark for humanoid VLN that models elevation-subtle hazards and locomotion-induced execution deviations, paired with a closed-loop VLN+locomotion framework to realign navigation with the robot's actual state.
AI.motivation: Humanoid navigation evaluation on physical hardware is costly and unsafe, making simulation benchmarks essential. Existing VLN benchmarks assume all hazards are observable from elevation maps and that realized motions match desired motions. In reality, ambiguities (e.g., fallen bottles, phones, water spills) and locomotion-policy avoidance cause command-execution mismatch that accumulates, driving robots to unintended locations.
AI.method: A benchmark modeling both elevation-subtle hazards and execution deviations, combined with a closed-loop VLN + locomotion control framework that continuously realigns high-level navigation with the robot's actual state. Evaluated in simulation, with the locomotion policy validated on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
AI.result: Semantic input reduces contact with hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, while anti-deviation improves navigation success. Validation on the physical Unitree G1 confirmed the locomotion policy.
AI.conclusion: Humanoid navigation should be evaluated jointly in terms of route completion and hazard avoidance, exposing failure modes overlooked by prior benchmarks.

title: A Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation
summary: Deterministic benchmark scores show that an agent received credit, but not whether that credit was earned, reported honestly, or would hold on a second run. We introduce a Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation, an additive post-hoc framework that reports, beside each recorded score, whether it should be believed. It verifies four properties: whether the result is supported by the benchmark's own grading logic, whether a passing answer was earned through traceable computation, whether the agent's completion claim matches what occurred, and whether the result is stable under repeated execution. The first three use only saved artifacts; the fourth re-runs the agent. Model judgments only label evidence under majority voting; all verdicts follow deterministic rules and never modify the recorded score. Applied to five agent configurations on 108 tasks from Agents' Last Exam, every model shows passing runs with no traceable computation (at rates varying tenfold), confirmed false completion claims, and unstable results: 18-46% of tasks do not stay in one score band over five runs. Only 22.6% of recorded passes clear all four checks (95% CI 15.0-32.6, n=84). Measuring what an agent can do and verifying that it did it are different problems, and current benchmarks address only the first.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a "Trust Layer" for agent evaluation, an additive, post-hoc framework that audits benchmark scores along four properties (grading support, traceable computation, honest completion claims, and stability), while never altering the recorded score. Applied to five agent configurations on 108 Agents' Last Exam tasks, only 22.6% of recorded passes clear all four checks.
AI.motivation: Deterministic benchmark scores only show that an agent received credit, not whether that credit was legitimately earned, honestly reported, or reproducible. Capability measurement and verification are distinct problems, yet current benchmarks address only the former, leaving scored results un-audited for validity and trustworthiness.
AI.method: The framework verifies four properties: (1) whether results are supported by the benchmark's own grading logic, (2) whether passing answers were earned through traceable computation, (3) whether completion claims match what actually occurred, and (4) whether results are stable across repeated executions. The first three rely solely on saved artifacts; the fourth re-runs the agent. Model judgments are used only to label evidence under majority voting, all verdicts follow deterministic rules, and recorded scores are never modified.
AI.result: Across five agent configurations on 108 Agents' Last Exam tasks, every model produced passing runs with no traceable computation (at rates varying tenfold), confirmed false completion claims, and unstable results, with 18–46% of tasks not staying within one score band over five runs. Only 22.6% of recorded passes cleared all four checks (95% CI 15.0–32.6, n=84).
AI.conclusion: Measuring what an agent can do and verifying that it did it are fundamentally different problems. Current benchmarks address only capability measurement, and the proposed Trust Layer exposes substantial gaps in score credibility, suggesting evaluation should report not just scores but also whether those scores should be believed.

title: An Autonomous, 3D Printed, Waterjet-Powered, Open-Source Robotic Trimaran for Environmental Inspection and Monitoring
comment: 8 pages. Accepted version. Published in the 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Finalist for the IROS 2024 Best Application Paper Award
summary: Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can offer excellent environmental inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, hard to reach, or access protected water bodies. This paper introduces such a platform in the form of an autonomous, cost-effective, waterjet-powered robotic trimaran. Motivated by the need for an efficient aquatic monitoring, particularly in Aotearoa - New Zealand's diverse environments, the trimaran provides an efficient, low-cost, and easy to replicate alternative to resource-intensive research vessels. The proposed platform, costs $600-1,500 USD to develop (depending on the sensing system configuration), weighs under 5 kg, and excels in bathymetry and water quality testing. The trimaran can reach speeds of up to 2 m/s offering obstacle avoidance of natural features, such as rocks. Utilizing off-the-shelf components and 3D printing technology, the proposed platform offers excellent reproducibility and robustness while operating in shallow waters with its jet propulsion system. The paper presents in detail the design characteristics, the sensing system employed, testing results focusing on bathymetry, and highlights the ability of vessel and the potential for future research and data collection.

AI.tldr: An autonomous, cost-effective waterjet-powered robotic trimaran is proposed for environmental inspection and monitoring of remote or protected water bodies, offering reproducible design, shallow-water operation, and strong bathymetry and water-quality testing performance.
AI.motivation: Efficient aquatic monitoring is needed, particularly in Aotearoa New Zealand's diverse environments, where resource-intensive research vessels are impractical. Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can provide inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, hard-to-reach, or protected water bodies.
AI.method: The platform is an autonomous, low-cost, waterjet-powered robotic trimaran weighing under 5 kg and costing $600-1,500 USD depending on sensing configuration. It uses off-the-shelf components and 3D printing for reproducibility and robustness, with a jet propulsion system for shallow-water operation, speeds up to 2 m/s, and obstacle avoidance of natural features such as rocks.
AI.result: The trimaran excels in bathymetry and water quality testing, achieving speeds up to 2 m/s while avoiding natural obstacles like rocks. Its design, sensing system, and testing results focused on bathymetry are presented in detail.
AI.conclusion: The proposed platform demonstrates excellent reproducibility, robustness, and capability in shallow waters, highlighting its potential for future research and data collection as a low-cost alternative to resource-intensive research vessels.

title: The Right Memory in the Wrong Context: Verifying Retrieval Admissibility in Long-Term Agent Memory
comment: 26 pages. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development". Code: https://github.com/ziwang11112/right-memory-wrong-context
summary: Long-term-memory agents can retrieve relevant information that is inadmissible for the current request because it belongs to another principal, violates policy, or reflects an incompatible lifecycle state. Recall and final-answer accuracy do not reveal this: a route can appear safe by missing required evidence, while a correct answer may follow inadmissible prompt exposure. We introduce a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that assigns each memory-query pair one of three statuses (admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved), compares routes at matched required-evidence recall with bounds for unresolved cases, and tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure while linking exposure to target-level disclosure. We evaluate its stages on separate, non-pooled populations. A post-hoc top-20 reanalysis of frozen rankings from two public long-term-memory benchmarks, RHELM and MemOps, covers 3,767 queries. All released anchors lie within trusted query namespaces; with within-namespace scores unchanged, off-namespace filtering cannot lower their ranks. Top-20 anchor recall increases from 0.432 to 0.533, 80% recall feasibility from 0.237 to 0.311, and exact similarity evaluations decrease by 98.3%. In a frozen 72-case development diagnostic, a released-metadata reference preserves required evidence, whereas neither text-only verifier detects violations under the 1% required-anchor false-denial limit. Across 1,523 paired benchmark-native cases, namespace routing is associated with judged-accuracy gains of 0.053-0.068 across three readers; recall also changes, so this comparison is observational. In 16 controlled exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% confidence intervals excludes zero for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]). Results motivate separate verification of candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that classifies memory-query pairs as admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved, and evaluates routing, exposure, and disclosure on separate non-pooled populations.
AI.motivation: Long-term-memory agents may retrieve information that is inadmissible for the current request due to principal mismatch, policy violation, or incompatible lifecycle state. Recall and final-answer accuracy conceal this problem, since a route can look safe by omitting required evidence, while a correct answer may stem from inadmissible prompt exposure.
AI.method: The framework assigns each memory-query pair one of three statuses (admissible, inadmissible, unresolved), compares routes at matched required-evidence recall with bounds for unresolved cases, and tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure, linking exposure to target-level disclosure. Stages are evaluated on separate, non-pooled populations, including a post-hoc top-20 reanalysis of frozen rankings from RHELM and MemOps, a frozen 72-case development diagnostic, 1,523 paired benchmark-native cases, and 16 controlled exposure scenarios.
AI.result: In the RHELM and MemOps reanalysis covering 3,767 queries, all released anchors lie within trusted query namespaces; with within-namespace scores unchanged, off-namespace filtering cannot lower their ranks. Top-20 anchor recall rises from 0.432 to 0.533, 80% recall feasibility from 0.237 to 0.311, and exact similarity evaluations drop by 98.3%. In the 72-case diagnostic, a released-metadata reference preserves required evidence, whereas neither text-only verifier detects violations under the 1% required-anchor false-denial limit. Across 1,523 paired cases, namespace routing is associated with judged-accuracy gains of 0.053-0.068 across three readers, though recall also changes, making the comparison observational. In 16 exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% confidence intervals excludes zero for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]).
AI.conclusion: Results motivate separate verification of candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure, since standard recall and accuracy metrics cannot expose inadmissible retrieval.

title: RACER: Residual-Adaptive Closed-Loop Estimation for Sampling-Based Planning in Wheeled-Quadruped Racing
summary: We present RACER, a hierarchical control framework for wheel-based quadruped racing that combines an MPPI planner with a learned residual dynamics model and a low-level RL velocity tracker. The planner augments a nominal unicycle kinematic model with a neural residual term to capture the closed-loop tracking behavior of the RL policy. To train this residual model under limited real-world data, we propose Low-Rank Residual Adaptation (LoRRA), a two-stage approach that pre-trains on large-scale simulation data for broad coverage and then fine-tunes on a small real-world dataset with a low-rank constraint. In simulation, we empirically validate our engineering choices by showing (A) Residual dynamics improve the overall performance of our pipeline by capturing the tracking error of RL velocity tracker at high-speed cornering. (B) Residual dynamics trained with both source-domain and target-domain data gives racing performance significantly better than the residual dynamics trained with only target-domain data. (C) Low-rank constraint at target-domain adaptation gives higher success rates and higher performance than full-tune and from-scratch when domain gap in ground coefficient or joint gain increases.

AI.tldr: RACER is a hierarchical control framework for wheel-based quadruped racing combining an MPPI planner, a learned residual dynamics model, and an RL velocity tracker, with a low-rank adaptation scheme (LoRRA) for training the residual model under limited real-world data.
AI.motivation: Wheel-based quadruped racing at high speed requires accurate planning, but a nominal unicycle kinematic model fails to capture the closed-loop tracking behavior of the low-level RL policy, especially the tracking error during high-speed cornering. Meanwhile, learning such residual dynamics is challenging because real-world data is scarce.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework: an MPPI planner that augments a nominal unicycle kinematic model with a neural residual term capturing the RL velocity tracker's closed-loop behavior; plus LoRRA, a two-stage residual-model training scheme that pre-trains on large-scale simulation data for broad coverage and then fine-tunes on a small real-world dataset with a low-rank constraint.
AI.result: Simulation experiments validate the design choices: (A) residual dynamics improve overall pipeline performance by capturing the RL velocity tracker's tracking error at high-speed cornering; (B) residuals trained with both source- and target-domain data significantly outperform those trained with target-domain data only; (C) the low-rank constraint yields higher success rates and performance than full-tune or from-scratch methods as the domain gap in ground coefficient or joint gain grows.
AI.conclusion: RACER demonstrates that combining an MPPI planner with a learned residual dynamics model and an RL velocity tracker, trained via low-rank residual adaptation, is an effective and data-efficient approach for wheel-based quadruped racing.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Inference-Time Overreliance Using Agentic Memory
summary: Agentic memory allows LLM agents to reuse past experience, yet retrieved memories can also distort inference even when they are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. We study this failure mode, which we call memory over-reliance. Across benchmarks and memory architectures, we find that memory is useful when past experience transfers to the current task, but can become misleading when only part of the evidence transfers. Failures are strongest under partial query-memory overlap, a pattern further confirmed by controlled experiments thatvary the amount of overlapping evidence. Motivated by this finding, we propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls its reuse at read time. MEMTRIM removes repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information, requires no retraining, and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory systems.Experiments show that MEMTRIM reduces memory overreliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory across models and memory settings.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "memory over-reliance," a failure mode where correctly stored and retrieved memories distort LLM agent inference when only partial evidence transfers, and proposes MEMTRIM, a training-free plug-and-play framework that indexes memory at write time and controls reuse at read time to reduce over-reliance while preserving useful memory benefits.
AI.motivation: Agentic memory enables LLM agents to reuse past experience, but retrieved memories can distort inference even when they are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. This failure mode, termed memory over-reliance, is most pronounced under partial query-memory overlap where only part of the evidence transfers to the current task.
AI.method: The authors diagnose memory over-reliance across benchmarks and memory architectures, including controlled experiments that vary the amount of overlapping evidence. They then propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls reuse at read time, removing repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information. MEMTRIM requires no retraining and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory systems.
AI.result: Experiments across models and memory settings show that MEMTRIM reduces memory over-reliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory.
AI.conclusion: Memory is beneficial when past experience transfers to the current task but misleading under partial evidence transfer; MEMTRIM offers a training-free, general solution to control memory reuse and mitigate over-reliance without sacrificing memory utility.

title: Entropy-Gated Belief Coordination for Decentralized Multi-Agent Search Under Intermittent Communication
summary: We study decentralized multi-agent target search where homogeneous agents communicate intermittently at Poisson-distributed times. Standard unconditional belief fusion wastes communication opportunities by synchronizing agents during high-entropy exploration, when diverse independent beliefs provide better coverage than a premature consensus. We introduce \emph{entropy-gated belief coordination}, in which agents skip fusion while their collective entropy ratio exceeds a threshold~\(θ\) and merge only during exploitation, consistent with the bifurcation structure of nonlinear opinion dynamics and the submodular structure of the per-step information gain objective. We further derive \(\Istep(α,β)\), the expected mutual information per observation step between two agents' binary sensors, as an interpretable, communication-free measure of sensor informativeness that motivates the gating design and guides system-level analysis. Experiments across 103{,}680 trials (nine grid sizes up to \(100{\times}100\), Poisson communication timing, four target movement patterns) show that the Entropy-Gated Trust-Decay Planner (\textsc{EG-TDP}), which adds a detection-probability planner switch in exploitation mode, achieves mean belief quality \(\bar{Q}=0.300\) (mean belief mass at the true target cell, averaged across all trials and steps), a \(58.9\%\) gain over arithmetic mean and a \(37.4\%\) gain over visit-weighted fusion. On representative configurations, EG-TDP also outperforms a joint-Bayesian reference that uses all agents'~observations at every step, despite operating under random intermittent contact only.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes entropy-gated belief coordination for decentralized multi-agent target search under intermittent Poisson communication, where agents skip fusion during high-entropy exploration and merge only during exploitation. The resulting EG-TDP planner (with a detection-probability switch) achieves mean belief quality Q=0.300, a 58.9% gain over arithmetic mean and 37.4% over visit-weighted fusion, and can outperform a fully joint-Bayesian reference under partial communication.
AI.motivation: In decentralized multi-agent target search, agents communicate only intermittently (Poisson-distributed contact), so each communication opportunity is scarce. Standard unconditional belief fusion wastes these opportunities by forcing synchronization during high-entropy exploration, when independent, diverse beliefs provide better coverage than premature consensus. A principled mechanism is therefore needed to decide when fusion is beneficial.
AI.method: The paper introduces entropy-gated belief coordination: agents skip belief fusion while their collective entropy ratio exceeds a threshold θ and merge only during exploitation. This gating design is motivated by (1) the bifurcation structure of nonlinear opinion dynamics and (2) the submodular structure of the per-step information gain objective. The authors also derive Istep(α,β), the expected mutual information per observation step between two agents' binary sensors, as an interpretable, communication-free measure of sensor informativeness that guides the gating threshold and system-level analysis. Building on this, they propose the Entropy-Gated Trust-Decay Planner (EG-TDP), which adds a detection-probability planner switch in exploitation mode.
AI.result: Across 103,680 trials (nine grid sizes up to 100×100, Poisson communication timing, four target movement patterns), EG-TDP achieves mean belief quality Q=0.300 (mean belief mass at the true target cell, averaged over all trials and steps). This represents a 58.9% gain over arithmetic mean fusion and a 37.4% gain over visit-weighted fusion. On representative configurations, EG-TDP also outperforms a joint-Bayesian reference that uses all agents' observations at every step, despite operating under random intermittent contact only.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-gated belief coordination provides an effective criterion for when decentralized agents should fuse beliefs, showing that selectively synchronizing during low-entropy exploitation rather than high-entropy exploration substantially improves belief quality. EG-TDP exceeds standard fusion baselines and even a full-information joint-Bayesian reference under realistic intermittent communication, demonstrating the value of communication-aware gating and the utility of the Istep measure for system-level analysis.

title: Rule-Based Languages for Neurosymbolic AI
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of Rules and Reasoning - 10th International Joint Conference, RuleML+RR 2026, Vilnius, Lithuania
summary: Logic programming is increasingly used as the symbolic component of neurosymbolic AI systems. We survey the main rule-based languages in this setting, namely Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs, along four axes: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanism. We analyse over 50 recent systems and applications, comparing formalism usage across four research areas: databases and programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics. We provide a decision matrix mapping application scenarios to required features and close by outlining open problems.

AI.tldr: A survey of rule-based logic programming languages (Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs) used as the symbolic component of neurosymbolic AI systems.
AI.motivation: Logic programming is increasingly adopted as the symbolic component of neurosymbolic AI, but the landscape of rule-based languages and their integration with neural methods is fragmented, motivating a structured, comparative survey.
AI.method: Surveys the main rule-based languages (Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs) along four axes: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanism. Analyzes over 50 recent systems and applications and compares formalism usage across four research areas: databases and programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics.
AI.result: Provides a comparative analysis of formalisms across the four axes and four research areas, yielding a decision matrix that maps application scenarios to required features.
AI.conclusion: The paper consolidates the neurosymbolic rule-based language landscape via a feature-based decision matrix and outlines open problems for future research.

title: Dynamics Modeling of a Multi-UAV Slung Load System Using a Discrete-Link Cable Approach
comment: Presented at ICRA 2026 as an accepted paper
summary: A common assumption to simplify the problem of controlling a multi-UAV slung load system (MUSLS) is that the flexible cables can be modeled as massless rigid rods. In this work, we propose an alternative Euler-Newton derived dynamical model which uses a series of rigid links to model the flexible cables. The model is specifically designed to allow efficient simulation using Featherstone's articulated body algorithm. We perform real-world validation of this model on gentle, aggressive, and tension-engagement maneuvers and run a parameter sweep to determine the number of links, joint damping, and joint friction to achieve the greatest model fidelity. The model closely matches real-world flight data with mean load translation errors below 132 mm (5.5% of the cable length) and orientation errors below 11.4 degrees. We make the real-world flight data publicly available for the development of future cable models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Euler-Newton dynamical model that represents flexible cables in a multi-UAV slung load system as a chain of rigid links, enabling efficient simulation via Featherstone's articulated body algorithm. Real-world experiments validate its fidelity, with mean load translation errors under 132 mm and orientation errors under 11.4°, and the flight data is released publicly.
AI.motivation: Controlling a multi-UAV slung load system is commonly simplified by modeling flexible cables as massless rigid rods, which neglects cable flexibility and may limit model accuracy. The authors seek a more faithful yet computationally tractable cable model suitable for real-world control and simulation.
AI.method: An Euler-Newton derived dynamical model is developed in which the flexible cables are represented by a series of rigid links. The formulation is specifically structured to permit efficient simulation using Featherstone's articulated body algorithm. Model fidelity is assessed through real-world validation on gentle, aggressive, and tension-engagement maneuvers, along with a parameter sweep over the number of links, joint damping, and joint friction.
AI.result: The model closely matches real-world flight data, achieving mean load translation errors below 132 mm (5.5% of the cable length) and orientation errors below 11.4 degrees. The parameter sweep identifies link count, joint damping, and joint friction values that maximize model fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Modeling flexible cables as a chain of rigid links yields a high-fidelity, efficiently simulable dynamical model for multi-UAV slung load systems, outperforming the massless rigid rod assumption. The real-world flight data is made publicly available to support the development of future cable models.

title: Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization: Learning to Reason with Adaptive Rationale Scaffolding
summary: On-policy reinforcement learning has become a central paradigm for improving the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, its effectiveness is often limited by reward sparsity: when a model fails to discover correct trajectories for difficult problems, the optimization process receives little useful signal and may stagnate. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by incorporating off-policy demonstrations, expert traces, or model-generated solutions, but they typically require the auxiliary data to match the format of the reinforcement-learning task, often relying on rejection sampling from stronger models to obtain suitable training trajectories. We introduce Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization (RGPO), a framework that adaptively leverages ground-truth rationale information according to the model's current capability while preserving its freedom to explore. Rather than treating reference solutions as fixed imitation targets, RGPO uses them as temporary scaffolds: rationales help the model generate improved responses, after which only higher-reward, model-generated solutions are transferred back to the original unguided setting. This design allows training to exploit available ground-truth information without requiring off-policy data to follow the same format as the RL task. Across both language-only and vision-language reasoning settings, RGPO consistently improves performance over RLVR baselines, and ablation studies show that adaptive rationale guidance is a key contributor to these gains. These results suggest that RGPO offers a practical and general approach for reducing reward sparsity, stabilizing reinforcement learning, and improving reasoning performance in both text-only and multimodal models.

AI.tldr: RGPO is a framework that adaptively uses ground-truth rationales as temporary scaffolds to reduce reward sparsity in on-policy RL, transferring only higher-reward model-generated solutions back to the unguided setting, improving reasoning in both text-only and vision-language tasks.
AI.motivation: On-policy RL is central to improving LLM reasoning, but reward sparsity limits its effectiveness: when models fail to discover correct trajectories on hard problems, optimization receives little useful signal and may stagnate. Existing remedies (off-policy demonstrations, expert traces, model-generated solutions) require auxiliary data to match the RL task format, often depending on rejection sampling from stronger models.
AI.method: Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization (RGPO) adaptively leverages ground-truth rationale information according to the model's current capability while preserving exploration freedom. Instead of treating reference solutions as fixed imitation targets, RGPO uses them as temporary scaffolds: rationales help the model generate improved responses, after which only higher-reward, model-generated solutions are transferred back to the original unguided setting. This exploits ground-truth information without requiring off-policy data to match the RL task format.
AI.result: Across language-only and vision-language reasoning settings, RGPO consistently outperforms RLVR baselines. Ablation studies show adaptive rationale guidance is a key contributor to the gains.
AI.conclusion: RGPO offers a practical, general approach for reducing reward sparsity, stabilizing reinforcement learning, and improving reasoning performance in both text-only and multimodal models.

title: SURGE: Sonar-fUsed Reconstruction and localization via image-gated Graph Estimation
summary: Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) are widely used to explore and inspect underwater environments such as caves, shipwrecks, and submerged infrastructure. These missions require accurate 3D understanding of the surrounding environment, which depends on both reliable vehicle localization and metric scene reconstruction. However, external positioning is often unavailable underwater, requiring small ROVs to rely primarily on onboard perception. Optic vision provides rich visual and geometric information but suffers from scale ambi- guity and trajectory drift, whereas 2D imaging sonar provides metric range but incomplete 3D geometry. Existing underwater reconstruction approaches typically address these limitations separately or assume known sensor poses, leaving localization and reconstruction disconnected. We present SURGE, a camera sonar framework that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and target location by integrating visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph, then uses the recovered metric poses for sonar Gaussian splatting. Experiments on real underwater RGB sonar observations show that SURGE substantially improves localization consistency over conventional vision based pose estimation and produces a more compact, natively metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian splatting baselines.

AI.tldr: SURGE jointly estimates ROV trajectory and target location by fusing camera and 2D imaging sonar in a factor graph, then uses the recovered metric poses for sonar Gaussian splatting.
AI.motivation: Underwater ROV missions (caves, shipwrecks, submerged infrastructure) need accurate 3D understanding, but external positioning is usually unavailable, forcing reliance on onboard perception. Optic vision suffers from scale ambiguity and trajectory drift, while 2D imaging sonar gives metric range but incomplete 3D geometry. Existing methods treat these limitations separately or assume known sensor poses, leaving localization and reconstruction disconnected.
AI.method: A camera-sonar framework integrating visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph to jointly estimate the ROV trajectory and target location, followed by sonar Gaussian splatting driven by the recovered metric poses.
AI.result: On real underwater RGB-sonar observations, SURGE substantially improves localization consistency over conventional vision-based pose estimation and yields a more compact, natively metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian splatting baselines.
AI.conclusion: Jointly coupling visual-acoustic localization with sonar Gaussian splatting enables consistent metric trajectory estimation and compact metric reconstruction for small ROVs without external positioning.

title: Trajectory-Retrieval Speculative Decoding: When Does a Model's Own History Help?
summary: Long chain-of-thought reasoning increases sequential decoding cost while creating a growing history of potentially reusable continuations. We investigate when this history supplies useful drafts and complements an existing drafter. Controlled source comparisons reveal trajectory-specific reuse, motivating our method Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR). TLAR retrieves approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory and uses recent verification outcomes to adapt retrieval activation and candidate width. TLAR combines retrieved continuations with model-generated drafts in a shared candidate tree, preserving the target model's output distribution through exact verification. Across code debugging, mathematics, and open-ended writing, our evaluation connects source reuse, incremental acceptance, and execution cost. Combining TLAR with strong retrieval baselines improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets and increases end-to-end throughput over the draft-model baseline. These findings support generated trajectories as runtime memory for adaptive inference.

AI.tldr: TLAR reuses prior continuations from the current reasoning trajectory as draft candidates, adaptively retrieving them to accelerate sequential decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution via exact verification.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning raises sequential decoding cost but also accumulates a growing history of potentially reusable continuations; the paper investigates when this history supplies useful drafts and complements existing drafters.
AI.method: Controlled source comparisons reveal trajectory-specific reuse, motivating Trajectory-Local Adaptive Retrieval (TLAR), which retrieves approximately matched continuations from the current trajectory, uses recent verification outcomes to adapt retrieval activation and candidate width, and merges retrieved continuations with model-generated drafts in a shared candidate tree under exact verification.
AI.result: Across code debugging, mathematics, and open-ended writing, the evaluation links source reuse, incremental acceptance, and execution cost; TLAR combined with strong retrieval baselines improves token acceptance under matched verification budgets and increases end-to-end throughput over the draft-model baseline.
AI.conclusion: The findings support generated trajectories as runtime memory for adaptive inference.

title: Risk-Sensitive Crowd Navigation with Adaptive Ellipsoidal Conformal Prediction
summary: Safe crowd navigation under distribution shift requires uncertainty representations that capture structured human-motion prediction errors and safety objectives that account for rare but consequential failures. Existing uncertainty-aware methods typically represent prediction errors using isotropic regions, which can be either overly conservative or poorly aligned with directional motion uncertainty. We introduce a risk-aware navigation framework that uses anisotropic conformal ellipsoids to translate structured prediction uncertainty into an episode-level conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) signal that regulates the Lagrangian safety penalty.
