In particular, adaptive ellipsoidal conformal prediction (AECP) captures directional prediction errors and adaptively calibrates uncertainty regions under distribution shift, while the resulting CVaR-regulated navigation policy is optimized using Lagrangian proximal policy optimization. We evaluate our proposed method under both in-distribution settings and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings involving shifts in pedestrian motion patterns. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, our method maintains competitive in-distribution performance while improving success rates by 5.68-7.44 percentage points and reducing collision rates by 5.44-6.64 percentage points across OOD settings. We further deploy the trained policy without fine-tuning on a physical robot with onboard perception and CPU-only inference, showing that the full pipeline is feasible in physical crowd navigation.

AI.tldr: A risk-aware crowd navigation framework uses anisotropic conformal ellipsoids to convert structured human-motion prediction uncertainty into an episode-level CVaR signal that regulates a Lagrangian safety penalty, improving OOD success and collision rates.
AI.motivation: Safe crowd navigation under distribution shift requires uncertainty representations that capture structured human-motion prediction errors and safety objectives that account for rare but consequential failures. Existing uncertainty-aware methods typically use isotropic prediction-error regions, which are either overly conservative or poorly aligned with directional motion uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors introduce a risk-aware navigation framework with adaptive ellipsoidal conformal prediction (AECP) to capture directional prediction errors and adaptively calibrate uncertainty regions under distribution shift. This structured uncertainty is translated into an episode-level conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) signal that regulates the Lagrangian safety penalty, and the resulting CVaR-regulated navigation policy is optimized with Lagrangian proximal policy optimization.
AI.result: Evaluated under in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with shifts in pedestrian motion patterns, the method maintains competitive in-distribution performance while improving success rates by 5.68-7.44 percentage points and reducing collision rates by 5.44-6.64 percentage points across OOD settings compared with state-of-the-art baselines. The trained policy was also deployed without fine-tuning on a physical robot with onboard perception and CPU-only inference.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic conformal ellipsoids combined with CVaR-regulated Lagrangian safety optimization yield a more effective and deployable uncertainty-aware policy for safe crowd navigation under distribution shift.

title: Evaluating Escalation Signals for LLM Routing: Targets, Controls, and Five Ways to Fool Yourself
summary: Deciding when to escalate a query from a small language model to a larger one requires a cheap signal that predicts, before the large model is called, whether escalating would help. Semantic entropy, originally developed to detect hallucinations, is a natural candidate: it measures how much a model's sampled answers disagree in meaning, and high disagreement often signals an unreliable answer. We test it across three benchmarks and two model families. On GSM8K, with a small/large pair about twelve times apart in size, semantic entropy reliably distinguishes the small model's mistakes (AUROC 0.871) and improves routed accuracy over random escalation by up to nine points at matched cost. An earlier strong-looking result on a synthetic benchmark proved misleading: a simple rule based only on question difficulty, with no model involved, matched semantic entropy almost exactly. This paper's main contribution is a set of checks that catch this before it is reported as real. We show that scoring a cheap, question-only difficulty estimate alongside any signal reveals whether the signal adds real information or just tracks how hard a question looks; that two reasonable definitions of "escalation worked" can produce very different results on the same data; that a benchmark can leave almost no room for any signal to beat simply always using the large model; and that the true cost of live sampling can make routing more expensive than calling the large model directly. For a cheaper alternative that reuses cached past outcomes, we show how to predict whether it will work on a new dataset -- confirmed by correctly forecasting a collapse from AUROC 0.908 to chance level (0.518) ahead of time. We offer these as a general checklist for evaluating escalation signals.

AI.tldr: This paper tests semantic entropy as a cheap escalation signal for routing queries between small and large language models, and contributes a set of validation checks that reveal when such signals only track question difficulty or benchmark artifacts rather than adding real routing value.
AI.motivation: Escalating a query from a small to a large model requires a cheap pre-call signal predicting whether escalation would help. Semantic entropy, used originally for hallucination detection, is a natural candidate, but its apparent success can be misleading if it merely reflects question difficulty or benchmark-specific artifacts.
AI.method: Semantic entropy is evaluated across three benchmarks and two model families. Validation checks include: scoring a cheap question-only difficulty estimate alongside any signal to test for incremental information; comparing two reasonable definitions of "escalation worked"; examining whether the benchmark leaves room to beat always using the large model; accounting for the true cost of live sampling; and forecasting the performance of a cheaper cached-outcome alternative on a new dataset.
AI.result: On GSM8K, with small/large models roughly twelve times apart in size, semantic entropy distinguishes the small model's mistakes (AUROC 0.871) and improves routed accuracy over random escalation by up to nine points at matched cost. On a synthetic benchmark, a question-difficulty-only rule matched semantic entropy almost exactly, exposing a misleading result. The cost of live sampling can make routing more expensive than directly calling the large model, and a cached-outcome alternative's collapse from AUROC 0.908 to chance level (0.518) was correctly forecast on a new dataset.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is a general checklist of checks for evaluating escalation signals, showing whether a signal adds genuine information beyond question difficulty, whether results depend on the definition of success, whether benchmarks permit improvement over always using the large model, and whether routing costs are actually justified.

title: MobileVISTA: Generative Data Augmentation for Pose Generalization in Mobile Manipulation
summary: Mobile manipulators such as humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in dynamic, unstructured environments to perform dexterous manipulation tasks. However, end-to-end manipulation policies trained to imitate demonstration data collected from a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale deviations in robot pose at deployment can drive ego-centric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, leading to sharp drops in performance. We introduce MobileVISTA, a data generation framework that transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes. Unlike prior methods, which assume a camera rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated robot geometry largely out of frame, MobileVISTA targets compatibility with egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the robot's kinematic chain as it moves. We study MobileVISTA in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments, and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro. We find policies trained on MobileVISTA-augmented data demonstrate improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses encountered at test time, without additional demonstration collection or a trained generative model. Additionally, we find MobileVISTA's benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame. Additional videos and appendix can be found on our website: https://mobilevista.github.io

AI.tldr: MobileVISTA is a data generation framework that converts demonstrations captured at a canonical robot pose into pose-perturbed training data by jointly augmenting egocentric visual observations and retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes, improving robustness of mobile manipulation policies.
AI.motivation: End-to-end imitation-learned manipulation policies trained from demonstration data at a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale pose deviations at deployment push ego-centric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, causing sharp performance drops. Prior augmentation methods assume cameras rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated geometry largely out of frame, so they do not fit egocentric platforms like humanoids where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the moving kinematic chain.
AI.method: MobileVISTA transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes, targeting egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera rides the actuated kinematic chain. It requires no additional demonstration collection and no trained generative model.
AI.result: Evaluated in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro, policies trained on MobileVISTA-augmented data show improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses at test time. The benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame.
AI.conclusion: MobileVISTA offers a simple, generative-model-free data augmentation approach that improves pose robustness of egocentric mobile manipulators without extra demonstration collection, with the strongest gains on humanoid platforms.

title: Evaluate the Stack, Not the Layer: Do Deterministic and LLM Gates for Agent Actions Fail Independently?
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 10 tables. Artifact (data, scripts, provenance): https://github.com/chenglin1112/evaluate-the-stack
summary: Runtime gates for agent tool calls are stacked on the assumption that their errors multiply. We test it on 1,119 labelled agent actions from three corpora, without an adaptive adversary. The stack has one deterministic rule layer and four LLM judges, three of them re-collected with the served model recorded on every call. We read each stack as a number of multiplication-equivalent layers, n_mult, with its floor under perfect coupling. Under the STRICT miss definition (escalation to a human scored as not stopped), any two judges compose to about 1.2 to 1.4 layers (φ median +0.430, 6 of 6 pairs significant, floors 1.02 to 1.17). The rule layer plus one judge composes to 1.86 to 2.09 layers (φ median +0.014, 0 of 4 significant, floors 1.01 to 1.09). Under PRIMARY (escalation scored as caught) the bands are 1.21 to 1.57 and 1.80 to 2.13. Intervals separate on the pooled data, point estimates split on each corpus, and a third-vendor judge lands in the judge band. Solo accuracy does not predict what a layer adds: a cloud rule pack lowers the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% and adds no new joint coverage. The difficulty share of judge coupling is not identifiable: 31.8% to 61.8% depending on the probe and the miss definition. One judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50 of 112 batches, concentrated on the external corpus. That event overturned a pre-declared analysis rule, and the scoring of review verdicts reversed five conclusions. We report both.

AI.tldr: Stacked runtime gates for agent tool calls do not multiply as assumed: two LLM judges compose to only ~1.2-1.4 multiplication-equivalent layers, while a rule layer plus one judge reaches ~1.86-2.09, and solo accuracy fails to predict marginal joint coverage.
AI.motivation: Runtime gates for agent tool calls are typically stacked on the assumption that their error rates multiply, so adding layers is expected to compound reliability. The paper tests whether that multiplicative assumption holds empirically, and whether a layer's marginal contribution can be inferred from its standalone accuracy.
AI.method: Evaluation on 1,119 labelled agent actions from three corpora, without an adaptive adversary. The stack comprises one deterministic rule layer and four LLM judges, three re-collected with the served model recorded per call. Each stack is summarized as multiplication-equivalent layers, n_mult, with its floor under perfect coupling. Two miss definitions are used: STRICT (human escalation scored as not stopped) and PRIMARY (escalation scored as caught). Coupling is probed via pairwise φ, with per-pair significance tests and pooled/corpus-level intervals.
AI.result: Under STRICT, any two judges compose to ~1.2-1.4 layers (φ median +0.430; 6/6 pairs significant; floors 1.02-1.17); rule+one judge composes to 1.86-2.09 layers (φ median +0.014; 0/4 significant; floors 1.01-1.09). Under PRIMARY the bands are 1.21-1.57 and 1.80-2.13. Intervals separate on pooled data, point estimates split per corpus, and a third-vendor judge falls in the judge band. A cloud rule pack cuts the rule layer's solo miss rate by 20% yet adds no new joint coverage. The difficulty share of judge coupling is unidentifiable (31.8%-61.8% depending on probe and definition). One judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50/112 batches, concentrated on the external corpus, overturning a pre-declared analysis rule; rescoring review verdicts reversed five conclusions.
AI.conclusion: The multiplicative-error assumption behind stacked runtime gates does not hold: judge-judge and rule-judge stacks behave very differently, and solo accuracy does not predict marginal joint coverage. Reported effects are sensitive to miss definition, probe, and corpus, with the difficulty share of coupling not identifiable, and served-model drift can invalidate pre-declared analysis rules and reverse conclusions; both analyses are reported.

title: ProCut: Probabilistic Cutting Topology for Autonomous Electrosurgical Tissue Dissection
summary: Accurately modeling and tracking the deformation of soft tissue is critical for a wide range of interventional and surgical procedures. However, current methods struggle in scenarios involving topological changes, such as cutting and dissection, due to the inherent non-linearity and discontinuity introduced by explicit changes in connectivity. In this work, we present a novel, fully differentiable framework that enables robust estimation and modeling of topological changes during deformable tracking. Our method introduces a continuous, sigmoid-based formulation to smooth the otherwise discrete event of tissue cutting, making it amenable to gradient-based optimization within a differentiable Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) simulation. To account for uncertainty and improve robustness in the presence of noisy visual data, we incorporate Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) for particle-based probabilistic inference, generating multiple hypotheses for topological state estimation. Building on this foundation, we develop an autonomous dissection algorithm for thin-shell tissues that leverages topological updates to guide closed-loop cutting trajectory control. We evaluate our approach in both simulated and real-world electrosurgical environments, demonstrating significant improvements in topological estimation accuracy and dissection precision over existing methods. Our results highlight the potential of this framework to advance automation in soft-tissue surgical procedures by enabling reliable perception and control in the presence of complex structural changes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully differentiable framework for modeling and tracking topological changes (cutting/dissection) in soft tissue deformation, using a sigmoid-based smoothing of discrete cutting events within differentiable Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) and Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) for probabilistic inference, enabling autonomous dissection of thin-shell tissues.
AI.motivation: Accurate modeling and tracking of soft tissue deformation is critical for interventional and surgical procedures, but current methods fail in scenarios involving topological changes such as cutting and dissection. These changes introduce inherent non-linearity and discontinuity from explicit connectivity alterations, making estimation and tracking difficult.
AI.method: The authors propose a fully differentiable framework with three key components: (1) a continuous, sigmoid-based formulation that smooths the discrete event of tissue cutting, rendering it amenable to gradient-based optimization within a differentiable Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) simulation; (2) incorporation of Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) for particle-based probabilistic inference, generating multiple hypotheses for topological state estimation to handle uncertainty and noisy visual data; (3) an autonomous dissection algorithm for thin-shell tissues that leverages topological updates to guide closed-loop cutting trajectory control.
AI.result: Evaluation in both simulated and real-world electrosurgical environments shows significant improvements in topological estimation accuracy and dissection precision over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates potential to advance automation in soft-tissue surgical procedures by enabling reliable perception and control under complex structural changes, offering robust estimation and modeling of topological changes during deformable tracking.

title: MemCo: Memory-Centric Collaboration for Generalizing LLM Agents to Unseen Environments
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in interactive environments, where they need to make sequential decisions through observation, action, and feedback. Although memory can help agents reuse experience, existing work designs memory in isolation, where collecting enough trajectories to populate it is expensive. Existing shared-memory approaches mitigate isolated experience by pooling episodic memories across tasks and environments. However, retrieving shared memory is challenged by the granularity, where retrieved memories can be either too specific to preserve current grounding or too coarse to support the next action. In this work, we propose MemCo, a memory-centric collaboration framework for generalizing LLM agents to unseen interactive environments. It maintains complementary local and global memory spaces, preserving environment-specific details locally while promoting transferable workflows induced from local trajectories to global memory. During online interaction, MemCo routes relevant local and global memories in terms of the agent's current state and decision phase, enabling agents to reuse the experience of other agents without blindly transferring environment-specific details. Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that MemCo improves task success and reduces redundant exploration compared with isolate-memory and shared-memory baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/SYannL/nvdamas.

AI.tldr: MemCo is a memory-centric collaboration framework that maintains complementary local and global memory spaces to generalize LLM agents to unseen interactive environments, improving task success and reducing redundant exploration.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate in interactive environments requiring sequential decisions via observation, action, and feedback. While memory helps reuse experience, existing designs build memory in isolation, making trajectory collection expensive. Shared-memory approaches pool episodic memories across tasks/environments but suffer from a granularity problem: retrieved memories are either too specific to preserve grounding or too coarse to support the next action.
AI.method: MemCo is a memory-centric collaboration framework. It maintains complementary local and global memory spaces: local memory preserves environment-specific details, while global memory promotes transferable workflows induced from local trajectories. During online interaction, MemCo routes relevant local and global memories based on the agent's current state and decision phase, enabling experience reuse without blindly transferring environment-specific details.
AI.result: Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that MemCo improves task success and reduces redundant exploration compared with isolate-memory and shared-memory baselines.
AI.conclusion: MemCo addresses the granularity challenge in shared memory by combining local and global memory with state- and phase-aware routing, effectively generalizing LLM agents to unseen interactive environments.

title: ReDex: Repairing Sim-to-Real Dexterous Policies by Finger-Level Compliant Interaction
summary: Dexterous manipulation policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world because of errors in contact timing and force regulation. Yet these policies can retain useful multi-finger coordination for task progression. We propose ReDex, a framework for adapting a simulation-trained base policy to the real world by correcting local contact failures and incorporating tactile feedback. Starting from a proprioception-only base policy, ReDex allows a human operator to physically correct contact failures at selected fingers under compliant control during real-world rollouts, while the frozen base policy continues to control the remaining fingers. These rollouts combine base policy execution, human-corrected finger motion, and fingertip force observations. We reconstruct force-informed targets from these rollouts to train a standalone force-conditioned policy via behavior cloning. This design reduces human correction effort, enables learning of contact regulation from real-world interaction, and introduces force feedback into a proprioception-only policy without tactile simulation or complex full-hand teleoperation. We evaluate ReDex on two challenging, contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks on real hardware. Compared with sim-to-real transferred base policies, ReDex increases Object Flipping success rate from 14\% to 86\% across two objects and average Screwdriver Rotation progress from 26.0% to 95.3% across three objects.

AI.tldr: ReDex adapts a simulation-trained, proprioception-only dexterous policy to real hardware by letting a human correct local fingertip contact failures under compliant control while the frozen base policy drives remaining fingers, then behavior-clones a force-conditioned policy from these rollouts.
AI.motivation: Sim-to-real transfer of dexterous manipulation fails largely due to errors in contact timing and force regulation, though the base policies still encode useful multi-finger coordination. Existing fixes typically require tactile simulation or complex full-hand teleoperation, which is costly and hard to scale.
AI.method: Start from a proprioception-only base policy trained in simulation. During real-world rollouts, a human operator physically corrects contact failures at selected fingers under compliant control while the frozen base policy controls the remaining fingers. Rollouts mix base policy execution, human-corrected finger motion, and fingertip force observations. Force-informed targets are reconstructed from these rollouts, and a standalone force-conditioned policy is trained via behavior cloning.
AI.result: On two contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks on real hardware, ReDex raises Object Flipping success from 14% to 86% across two objects and average Screwdriver Rotation progress from 26.0% to 95.3% across three objects, versus sim-to-real transferred base policies.
AI.conclusion: Local, human-corrected contact failures combined with reconstructed force targets are sufficient to learn real-world contact regulation. This reduces human correction effort, injects force feedback into a proprioception-only policy without tactile simulation or full-hand teleoperation, and yields large gains over direct sim-to-real transfer.

title: Defense-in-Depth for LLMs: Evaluating Memory Gates Against Activation-Induced and Memory-Induced Sycophancy
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS (IAB, RTCA, AIWILD, and CL4FM)
summary: Long-term memory allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain personalized context across interactions, but retrieved user history can induce memory-induced sycophancy, causing models to favor stored user beliefs over objective evidence. Existing defenses primarily operate on retrieved context and are rarely evaluated jointly with internal behavioral bias. We introduce a $2 \times 2$ defense-in-depth framework separating internal activation steering from external memory handling. We extract sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and evaluate four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench (answers for all 1,550 items; defense conditions judged on a fixed 250-item subsample), with three LLM judges. Three of the five configurations are new (rewriting every memory, a Router Gate that keeps, rewrites, or drops each memory, and dropping all memory); the other two are MemSyco's baselines. Selective Router Gate filtering preserves substantially more of MemSyco's average accuracy than complete memory removal, and this separation persists when the models are steered toward sycophancy. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering ($α= -1.5$) lowers judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while average accuracy moves from 43.99% to 43.31%; this reduction has the same direction under all three judges but is not statistically significant (paired $p = 0.08$ to $0.63$ on 149 items). External memory filtering is the part of the design that holds up; our data do not show that inverse steering adds to it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 2x2 defense-in-depth framework combining internal activation steering and external memory handling to mitigate memory-induced sycophancy in LLMs, finding that external memory filtering (particularly selective Router Gate) is the robust component while inverse steering does not demonstrably add benefit.
AI.motivation: Long-term memory enables personalized LLM interactions, but retrieved user history can trigger memory-induced sycophancy, where models prioritize stored user beliefs over objective evidence. Existing defenses focus mainly on retrieved context and are seldom evaluated alongside internal behavioral bias.
AI.method: A 2x2 defense-in-depth framework separating internal activation steering from external memory handling. Sycophancy steering directions are extracted from 100 paired prompts. Four open-weight models are evaluated across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench (all 1,550 items answered; defense conditions judged on a fixed 250-item subsample), using three LLM judges. Five configurations: two MemSyco baselines plus three new ones (rewriting every memory, a Router Gate that keeps/rewrites/drops each memory, and dropping all memory).
AI.result: Selective Router Gate filtering retains substantially more of MemSyco's average accuracy than complete memory removal, and this separation persists under sycophancy steering. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering (α = -1.5) reduces judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while accuracy shifts from 43.99% to 43.31%; the reduction is directionally consistent across all three judges but not statistically significant (paired p = 0.08 to 0.63 on 149 items).
AI.conclusion: External memory filtering is the component of the design that holds up. The data do not show that inverse steering adds to it, indicating internal activation steering provides no demonstrated complementary benefit to memory filtering in this setting.

title: Task-Space Imitation Guidance for Efficient Reinforcement Learning
summary: We introduce Task-Space Imitation Guidance for Efficient Reinforcement Learning (TIGER), a reward-construction and pretraining framework for sparse-reward tabletop robotic manipulation. TIGER treats an action-chunked imitation policy not as an executable controller or action prior, but as a local task-space progress estimator: predicted action chunks are converted, using controller-aware action-to-motion mapping, into short-horizon end-effector references, and the RL agent receives dense progress rewards toward these references while the sparse environment reward remains the dominant objective. During pretraining, TIGER uses imitation-guided look-ahead signals to relax conservative value penalties for actions predicted to make task-space progress, reducing off-manifold exploration during early online RL. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, TIGER improves early sample efficiency and reduces measured safety violations while matching or improving final success rates relative to prior RL and IL-RL baselines on the evaluated tasks.

AI.tldr: TIGER is a reward-construction and pretraining framework that uses an action-chunked imitation policy as a task-space progress estimator rather than a controller, providing dense progress rewards and relaxed conservative value penalties for sparse-reward robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Sparse-reward tabletop robotic manipulation is hard for RL due to limited reward signal and inefficient, unsafe early exploration. Existing IL-RL approaches typically use imitation policies as controllers or action priors, which may constrain or misguide the RL agent.
AI.method: TIGER treats an action-chunked imitation policy as a local task-space progress estimator. Predicted action chunks are mapped via controller-aware action-to-motion mapping into short-horizon end-effector references, from which dense progress rewards are derived while the sparse environment reward remains dominant. During pretraining, imitation-guided look-ahead signals relax conservative value penalties for actions predicted to yield task-space progress, reducing off-manifold exploration in early online RL.
AI.result: In simulation and real-robot experiments, TIGER improves early sample efficiency and reduces measured safety violations while matching or improving final success rates compared with prior RL and IL-RL baselines on the evaluated tasks.
AI.conclusion: Repurposing an imitation policy as a task-space progress estimator, rather than a controller or action prior, yields denser guidance and safer, more sample-efficient RL for sparse-reward robotic manipulation without sacrificing final success rates.

title: 2d-fet-bench: from spatial reasoning to fet design on flakes
summary: Field-effect transistor (FET) layouts on exfoliated two-dimensional flakes are typically drawn by hand for each flake, placing contacts and gates to match its position and outline in optical micrographs. To our knowledge, no executable benchmark tests whether language-model agents can perform this flake-specific construction reliably. We introduce 2D-FET-Bench V2, a benchmark of 128 layout tasks built from microscopy-derived flake contours, including hole-containing flakes and multi-flake tasks. Each task supplies a textual device specification and contour coordinates. An agent generates typed polygon and path operations rendered to GDSII. A deterministic verifier checks geometric and structural requirements, and a separate integrity check verifies that the supplied contours remain unchanged. Scripted reference layouts pass all 128 tasks, showing that every task is solvable. We evaluate six models and seven workflow and scaffold variants of GPT5.6-Luna, with five attempts per task. The best-performing configuration in the six-model panel, GPT5.6-Luna with ReAct-3, passes 62.3% of attempts and solves 80.5% of tasks at least once (coverage) and 43.8% in all five attempts (consistency). ReAct-3 exceeds the one-pass Plan-and-Execute by 27.0 pass@1 points at 2.46 times the tokens. An expert audit of one sampled verifier-passing layout per covered task, across five ReAct-3 configurations, accepts 56.4% to 63.5% of them. The benchmark evaluates geometric and structural FET layout construction.

AI.tldr: 2D-FET-Bench V2 is a new 128-task benchmark for testing whether language-model agents can construct field-effect transistor layouts on exfoliated 2D flakes from microscopy-derived contours, using GDSII output and deterministic geometric verification.
AI.motivation: FET layouts on exfoliated 2D flakes are normally drawn by hand for each individual flake, placing contacts and gates to match its position and outline. No executable benchmark previously tested whether language-model agents can perform this flake-specific construction reliably.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 128 layout tasks built from microscopy-derived flake contours, including hole-containing and multi-flake tasks. Each task provides a textual device specification and contour coordinates; an agent emits typed polygon and path operations rendered to GDSII. A deterministic verifier checks geometric and structural requirements, and a separate integrity check confirms supplied contours remain unchanged. Scripted reference layouts validate solvability. Six models and seven workflow/scaffold variants of GPT5.6-Luna are evaluated with five attempts per task.
AI.result: Scripted reference layouts pass all 128 tasks. The best configuration, GPT5.6-Luna with ReAct-3, passes 62.3% of attempts, achieves 80.5% task coverage, and 43.8% consistency (all five attempts). ReAct-3 exceeds one-pass Plan-and-Execute by 27.0 pass@1 points at 2.46x token cost. An expert audit of one sampled verifier-passing layout per covered task, across five ReAct-3 configurations, accepts 56.4%-63.5%.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reliably evaluates geometric and structural FET layout construction by language-model agents, showing that reference layouts are fully solvable while current agent performance remains partial, with meaningful gaps between attempt-level success, coverage, and consistency.

title: Seeing the Invisible: Physics-Guided Visual Prompting for Temperature- and Radiation-Aware VLA Navigation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a major paradigm for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN). However, in safety-critical facilities, invisible risks such as radiation or temperature spikes cannot be detected by an RGB camera, and handling each risk is expensive, requiring a new encoder, new data, and model retraining. We propose Physics-Guided Visual Prompting (PG-VP), a plug-and-play multimodal perception module that instead reuses what a frozen VLA model already does well: avoiding visible obstacles. Given a proximal radiation or thermal source, PG-VP performs a physics-guided risk assessment to determine the avoidance direction and overlays a corresponding virtual obstacle that moves across consecutive frames (Dynamic Visual Prompting). The navigation policy then naturally detours around this invisible hazard. The identical virtual obstacle is used regardless of hazard type, so the visual prompting pattern remains fixed as sensors are added. When no hazard is detected, nothing is rendered, and the policy behaves exactly as it would without PG-VP. We evaluate PG-VP on OmniNav using the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, where it guides the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9% and 83.2% of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate. We further test it with distinct scenarios on a real robot in the presence of actual thermal and radiation sources, all without any retraining. The real test shows that PG-VP effectively avoids these invisible hazards, improving worst-10% average trajectory safety by 63.45% and 32.59% against thermal and radiation sources, respectively.

AI.tldr: PG-VP is a plug-and-play module that overlays a moving "virtual obstacle" in the front of a frozen VLA navigation model to steer it away from invisible hazards (radiation, heat) without retraining, trading a few points of success rate for large safety gains.
AI.motivation: In safety-critical facilities, hazards such as radiation or temperature spikes are invisible to RGB cameras. Standard VLA models therefore cannot perceive them, and building dedicated perception pipelines is costly: each new risk type requires a new encoder, new data, and model retraining.
AI.method: Physics-Guided Visual Prompting (PG-VP) reuses the frozen VLA model's existing obstacle-avoidance behavior. From a proximal radiation/thermal source, it computes a physics-guided risk assessment that determines the avoidance direction, then overlays a corresponding virtual obstacle moving across consecutive frames (Dynamic Visual Prompting). The policy then detours around the hazard. The same virtual-obstacle pattern is used for every hazard type, so the prompting scheme stays fixed as sensors are added; when no hazard is detected, nothing is rendered and the policy is unchanged.
AI.result: On OmniNav with the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, PG-VP steers the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9% and 83.2% of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate. Real-robot tests with actual thermal and radiation sources, without any retraining, improve worst-10% average trajectory safety by 63.45% (thermal) and 32.59% (radiation).
AI.conclusion: Invisible, safety-critical hazards can be handled by prompting a frozen VLA navigator rather than retraining it, yielding strong worst-case safety improvements across simulation and real hardware with a modest success-rate trade-off.

title: Adaptive Gait Biofeedback With Participant-Held-Out Modeling and Participant-Specific Updating in Chronic Ankle Instability
comment: 28 pages (14-page main manuscript and 14-page supplementary material), 5 main figures
summary: Adaptive gait biofeedback may support repeated practice in chronic ankle instability, but its evaluation must address model performance and human response. We evaluated a temporal convolutional classifier on protocol-defined, angle-derived GOOD/BAD gait-cycle labels using participant-held-out leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation in 20 participants. Seven participants in the adaptive-intervention group completed nine sessions over three weeks, with one motion-capture recording analyzed per session. Models updated after failed sessions were compared offline with their parent models on the same-session validation subset used for candidate selection and the first subsequent adaptive-session recording. Frontal-plane ankle angle was compared between the adaptive group and 10 sequentially enrolled controls at Baseline, Post, and 7-day Retention. Across 20 held-out folds, mean fold-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.948, sensitivity for angle-threshold-exceeding BAD cycles was 0.941, and specificity for angle-threshold-meeting GOOD cycles was 0.366. Mean BAD-class F1 was higher in candidate models by 0.187 on the same-session subset and 0.118 on the first subsequent recording. At Post, the adaptive group had a baseline-adjusted frontal-plane ankle angle 5.168 degrees lower than controls (95% confidence interval, 1.766-8.569 degrees lower); the Retention contrast was uncertain. These findings characterize population-model discrimination and offline participant-specific updating during repeated biofeedback use, alongside a nonrandomized Post frontal-plane ankle angle association. They do not establish independent clinical gait classification or a causal benefit of updating.

AI.tldr: A temporal convolutional classifier distinguished GOOD/BAD gait cycles in chronic ankle instability with high AUROC (0.948) using leave-one-subject-out validation (n=20). Offline participant-specific model updating improved BAD-class F1 across sessions. A nonrandomized adaptive-biofeedback group (n=7) showed a baseline-adjusted frontal-plane ankle angle 5.168 degrees lower than controls at Post, with uncertain Retention effects.
AI.motivation: Adaptive gait biofeedback may support repeated practice in chronic ankle instability, but its evaluation must jointly address model performance and human response, motivating combined assessment of classifier generalization and intervention-related biomechanical change.
AI.method: Temporal convolutional classifier trained on protocol-defined, angle-derived GOOD/BAD gait-cycle labels, evaluated by participant-held-out leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation in 20 participants. Seven adaptive-intervention participants completed nine sessions over three weeks with one motion-capture recording per session. Models updated after failed sessions were compared offline with parent models on the same-session validation subset and the first subsequent adaptive-session recording. Frontal-plane ankle angle was compared between the adaptive group and 10 sequentially enrolled controls at Baseline, Post, and 7-day Retention.
AI.result: Mean fold-level AUROC was 0.948; sensitivity for angle-threshold-exceeding BAD cycles was 0.941; specificity for angle-threshold-meeting GOOD cycles was 0.366. Mean BAD-class F1 was higher in candidate models by 0.187 on the same-session subset and 0.118 on the first subsequent recording. At Post, the adaptive group had a baseline-adjusted frontal-plane ankle angle 5.168 degrees lower than controls (95% CI, 1.766-8.569 degrees lower); the Retention contrast was uncertain.
AI.conclusion: These findings characterize population-model discrimination and offline participant-specific updating during repeated biofeedback use, alongside a nonrandomized Post frontal-plane ankle angle association. They do not establish independent clinical gait classification or a causal benefit of updating.

title: OpenSplatGraph: From Dense Semantic Maps to Structured Scene Graphs for Open-Vocabulary Robot Perception
summary: Dense 3D mapping with semantic understanding is essential for robotic perception in complex environments. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting-based mapping approaches enable high-fidelity geometry and efficient open-vocabulary perception, but typically represent semantics as unstructured feature fields that limit object-centric reasoning. In contrast, 3D scene graphs explicitly model objects and their relationships for structured reasoning, but are commonly constructed from sparse geometric representations that do not fully exploit dense semantic maps. In this work, we present OpenSplatGraph, a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from an online Gaussian-based open-vocabulary semantic map. The proposed framework augments the dense semantic map with a reliability-aware semantic field that maintains lightweight observation statistics for confidence-aware, query-conditioned object extraction. Extracted object instances are associated with persistent graph nodes, allowing object attributes and relationships to be incrementally updated across observations and queries. By tightly coupling dense semantic mapping with persistent object-centric representations, our framework supports both language-guided object grounding and structured relational reasoning while preserving the geometric fidelity of Gaussian-based mapping. Comprehensive evaluations on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments demonstrate that OpenSplatGraph achieves competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks. Project page: https://csiro-robotics.github.io/OpenSplatGraph.

AI.tldr: OpenSplatGraph is a unified framework that builds persistent 3D scene graphs directly from an online Gaussian-based open-vocabulary semantic map, enabling structured object-centric reasoning while retaining dense geometric fidelity.
AI.motivation: Dense 3D semantic mapping is vital for robotic perception, yet current 3D Gaussian Splatting approaches encode semantics as unstructured feature fields that hinder object-centric reasoning, whereas 3D scene graphs offer structured reasoning but are typically built from sparse geometry that underuses dense semantic maps.
AI.method: The framework augments the dense semantic map with a reliability-aware semantic field that keeps lightweight observation statistics for confidence-aware, query-conditioned object extraction. Extracted instances are linked to persistent graph nodes so that attributes and relationships are incrementally updated across observations and queries, tightly coupling dense mapping with persistent object-centric representations.
AI.result: Evaluations on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments show competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks.
AI.conclusion: OpenSplatGraph supports both language-guided object grounding and structured relational reasoning while preserving the geometric fidelity of Gaussian-based mapping, bridging dense open-vocabulary mapping and persistent scene graphs.

title: When Does AI Supervision Help? A Role-Aware Study of Network Fraud Decision Management with Blockchain Auditability
summary: When does a second artificial intelligence (AI) component improve a primary network-fraud decision rather than add operational burden? We study this question through a role-aware Decider-Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations that combine centralised machine learning, a Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and Base or Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) large language model variants. The analysis compares primary-only and supervised decisions using non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, conditional calibration, traffic-mix and Review-capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls. The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, leaving the non-hard population as the main AI decision setting. Conditional validation calibration does not produce a consistently transferable supervisory advantage on deployment replay. DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive supervised configuration, but it still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, while exposing a pre-finalisation single-write limitation. The results show that the value of AI supervision depends on role assignment, calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than on the presence of a second model alone.

AI.tldr: A role-aware Decider-Supervisor framework shows a second AI component improves primary network-fraud decisions only under specific role assignments, calibration, traffic mixes, and lifecycle controls—not merely by being added.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses when a second AI component improves a primary network-fraud decision versus adding operational burden. It questions whether AI supervision value comes from the presence of a second model alone or from configuration and deployment factors.
AI.method: The study uses a role-aware Decider-Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations combining centralised ML, a FedAvg-trained federated meta-model, and Base or QLoRA LLM variants. It compares primary-only and supervised decisions using non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, conditional calibration, traffic-mix and Review-capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls.
AI.result: The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, leaving the non-hard population as the main AI decision setting. Conditional validation calibration does not yield a consistently transferable supervisory advantage. DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive supervised configuration but still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, but expose a pre-finalisation single-write limitation.
AI.conclusion: The value of AI supervision depends on role assignment, calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than on the presence of a second model alone.

title: BiGym 2.0: Benchmarking Learned and Agent-Developed Policies for Humanoid Household Manipulation
summary: Humanoid household manipulation requires the arms to act while the body balances, steps and changes posture. We present BiGym 2.0, an adaptation of BiGym for the Unitree G1 across 20 household tasks using a unified whole-body controller for demonstration and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronised multi-camera views and full-body execution records. We benchmark vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents given the interaction budget of online reinforcement learning. With the same onboard views, proprioception and whole-body controller for every method, vision-language-action fine-tuning has the highest nine-task mean, and agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven reinforcement learning baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains open, $π_{0.5}$ stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is hard for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and coding agents. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at https://github.com/swirl-uk/BiGym2.

AI.tldr: BiGym 2.0 adapts BiGym to the Unitree G1 humanoid, offering 20 household tasks with a unified whole-body controller, 60 human VR demonstrations per task, and a benchmark comparing VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven RL, and coding agents.
AI.motivation: Humanoid household manipulation requires arms to act while the body balances, steps, and changes posture, creating a whole-body control challenge that existing benchmarks for fixed-base or wheeled platforms do not adequately address.
AI.method: The authors build BiGym 2.0 on the Unitree G1 with 20 household tasks, using a unified whole-body controller for both demonstration collection and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronized multi-camera views and full-body execution records. They benchmark four paradigms: vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents under an online RL interaction budget, keeping onboard views, proprioception, and the whole-body controller identical across methods.
AI.result: VLA fine-tuning achieves the highest nine-task mean. Agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven RL baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains unsolved, π0.5 stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is difficult for imitation learning, demo-driven RL, and coding agents.
AI.conclusion: Whole-body humanoid household manipulation remains challenging, with VLA fine-tuning and coding agents showing the strongest overall performance while several tasks (cross-workspace stacking, pick-box for π0.5, multi-object transport) stay open. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced.

title: Auditable Claims about AI Agents
summary: Organizations make claims about their AI agents: a person approves every external email, every action is logged, an evaluation shows the agent is safe to deploy. Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to allow the automatic recording of events but does not say which records settle a given claim. The position is one sentence: to be checked, a claim about an agent must first name its policy, its scope, the records that would settle it, and who writes them. Adapting the preconditions of an assurance engagement, we call a claim auditable when these elements and a decision rule are fixed before any verdict and the records are obtainable. This extends the Policy Checkability dimension of our Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims. Agents add three conditions: coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity. Under an explicit model, we prove that support is impossible without each wherever its hypotheses hold. A claim-check table applies the method to six common claims, anchored in current NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts. A worked case follows one claim through five evidence states. We close with a practice box and steps for operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters.

AI.tldr: To be checkable, a claim about an AI agent must first name its policy, its scope, the records that would settle it, and who writes those records. Adapting assurance-engagement preconditions, the authors define a claim as "auditable" when these elements plus a decision rule are fixed before any verdict and the records are obtainable, extending the Policy Checkability dimension of their Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims.
AI.motivation: Organizations make claims about AI agents (e.g., every email is human-approved, every action is logged, evaluations show safe deployment), but Article 12 of the EU AI Act only mandates automatic event recording for high-risk systems and does not specify which records settle a given claim. A gap exists between the claims made and the evidence required to verify them, motivating a formal account of claim checkability.
AI.method: The authors adapt the preconditions of an assurance engagement to define auditable claims, extending the Policy Checkability dimension of their Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims. They identify three additional agent-specific conditions—coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity—and, under an explicit model, prove that support is impossible without each condition wherever its hypotheses hold. They apply the method via a claim-check table covering six common claims anchored in current NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts, along with a worked case tracing one claim through five evidence states.
AI.result: The paper establishes formal conditions under which a claim about an AI agent is auditable, proves necessity of the three agent-specific conditions, and demonstrates applicability through a six-claim check table grounded in current standards drafts and a worked case spanning five evidence states.
AI.conclusion: Claim checkability requires pre-fixing an agent's policy, scope, settling records, record authors, and decision rule before any verdict. The work offers a practical framing and procedural steps for operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters seeking to make agent claims auditable.

title: The Robot Is Not Its Description: GaugeBench for Representation Robustness in Morphology-Aware Policies
summary: A robot description does more than specify a physical mechanism: it also encodes arbitrary conventions, such as joint-axis direction, joint-angle zero, and the order and names of links and joints. Morphology-aware policies consume interfaces built from these descriptions, yet cross-embodiment evaluation typically changes the robot while keeping those conventions fixed. This leaves a simple question unanswered: does behavior survive when the robot stays fixed but its description changes? GaugeBench isolates this case by rewriting a fixed mechanism under physically equivalent conventions, verifying that its physics and policy interface are preserved, and then evaluating the same policy weights. The result is stark: three MetaMorph policies score 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots, but only 51.6 when those same robots are equivalently re-described, while 98 genuinely held-out robots score 1489.6. A new description can therefore be more damaging than a new robot. Tracing the failure reveals that axis reversal alone reproduces the collapse, joint-angle zero changes are nearly harmless, and reordering lies between them; moreover, changing joint-state and torque coordinates alone is sufficient to cause the failure, while changing description-derived features alone is not. The same phenomenon appears in ModuMorph and an unrelated PyBullet framework. Yet it is not irreversible: exact two-description transport restores the original controller, and training across equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6% to 80.6%. Together, these results separate mechanism robustness from representation robustness and show that cross-embodiment evaluation should test both.

AI.tldr: GaugeBench shows that physically equivalent rewrites of a robot's description can collapse a morphology-aware policy far more than swapping in a new robot, revealing that representation robustness is distinct from mechanism robustness.
AI.motivation: Robot descriptions encode arbitrary conventions (joint-axis direction, joint-angle zero, link/joint order and names) beyond physical mechanism. Cross-embodiment evaluation typically varies the robot while fixing these conventions, leaving open whether behavior survives when the mechanism is fixed but its description changes.
AI.method: GaugeBench rewrites a fixed mechanism under physically equivalent conventions, verifies that physics and the policy interface are preserved, and then evaluates the same policy weights. Ablations isolate which convention changes cause failure, and the phenomenon is checked in ModuMorph and an unrelated PyBullet framework. Mitigations include exact two-description transport and training across equivalent axis conventions.
AI.result: Three MetaMorph policies score 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots, but only 51.6 when the same robots are equivalently re-described, versus 1489.6 on 98 genuinely held-out robots. Axis reversal alone reproduces the collapse; joint-angle zero changes are nearly harmless; reordering lies between. Changing joint-state and torque coordinates alone suffices to cause failure, while changing description-derived features alone does not. Exact two-description transport restores the original controller, and training across equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6% to 80.6%.
AI.conclusion: A new description can be more damaging than a new robot. Mechanism robustness and representation robustness are separable properties, and cross-embodiment evaluation should test both.

title: COMPASS: Finding Where Reasoning Lives in Language Models
summary: Explicitly eliciting reasoning substantially improves LLM performance. Existing approaches require a predefined characterization of reasoning, whether through CoT prompt design, contrastive CoT directions, or via SAE derived reasoning features. For mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, we show that a much simpler signal suffices, which is the correctness of the model's own direct answer attempts. This signal yields a latent direction that elicits reasoning. This direction is decodable within the activations of most attention heads, but only a small subset of them can be effectively intervened. We introduce COMPASS, an inference-time steering method that identifies these heads using a logit-space attribution score and steers their activations along the correctness direction, requiring only per-head activation statistics. Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, COMPASS outperforms the activation-steering baselines we compare against, improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average, and approaches CoT accuracy with 20-70\% fewer generated tokens. Interventions transfer without re-fitting to unseen benchmarks, and ablations show that both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces COMPASS, an inference-time activation steering method that elicits reasoning by using the correctness of a model's own direct answer as a simple signal, identifying a small subset of attention heads via logit-space attribution and steering them along a correctness direction.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to elicit reasoning require a predefined characterization of reasoning, such as CoT prompt design, contrastive CoT directions, or SAE-derived reasoning features. For math reasoning with verifiable answers, this complexity may be unnecessary, motivating a simpler signal.
AI.method: COMPASS uses the correctness of the model's own direct answer attempts as the signal, yielding a latent correctness direction that elicits reasoning. This direction is decodable in most attention heads, but only a small subset supports effective intervention. COMPASS identifies these heads via a logit-space attribution score and steers their activations along the correctness direction, requiring only per-head activation statistics.
AI.result: Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, COMPASS outperforms activation-steering baselines, improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average, and approaches CoT accuracy with 20-70% fewer generated tokens. Interventions transfer to unseen benchmarks without re-fitting.
AI.conclusion: Both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads, showing a simple correctness signal suffices to elicit reasoning.

title: Modeling Latent Disturbances for Robust Decision-Making in World Models
summary: In this paper, we study robust decision-making in the latent space of world models (WMs). Robust optimization is a mathematical framework where, given explicitly specified dynamics and physically meaningful disturbances, a robot can select actions that remain effective even under worst-case disturbances. However, applying this principle to the learned latent space of WMs introduces a fundamental challenge: because WMs have fully learned state spaces and dynamics inferred from high-dimensional observations, it is unclear how to define latent-space disturbances that faithfully represent uncertainty in the underlying system. Our key idea is to model a latent-space disturbance as a perturbation to the learned latent dynamics that induces pessimistic but plausible transitions. Specifically, we construct a set of plausible latent dynamics by combining a dynamics-aware similarity metric that captures plausible transitions with out-of-distribution detection that excludes implausible latent states. We calibrate this uncertainty set over latent dynamics using conformal prediction, ensuring that WM imaginations induced by the latent disturbance remain plausible without becoming overly pessimistic. We then jointly optimize robust robot actions and the worst-case latent disturbances through game-theoretic optimization. We leverage this latent-space robust optimization to robustify policy steering, considering two paradigms: latent safety filtering and sample-and-verify steering of a generative control policy. Our controlled simulation experiments show that our latent disturbance enables robust decision-making directly in WM latent spaces, and hardware experiments with a Franka manipulator show that modeling latent disturbances enables robust policy steering, reducing failures by 70% in safety filtering and 54% in sampling-based policy steering. Project website: https://junwon.me/LatentDisturbance/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for robust decision-making directly in the latent space of world models by modeling latent disturbances as perturbations to learned latent dynamics that induce pessimistic but plausible transitions, calibrated via conformal prediction and optimized through game-theoretic robust optimization.
AI.motivation: Robust optimization typically requires explicitly specified dynamics and physically meaningful disturbances. Applying it to the learned latent spaces of world models is challenging because these spaces and dynamics are inferred from high-dimensional observations, making it unclear how to define latent-space disturbances that faithfully represent real system uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors model a latent-space disturbance as a perturbation to the learned latent dynamics that induces pessimistic yet plausible transitions. They construct a set of plausible latent dynamics using a dynamics-aware similarity metric (capturing plausible transitions) combined with out-of-distribution detection (excluding implausible latent states). The uncertainty set over latent dynamics is calibrated using conformal prediction to keep WM imaginations plausible without excessive pessimism. Robust actions and worst-case latent disturbances are then jointly optimized via game-theoretic optimization, and this latent-space robust optimization is applied to robustify policy steering via two paradigms: latent safety filtering and sample-and-verify steering of a generative control policy.
AI.result: Controlled simulation experiments show that the latent disturbance enables robust decision-making directly in WM latent spaces. Hardware experiments with a Franka manipulator demonstrate that modeling latent disturbances enables robust policy steering, reducing failures by 70% in safety filtering and 54% in sampling-based policy steering.
AI.conclusion: Modeling latent-space disturbances as calibrated perturbations to learned latent dynamics provides an effective means of achieving robust decision-making and robust policy steering within world model latent spaces, validated in both simulation and real-world manipulator experiments.

title: PsyCIDRA: A Dual-Agent Framework for Psychiatric Interviewing and Diagnostic Reasoning
summary: Large language models show promise in clinical reasoning, but psychiatric interviewing requires guiding an evolving conversation. Their ability to carry out this interactive assessment remains less studied. We present PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework linking free-form psychiatric interviewing with diagnostic reasoning for expert review. Its interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry. Its diagnostic reasoning agent then receives the completed interview transcript and reports hypotheses alongside supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, withholding a final hypothesis when none is sufficiently supported. Using patient profiles generated with PsyCPG, we first evaluate PsyCIDRA in simulation. Across four models on 53 evaluation cases, it achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% versus 51.9%. In a blinded study of 101 human participants in separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, compared with 65.4% for direct prompting. Together, these findings support the potential of LLM agents to assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety together, this study contributes to understanding the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.

AI.tldr: PsyCIDRA is a dual-agent LLM framework that pairs a free-form psychiatric interviewer agent with a diagnostic reasoning agent, showing improved diagnostic agreement and hypothesis-withholding behavior versus direct prompting in both simulation and a blinded human study.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in clinical reasoning, but psychiatric interviewing requires guiding an evolving conversation rather than single-shot reasoning. The ability of LLMs to conduct this interactive assessment is understudied, and prior work rarely examines diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety jointly.
AI.method: PsyCIDRA couples two agents. The interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry. The diagnostic reasoning agent receives the completed transcript and reports hypotheses with supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, abstaining when no hypothesis is sufficiently supported. Evaluation used patient profiles generated with PsyCPG: simulation across four models on 53 cases, 81 held-out simulated cases, plus a blinded study of 101 human participants in separate arms.
AI.result: PsyCIDRA achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting across four models on 53 cases. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% vs 51.9%. In the blinded human study, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, versus 65.4% for direct prompting.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the potential of LLM agents to assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By jointly examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety, the study clarifies both the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.

title: Learning Grasp Targeting from Point Clouds for Log Pile Clearing on a Hydraulic Crane
summary: In mill yards, log loaders clear dense piles by a sequence of bundle grasps: hundreds of logs rest in contact, and each removal changes the pile available to the next grasp. A learned policy chooses where to place and orient the grapple from unsegmented point clouds and runs on a trailer-mounted hydraulic forestry crane. The policy classifies at which observed point to grasp and predicts depth and grapple orientation there. The same network outputs support behavior cloning (BC), reinforcement learning (RL), and deployment. BC learns from successful top-of-pile demonstrations; RL explores for improvements by fine-tuning the cloned policy (BC$\to$RL) or by training from scratch. In simulation, BC clears 98 of 100 piles of 200 logs, while BC$\to$RL improves load stability. Twelve field trials compare a geometric heuristic, RL from scratch, BC, and BC$\to$RL through complete grasp-transport-deposit cycles. BC and BC$\to$RL deposit 93.8% and 88.9% of pooled inventory, against 80.4% for the heuristic. BC$\to$RL deposits logs on 83.6% of its cycles, against 79.6% for the heuristic and 65.7% for BC, while its simulated stability gain does not carry over to the crane testbed. Trained entirely in simulation and run unchanged on the crane, the learned policies clear more than the hand-filtered heuristic while observing unfiltered clouds that still contain the storage rack's rails and poles.

AI.tldr: A learned grasping policy for a hydraulic forestry crane picks and orients its grapple on unsegmented point clouds to clear log piles, trained in simulation via behavior cloning or BC→RL and deployed unchanged, outperforming a geometric heuristic in field trials.
AI.motivation: Clearing dense log piles is a sequential bundle-grasping problem: hundreds of logs rest in contact, and each removal changes the remaining pile, so a fixed heuristic is limited. The authors aim for a learned policy that selects grasp point and grapple orientation directly from unsegmented point clouds and transfers from simulation to a real trailer-mounted crane.
AI.method: The policy classifies which observed point to grasp and predicts depth and grapple orientation at that point. One network supports behavior cloning (BC) from successful top-of-pile demonstrations, reinforcement learning (RL) from scratch, and BC→RL fine-tuning, and is used for both simulation and deployment. Evaluated in simulation and in twelve field trials against a geometric heuristic, RL from scratch, BC, and BC→RL over complete grasp-transport-deposit cycles.
AI.result: In simulation, BC clears 98/100 piles of 200 logs, and BC→RL improves load stability. In field trials, BC and BC→RL deposit 93.8% and 88.9% of pooled inventory versus 80.4% for the heuristic; BC→RL deposits on 83.6% of cycles versus 79.6% (heuristic) and 65.7% (BC), though the simulated stability gain does not carry over to the crane testbed.
AI.conclusion: Policies trained entirely in simulation and run unchanged on the crane clear more logs than the hand-filtered heuristic while operating on unfiltered clouds that still contain the storage rack's rails and poles.

title: In With the Old: Enhancing 'Classical' Document Automation with Generative AI
comment: 10 pages. AI for Access to Justice Workshop at ICAIL 2025
summary: Software-based legal assistance systems have leveraged many different forms of knowledge representation and reasoning. This article explores how document automation services rooted in expert system style and other symbolic approaches can usefully enhance and be enhanced by current generative AI approaches. We discuss the possible benefits and challenges, and report on preliminary experiments in using large language models to identify and fix issues in texts written by laypeople.

AI.tldr: This article examines how document automation services based on expert-system and symbolic approaches can mutually enhance and be enhanced by current generative AI methods, reporting preliminary experiments using LLMs to identify and fix issues in layperson-written legal texts.
AI.motivation: Software-based legal assistance systems have drawn on many forms of knowledge representation and reasoning. The paper is motivated by the question of how document automation rooted in expert system and other symbolic approaches can usefully complement, and be complemented by, modern generative AI approaches.
AI.method: Conceptual discussion of benefits and challenges of combining symbolic expert-system-style document automation with generative AI, supplemented by preliminary experiments in which large language models are used to identify and fix issues in texts written by laypeople.
AI.result: Preliminary experimental results indicate that large language models can be applied to identify and repair problems in layperson-written legal texts, illustrating a practical integration of generative AI with symbolic legal assistance systems.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic, expert-system-based legal document automation and generative AI can mutually reinforce each other; the paper outlines the associated benefits and challenges and provides initial evidence for LLM-based text repair as one promising direction.

title: Nine Trials to Recover: A Reproducible Benchmark for Repertoire-Free Soft-Robot Damage Adaptation
summary: We present a repertoire-free benchmark for soft-robot damage recovery under nine online trials. The protocol pairs damage masks within each morphology, retains a measured nominal fallback, and separates method development from evaluation on new bodies. A Gaussian-process expected-improvement (GP-EI) reference controller adapts actuator phases using three initialization probes and six feedback-selected rollouts. Across two disjoint 75-body cohorts, it outperforms random search, Sobol, CEM, and CMA-ES under equal budgets. GP-EI improves the worst-mask gain on 69/75 confirmation bodies and exceeds these four baselines by 0.235-0.310 mean worst-mask reward. A TuRBO-style local GP is the closest comparator; the paired confidence interval includes zero. Post-confirmation fixed-controller replay finds 5.06 voxel widths of mean recovery together with a 0.0031 increase in worst-mask p99 geometric edge strain; a strict no-added-demand deployment gate retains 48.7% of mean gain. In a frozen development stress test that physically removes 10% of occupied voxels, GP-EI improves 71/75 bodies and exceeds official BoTorch TuRBO by 0.356 mean worst-mask gain. Together, the replayable controllers, body-level inference, and frozen-cohort evaluation provide a reference for measuring the added value of learned damage priors and future adaptation methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a repertoire-free benchmark for soft-robot damage recovery, using a Gaussian-process expected-improvement (GP-EI) controller as a reference and evaluating it against five baselines across two disjoint 75-body cohorts under equal budgets.
AI.motivation: Damage recovery in soft robots is typically studied with precomputed repertoires and single-morphology trials, which confounds method development with evaluation and limits generalization claims. The authors seek a reproducible, body-level protocol that separates development from confirmation on new bodies.
AI.method: A repertoire-free benchmark with nine online trials per morphology, pairing damage masks within each morphology and retaining a measured nominal fallback. GP-EI adapts actuator phases using three initialization probes and six feedback-selected rollouts. Baselines: random search, Sobol, CEM, CMA-ES, and a TuRBO-style local GP. Evaluation uses two disjoint 75-body cohorts, equal budgets, paired confidence intervals, post-confirmation fixed-controller replay, and a strict no-added-demand deployment gate.
AI.result: GP-EI improves worst-mask gain on 69/75 confirmation bodies and exceeds the four baselines by 0.235-0.310 mean worst-mask reward. TuRBO-style local GP is the closest comparator, with a paired CI including zero. Fixed-controller replay yields 5.06 voxel widths of mean recovery with a 0.0031 increase in worst-mask p99 geometric edge strain; the no-added-demand gate retains 48.7% of mean gain. In a frozen stress test removing 10% of occupied voxels, GP-EI improves 71/75 bodies and beats official BoTorch TuRBO by 0.356 mean worst-mask gain.
AI.conclusion: The replayable controllers, body-level inference, and frozen-cohort evaluation form a reference protocol for quantifying the added value of learned damage priors and future adaptation methods, establishing GP-EI as a strong repertoire-free reference baseline under strict, budget-matched conditions.

title: Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping?
summary:
Muon combines current and past gradients into matrix momentum. For $M=UΣV^\top$, the idealized polar update $Q=UV^\top$ gives every singular direction the same weight. We refer to this as the flat profile. Several recent optimizers replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that give each direction its own gain. We ask how much of this spectral detail a Muon update needs. Our spectral diagnostics show that approximately $94$--$97\%$ of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient.
  We introduce BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants.
