The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko--Pastur reference edge for Muon's Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk's relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix's unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. Across 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia-14M to 410M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon and outperforms Spectra. Measured against Muon's flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by $0.022\%$ of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of $0.073$--$0.147\%$. These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles.

AI.tldr: BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework for Muon, shows that a single bulk-to-spike gain captures as much benefit as fine-grained spectral profiles, since 94-97% of singular modes lie below a noise edge yet align positively with the reference gradient.
AI.motivation: Muon's idealized polar update (Q=UV^T) assigns equal weight to every singular direction, termed the flat profile. Recent optimizers replace this with fine-grained spectral maps giving each direction its own gain. The authors question how much spectral detail a Muon update actually needs, given empirical evidence that most singular modes are noise-dominated.
AI.method: The authors propose BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The noise-calibrated variant uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko-Pastur reference edge for Muon's Nesterov input, separating bulk (below edge) from spikes (above edge). Both variants increase the bulk's relative weight via one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix's unreweighted direction. Theory derives the first-order condition under which shifting weight toward the bulk lowers loss, and quantifies the fraction of maximal first-order improvement rate capturable by two bands over all per-mode reallocations.
AI.result: Spectral diagnostics show approximately 94-97% of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient. Across 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia-14M to 410M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with Freon's fine-grained power-law profile and outperforms Spectra. Relative to Muon's flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by 0.022% of pre-adaptation loss on average, while the two-band variants achieve 0.073-0.147% reductions.
AI.conclusion: Useful departures from Muon's flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as fine-grained spectral profiles, suggesting that elaborate per-mode spectral maps may be unnecessary.

title: TacZero: Training-Free Peg Insertion Using a General-Purpose Vision-Language Model with Tactile Feedback
summary: Robots that autonomously determine their actions from language instructions and sensory observations could perform new contact-rich manipulation tasks without task-specific training or hand-designed rules. To perform these tasks, robots must infer how objects contact one another and move as a result, then select actions. For contact inference and action selection, prior approaches involve designing estimation models and tactile feedback control laws, or learning models for object-motion estimation, action-outcome prediction, and action selection from tactile data. Instead, we propose TacZero, which uses a pretrained general-purpose vision-language model (VLM) to interpret visual and tactile observations and select robot actions without additional tactile or manipulation training or task-specific rules for contact interpretation or action selection. TacZero provides the VLM with camera images, robot state, and three-axis tactile responses represented as numerical values or vectors overlaid on the images. From these observations and interaction history, the VLM generates commands specifying target end-effector positions and gripper opening or closing, which a low-level controller executes. In real-world cylindrical-peg insertion experiments, TacZero succeeded in 15 of 20 trials with numerical tactile input, compared with 10 of 20 without tactile input. This study provides a concrete starting point for further research on contact-rich manipulation using general-purpose VLMs and highlights challenges in pursuing this direction.

AI.tldr: TacZero uses a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) to interpret visual and tactile observations and directly select robot actions for contact-rich manipulation, without any task-specific training or rules.
AI.motivation: Robots that autonomously determine actions from language instructions and sensory observations could perform new contact-rich manipulation tasks without task-specific training or hand-designed rules. This requires inferring how objects contact and move, then selecting actions—a challenge prior work addressed with engineered estimation models, tactile control laws, or learned task-specific models.
AI.method: TacZero provides a pretrained general-purpose VLM with camera images, robot state, and three-axis tactile responses represented as numerical values or vectors overlaid on the images. From these observations and interaction history, the VLM generates commands specifying target end-effector positions and gripper opening or closing, which a low-level controller then executes.
AI.result: In real-world cylindrical-peg insertion experiments, TacZero succeeded in 15 of 20 trials with numerical tactile input, compared with 10 of 20 without tactile input.
AI.conclusion: This study provides a concrete starting point for further research on contact-rich manipulation using general-purpose VLMs and highlights challenges in pursuing this direction.

title: MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Long-history recommenders often compress each user's history into a compact, candidate-independent memory that is cached and reused to score large candidate pools. We show that real user histories exhibit multi-scale semantic structure, with short-lived intent, medium-term interests, and long-term preferences coexisting in one sequence, and that monolithic cached memories preserve these scales unevenly: linear probes recover recent and mid-range content far worse than long-range content. We call this failure mode \textit{temporal aliasing}. We propose \textbf{MARS}, a multi-resolution user memory that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives, and a sparse routing reader that materializes compact seed memories by selecting the relevant temporal resolutions for each seed, preserving fixed-size candidate scoring. MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains that grow with history length. Component-matched ablations with paired tests show that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond what hard-window memories or added capacity provide. The advantage of MARS over its interface-matched baseline also widens after within-user behavioral shifts, at about $1.02\times$ that baseline's warm-cache serving latency for $1{,}000$ candidates per user.

AI.tldr: MARS introduces a multi-resolution user memory for long-history recommenders that writes history into recurrent state tracks with different half-lives and uses sparse routing to build compact seed memories, overcoming "temporal aliasing" in monolithic cached memories.
AI.motivation: Real user histories exhibit multi-scale semantic structure (short-lived intent, medium-term interests, long-term preferences) in a single sequence. Existing long-history recommenders compress each user's history into a single candidate-independent cached memory, which preserves these temporal scales unevenly. Linear probes reveal that recent and mid-range content is recovered far worse than long-range content—a failure mode the authors term temporal aliasing.
AI.method: MARS is a multi-resolution user memory that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives. A sparse routing reader materializes compact seed memories by selecting relevant temporal resolutions for each seed, preserving fixed-size candidate scoring for large candidate pools.
AI.result: MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains growing with history length. Component-matched ablations with paired tests show temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond hard-window memories or added capacity. Its advantage over an interface-matched baseline widens after within-user behavioral shifts, at about 1.02× that baseline's warm-cache serving latency for 1,000 candidates per user.
AI.conclusion: Monolithic cached memories suffer from temporal aliasing, unevenly preserving multiple temporal scales in user history. MARS addresses this with half-life-anchored recurrent state tracks and sparse routing, delivering superior and more robust recommendations at near-parity serving latency.

title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence
summary: Co-design methods optimize a robot's body and controller jointly and judge the result by one number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym locomotion tasks, task reward explains only $39\%$, $33\%$ and $10\%$ of the variance in this quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC$(2,k) = 0.956$--$0.986$) but depends on the declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same morphologies at Spearman $0.50$--$0.63$ and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in $3$ of $5$ paired runs, short of a pre-registered bar of $4$. Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all $8$ runs offering a choice, at a cost of at most $0.10$ reward units, and in $6$ of $8$ that body also scored higher under a held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "restricted-control competence" as a morphology property: the task competence a body retains under an explicitly declared low-complexity controller family, and shows task reward alone cannot capture it.
AI.motivation: Co-design methods judge morphologies by a single number (task reward of the fully optimized body-controller pair). This number cannot distinguish morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees, hiding important morphological properties.
AI.method: A morphology is evaluated by restricting its controller: record retained task competence under a declared low-complexity controller family, environment, task, and search budget. Tested on three EvoGym locomotion tasks, with reliability checks across optimizer restarts, sensitivity to controller-family definition (actuator-index vs. position phasing), and use as a secondary search objective and as a post-hoc selector within top reward bands.
AI.result: Task reward explains only 39%, 33%, and 10% of variance in restricted-control competence; geometric descriptors fail to predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. Measurement is reliable across restarts (ICC(2,k)=0.956-0.986) but family-dependent, with Spearman 0.50-0.63 between phasing schemes and reversal of reward-matched pairs. As a secondary objective it improved competence at matched reward in 3/5 paired runs (below pre-registered bar of 4). Used post-hoc to choose within the top reward band, it selected a different body in all 8 runs offering a choice, costing at most 0.10 reward units, and in 6/8 that body scored higher under a held-out family.
AI.conclusion: Restricted-control competence is a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, but it is interpretable only together with the controller family that defines it.

title: On Open-Ended Information Seeking for Information Elicitation Agents
summary: Information elicitation is an open-ended information-seeking problem in which an interaction can unfold in many potentially valuable directions, requiring an elicitor to continually determine which information to pursue as new information emerges. In agentic elicitation, these decisions may be delegated to a foundation model, yet how model choice shapes the resulting information-seeking behavior remains understudied. We study how judgments about information value vary across LLMs and how these differences shape sequential information seeking. We first examine these judgments across 11 LLMs spanning multiple model families and parameter scales, using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives. We then develop a controlled elicitation simulation in which different models encounter the same information space and use the same selection rule, isolating these judgments from question generation and respondent behavior. Using this setting, we characterize the breadth-depth behavior that emerges from model-specific information-seeking preferences over the course of elicitation. We further examine how interaction history changes the evaluation and subsequent selection of prospective information. We test the robustness and boundaries of these findings through sensitivity analyses and ablations over the opportunities available to the elicitor, the response labels used to operationalize information-seeking preferences, the presence of interaction history, and whether redundancy is explicitly relevant to the assessment. The project code, data, and trajectory files are available at https://github.com/infosenselab/open-elicitation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how different LLMs judge the value of information and how those judgments shape sequential, agentic information elicitation, using a controlled elicitation simulation across 11 models.
AI.motivation: Information elicitation is open-ended, and when delegated to foundation models, it remains unclear how the choice of model shapes information-seeking behavior. Model-specific judgments about information value and their downstream effects on sequential seeking are understudied.
AI.method: The authors examine information-value judgments across 11 LLMs spanning multiple model families and parameter scales using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives. They build a controlled elicitation simulation where models encounter the same information space and use the same selection rule, isolating judgments from question generation and respondent behavior. They then characterize emergent breadth-depth behavior and examine how interaction history affects evaluation and subsequent selection. Robustness is tested via sensitivity analyses and ablations over elicitor opportunities, response labels, interaction history, and redundancy relevance.
AI.result: Judgments about information value vary systematically across LLMs and produce distinct sequential information-seeking behaviors. Model-specific preferences yield different breadth-depth patterns over the course of elicitation, and interaction history alters both the evaluation and selection of prospective information. Findings are robust across the tested ablations and sensitivity conditions.
AI.conclusion: Model choice materially shapes agentic elicitation behavior, with differences in information-value judgments driving divergent breadth-depth strategies. The controlled simulation isolates these effects and offers a reproducible basis for studying elicitation, with code, data, and trajectories released publicly.

title: OntoPlan: An Ontology-Grounded Scene Representation and Agentic Framework for Scalable Robot Task Planning
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based robot task planning is promising for open-ended instruction following, but degrades on long-horizon tasks in large environments. When spatial information is conveyed to the LLM through text, the model can fail to capture spatial context, and token cost grows with environment size. Generating action sequences directly with an LLM also makes it difficult to satisfy the current world state and action preconditions. We address this with an ontology-grounded scene representation that aligns objects, spaces, relations, and states in a shared symbolic vocabulary for spatial reasoning and task planning, and with OntoPlan, an agentic framework that interprets instructions, selectively retrieves task-relevant information, formalizes goals and constraints, and produces executable plans. Across 150 general tasks spanning five indoor environments and three scene scales, OntoPlan achieves 0.89 average task success, compared with 0.27 for the strongest baseline, while using 18.1k total tokens per task on average, about 5.6$\times$ fewer than the most efficient baseline. These advantages persist as scene scale increases, whereas prior methods degrade more sharply in success and remain far more costly in tokens. OntoPlan also responds appropriately to ambiguous or infeasible instructions by asking follow-up questions or reporting insufficient information rather than committing to invalid plans. Code available at https://github.com/namhyeongwoo/OntoPlan.

AI.tldr: OntoPlan combines an ontology-grounded scene representation with an agentic planning framework to improve LLM-based robot task planning, achieving 0.89 task success vs. 0.27 for the best baseline while using ~5.6x fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: LLM-based robot task planning struggles on long-horizon tasks in large environments: text-based spatial information causes the model to miss spatial context and token cost scales with environment size. Directly generating action sequences also makes it hard to respect current world state and action preconditions.
AI.method: An ontology-grounded scene representation aligns objects, spaces, relations, and states in a shared symbolic vocabulary for spatial reasoning and task planning. OntoPlan is an agentic framework that interprets instructions, selectively retrieves task-relevant information, formalizes goals and constraints, and produces executable plans.
AI.result: Across 150 general tasks spanning five indoor environments and three scene scales, OntoPlan achieves 0.89 average task success vs. 0.27 for the strongest baseline, using 18.1k tokens per task on average (~5.6x fewer than the most efficient baseline). Advantages persist as scene scale increases, whereas prior methods degrade more sharply in success and cost far more tokens. OntoPlan also handles ambiguous or infeasible instructions by asking follow-up questions or reporting insufficient information instead of committing to invalid plans.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-grounded symbolic scene representation plus selective, agentic planning yields substantially higher success and lower token cost than prior LLM planning methods, with robust scaling and appropriate handling of ambiguous or infeasible instructions.

title: From Local Evidence to Safety Verdicts: Causal Tracing in Vision-Language Models
summary: A vision-language model may need to combine an image with a prompt to recognize a safety risk that neither reveals alone. Where does this joint safety judgment become accessible inside the model? We introduce SSU-Bench, a dataset of matched safe and unsafe image-text combinations constructed using single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated intended regions. Using three vision-language models, we transfer internal states between paired inputs and measure the resulting change in the safety verdict. Across models and both types of counterfactual, interventions at the changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective later. Directions estimated from other examples produce similar late-layer effects. A linear readout of the final-token state also predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect judgments, and cross-model comparisons reveal similarities in the patterns of counterfactual change. These findings identify a recurring transition in where interventions can influence a joint safety verdict and distinguish a readable model decision from a correct safety judgment.

AI.tldr: A recurring layer-wise transition determines where internal interventions can flip a vision-language model's joint safety verdict, and the readable final-token decision can be separated from actual safety correctness.
AI.motivation: Safety risks in vision-language models often arise from the combination of an image and a prompt, where neither modality alone reveals the risk. It is unclear where inside the model this joint safety judgment becomes accessible and causally influenceable. The paper aims to localize this internal decision point across models and counterfactual input types.
AI.method: The authors introduce SSU-Bench, a dataset of matched safe/unsafe image-text pairs built via single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated intended regions. Using three vision-language models, they transfer internal states between paired inputs and measure changes in the safety verdict. They perform interventions at changed input positions versus the final input token across decoder layers, estimate directions from other examples, apply a linear readout of the final-token state, and conduct cross-model comparisons.
AI.result: Across models and both counterfactual types, interventions at changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective in later layers. Directions estimated from other examples yield similar late-layer effects. A linear readout of the final-token state predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect judgments, and cross-model comparisons show similarities in counterfactual-change patterns.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a recurring transition in where interventions can influence a joint safety verdict and distinguishes a readable model decision from a correct safety judgment, providing a layer-resolved account of multimodal safety processing.

title: Silicon Language: A Robot-Native Knowledge Exchange Framework for Heterogeneous Robots
summary: Reusing a capability across heterogeneous robots still requires substantial human adaptation and verification: transferring a skill often means re-engineering interfaces, retuning parameters, and re-validating safety. We introduce Silicon Language, a robot-native knowledge exchange framework that treats the robot as the active subject of its own capability evolution. In this framework, a robot that wants a capability encodes its own experience into knowledge packets, publishes them, retrieves peer packets, translates them for its own sensors and actuators, and reviews them through independent local trial. A receiver-side usability evaluation procedure lets each robot decide for itself whether an external packet is useful, and progressive blending with automatic rollback is designed to reduce the risk of negative transfer when adopting it. The system combines three infrastructure layers (edge agent, Silicon Transfer Protocol (STP), and knowledge hub) with a capability stack inspired by the human scholarly system. We report a 30-day proof-of-concept deployment at an above-ground simulated-mine laboratory in Yulin, with following trials on an outdoor sand road and an indoor factory floor. Two heterogeneous robots encoded and translated three capabilities across embodiments through operator-assisted file copies mediated by the Silicon Language translation layer; source-side trials of the dust-locked following behavior were recorded on Taurus. Project records indicate that per-capability adaptation time dropped from days to hours; we present these figures as descriptive deployment records rather than controlled measurements. The deployment provides initial evidence for cross-embodiment knowledge exchange; fleet-level autonomous evolution and controlled with/without-packet comparisons remain future work.

AI.tldr: Silicon Language is a robot-native knowledge exchange framework enabling cross-embodiment capability transfer via self-encoded knowledge packets, peer retrieval, translation, receiver-side usability evaluation, and progressive blending with rollback; a 30-day proof-of-concept across three sites reported adaptation time dropping from days to hours (descriptive records, not controlled measurements).
AI.motivation: Reusing a capability across heterogeneous robots currently demands substantial human effort: re-engineering interfaces, retuning parameters, and re-validating safety. The paper aims to reposition the robot as the active subject of its own capability evolution rather than a passive recipient of engineered transfers.
AI.method: The framework has a robot encode its own experience into knowledge packets, publish them, retrieve peer packets, translate them for its own sensors/actuators, and review them through independent local trial. A receiver-side usability evaluation lets each robot judge external packet usefulness, and progressive blending with automatic rollback mitigates negative transfer risk. It combines three infrastructure layers (edge agent, Silicon Transfer Protocol (STP), knowledge hub) with a capability stack inspired by the human scholarly system.
AI.result: A 30-day proof-of-concept deployment at an above-ground simulated-mine laboratory in Yulin, with follow-up trials on an outdoor sand road and an indoor factory floor. Two heterogeneous robots encoded and translated three capabilities across embodiments via operator-assisted file copies mediated by the Silicon Language translation layer; source-side trials of dust-locked following behavior were recorded on Taurus. Per-capability adaptation time reportedly dropped from days to hours, presented as descriptive deployment records rather than controlled measurements.
AI.conclusion: The deployment provides initial evidence for cross-embodiment knowledge exchange, but fleet-level autonomous evolution and controlled with/without-packet comparisons remain future work.

title: Grounding What Shapes the Plan: Rethinking Groundedness for Physical Intelligence in Autonomous Driving
summary: Driving models increasingly ground reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures. These advances make reasoning more faithful to the driving scene, but leave a fundamental question unresolved: what should groundedness mean when the model ultimately outputs an action? Correctly grounded reasoning does not, by itself, ensure desirable driving outcomes. We introduce GroundAct, which starts from a simple premise: driving unfolds through physical entities and their interactions. Entities therefore become the unit of grounding; a lightweight reference token keeps each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning; and only the referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal correct the plan. The result is an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does, which we call grounded planning. To assess its practical value, we evaluate GroundAct in both open- and closed-loop settings. GroundAct shows strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, with closed-loop results extending this evidence to driving in simulation.

AI.tldr: GroundAct reframes groundedness in driving models around physical entities and their interactions, using reference tokens to link symbolic reasoning to predictable entity states, yielding an explicit "grounded planning" path that improves open- and closed-loop driving performance.
AI.motivation: Existing driving models increasingly ground reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures, but this leaves a fundamental question unresolved: what groundedness should mean when the model ultimately outputs an action. Correctly grounded reasoning does not by itself guarantee desirable driving outcomes, so the paper seeks a grounding formulation that directly shapes the resulting plan.
AI.method: The authors propose GroundAct, built on the premise that driving unfolds through physical entities and their interactions. Entities become the unit of grounding; a lightweight reference token keeps each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning; and only the referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal are used to correct the plan. This creates an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does, termed grounded planning.
AI.result: GroundAct is evaluated in both open- and closed-loop settings. It shows strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, and closed-loop results extend this evidence to driving in simulation.
AI.conclusion: Grounding on entities and their interactions, rather than on reasoning alone, provides an explicit and effective link from grounded reasoning to planning, demonstrating practical value for driving across diverse open- and closed-loop conditions.

title: SMART: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Articulated Object Manipulation via Large-Scale Synthetic Pretraining
summary: The ability to interact with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligent systems, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations for these interactions remains challenging due to the precise contact and constraint-following motions involved. Although simulation provides a promising alternative, existing synthetic data efforts cover limited articulated-object categories, while general-purpose synthesis pipelines lack explicit designs for part-level semantics and articulation constraints, hindering agentic task generation and scalable synthesis of high-quality articulated-manipulation demonstrations. To bridge this gap, we introduce SMART, a scalable system leveraging large-scale Synthesized Manipulation demonstrations for ARTiculated-object manipulation. At its core, we develop SMART-Sim, a simulation platform with articulation-aware design that enables effective task generation and efficient demonstration collection. Building on SMART-Sim, we apply agentic task generation and design a scalable distributed synthesis system, using them to synthesize SMART-Data, comprising over 1M demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects. The vision-language-action (VLA) model pretrained on SMART-Data shows competitive performance on simulation benchmarks and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and scalable performance in real-world articulated-object manipulation tasks. This highlights the potential of synthetic demonstrations in providing effective and scalable supervision for improving VLA model performance in contact-rich articulated-object manipulation.

AI.tldr: SMART is a scalable simulation-based system that synthesizes over 1M manipulation demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects; a VLA model pretrained on this data shows strong simulation performance and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Interacting with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligence, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations is difficult due to precise contact and constraint-following motions. Existing synthetic data efforts cover limited object categories, and general-purpose synthesis pipelines lack part-level semantics and articulation constraints, limiting agentic task generation and scalable synthesis of high-quality demonstrations.
AI.method: The authors introduce SMART, a scalable system for articulated-object manipulation using large-scale synthesized demonstrations. Its core, SMART-Sim, is a simulation platform with articulation-aware design enabling effective task generation and efficient demonstration collection. On top of it, they apply agentic task generation and a scalable distributed synthesis system to produce SMART-Data, comprising over 1M demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects. A vision-language-action (VLA) model is pretrained on this data.
AI.result: The VLA model pretrained on SMART-Data achieves competitive performance on simulation benchmarks and demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with scalable performance on real-world articulated-object manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic demonstrations can provide effective and scalable supervision for improving VLA model performance in contact-rich articulated-object manipulation, highlighting the potential of the proposed SMART system and SMART-Data.

title: A Systematic Investigation of Bias in Large Language Models for Advertising Relevance
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge how well an advertisement matches a query, but the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention. We conduct a systematic study of fairness in relevance judgments made by LLMs for queries and advertisements. Our counterfactual framework examines the effects of advertiser identity and possible popularity, input language, and demographic wording. We study GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model trained specifically for relevance prediction. The advertiser and language experiments use query and advertisement pairs sampled from real advertising logs. Controlled synthetic queries are used to study demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit. For both models, changing the advertiser identity or input language can alter the relevance assessment. Selected demographic comparisons also show patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly those involving gender and occupation. We further study mitigation during model inference and training. The results indicate that its effectiveness depends on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in the training data. These findings can help advertising practitioners identify fairness risks and develop suitable mitigation methods for LLM relevance systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies fairness in LLM-based ad relevance judgments using a counterfactual framework, testing GPT-4o and a Qwen-7B relevance model across advertiser identity, popularity, input language, and demographic wording, and evaluating inference- and training-time mitigation.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to judge advertisement-query relevance, yet the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention, creating unexamined fairness risks for advertising practice.
AI.method: A counterfactual framework manipulates advertiser identity and possible popularity, input language, and demographic wording. Two judges are examined: GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model trained specifically for relevance prediction. Advertiser and language experiments use query-advertisement pairs sampled from real advertising logs, while controlled synthetic queries probe demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit. Mitigation is studied during both model inference and training.
AI.result: For both models, changing advertiser identity or input language can alter relevance assessments. Selected demographic comparisons show patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly involving gender and occupation. Mitigation effectiveness depends on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in the training data.
AI.conclusion: LLM relevance judgments exhibit measurable fairness risks tied to advertiser identity, language, and demographic wording. Practitioners should identify these risks and select mitigation methods informed by advertiser-query relevance and training-label distribution.

title: EigenDEXplore: Structured Exploration for Dexterous Manipulation with Human Priors
summary: Dexterous manipulation poses a challenging high-dimensional optimization problem, as useful behaviors require coordinated motion across many hand joints. In reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization, exploration commonly relies on independent robot joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover. Prior work reduces this search space for grasp learning using low-dimensional spaces of coordinated joint motions learned from human hand data, but this restricts the expressivity required for general manipulation. Some combine learned and joint-space actions to restore expressivity, but this increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy. We study these effects across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data. Our experiments suggest that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation. Motivated by this finding, we propose EigenDEXplore, which induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged. Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EigenDEXplore, a method that improves dexterous manipulation by structuring exploration with human-derived eigenvectors added as correlated noise to joint-space perturbations, rather than altering the action representation. It consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines across multiple tasks and settings.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation is a high-dimensional optimization problem requiring coordinated motion across many hand joints. Standard RL and trajectory optimization rely on independent joint perturbations for exploration, which makes discovering coordinated behaviors difficult. Prior work reduces the search space using low-dimensional coordinated joint motion spaces learned from human hand data, but this restricts expressivity for general manipulation. Combining learned and joint-space actions restores expressivity but increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy. The authors aim to study these trade-offs across diverse manipulation settings.
AI.method: The authors investigate the effects of action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data across diverse manipulation settings. Based on the finding that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation, they propose EigenDEXplore. This method induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged.
AI.result: Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design.
AI.conclusion: Human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than to change the action representation. EigenDEXplore demonstrates that adding human-derived eigenvector perturbations to joint-space noise improves dexterous manipulation performance across various tasks, learning paradigms, and hardware, with the greatest benefits in settings lacking extensive reward shaping and curriculum design.

title: Decoupled Multi-Agent Orchestration
summary: Learned orchestration can automatically construct effective language-model multi-agent systems, but existing approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome, limiting transfer and obscuring credit assignment. We introduce DeOrch, which separates worker-agnostic planning from concrete worker selection. Its two-stage planner first decomposes the task without worker information, then chooses collaboration operations using compact, worker-identity-free matchability feedback from the pool, enabling conditional credit assignment to decomposition and collaboration decisions. A lightweight matcher estimates worker suitability from behavior on a fixed probe set and adapts online with a contextual bandit, allowing new workers to be incorporated without retraining the planner or matcher. Across diverse in- and out-of-distribution tasks, DeOrch outperforms prior automatic MAS orchestration methods with fewer worker calls than competing learned orchestrators, remains effective when transferred to an entirely unseen worker pool without retraining, and shows consistent gains from both components.

AI.tldr: DeOrch is a learned orchestration framework that decouples worker-agnostic planning from worker selection, enabling better transfer and credit assignment for language-model multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Existing learned orchestration approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train both decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome. This limits transferability to new worker pools and obscures credit assignment between planning and collaboration decisions.
AI.method: DeOrch uses a two-stage planner: it first decomposes the task without worker information, then selects collaboration operations using compact, worker-identity-free matchability feedback from the pool, enabling conditional credit assignment. A lightweight matcher estimates worker suitability from behavior on a fixed probe set and adapts online via a contextual bandit, allowing new workers to be added without retraining the planner or matcher.
AI.result: DeOrch outperforms prior automatic MAS orchestration methods on diverse in- and out-of-distribution tasks, using fewer worker calls than competing learned orchestrators. It remains effective when transferred to an entirely unseen worker pool without retraining, and both components yield consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: Separating worker-agnostic planning from worker selection improves transfer and credit assignment in learned multi-agent orchestration, enabling adaptive integration of new workers without retraining.

title: ExoBridge: Learning a Bare Hand to Hand-Worn Exoskeleton Mapping through Human Limb Coupling
summary: Human video offers a scalable source of experience for dexterous robot learning, but obtaining motion and tactile supervision while preserving bare hand interaction remains challenging. We present ExoBridge, a framework that leverages human limb coupling to learn a bridging function from bare hand video to the motion and tactile state of a sensorized exoskeleton. Our central idea is to use coordinated bimanual behavior to connect an uninstrumented visual source with a measured manipulation interface. During collection, one hand remains bare and provides visual observations, while the opposite hand wears the exoskeleton and supplies synchronized motion and tactile measurements. These paired demonstrations train a temporal visual model to predict fingertip contact, continuous tactile intensity, and relative encoder motion from bare hand video alone. The exoskeleton defines an intermediate state space whose motion coordinates are linked to a dexterous robot hand through existing calibration. Evaluation on 1,215 demonstrations across four manipulation tasks uses held out collection sessions and yields a pooled any contact AUROC of 0.916 and a Pearson correlation of 0.790 for tactile intensity. The learned bridge also predicts relative changes in exoskeleton configuration from bare hand video. These results demonstrate that human limb coupling can turn exoskeleton measurements into supervision for bare hand video, establishing a learned bridge between human visual demonstrations and a robot oriented manipulation interface.

AI.tldr: ExoBridge learns a bridging function from bare hand video to exoskeleton motion and tactile states using coordinated bimanual human demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Human video is a scalable source of robot learning experience, but obtaining motion and tactile supervision while preserving bare hand interaction is difficult.
AI.method: During collection, one bare hand provides visual observations while the opposite hand wears a sensorized exoskeleton supplying synchronized motion and tactile measurements. Paired demonstrations train a temporal visual model to predict fingertip contact, continuous tactile intensity, and relative encoder motion from bare hand video, with exoskeleton motion coordinates linked to a dexterous robot hand via calibration.
AI.result: On 1,215 demonstrations across four manipulation tasks with held-out collection sessions, the method achieves pooled any-contact AUROC of 0.916 and Pearson correlation of 0.790 for tactile intensity, and predicts relative exoskeleton configuration changes from bare hand video.
AI.conclusion: Human limb coupling turns exoskeleton measurements into supervision for bare hand video, establishing a learned bridge between human visual demonstrations and a robot-oriented manipulation interface.

title: Navigating Route Latent Space for Synthesizable Molecular Design
summary: Goal-directed molecular design has advanced rapidly, yet a substantial proportion of designed molecules remain difficult to synthesize in practice, limiting their real-world utility. Prior synthesizability-aware methods either project generated molecules back to synthesizable analogs that deviate from the intended target, or optimize directly in discrete synthesis spaces that lack a continuous landscape for efficient search. We argue that this limitation mainly comes from the search space rather than the optimizer. To address this, we propose RouteFlow, a framework that reformulates synthesizable molecular design as a search over a continuous route latent space, where each latent maps back to a complete synthesis route and synthesizability is inherently preserved. To navigate this space, we adopt reward-guided flow matching as an efficient sampler that steers toward high-property regions. Since reward optimization may push latents off the manifold of real synthesis routes, where decoding becomes unreliable, we further introduce a cycle-consistency mechanism to stabilize fine-tuning. Across 16 optimization tasks from Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow achieves the best sample efficiency among synthesizability-aware baselines, with the best synthetic accessibility and the highest retrosynthesis success rate. Our results also confirm that the proposed cycle-consistency reliably keeps optimization on-manifold while improving target properties, supporting effective synthesizable molecular discovery.

AI.tldr: RouteFlow reformulates synthesizable molecular design as search over a continuous route latent space, using reward-guided flow matching with cycle-consistency to achieve efficient, synthesizable optimization.
AI.motivation: A large fraction of designed molecules remain hard to synthesize, limiting practical utility. Prior synthesizability-aware methods either project generated molecules back to synthesizable analogs that deviate from the intended target, or optimize directly in discrete synthesis spaces lacking a continuous landscape for efficient search. The authors argue this limitation stems from the search space rather than the optimizer.
AI.method: RouteFlow searches over a continuous route latent space, where each latent maps back to a complete synthesis route, inherently preserving synthesizability. Reward-guided flow matching serves as an efficient sampler steering toward high-property regions. A cycle-consistency mechanism stabilizes fine-tuning, since reward optimization may push latents off the manifold of real synthesis routes, making decoding unreliable.
AI.result: Across 16 optimization tasks from Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow achieves the best sample efficiency among synthesizability-aware baselines, with the best synthetic accessibility and the highest retrosynthesis success rate. Cycle-consistency reliably keeps optimization on-manifold while improving target properties.
AI.conclusion: Searching a continuous route latent space with reward-guided flow matching and cycle-consistency supports effective synthesizable molecular discovery.

title: ESP: Energy-Score Policy for One-Step Multimodal Action Generation
summary: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. Their iterative sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to generate each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), a teacher-free approach that maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. ESP trains the action head with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Whereas squared-error regression targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper: its expected value is uniquely minimized by the target distribution. This provides a principled objective for learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling, with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution. Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline. These results support direct distributional learning as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies.

AI.tldr: ESP (Energy-Score Policy) is a teacher-free, single-step action head that trains with an energy score instead of MSE, learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling and achieving lower latency than flow matching baselines.
AI.motivation: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching capture diverse, multimodal behaviors in VLA policies but require repeated network evaluations for each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. The paper seeks an efficient alternative that retains multimodal distributional learning without iterative sampling.
AI.method: ESP maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. The action head is trained with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Unlike squared-error regression, which targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper, with its expected value uniquely minimized by the target distribution, providing a principled objective for multimodal action learning with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution.
AI.result: Experiments on simulation and real-world manipulation tasks show competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline.
AI.conclusion: Direct distributional learning is supported as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies.

title: Unanimously Wrong: Certified Abstention from How Medical LLM Consensus Forms
comment: Accepted at the GenAI4Health Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: In clinical practice, agreement among independent experts is treated as evidence of reliability, and multi-round consensus has become a core mechanism of agentic medical question-answering systems. When such a system must decide whether to trust its own answer, the prevailing signal is again agreement, now among the sampled answers. But agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong, returning the same incorrect answer on every sample, and on these questions agreement-based signals carry no information. The cause is that these signals read only the final state of the consensus and discard how it was reached. Agreement that was reached by resolving disagreement with evidence looks identical, at the end, to agreement that was present from the first sample because every sample shares one misconception. ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework that bases the abstention decision on how the consensus formed. Process features trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration then converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk. We evaluate ProbeGuard on three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference, with a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong, and no agreement-based signal can flag them. Process signals raise the discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at an observed selective risk of 9.0%, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.

AI.tldr: ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework for medical QA that decides trust based on how consensus formed rather than whether it formed, using process features, rationale semantic entropy, and active counter-evidence probes, then calibrating via stratified Learn-then-Test for a distribution-free selective-risk bound.
AI.motivation: In agentic medical QA, agreement among sampled answers—and among experts—is treated as evidence of reliability, but agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong: every sample returns the same incorrect answer because all samples share one misconception, and on such questions agreement-based signals carry no information. Existing signals read only the final consensus state and discard how it was reached, so evidence-resolved agreement is indistinguishable from agreement present from the first sample.
AI.method: ProbeGuard bases the abstention decision on consensus formation. It uses process features that trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk.
AI.result: Evaluated on three medical QA benchmarks plus a hard-frontier reference, on a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong and no agreement-based signal flags them; process signals raise discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at 9.0% observed selective risk, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.
AI.conclusion: Treating final-state agreement as a reliability signal is insufficient because unanimous errors leave agreement-based signals uninformative. Monitoring how consensus forms—via process features, rationale coherence under semantic entropy, and active counter-evidence probing—restores discriminative power and, with stratified Learn-then-Test calibration, yields a certified, distribution-free selective-risk guarantee for abstention in agentic medical QA.

title: Seeing Through the Displaced Frame: Privileged Noise Distillation for Vision-Force Precision Assembly
summary: Pose error in precision assembly can corrupt not only what a robot observes but also the coordinate frame in which it acts. On the FORGE benchmark, the official state-based policy succeeds in 97% to 99% of episodes with the true pose but only 32% to 60% at the benchmark's $σ=5$ mm pose-noise setting. The same estimated pose enters the observation and anchors the action frame, making the offset unidentifiable from proprioceptive state alone before contact. We supply this missing information during training in two ways. A privileged teacher observes the offset in simulation, while clean demonstrations can instead be relabelled into the displaced frame in closed form. The deployed student is trained with behaviour cloning followed by one DAgger round and receives only noisy state, a raw wrench window, and two RGB cameras at test time. On the unmodified FORGE tasks, the teacher-route student maintains 92% to 99% success across $σ=0$ to 5 mm, while six non-privileged baselines fall to 2% to 80%. A matched behaviour-cloning experiment isolates the source of this robustness. With the same student architecture, data budget, and training procedure, demonstrations generated without offset access yield only 31.5% success at $σ=5$ mm, whereas privileged and relabelled demonstrations reach 88.7% and 95.8%. Deployed zero-shot on a Franka, the student reaches 83.3% pooled success at $σ=5$ mm against 34.4% for the strongest state-based policy. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient. Robustness requires supervision that encodes compensation for the latent frame offset.Project page: https://drychang.github.io/displaced-frame/

AI.tldr: Pose error in precision assembly shifts both the observation and the action frame, a latent offset unidentifiable from proprioception alone. Providing frame-offset supervision during training (via a privileged teacher or closed-form demonstration relabelling) yields a student policy that stays robust (92–99%) across σ=0–5 mm, versus 2–80% for non-privileged baselines and 83.3% zero-shot on a Franka.
AI.motivation: In precision assembly, pose error corrupts more than observations: because the same estimated pose anchors the action coordinate frame, the resulting latent frame offset cannot be identified from proprioceptive state before contact. This makes robustness fundamentally a supervision problem, motivating the provision of the missing offset information during training.
AI.method: The authors supply frame-offset information during training through two routes: (1) a privileged teacher that observes the offset in simulation, and (2) closed-form relabelling of clean demonstrations into the displaced frame. The deployed student is trained via behaviour cloning plus one DAgger round, and at test time receives only noisy state, a raw wrench window, and two RGB cameras (no privileged signals).
AI.result: On unmodified FORGE tasks the teacher-route student achieves 92–99% success across σ=0–5 mm, while six non-privileged baselines drop to 2–80%. A matched behaviour-cloning ablation (same architecture, data budget, and procedure) shows 31.5% success at σ=5 mm without offset access, versus 88.7% (privileged) and 95.8% (relabelled). Zero-shot on a Franka, the student reaches 83.3% pooled success at σ=5 mm versus 34.4% for the strongest state-based policy.
AI.conclusion: Deployable sensing alone is insufficient for robust precision assembly. Robustness requires supervision that explicitly encodes compensation for the latent coordinate-frame offset induced by pose error.

title: Cooperating with Future Collaborators: Multi-Agent RL under Staggered Participation
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are often trained under concurrent participation, while in many tasks some agents act earlier and leave task-relevant information that becomes useful to agents participating later. We study this setting as staggered participation (SP), which introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency because an early action may affect the return through the information it provides and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP therefore requires both identifying what information is useful for future decisions and learning how later agents should use it. We propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that addresses these two parts with prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average difference of 14.1%. The gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies staggered participation (SP) in cooperative MARL, where early agents leave useful information for later agents, and proposes Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that improves task completion across backbones and environments.
AI.motivation: In cooperative MARL, agents are typically trained under concurrent participation, but many tasks involve agents acting earlier and leaving task-relevant information for later agents. This staggered participation introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency: early actions affect returns through the information they provide and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP thus requires identifying useful information for future decisions and learning how later agents should exploit it.
AI.method: The authors propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation with two components: prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents.
AI.result: SPL is evaluated across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone-setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average improvement of 14.1%. Gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab.
AI.conclusion: SPL provides consistent improvements across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings, offering evidence that explicitly addressing staggered participation benefits cooperative MARL.

title: CoRE: Learning Collaboration-Role Experts for Decentralized Collaborative Manipulation with One Policy
summary: Collaborative manipulation requires robots to perform complementary actions as interactions unfold. We study single-policy decentralized collaboration: every robot runs the same policy from its visual observations and proprioception, without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages. The challenge is to learn complementary team behaviors within shared parameters and select appropriate actions from each robot's local observations. We introduce CoRE, which learns Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations. Fused appearance and geometry provide local interaction evidence. Query-conditioned cross-attention experts provide adaptable prediction paths, which a local router combines at each action-chunk position. During training, an action-expert alignment loss supervises expert selection using relative forced-route prediction errors against demonstrations under fixed inputs, without role labels. Across simulation benchmarks, CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods. Physical experiments demonstrate effective collaboration across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to partner delays and slowdowns. Project page: https://aus.bot/research/core/.

AI.tldr: CoRE learns Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-robot demonstrations, enabling single-policy decentralized collaboration without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages.
AI.motivation: Collaborative manipulation requires robots to perform complementary actions as interactions unfold. The paper studies single-policy decentralized collaboration, where every robot runs the same policy from visual observations and proprioception, without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages. The core challenge is learning complementary team behaviors within shared parameters and selecting appropriate actions from each robot's local observations.
AI.method: CoRE learns Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations. Fused appearance and geometry provide local interaction evidence. Query-conditioned cross-attention experts provide adaptable prediction paths, which a local router combines at each action-chunk position. During training, an action-expert alignment loss supervises expert selection using relative forced-route prediction errors against demonstrations under fixed inputs, without role labels.
AI.result: Across simulation benchmarks, CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods. Physical experiments demonstrate effective collaboration across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to partner delays and slowdowns.
AI.conclusion: CoRE enables effective decentralized, single-policy collaborative manipulation by learning collaboration-role experts from pooled demonstrations, achieving strong simulation performance and robust real-world collaboration without role labels, task prompts, or inter-robot communication.

title: LOGIC: An LLM Benchmark for Intent-Grounded Change Impact in Aerospace Electrical Systems
summary: Aerospace electrical-design revisions can contain multiple genuine changes, although an engineering request may authorize only a subset. Propagating every detected difference can therefore produce overly broad impact reports. We present LOGIC, a controlled benchmark and evaluation framework in which locally deployable language models ground a request in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before selected changes are propagated through a typed electrical traceability graph. This separation permits candidate-selection errors to be distinguished from downstream propagation errors. LOGIC contains 168 scenarios, including 144 selection and 24 abstention cases. We evaluate three 7--8B models against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods, with an oracle-root upper bound. On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, gate-only structured evidence achieves candidate F1 of 1.0000, compared with 0.9677 for token-lexical matching. On 12 relational-paraphrase cases, token-lexical F1 is 0.1772 and gate-only F1 is 0.0000, compared with 0.5000--0.6400 for the large language models. Model grounding degrades as candidate inventories grow from 4 to 64 changes, while affected-element and typed-path accuracy remain comparatively stable when frozen selections are replayed over graphs of approximately 1K to 100K nodes. Strict evidence gating suppresses false positives but can remove correct semantic selections. An exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raises strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 for all three models and reduces unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, while decreasing answerable-case coverage by 16.0--27.1 percentage points. Four of six conflicting requests remain unsafe for each model. These findings support combining literal evidence and language-model reasoning with engineering review when intent cannot be established reliably.

AI.tldr: LOGIC is a controlled benchmark and evaluation framework that separates candidate-selection errors from downstream propagation errors in aerospace electrical-design revisions, using locally deployable language models grounded in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before propagating selected changes through a typed traceability graph.
AI.motivation: Aerospace electrical-design revisions can contain multiple genuine changes, although an engineering request may authorize only a subset. Propagating every detected difference can therefore produce overly broad impact reports, so there is a need to isolate the candidate-selection step from downstream propagation and to evaluate both separately.
AI.method: LOGIC grounds a request in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before selected changes are propagated through a typed electrical traceability graph, allowing candidate-selection errors to be distinguished from propagation errors. The benchmark contains 168 scenarios (144 selection and 24 abstention). Three 7--8B models are evaluated against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods, with an oracle-root upper bound, and frozen selections are replayed over graphs of approximately 1K to 100K nodes.
AI.result: On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, gate-only structured evidence achieves candidate F1 of 1.0000 versus 0.9677 for token-lexical matching. On 12 relational-paraphrase cases, token-lexical F1 is 0.1772 and gate-only F1 is 0.0000, compared with 0.5000--0.6400 for the large language models. Model grounding degrades as candidate inventories grow from 4 to 64 changes, while affected-element and typed-path accuracy remain comparatively stable. Strict evidence gating suppresses false positives but can remove correct semantic selections. An exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raises strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 for all three models and reduces unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, while decreasing answerable-case coverage by 16.0--27.1 percentage points. Four of six conflicting requests remain unsafe for each model.
AI.conclusion: These findings support combining literal evidence and language-model reasoning with engineering review when intent cannot be established reliably.

title: StairVLA: Stage-Aware Hierarchical Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly rely on diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to generate continuous robot actions. These action heads typically process the denoising trajectory in a largely uniform manner. However, we observe that the conditioning focus naturally shifts across denoising stages: early stages combine language instructions and visual observations to establish a coarse action trajectory, whereas later stages place greater emphasis on current visual observations for action alignment. Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce a reusable long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, while a lightweight refiner operates at a higher frequency to refine local action chunks using the latest observations. This design amortizes expensive high-level VLA computation while preserving frequent closed-loop correction. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk. More broadly, across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, StairVLA consistently reduces inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.

AI.tldr: StairVLA introduces a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework for VLA models that splits denoising into a high-level VLA for coarse long-horizon trajectories and a lightweight high-frequency refiner for local correction, improving success rates and cutting inference latency.
AI.motivation: Diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads in VLA models typically process the entire denoising trajectory uniformly. The authors observe that the conditioning focus actually shifts across denoising stages: early stages fuse language instructions and visual observations to form a coarse action trajectory, while later stages emphasize current visual observations for action alignment. This mismatch motivates a stage-aware, hierarchical approach.
AI.method: StairVLA uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce a reusable long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, while a lightweight refiner runs at higher frequency to refine local action chunks with the latest observations. This amortizes expensive high-level VLA computation while retaining frequent closed-loop correction.
AI.result: On LIBERO, a GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% and reduces amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk. Across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, StairVLA consistently lowers inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.
AI.conclusion: Stage-aware hierarchical action generation effectively exploits the shifting conditioning focus across denoising stages, enabling VLA models to achieve both higher task success and substantially lower inference latency, with consistent gains across backbones, benchmarks, and real-robot settings.

title: Representation Bias, Correction Transfer, and Resolution Sensitivity in Three-Dimensional Mitochondrial Morphometry
summary: Quantitative imaging pipelines can produce precise but systematically different measurements of the same object. We present an empirical reliability assessment of three-dimensional mitochondrial morphometry that connects representation bias, a controlled processing intervention, correction transfer, and resolution sensitivity. Using 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy, we find that occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average despite an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.994. Boundary analysis identifies an outward label displacement of 0.00304 normalized units. In a controlled label-pipeline reimplementation, removing the depth offset reduces volume error in all 55 analyzed objects by a mean of 1.57 percentage points, approximately 45% of mean reproduced inflation; the source of the remainder is not isolated. A frozen regression using occupancy-derived features reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664% in 2,728 previously unused objects from the same resource. However, its calibrated error bound covers only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in a low-occupancy subgroup, demonstrating that accuracy and uncertainty transfer must be evaluated separately. In 550 rat-cortex objects from the MitoEM resource, coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nanometers changes median surface area by minus 10.60% and sphericity by plus 11.76%, despite a rank correlation of 0.994. These results provide quantitative checks for distinguishing processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences, without establishing biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically assesses reliability of 3D mitochondrial morphometry, showing that pipelines produce precise but systematically biased measurements; representation bias is partly corrected by a controlled intervention, yet error-bound and resolution transfer remain incomplete.
AI.motivation: Quantitative imaging pipelines can yield precise but systematically different measurements of the same object, so processing-induced descriptor changes may be mistaken for biological differences; the authors aim to quantify these effects and provide reliability checks.
AI.method: Using 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy, they assess occupancy-derived versus reference mesh volumes, ICC, boundary displacement, and a controlled label-pipeline reimplementation removing a depth offset. They test frozen regression correction on 2,728 previously unused objects, evaluate calibrated error-bound coverage overall and in a low-occupancy subgroup, and analyze resolution sensitivity in 550 rat-cortex objects from MitoEM by coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nm.
AI.result: Occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average, with ICC 0.994 and outward label displacement of 0.00304 normalized units. Removing the depth offset reduces volume error in all 55 analyzed objects by a mean of 1.57 percentage points, about 45% of mean reproduced inflation. Frozen regression reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664% in 2,728 previously unused objects, but its calibrated error bound covers only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in the low-occupancy subgroup. In 550 MitoEM rat-cortex objects, coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nm changes median surface area by -10.60% and sphericity by +11.76%, despite a rank correlation of 0.994.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide quantitative checks to distinguish processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences, but they do not establish biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

title: Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization for Constrained Locomotion Planning
summary: Constrained Locomotion Planning (CLP) for quadrupeds and humanoids, where robots must satisfy collision avoidance, contact consistency, kinematic feasibility, and support constraints, is challenging under high-dimensional dynamics and highly non-convex environments. Recent Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) approaches recast trajectory optimization as posterior sampling over trajectories, using known dynamics and Monte Carlo rollouts to analytically estimate the denoising score function without demonstration learning. While constrained variants further incorporate feasibility into model-based score rollouts and show promising performance, they are still limited by (1) lacking a task-modulated active constraint geometry that shapes the score direction and reverse stochasticity, and (2) using deterministic DDPM-style reverse transport without adaptive scheduling across different generative transports.
