Therefore, we introduce Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization (2GO) for constrained locomotion, which turns active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators through normal- induced metric shaping, tangent-space stochastic filtering, and CFS-based retraction. 2GO further decouples generative transport from reverse stochasticity through an adaptive diffusion and flow-like schedule. Experiments on constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion demonstrate strong performance in discrete foothold selection and continuous posture planning, with higher success rates, fewer violations, and improved execution compatibility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization (2GO), which addresses limitations of constrained Model-Based Diffusion for legged locomotion by turning active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators and decoupling generative transport from reverse stochasticity.
AI.motivation: Constrained Locomotion Planning for quadrupeds and humanoids is difficult due to high-dimensional dynamics and non-convex environments requiring collision avoidance, contact consistency, kinematic feasibility, and support constraints. Existing constrained Model-Based Diffusion variants are limited: (1) they lack task-modulated active constraint geometry that shapes the score direction and reverse stochasticity, and (2) they use deterministic DDPM-style reverse transport without adaptive scheduling across different generative transports.
AI.method: 2GO converts active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators via normal-induced metric shaping, tangent-space stochastic filtering, and CFS-based retraction. It additionally decouples generative transport from reverse stochasticity through an adaptive diffusion and flow-like schedule.
AI.result: Experiments on constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion show strong performance in discrete foothold selection and continuous posture planning, achieving higher success rates, fewer violations, and improved execution compatibility.
AI.conclusion: 2GO improves constrained locomotion planning by integrating task-modulated constraint geometry into the denoising process and enabling adaptive scheduling, yielding more feasible and executable trajectories for quadruped and humanoid robots.

title: Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation with Cross-Platform User History
summary: Modern recommendation is shifting from platform-centric personalization toward user-governed personalization, where a personal LLM agent can act on the user's behalf across services. We formalize this emerging paradigm as Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation: a platform recommender ranks a candidate set using platform-local information, and a personal agent uses user-authorized cross-platform history to mediate the resulting ranking and produce the final top-K slate. Such mediation is nontrivial: the platform ranking can encode strong population evidence that the personal agent cannot observe, so effective mediation must therefore balance beneficial rescues against harmful overrides. To study this trade-off, we introduce MediateRec, a benchmark that includes scalable proxy cross-platform environments and a real cross-platform test under a controlled platform-agent information boundary. To train the agent to use cross-platform history effectively, we further propose Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization (PAMO), which counterfactually masks that history to estimate personal mediation support and reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor. We theoretically prove that PAMO preserves cutoff-level advantage mass and is locally optimal among first-order reallocations that preserve this mass without lowering average platform-relative value. Experiments on MediateRec show that personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, yet even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently improves over matched outcome-only RL across seen and unseen target platforms and on the real cross-platform test, while achieving a better rescue-harm balance.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation, introduces the MediateRec benchmark, and proposes PAMO to train a personal LLM agent to mediate platform rankings using cross-platform history while balancing beneficial rescues against harmful overrides.
AI.motivation: Recommendation is shifting from platform-centric personalization to user-governed personalization, where a personal LLM agent acts on the user's behalf across services. In this setting, mediation is nontrivial: the platform ranking encodes strong population evidence the agent cannot observe, so effective mediation must trade off beneficial rescues against harmful overrides.
AI.method: The authors formalize Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation, where a platform ranks candidates with platform-local information and a personal agent uses user-authorized cross-platform history to mediate the ranking into a final top-K slate. They build MediateRec, a benchmark with scalable proxy cross-platform environments and a real cross-platform test under a controlled platform-agent information boundary. They propose Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization (PAMO), which counterfactually masks cross-platform history to estimate personal mediation support and reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor.
AI.result: PAMO is theoretically proven to preserve cutoff-level advantage mass and to be locally optimal among first-order reallocations preserving that mass without lowering average platform-relative value. On MediateRec, personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, but even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently outperforms matched outcome-only RL across seen and unseen target platforms and on the real cross-platform test, with a better rescue-harm balance.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes personal-agent mediated recommendation as a formal paradigm and shows that principled mediation training can improve cross-platform correction while mitigating harmful overrides relative to outcome-only RL.

title: Multi-Robot Multi-Goal Motion Planning with Stochastic Skills
summary: As robots are increasingly deployed in groups and share workspaces to execute real-world tasks, planning their concurrent motions around complex manipulation skills becomes essential. These skills involve continuous physical execution and may exhibit stochastic behavior, resulting in variable execution times and uncertain continuous trajectories. Existing planners either limit execution to single-robot scenarios, rely on open-loop paths, or use post-hoc scheduling that prevents dynamic coordination. In this paper, we address this gap by integrating stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning by formulating the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite roadmap. For stochastic skills, solving the MDP yields a reactive policy that allows controllable robots to dynamically adapt their motions in response to other robots' execution of manipulation skills. By resolving skill uncertainty directly at planning time, this approach avoids the pessimism of conservative baselines and unlocks robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination. Code for the planners is available at https://www.vhartmann.com/stochastic-skills.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates stochastic manipulation skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning by formulating the problem as an MDP over a multi-modal composite roadmap, yielding a reactive policy that enables dynamic coordination.
AI.motivation: As robots are increasingly deployed in groups and share workspaces, planning concurrent motions around complex manipulation skills becomes essential. These skills involve continuous physical execution and may be stochastic, resulting in variable execution times and uncertain trajectories. Existing planners either limit execution to single-robot scenarios, rely on open-loop paths, or use post-hoc scheduling that prevents dynamic coordination.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite roadmap, integrating stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning. Solving the MDP for stochastic skills yields a reactive policy that allows controllable robots to dynamically adapt their motions in response to other robots' execution of manipulation skills.
AI.result: By resolving skill uncertainty directly at planning time, the approach avoids the pessimism of conservative baselines and unlocks robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination. Code for the planners is available at https://www.vhartmann.com/stochastic-skills.
AI.conclusion: Integrating stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning via an MDP formulation over a multi-modal composite roadmap enables robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination and overcomes the limitations of open-loop and post-hoc scheduling approaches.

title: LSC-DPO: Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a standard reward-model-free approach for aligning language models with preference data. However, as the scaled preference margin grows during training, the logistic DPO loss becomes progressively less sensitive to further changes. We study DPO from a loss-level geometric perspective and identify the sigmoid factor as a learning signal that characterizes the local sensitivity of the objective. Based on this view, we propose Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization (LSC-DPO), which dynamically regulates the learning signal near a target regime. A log-space analysis establishes conditions for stable tracking of the target learning-signal regime. Experiments on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH show that LSC-DPO consistently improves over DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines. We further find that different coefficient initializations induce distinct transient learning-signal trajectories even when their later signal levels become similar. Based on this observation, we derive a signal-budget compensation rule that adjusts the target learning signal to compensate for these transient differences. The resulting compensation substantially reduces performance variation across coefficient initializations.

AI.tldr: LSC-DPO treats the sigmoid factor in the DPO loss as a controllable learning signal that is dynamically regulated near a target regime, improving alignment performance and reducing sensitivity to coefficient initialization.
AI.motivation: In DPO training, as the scaled preference margin grows, the logistic loss becomes progressively less sensitive to further changes, weakening the learning signal. The paper aims to understand and control this local sensitivity from a loss-level geometric perspective.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret DPO's sigmoid factor as a learning signal characterizing local objective sensitivity, and propose Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization (LSC-DPO), which dynamically regulates this signal near a target regime. A log-space analysis establishes conditions for stable tracking of the target learning-signal regime. A signal-budget compensation rule is further derived to adjust the target learning signal, compensating for transient trajectory differences induced by different coefficient initializations.
AI.result: On AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH, LSC-DPO consistently outperforms DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines. The signal-budget compensation rule substantially reduces performance variation across different coefficient initializations.
AI.conclusion: Viewing DPO through a learning-signal lens enables effective control of the objective's sensitivity, yielding consistent gains and improved robustness to initialization choices.

title: CUSP: CUSUM-Governed Survival Hazard Alarms at the Perception Onset for Off-Road Navigation
summary: Off-road navigation exposes a robot to potentially hazardous terrain en route. Although learning-based navigation uses safety supervision to choose which path to drive, it provides no runtime alarm when the robot following that path is heading into danger. Such an alarm must be learned from field logs, where human intervention preempts the failure and the failure itself is therefore never observed. The human judges driving unsafe early but typically intervenes only once failure is clearly near, so the intervention marks that judgment late. That earlier judgment is what a runtime alarm must detect, yet no prior intervention-supervised method has targeted it. To address this problem, we introduce CUSP (CUSUM-governed Survival model of the Perception onset), a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm that learns this moment from intervention-terminated logs. "Cusp" is a word for the point at which one state is about to turn into another, and the moment we target is exactly such a cusp: the point at which safe driving turns unsafe in a human's judgment. We call this point the perception onset and annotate it separately from the intervention. A visual hazard head is trained on the annotated onset with a discrete-time survival objective so that driving with and without an onset both supervise the head, and a CUSUM accumulates the predicted onset risk into alarms. We evaluate CUSP at five unseen sites, two autonomous and three teleoperated, with 142 events and every method tuned to the same rate of ten false alarms per hour. CUSP detected 85 events compared to 26 for the best of nine adapted baselines, and the margin comes from hazards to which every signal in the navigation model is blind.

AI.tldr: CUSP is a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm for off-road navigation that learns the moment a human judges driving unsafe ("perception onset") from intervention-terminated logs, using a discrete-time survival head plus CUSUM accumulation, and detects 85/142 events vs. 26 for the best baseline at equal false-alarm rate.
AI.motivation: Off-road robots face hazardous terrain, and learning-based navigation selects safe paths but offers no runtime alarm when the robot on that path heads into danger. Such an alarm must be learned from field logs where human intervention preempts failure, so the failure is never observed. The human judges driving unsafe early but intervenes late, meaning the intervention marks that judgment belatedly; this earlier judgment is exactly what a runtime alarm must detect, yet no prior intervention-supervised method has targeted it.
AI.method: CUSP (CUSUM-governed Survival model of the Perception onset): a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm. A "perception onset" is annotated as the cusp where safe driving turns unsafe in human judgment, separately from the intervention. A visual hazard head is trained on the annotated onset with a discrete-time survival objective so that logs with and without an onset both supervise the head; a CUSUM then accumulates predicted onset risk into alarms.
AI.result: Evaluated at five unseen sites (two autonomous, three teleoperated) with 142 events, all methods tuned to ten false alarms per hour. CUSP detected 85 events versus 26 for the best of nine adapted baselines, with the margin coming from hazards to which every signal in the navigation model is blind.
AI.conclusion: CUSP provides an effective, model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm by supervising on the perception onset rather than the intervention, substantially outperforming adapted baselines and catching hazards invisible to the navigation model's signals.

title: Beyond Scalar IoU: Structured Verification from Rollout Groups for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a natural framework for adapting pretrained models to video temporal grounding, where generated temporal intervals can be scored directly against ground truth intervals. Yet existing overlap verifiers typically score each rollout independently, leaving the joint structure of the rollout group unused. We introduce SUTURE, which conditions verification on the rollout group and exploits its structure at two complementary scales: disagreement across rollouts controls how strongly the target is reweighted, while coverage at each position determines where reward mass is redistributed. We show that the resulting verifier admits an exact decomposition into the standard IoU term and a covariance correction determined by the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic finds a preference for responses covering relatively less supported target regions in the analyzed groups. Across five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE improves grounding performance at every reported IoU threshold. Its trained policy also shows less video-start anchoring in reasoning traces: for later events, the first temporal mention more often overlaps the annotated target. Together, these results show that the joint structure of a rollout group can support a more informative temporal verifier.

AI.tldr: SUTURE introduces a group-conditioned verifier for RLVR in video temporal grounding, using rollout disagreement for target reweighting and coverage for reward redistribution, decomposing exactly into standard IoU plus a covariance correction.
AI.motivation: Existing overlap verifiers in RLVR for video temporal grounding score each rollout independently, ignoring the joint structure of the rollout group, which limits the informativeness of the temporal reward signal.
AI.method: SUTURE conditions verification on the rollout group at two scales: disagreement across rollouts controls target reweighting, and coverage at each position determines reward mass redistribution. The verifier admits an exact decomposition into a standard IoU term plus a covariance correction governed by the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic is used to analyze response preferences.
AI.result: Across five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE improves grounding performance at every reported IoU threshold. The trained policy exhibits less video-start anchoring in reasoning traces, with the first temporal mention for later events more often overlapping the annotated target.
AI.conclusion: The joint structure of a rollout group can support a more informative temporal verifier, yielding consistent grounding gains and improved temporal reasoning behavior.

title: Beyond Retargeting: Low-Latency and Robust Humanoid Whole-Body Teleoperation with Learned Atomic Motion Primitives
summary: Humanoid whole-body teleoperation translates human motion into stable robot behavior in real time. Existing systems typically rely on online motion retargeting to bridge human--robot morphological differences, but this process adds latency and can produce physically infeasible targets. Meanwhile, diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations often fall outside the training distribution, potentially causing unstable robot behavior. We propose a retargeting-free policy that maps raw human motion directly to robot joint commands in a single forward pass, eliminating online kinematic adaptation. To improve robustness, we learn a codebook of full-body motion primitives that projects out-of-distribution observations onto plausible motion prototypes and recovers full-body motion from partial inputs. Experiments on a Unitree~G1 in simulation and on hardware, using virtual reality, optical mocap, text-to-motion generation, and monocular video inputs, show that our method outperforms baselines in latency and robustness.

AI.tldr: A retargeting-free policy maps raw human motion directly to humanoid robot joint commands in a single forward pass, using a learned codebook of motion primitives to robustly handle out-of-distribution and partial observations, achieving lower latency and higher robustness than baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid whole-body teleoperation systems rely on online motion retargeting to bridge human–robot morphological differences, but this adds latency and can generate physically infeasible targets. Additionally, diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations frequently fall outside the training distribution, risking unstable robot behavior.
AI.method: The authors propose a retargeting-free policy that directly maps raw human motion to robot joint commands in a single forward pass, eliminating online kinematic adaptation. To improve robustness, they learn a codebook of full-body motion primitives that projects out-of-distribution observations onto plausible motion prototypes and recovers full-body motion from partial inputs.
AI.result: Experiments on a Unitree G1 in simulation and on hardware—using VR, optical mocap, text-to-motion generation, and monocular video inputs—show the method outperforms baselines in latency and robustness.
AI.conclusion: A retargeting-free, codebook-based policy enables low-latency, robust humanoid whole-body teleoperation that handles out-of-distribution and partial motion observations more effectively than retargeting-based baselines.

title: VALSE: Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficient Inference in Large Language Models
summary: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for vertical adaptive layer skipping, proving three foundational results: (i) an Expected FLOPs formula (theorem 2) giving a closed-form expression for the computational cost of arbitrary per-sample skip schedules as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities; (ii) function-space superset (theorem 10) and strict inclusion (theorem 11) theorems showing that skip-layer models are strictly contained in---yet meaningfully approximate---the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example; and (iii) a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (proposition 6), positioning vertical depth-wise sparsity as the orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity. Building on this theory, we propose VALSE (Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficiency), a per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping method: a lightweight difficulty estimator scores each input from the first few layers, and per-layer gates selectively skip redundant layers---including arbitrary middle layers while retaining deeper ones---so that only the necessary depth is activated for each input, whose feasibility is preliminarily assessed at prototype scale.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for vertical adaptive layer skipping, proving an Expected FLOPs formula, function-space superset/strict-inclusion theorems relative to full-layer models, and a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts, then proposes VALSE, a per-sample non-contiguous layer skipping method driven by a lightweight difficulty estimator and per-layer gates.
AI.motivation: Existing work on adaptive computation largely explores horizontal (width-wise) sparsity via Mixture-of-Experts, leaving vertical (depth-wise) sparsity theoretically under-characterized. The paper aims to fill this gap by grounding per-sample layer skipping in formal theory and establishing its relationship to the full-layer function space and to MoE architectures.
AI.method: The authors derive three foundational theoretical results: (i) an Expected FLOPs formula (Theorem 2) giving a closed-form expression for computational cost of arbitrary per-sample skip schedules as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities; (ii) function-space superset (Theorem 10) and strict inclusion (Theorem 11) theorems showing skip-layer models are strictly contained in—yet meaningfully approximate—the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example; and (iii) a structural duality (Proposition 6) between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts, positioning vertical depth-wise sparsity as the orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity. Building on this theory, they propose VALSE, which uses a lightweight difficulty estimator scoring each input from the first few layers and per-layer gates that selectively skip redundant layers, including arbitrary middle layers while retaining deeper ones.
AI.result: The paper establishes the Expected FLOPs closed form, proves the strict inclusion of skip-layer models within the full-layer function space with an explicit separating example, and formalizes the VALSE–MoE duality. The VALSE method is described as enabling per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping so that only necessary depth is activated, with feasibility preliminarily assessed at prototype scale.
AI.conclusion: Vertical adaptive layer skipping is provided with a rigorous theoretical foundation linking skip schedules to FLOPs, function-space approximation, and MoE duality. VALSE operationalizes this theory as a per-sample, non-contiguous depth-sparsity method, positioning vertical depth-wise sparsity as the orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity, with prototype-scale evidence of feasibility.

title: From Model to Prototype: Design and Motor-Flap Propulsion Control of a Twin-Wing Metamorphic UAV
summary: This paper presents the design and control strategy for MetaMorpher, a metamorphic Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), capable of both spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise flight. Since control of the cruise configuration is comparatively well established in the literature, this paper focuses on control of the MetaMorpher in hover mode, building on the flight dynamics model and conceptual design validated in previous work. The control algorithm is implemented using one of two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in synchrony with the vehicle's rotation, or flap propulsion, a novel strategy that pulses the deflection of the wing-mounted elevons. We evaluate both strategies in simulation through different flight experiments. Simulation results confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, demonstrating flap propulsion as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model against the physical prototype, demonstrating very good steady-state agreement across different configurations.

AI.tldr: MetaMorpher is a metamorphic UAV that can spin its wings for hover and lock them into a fixed flying-wing for cruise. This paper develops hover-mode control using two phase-synchronized strategies—pulsing motor thrust or pulsing elevon deflection (flap propulsion)—validated in simulation and partly on a physical prototype.
AI.motivation: The cruise configuration of the MetaMorpher UAV is already well covered in the literature, so the control challenge lies in the hovering, spinning-wing mode. This work aims to provide a validated control approach for that under-addressed hover regime and to explore a lightweight alternative actuation strategy.
AI.method: Building on a previously validated flight dynamics model and conceptual design, the authors implement hover control with two phase-synchronized strategies: (1) motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in sync with the vehicle's rotation, and (2) flap propulsion, which pulses the deflection of wing-mounted elevons. Both strategies are evaluated through multiple simulated flight experiments.
AI.result: Simulations confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, with flap propulsion emerging as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing of the physical prototype validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model, showing very good steady-state agreement across different configurations.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that phase-synchronized control strategies enable stable hover control of MetaMorpher, and that flap propulsion offers a lightweight, decoupled option. The vertical-dynamics model is experimentally validated, supporting the design's feasibility, though broader flight testing remains for future work.

title: BioStudyBench: Evaluating Agents on Post-Cutoff Biomedical Studies
summary: We evaluate whether AI agents can match the reported findings of published biomedical studies using public data. Existing evaluations do not consistently separate analysis from prior knowledge or retrieval of the published answer. We introduce BioStudyBench, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon analysis tasks drawn from studies first published between July and September 2026, after the developer-reported knowledge cutoffs of the models we evaluate, semi-automatically filtered down from 404,019 PubMed records. In each task, the agent receives a neutral research question but no data files, so it must find and download the relevant public data, search the literature through tools that return only records dated before its cutoff, and report findings through data analysis. To measure gains over prior knowledge, we run every task both with and without access to data and tools. Across eight models, access to data and tools raises the pass rate by 47 percentage points on average over the no-data baseline. Open-weight models across sizes trail closed-weight models, with the best open-weight model passing 81.3% of tasks against 94.7% for the best closed-weight model.

AI.tldr: BioStudyBench evaluates whether AI agents can reproduce findings of recent biomedical studies using public data, showing that data/tool access boosts pass rates by 47 points on average, though open-weight models lag behind closed-weight ones.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI agents in biomedicine fail to cleanly separate genuine data analysis from prior knowledge or retrieval of already-published answers, making it unclear whether agents can truly conduct analyses matching published findings.
AI.method: The authors build BioStudyBench, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon analysis tasks derived from studies published between July and September 2026—after the models' knowledge cutoffs—semi-automatically filtered from 404,019 PubMed records. Agents receive a neutral research question with no data files, and must locate and download public data, search literature via tools limited to pre-cutoff records, and report findings via analysis. Each task is run with and without data/tool access to isolate gains over prior knowledge, across eight models.
AI.result: Access to data and tools raises the average pass rate by 47 percentage points over the no-data baseline. Open-weight models trail closed-weight models at all sizes, with the best open-weight model passing 81.3% of tasks versus 94.7% for the best closed-weight model.
AI.conclusion: Access to data and tools substantially improves agents' ability to reproduce reported biomedical findings beyond prior knowledge, but a performance gap persists between open-weight and closed-weight models.

title: PACE: Stage-Consistent Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Progress-Aligned Context for Execution
summary: Demonstration-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for specifying robot behavior, yet long-horizon manipulation remains difficult when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. We identify the resulting failure mode as stage confusion and introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful method that continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. PACE compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens and uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose its latent stage structure. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action-observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention, producing a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies. PACE improves success from 88.9% to 94.0% on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1% to 83.3% on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3% to 73.3% on the two-step Block Routing tasks. Failure analysis further indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion.

AI.tldr: PACE is a stateful, demonstration-conditioned policy that aligns a full demonstration with realized execution progress using fast-weight memory and dual-edge attention, resolving "stage confusion" in long-horizon manipulation without test-time stage labels.
AI.motivation: Demonstration-conditioned policies are a natural interface for robot behavior specification, but long-horizon manipulation fails when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions run at different speeds. The authors identify this failure mode as "stage confusion."
AI.method: PACE continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. It compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens, uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose latent stage structure, and during execution employs an episode-local fast-weight memory that causally encodes realized action-observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention. This yields a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert, requiring no test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies.
AI.result: Success improves from 88.9% to 94.0% on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1% to 83.3% on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3% to 73.3% on two-step Block Routing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Failure analysis indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion, validating PACE's stateful, progress-aligned design for long-horizon manipulation.

title: Explore, Then Commit: Measurement-Efficient Scientific Law Discovery with Language Models
comment: 19 pages, including Supplementary Material S1; code and data included as ancillary files. Preprint
summary: Scientific law discovery requires selecting measurements and converting evidence into a governing equation. We evaluate an explore-then-commit protocol in which a large language model proposes hypotheses, a programmatic planner gathers measurements, and a fresh prompt synthesizes the final law from fixed observations. The protocol combines structured probes, automatic numerical diagnostics, restricted measurement batches, and optional interpreter access. Across 576 NewtonBench trials, we compare eight configurations on 12 physics modules using GPT-4.1-mini and a medium-difficulty GPT-4.1 replication. On medium tasks, interpreter-enabled planners use 8.6 versus 22.5 measurements per trial for GPT-4.1-mini and 8.9 versus 43.0 for GPT-4.1. Their mean magnitude-based root-mean-squared logarithmic error falls from 2.514 to 0.202 and from 0.626 to 0.149, respectively. An additional audit retains incomplete and invalid submissions in a coverage-sensitive analysis. Observed symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent across modules, and random acquisition is competitive with disagreement scoring. Measurement savings occur in every module, but unequal batch constraints prevent attributing them solely to acquisition quality. These results support the complete protocol as a promising measurement-efficient configuration, while leaving its causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks unresolved.

AI.tldr: An explore-then-commit protocol where an LLM proposes hypotheses, a planner gathers measurements, and a fresh prompt synthesizes the law yields large measurement savings and lower error on NewtonBench, though symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent.
AI.motivation: Scientific law discovery requires selecting which measurements to take and converting evidence into a governing equation. The paper evaluates whether an LLM-driven, measurement-efficient protocol can do this well, and whether acquisition quality or interpreter access drives the observed benefits.
AI.method: An explore-then-commit protocol: a large language model proposes hypotheses, a programmatic planner gathers measurements, and a fresh prompt synthesizes the final law from fixed observations. It combines structured probes, automatic numerical diagnostics, restricted measurement batches, and optional interpreter access. Across 576 NewtonBench trials, eight configurations are compared on 12 physics modules using GPT-4.1-mini and a medium-difficulty GPT-4.1 replication, including a coverage-sensitive audit and a disagreement-vs-random acquisition comparison.
AI.result: On medium tasks, interpreter-enabled planners use 8.6 vs 22.5 measurements per trial (GPT-4.1-mini) and 8.9 vs 43.0 (GPT-4.1). Mean magnitude-based RMSLE falls from 2.514 to 0.202 and from 0.626 to 0.149, respectively. Measurement savings occur in every module. Symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent across modules, and random acquisition is competitive with disagreement scoring; unequal batch constraints prevent attributing savings solely to acquisition quality.
AI.conclusion: The complete protocol is a promising measurement-efficient configuration, but its causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks remain unresolved.

title: OpenWAM: An Open Framework for Composable World-Action Models
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://openwam.stanford.edu ; Code: https://github.com/OpenWAM/OpenWAM ; Code and project page released June 4, 2026. Equal contribution: Heng Yu, David D. Yuan, Juze Zhang
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with robot control, yet existing systems often vary the video backbone, interaction structure, supervision, and inference procedure simultaneously, making their design choices difficult to compare. We introduce OPENWAM, an open world-action modeling framework built around a common causal robot-video foundation and configurable video-action interaction. Starting from Wan2.2-5B, we perform causal robot-video pretraining on over 10,000 hours of video, then integrate an action expert through a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. OPENWAM achieves high success rates on four LIBERO suites and real-world bimanual tasks; robot-video training with causal adaptation improves VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%. The same configurable architecture naturally extends to inverse and forward dynamics, allowing us to study how counterfactual transitions improve independently trained dynamics models beyond demonstrations alone. When only the video predictor is adapted to a new task, a frozen local-context inverse dynamics model trained on counterfactual data and demonstrations achieves 84.0% mean success across four held-out LIBERO-90 tasks, compared with 47.0% for a full-context inverse model and 21.5% for a local-context model trained only on demonstrations. For forward dynamics, counterfactual supervision reduces RGB prediction error by 34.5% and raises outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% among 16 same-state outcomes. OPENWAM provides a common testbed for comparing WAM interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations.

AI.tldr: OPENWAM is an open world-action modeling framework with a shared causal robot-video foundation and configurable video-action interaction, serving as a testbed to compare WAM designs and study dynamics learning beyond demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models vary video backbone, interaction structure, supervision, and inference procedure simultaneously, making design choices hard to compare fairly; there is no common testbed for these designs or for studying dynamics learning from video beyond successful demonstrations.
AI.method: Built on Wan2.2-5B, the authors perform causal robot-video pretraining on over 10,000 hours of video, then integrate an action expert via a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. The architecture extends to inverse and forward dynamics, and counterfactual transitions are used as supervision.
AI.result: OPENWAM achieves high success on four LIBERO suites and real-world bimanual tasks; causal robot-video training raises VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%. With only the video predictor adapted, a frozen local-context inverse dynamics model trained on counterfactual data plus demonstrations reaches 84.0% mean success on four held-out LIBERO-90 tasks (vs 47.0% full-context, 21.5% demonstrations-only). Counterfactual supervision cuts forward-dynamics RGB error by 34.5% and raises outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% among 16 same-state outcomes.
AI.conclusion: OPENWAM offers a common testbed for comparing world-action model interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations.

title: Learning to Outgrow a Theory: Experimental Discovery Beyond the Initial Hypothesis Space
summary: Scientific discovery systems typically optimize experiments within a fixed hypothesis space. This creates a failure mode when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism: candidate disagreement can collapse even while the model class is systematically wrong. We formulate experimental model-class revision, in which a discovery policy jointly proposes a structural edit and a diagnostic experiment that tests whether that edit is necessary. The method couples a class-level distinguishability objective, in which one shared parameterization must explain all selected experiments, with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current class is rejected. On 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the joint policy reaches 89.5% exact recovery with a budget of 32 real experiments, improving the strongest matched baseline by 10.0 percentage points while requiring fewer executed experiments and candidate fits. The learned revision-experiment pairing transfers across unseen mechanism combinations, held-out but expressible primitives, parameter extrapolation, and shifted experiment costs; when the true mechanism is outside the edit grammar, it detects library insufficiency in 88% of cases with a 5.5% false-support rate. Revision gains also transfer to ODEBench and ODEBase model-library tasks, as well as DiscoverPhysics worlds. These results support a view of scientific discovery in which deciding what mechanisms a theory should make expressible and where to collect evidence are treated as a single sequential decision problem.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates experimental model-class revision, where a discovery policy jointly proposes structural edits to a hypothesis space and diagnostic experiments testing their necessity, achieving 89.5% exact recovery on controlled dynamical environments and detecting library insufficiency when the true mechanism lies outside the edit grammar.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery systems typically optimize experiments within a fixed hypothesis space, which fails when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism: candidate disagreement can collapse even while the model class is systematically wrong. This motivates treating the revision of what mechanisms a theory makes expressible and where to collect evidence as a single sequential decision problem.
AI.method: The method couples a class-level distinguishability objective, in which one shared parameterization must explain all selected experiments, with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current class is rejected. The discovery policy jointly proposes a structural edit and a diagnostic experiment that tests whether that edit is necessary.
AI.result: On 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the joint policy reaches 89.5% exact recovery with a budget of 32 real experiments, improving the strongest matched baseline by 10.0 percentage points while requiring fewer executed experiments and candidate fits. The learned revision-experiment pairing transfers across unseen mechanism combinations, held-out but expressible primitives, parameter extrapolation, and shifted experiment costs. When the true mechanism is outside the edit grammar, it detects library insufficiency in 88% of cases with a 5.5% false-support rate. Revision gains also transfer to ODEBench and ODEBase model-library tasks, as well as DiscoverPhysics worlds.
AI.conclusion: The results support a view of scientific discovery in which deciding what mechanisms a theory should make expressible and where to collect evidence are treated as a single sequential decision problem, with the joint policy outperforming fixed-hypothesis-space approaches and generalizing across varied tasks and conditions.

title: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Models to Unknown Visual Disruptions During Execution
summary: Visual disruptions can arise while a robot is executing a task, leaving a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. We introduce Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), which uses the leftover trajectory, the unexecuted part of the previous action chunk, as self-supervision for test-time adaptation. Because consecutive chunks overlap in time, the leftover provides a temporally aligned target for the current prediction over the same future control interval. At the onset of a visual shift, the leftover can retain a plan formed before the corruption, so updating the policy toward it anchors the adaptation across the shift (Transition Anchoring). SALT keeps the adapted policy and regenerates the current chunk, whose leftover becomes the target at the next replan, carrying the correction forward along the execution trajectory (Sequential Correction Propagation). Supervision comes entirely from the policy's own predictions, requiring no disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations, and a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin. On LIBERO-10, SALT increases average success across five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while largely preserving nominal performance. On a real robot, it raises task progress averaged over digital and physical disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61.

AI.tldr: SALT is a test-time adaptation method for VLA policies that uses the unexecuted leftover of the previous action chunk as a self-supervised target, enabling adaptation to visual disruptions without annotations or expert actions.
AI.motivation: Robots may encounter visual disruptions during task execution, and a VLA policy must respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. Existing adaptation approaches would typically require disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations.
AI.method: SALT treats the leftover trajectory (the unexecuted portion of the previous action chunk) as a temporally aligned self-supervision target for the current prediction over the same future control interval. At visual shift onset, the leftover can retain a pre-corruption plan, so updating toward it anchors adaptation across the shift (Transition Anchoring). The adapted policy regenerates the current chunk, and its leftover becomes the next target at replanning, propagating correction along the trajectory (Sequential Correction Propagation). A lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin.
AI.result: On LIBERO-10, SALT raises average success under five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while largely preserving nominal performance. On a real robot, it improves average task progress under digital and physical disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61.
AI.conclusion: SALT provides effective test-time adaptation for VLA policies under visual disruptions using only the policy's own predictions as supervision, requiring no disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations.

title: Measuring climate backlash in Twitter and Reddit archives: Lexical definitions, recorded responses and participant turnover
summary: Social media archives are often used to study resistance to climate action, but words, response counters and observed participants do not measure the same social process. We examine four supplied Twitter and Reddit archives by processing all registered files without sampling and applying transparent, non-exclusive lexical rules. The study links frame co-occurrence to source-specific temporal and response models, then separates event-period changes among returning authors from participant turnover. Renewable-energy terms accompany cost-related language on Reddit, yet narrower backlash phrases sharply reduce cross-source contrasts and reverse the sign of the Paris Agreement contrast in submissions. Cross-discourse history does not improve eligible primary-context forecasts. Denial/hoax terms are associated with higher recorded Twitter likes, whereas Reddit response associations depend on frame, outcome and author specification. Around the 2019 global climate strike, returning-author expression and participant turnover both contribute to increased protest-language shares. An archive endpoint prevents the corresponding Climate Twitter migration inference. Most crossed-cluster estimates lack released intervals, and joint author/month response covariance estimates fail, restricting formal inference. These results show how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields and observation boundaries shape what can be claimed about climate backlash. The contribution is an archive-based account of these measurement consequences, rather than a measure of individual opposition, persuasion or advocacy-induced backlash.

AI.tldr: This archive-based study of four supplied Twitter and Reddit climate corpora shows how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields, and observation boundaries shape what can be claimed about climate backlash, rather than measuring individual opposition or persuasion.
AI.motivation: Social media archives are frequently used to study resistance to climate action, but words, response counters, and observed participants do not capture the same social process. The authors aim to clarify the measurement consequences of operational choices.
AI.method: The authors process all registered files of four supplied Twitter and Reddit archives without sampling, applying transparent, non-exclusive lexical rules. They link frame co-occurrence to source-specific temporal and response models, and separate event-period changes among returning authors from participant turnover.
AI.result: Renewable-energy terms co-occur with cost language on Reddit, but narrower backlash phrases sharply reduce cross-source contrasts and reverse the sign of the Paris Agreement contrast in submissions. Cross-discourse history does not improve eligible primary-context forecasts. Denial/hoax terms associate with higher recorded Twitter likes, while Reddit response associations depend on frame, outcome, and author specification. Around the 2019 global climate strike, both returning-author expression and participant turnover raise protest-language shares. An archive endpoint blocks the corresponding Climate Twitter migration inference; most crossed-cluster estimates lack released intervals and joint author/month response covariance estimates fail.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers an archive-based account of how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields, and observation boundaries constrain claims about climate backlash, not a measure of individual opposition, persuasion, or advocacy-induced backlash.

title: Commit While Futures Agree: Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking for Robot Manipulation
summary: Action-chunking policies predict multi-step control sequences, but a fundamental question remains: how much of a predicted action chunk should be committed before replanning? Existing systems typically execute a fixed-length prefix, implicitly assuming that the same execution horizon remains trustworthy across states. Some adaptive methods estimate this horizon from the similarity or stability of predicted actions. However, different actions may lead to the same successful outcome, whereas similar actions can produce different futures, suggesting that commitment should be determined by agreement among imagined futures rather than by similarity in action space. To this end, we propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA$^3$C), an inference-time framework built on a simple principle: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge. Without modifying or retraining the base policy, CA$^3$C uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine the future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Using these imagined consequences, we formulate execution-horizon estimation as a Bayesian change-point inference problem and select the execution candidate through future consensus. Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA$^3$C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate over the corresponding base policies.

AI.tldr: CA$^3$C is an inference-time framework for action-chunking policies that adaptively decides how much of a predicted action chunk to execute, by committing while imagined futures agree and replanning when they diverge, via a Bayesian change-point formulation.
AI.motivation: Action-chunking policies predict multi-step control sequences, but it is unclear how much of a predicted chunk should be committed before replanning. Existing systems use a fixed-length prefix, assuming a static trustworthy horizon across states. Adaptive methods estimate the horizon from similarity or stability of predicted actions, yet this is flawed: different actions can yield the same outcome, and similar actions can produce different futures. Thus commitment should depend on agreement among imagined futures, not action-space similarity.
AI.method: The authors propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA$^3$C), an inference-time framework requiring no modification or retraining of the base policy. It uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Execution-horizon estimation is formulated as a Bayesian change-point inference problem, and the execution candidate is selected through future consensus.
AI.result: Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA$^3$C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate compared to the corresponding base policies.
AI.conclusion: Determining action-chunk commitment from agreement among imagined futures, rather than action-space similarity, provides an effective, retraining-free adaptive action-chunking strategy that substantially reduces failure rates across simulated and real robot manipulation tasks.

title: Learning Explainable Representations of Complex Game-playing Strategies
summary: As part of learning to play complex games, human players develop develop abstractions for concepts and strategies of gameplay consistent with game rules to improve their performance. These concepts are applied to explain other players' actions, and to inform their own actions in-game. Understanding other players' strategies is a crucial part of such improvement, but requires time and effort. In this paper, we propose a strategy similar to human cognition for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures based on sequences of gameplay actions. We present methods to automatically learn such programs to play chess and to solve tasks in a grid-based environment. We show that the learned strategies produce effective actions, and can be learned from gameplay data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a human-cognition-inspired approach for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures from sequences of gameplay actions, demonstrated on chess and a grid-based environment.
AI.motivation: Human players develop abstractions for concepts and strategies consistent with game rules to improve performance, using these to explain others' actions and inform their own. Understanding other players' strategies is crucial for improvement but is time- and effort-intensive. The paper aims to replicate this cognitive process in RL agents.
AI.method: The authors propose a strategy inspired by human cognition for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures, based on sequences of gameplay actions. They present methods to automatically learn such programs for playing chess and for solving tasks in a grid-based environment.
AI.result: The learned strategies produce effective actions and can be learned from gameplay data.
AI.conclusion: Synthesizing strategies as executable procedures from gameplay action sequences is a viable approach, yielding effective policies learnable directly from gameplay data.

title: IronMan: Information-Constrained Video-Action Learning for Robot Manipulation
summary: Video Action Models (VAMs) couple visual dynamics modeling with action generation for robot manipulation. However, video representations are not naturally suited to action generation, as exposing the action policy to excessive visual detail can impair its generalization ability. Therefore, we introduce IronMan (Information-constRained videO-actioN learning for robot MANipulation), a robust video-action learning framework built on the information bottleneck principle. The core principle of this framework is to impose information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues. IronMan employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong in-distribution (ID) performance and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness while maintaining efficient inference. IronMan achieves success rates of 99.0% on LIBERO and 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean, outperforming all the evaluated baselines. Under OOD shifts, IronMan achieves a success rate of 79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points. Project page: https://youngsoul0731.github.io/ironman-project-page/

AI.tldr: IronMan is an information-bottleneck-based video-action learning framework for robot manipulation that constrains one-step video features into compact world representations, achieving strong in-distribution performance and superior out-of-distribution robustness.
AI.motivation: Video Action Models couple visual dynamics modeling with action generation, but video representations are not naturally suited to action generation: exposing the action policy to excessive visual detail can impair its generalization ability. This motivates suppressing irrelevant visual information while retaining action-relevant dynamics cues.
AI.method: IronMan (Information-constRained videO-actioN learning for robot MANipulation) is built on the information bottleneck principle, imposing information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues. It employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show strong ID performance and OOD robustness with efficient inference. Success rates: 99.0% on LIBERO and 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean, outperforming all evaluated baselines. Under OOD shifts, 79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Applying information constraints to video-action learning yields compact, action-relevant representations that improve generalization and robustness in robot manipulation, as validated across simulation and real-world settings.

title: Towards the Automatic Synthesis of Interpretable Chess Tactics
summary: State-of-the-art reinforcement learning agents are capable of outperforming human experts at games like chess, Go and StarCraft II. These agents do not simply take advantage of their digital hardware in being able to react and calculate faster than humans, but employ better strategies that lead to more victories. Interpreting these strategies would give human players valuable insight into how to improve their play. In this preliminary work, we propose a symbolic sub-policy model for playing chess. Inspired by chess tactics, our model attempts to incorporate domain knowledge to improve interpretability. We adapt patterns learned by an inductive logic programming system called PAL to derive our model. We contribute a divergence metric to evaluate our model against a random baseline, and find a set of tactics that is able to suggest moves of similar playing strength to a human beginner. Finally, we propose a computational evaluation scheme for the model by augmenting an off-the-shelf engine with it.

AI.tldr: This preliminary work proposes a symbolic, interpretable sub-policy model for chess that incorporates tactical domain knowledge via patterns learned by the ILP system PAL, evaluates it with a divergence metric against a random baseline, and finds it suggests moves of human-beginner strength.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art RL agents beat human experts at chess, Go and StarCraft II not merely through faster computation but via superior strategies. Interpreting these strategies would give human players valuable insight into improving their play, yet such strategies remain hard to interpret.
AI.method: Inspired by chess tactics, the authors design a symbolic sub-policy model that encodes domain knowledge to improve interpretability. They adapt patterns learned by an inductive logic programming system called PAL to derive the model. They introduce a divergence metric to evaluate the model against a random baseline, and propose a computational evaluation scheme that augments an off-the-shelf engine with the model.
AI.result: Using the divergence metric, the derived set of tactics is found to suggest moves of playing strength similar to that of a human beginner.
AI.conclusion: A symbolic, tactic-based sub-policy derived from PAL patterns offers an interpretable chess model with human-beginner-level move suggestions; future work will use the proposed engine-augmentation evaluation scheme to assess it computationally.

title: Reactive Task-Oriented Robot-Human Handovers via Generative Hypothesis Selection
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
summary: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.

AI.tldr: GENESIS-Handover uses VLM image generation to synthesize task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses, matches them in real time to observed human hand poses, and infers the best handover configuration for task-oriented robot-human handovers.
AI.motivation: Human handovers embed both geometric and semantic cues (e.g., passing a knife by the handle). Existing state-of-the-art methods moved from object geometry to affordances but typically omit explicit, task-specific hand poses, despite many objects supporting multiple interaction modalities (e.g., a claw hammer for striking or pulling). This variability must be modeled for robust task-oriented handovers.
AI.method: The proposed approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), leverages VLM image generation to produce diverse task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These generated hypotheses are matched in real time against the observed human hand pose, allowing inference of the most suitable handover configuration. VLMs act as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, yielding task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs.
AI.result: The standalone interaction proposal module was evaluated before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived the method as having better task understanding than the previous state of the art.
AI.conclusion: GENESIS-Handover shows that generative VLM priors can produce task-conditioned handover strategies for unseen object-task pairs, improving perceived task understanding over prior state-of-the-art methods and supporting robust task-oriented robot-human handovers.

title: Matching Object or Relation? Tracing Abstract Reasoning Inside VLMs
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel on visual benchmarks but fail systematically on tasks requiring abstract reasoning. Existing benchmarks document this failure but cannot say \emph{why} it happens or which cognitive capability is missing. We close this gap by adopting the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology and pairing it with a mechanistic analysis of the model's internals. On a parametrically controlled stimulus set evaluated across frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3), we identify four levers that shift VLMs toward the relational match---capability tier, model scale, the number of objects per scene, and the absence of per-object stimulus noise---together producing a developmental-like trajectory that mirrors the human \emph{relational shift}. Opening up the model, a per-layer representational similarity analysis and a causal mediation analysis reveal that VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by two competing circuits: an early circuit that organises images by their surface object features, and a late circuit that organises them by their abstract relation. Extending the analysis to ARC-AGI-1, we find that ablating the relational heads identified on RMTS degrades performance more than ablating random heads, indicating that the relational circuit is recruited beyond our controlled stimuli. We hope this mechanism-level view serves as a step toward understanding how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the Relational Match-to-Sample paradigm plus mechanistic interpretability to explain why VLMs fail at abstract reasoning, identifying four factors that drive a developmental-like relational shift and uncovering two competing circuits (surface-feature vs. abstract-relation) in the model.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks show VLMs fail on abstract reasoning but cannot explain why or which cognitive capability is missing. This gap between documenting failure and understanding its mechanism motivates a cognitive-paradigm-driven, internals-level investigation.
AI.method: Adopts the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative/developmental psychology with a parametrically controlled stimulus set. Evaluates frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3). Applies per-layer representational similarity analysis and causal mediation analysis to probe model internals, then extends to ARC-AGI-1 via head ablation.
AI.result: Four levers shift VLMs toward the relational match: capability tier, model scale, number of objects per scene, and absence of per-object stimulus noise, together producing a developmental-like trajectory mirroring the human relational shift. Mechanistic analysis reveals two competing circuits: an early circuit organizing images by surface object features and a late circuit organizing by abstract relation. Ablating relational heads identified on RMTS degrades ARC-AGI-1 performance more than ablating random heads.
AI.conclusion: VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by competing surface-feature and relational circuits, with the relational circuit recruited beyond controlled stimuli. This mechanism-level view is a step toward understanding how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs.

title: Vector Map Quality Metrics for Contextual Autonomous Driving Systems
summary: Ensuring safety in autonomous driving requires continuous map maintenance supported by reliable quality indicators. In this context, it is crucial to identify when and where map updates should be triggered, for instance through crowdsourced data, and under which conditions a new map compilation should be deployed. This paper focuses on effective metrics for assessing the quality of vector maps and guiding such decisions. We present a new metric called GOSPAM designed to measure map discrepancies in terms of location errors, existence, and completeness. Through detailed simulations on both point and polyline feature maps, we analyze its sensitivity to common map degradation such as bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors. The results demonstrate that GOSPAM offers a unified and interpretable measure that effectively captures various forms of map deviation, making it a strong candidate for map quality assessment in automotive applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GOSPAM, a unified metric for assessing vector map quality in autonomous driving by capturing location errors, existence, and completeness, validated through simulations on point and polyline maps.
AI.motivation: Continuous map maintenance is essential for autonomous driving safety, requiring reliable quality indicators to decide when and where map updates should be triggered and when a new map compilation should be deployed. Existing needs call for effective metrics to assess vector map quality and guide these decisions.
AI.method: The authors propose GOSPAM, a new metric designed to measure map discrepancies in terms of location errors, existence, and completeness. They conduct detailed simulations on both point and polyline feature maps and analyze the metric's sensitivity to common map degradations such as bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors.
AI.result: GOSPAM provides a unified and interpretable measure that effectively captures various forms of map deviation, showing sensitivity to bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors across point and polyline feature maps.
AI.conclusion: GOSPAM is a strong candidate for map quality assessment in automotive applications, supporting decisions on map update triggering and new map compilation deployment.

title: Where Rules End and Judges Begin: Measuring the Judgment Boundary in Multi-Agent Systems Security
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, often encountering adversarial content. Current defenses for MAS are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which can lead to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. This study organizes defenses into five principles, implementing them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment), which includes a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. In independent testing across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%, with 78% of blocked attacks handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain, illustrating that the rules provide security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges manage those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, such as a risk-score approval gate that inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, highlighting the challenges in assessing threats accurately.

AI.tldr: The paper structures multi-agent system (MAS) defenses into five principles and implements them as DEFER1, a deterministic-first cascade of 28 checks with residual referral to a four-judge panel, cutting attack success rates from ~30% to ~3% across four domains.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, and thus frequently encounter adversarial content. Existing MAS defenses are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which leads to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes and leaves defenses untested against the broader threat landscape.
AI.method: The study organizes defenses into five principles and implements them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment). DEFER1 is a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it deterministically can and refers the remainder to a panel of four judges. It is evaluated via independent testing across four domains, with measurement of attack success rates, the share of blocks handled deterministically, and the proportion of proposals reaching judges.
AI.result: Across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%. Deterministic checks handle 78% of blocked attacks, and only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain. Both systems exhibit weaknesses: a risk-score approval gate inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, underscoring the difficulty of accurate threat assessment.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic rules secure against attacks that violate clear policies, while judges manage cases that only misrepresent intent. The division of labor is effective overall, but residual weaknesses, notably the unreliable risk-score approval gate, highlight the ongoing challenge of assessing threats accurately.

title: Navigation with RF Cues: Embodied Perception Action under Multipath Uncertainty
summary: Smart factory inspection requires robots to reach connected equipment without a prior map or known target coordinates. Radio frequency (RF) signals from the target can provide directional cues to complement visual observations when occlusion or poor lighting limits target detection. However, multipath propagation can distort these cues, making it difficult to infer the target's true direction from instantaneous RF measurements. To enable navigation research under these conditions, we first construct a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark that uses detailed scene geometry and assigned material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations in response to robot actions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an uncertainty aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty from a history of RF, visual, and pose observations. These estimates inform action selection alongside visual context. Experiments in unseen scenes show relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the strongest evaluated baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark for RF-visual navigation in smart factory inspection and proposes an uncertainty-aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty, achieving +18.2% SR and +11.5% SPL over the strongest baseline in unseen scenes.
AI.motivation: Smart factory inspection robots must reach connected equipment without a prior map or known target coordinates. RF signals from the target offer directional cues that complement vision when occlusion or poor lighting limits target detection, but multipath propagation distorts instantaneous RF measurements, complicating inference of the true target direction. Navigation research under these conditions lacks a suitable benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark that leverages detailed scene geometry and assigned material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations in response to robot actions. On this benchmark, they propose an uncertainty-aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty from a history of RF, visual, and pose observations; these estimates inform action selection together with visual context.
AI.result: Experiments in unseen scenes show relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and uncertainty-aware multimodal framework enable effective RF-visual navigation for smart factory inspection, improving SR and SPL in unseen scenes over the strongest evaluated baseline.

title: Massive Activation Gating Channel in Large Language Models
summary: Massive activations, a phenomenon in which a small number of hidden channels exhibit exceptionally large magnitudes, are pervasive in large language models (LLMs). However, the mechanism by which a token develops massive activations as it propagates through a pretrained LLM remains poorly understood. In this paper, we find that the emergence of massive activations is controlled by a single channel in the input embedding to a spike feed-forward network (FFN). The position of this channel is fixed for a particular LLM. We name this channel the massive activation gating channel (MAGC). When the value of the MAGC is sufficiently large (or small, depending on the LLM), the output of the spike FFN exhibits massive activations. Examining six LLMs across four model families and different model sizes, we verify the existence and effect of MAGC. We further provide a theoretical explanation of the mechanism by which MAGC induces massive activations. When the value of MAGC is sufficiently large (or small), the output of a spike FFN asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form that mixes a few columns of the down-projection matrix of the FFN. Since these columns exhibit the shape of massive activations, the output therefore exhibits massive activations.
