AI.tldr: Massive activations in LLMs are gated by a single, position-fixed channel in the spike FFN's input, termed the massive activation gating channel (MAGC); when MAGC's value is extreme, the FFN output asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form mixing a few down-projection columns, producing massive activations. Verified across six LLMs/four families.
AI.motivation: Massive activations—a few hidden channels with exceptionally large magnitudes—are pervasive in LLMs, yet how a token develops them while propagating through a pretrained LLM is poorly understood. The paper aims to identify the controlling mechanism.
AI.method: The authors trace the emergence of massive activations to the input embedding of a spike feed-forward network (FFN). They identify a single fixed channel, the massive activation gating channel (MAGC), whose sufficiently large (or small, model-dependent) value triggers massive activations in the FFN output. They test this on six LLMs across four model families and different sizes, and provide a theoretical analysis.
AI.result: The existence and effect of MAGC are confirmed across six LLMs spanning four model families and multiple sizes. Theoretically, when MAGC's value is extreme, the spike FFN output asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form that mixes a few columns of the FFN's down-projection matrix; because these columns exhibit the shape of massive activations, the output inherits them.
AI.conclusion: Massive activations are governed by a single fixed channel (MAGC) at the spike FFN input, with a quadratic-form asymptotic explanation linking that channel to the down-projection columns. This offers a mechanistic account of how tokens develop massive activations in pretrained LLMs.

title: Reactive Exploration of Unknown Environments for Redundant Robots using Virtual Model Control
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures, This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The exploration of confined, occluded, and partially known spaces poses significant challenges in robotic manipulation. The overall pose of the robotic arm must be carefully controlled to respect tight geometric constraints while avoiding newly discovered obstacles. We address this problem by proposing an active exploration approach for redundant robotic arms with an eye-in-hand camera configuration. Our approach navigates and acquires information in real-time based on a novel scoring method that directly selects a target voxel from the unexplored space using the robot's current state and expected information gain. To move the robot safely toward the target voxel, we utilize Virtual Model Control, which guarantees compliance and enables whole-body reactive obstacle avoidance without the need for path replanning. Simulated and real-robot experiments in both confined and open environments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving over $90\%$ mapping coverage across all tested environments in under $120$ seconds without colliding with obstacles.

AI.tldr: A novel active exploration method for redundant robot arms with eye-in-hand cameras that navigates confined/occluded spaces using voxel-based information gain scoring and Virtual Model Control for compliant, reactive obstacle avoidance without path replanning.
AI.motivation: Exploring confined, occluded, and partially known spaces is challenging in robotic manipulation. The robot arm's pose must be precisely controlled to satisfy tight geometric constraints while avoiding newly discovered obstacles, which is difficult with conventional planning approaches.
AI.method: The approach performs real-time exploration using a novel scoring method that directly selects a target voxel from unexplored space based on the robot's current state and expected information gain. To move safely toward the target voxel, the method employs Virtual Model Control, which guarantees compliance and enables whole-body reactive obstacle avoidance without path replanning.
AI.result: Simulated and real-robot experiments in confined and open environments achieved over 90% mapping coverage in all tested environments within under 120 seconds without colliding with obstacles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed active exploration approach is effective for redundant robot arms in confined and open spaces, providing safe, high-coverage, and time-efficient exploration without collisions.

title: EIO-Agents: The Missing Semantic Layer for AI Agent Evaluation
summary: AI agents are entering production in increasingly consequential environments without a shared semantic standard for what their evaluations actually mean. Scores, traces, judge outputs, and multi juror findings are increasingly used to justify readiness and release decisions, yet they often do not specify what evidence supports a claim, what that evidence can establish, or how the claim leads to a decision. We introduce EIO-Agents, an open specification for interoperable AI agent evaluation built on two layers. The Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) provides the semantic layer through typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and PASS, REVIEW, or BLOCK decisions. The Portable Evaluation Record (PER) provides the system of record: a canonical, content addressed representation of one evaluation that preserves the evidence to decision chain and can be re derived, explained, and verified. Scores summarize, juries interpret, and traces record, but none of them define what the evidence means or what it can prove. EIO provides that missing semantic contract, while PER preserves the resulting evaluation as a portable and verifiable system of record. As AI agents assume greater operational responsibility, evaluation must become more than a collection of scores and verdicts; it must become an accountable artifact whose meaning, evidence, limitations, and decisions can be independently checked.

AI.tldr: EIO-Agents is an open specification for interoperable AI agent evaluation, comprising a semantic layer (Evaluation Intelligence Ontology, EIO) and a system of record (Portable Evaluation Record, PER), to make evaluation an accountable, verifiable artifact.
AI.motivation: AI agents are being deployed in high-stakes production environments without a shared semantic standard for evaluation. Existing artifacts (scores, traces, judge outputs, multi-juror findings) are used to justify readiness and release decisions but fail to specify supporting evidence, what it establishes, or how it maps to a decision.
AI.method: The framework has two layers: (1) the Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO), a semantic layer with typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and PASS/REVIEW/BLOCK decisions; (2) the Portable Evaluation Record (PER), a canonical, content-addressed representation of a single evaluation that preserves the evidence-to-decision chain and supports re-derivation, explanation, and verification.
AI.result: The specification supplies the missing semantic contract that scores, juries, and traces lack, and preserves each evaluation as a portable, verifiable system of record that can be independently re-derived and checked.
AI.conclusion: As AI agents take on greater operational responsibility, evaluation must transcend collections of scores and verdicts and become an accountable artifact whose meaning, evidence, limitations, and decisions are independently checkable.

title: Energy-Aware Path Following: Comparative Analysis of Reinforcement Learning and NMPC for Electric Vehicles
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, currently submitted for review at the journal (Robotics and Autonomous Systems) https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/robotics-and-autonomous-systems
summary: Path-following control strategies typically follow the bi-objective optimization dilemma: minimizing deviations from a reference path while maintaining smooth speed profiles. The latter objective is especially relevant for Electric Vehicles (EVs), since their limited driving range can be extended by recovering energy through regenerative braking, a feature that has not yet been sufficiently studied in the literature. In this work, we perform a comparative analysis of four controllers under one common Frenet frame-based kinematic vehicle model, utilizing a validated energy model (VT-CPEM) with explicit regenerative braking. Herein, we implement the following controllers: Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), gain-scheduled Ackermann state-feedback baseline (PID-SF), and a Stanley geometric baseline. To satisfy real-time requirements, we implement the NMPC using JIT-compiled CasADi. Moreover, we train the PPO using traditional straight and S-curve tracks, after which we successfully transfer the unmodified policy to unseen tracks, including: an ISO 3888-1 lane-change, a chicane, randomly-generated parameterized-splines, and a $\pm3^\circ$ graded road. In addition, the policy transfers to a dynamic single-track vehicle model with linear tires, zero-shot with an acceptable initial performance, which was optimized after brief fine-tuning. Thereby, we demonstrate that our PPO is readily transferable to more comprehensive vehicle models. We conclude with a performance analysis of developed controllers and discuss ideas for future work.

AI.tldr: This paper compares four path-following controllers—NMPC, PPO, a gain-scheduled Ackermann PID state-feedback baseline, and a Stanley geometric baseline—on a Frenet-frame kinematic vehicle model using the VT-CPEM energy model with explicit regenerative braking, finding that PPO transfers well to unseen tracks and even to a dynamic vehicle model.
AI.motivation: Path-following control involves a bi-objective trade-off between minimizing path deviation and maintaining smooth speed profiles. The latter matters particularly for EVs, whose limited range can be extended via regenerative braking energy recovery—an aspect insufficiently studied, especially regarding how controllers affect energy recuperation.
AI.method: A comparative analysis of four controllers (NMPC, PPO, gain-scheduled Ackermann state-feedback baseline PID-SF, and a Stanley geometric baseline) under a shared Frenet frame-based kinematic vehicle model, using the validated VT-CPEM energy model with explicit regenerative braking. NMPC is implemented with JIT-compiled CasADi for real-time requirements; PPO is trained on straight and S-curve tracks.
AI.result: The unmodified PPO policy transfers to unseen tracks—an ISO 3888-1 lane-change, a chicane, randomly-generated parameterized splines, and a ±3° graded road—and also transfers zero-shot to a dynamic single-track vehicle model with linear tires with acceptable initial performance, improved after brief fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: PPO is readily transferable to more comprehensive vehicle models, and the work concludes with a performance analysis of the developed controllers and ideas for future work.

title: BluffJAX: Adversarial Imperfect Information Games in JAX
summary: We introduce BluffJAX: an open-source suite of adversarial imperfect information games in JAX. We provide canonical implementations of games designed for high simulation throughputs and parallelization on GPU accelerators. Our suite consists of well-studied benchmarks such as Texas Hold'Em Poker and Kuhn Poker, as well as games that have not been previously studied in reinforcement learning research, such as Bluff, Stud Poker, and Kemps. We hope that implementing a variety of game mechanics and difficulties will introduce new challenges and foster novel research directions in game-theoretic methods for RL. We benchmark the throughput performance and memory usage of our environments in single and multi-GPU settings, demonstrating scaling of up to hundreds of millions of samples per second, and motivating the usage of BluffJAX over related GPU and CPU-based libraries. We benchmark reinforcement learning, tree search, and game-solving algorithms in JAX in order to provide users with baseline results and facilitate future comparisons.

AI.tldr: BluffJAX is an open-source JAX suite of adversarial imperfect information games with canonical, high-throughput GPU-parallel implementations of benchmarks (Texas Hold'Em, Kuhn Poker) and novel games (Bluff, Stud Poker, Kemps), plus throughput/memory benchmarks and RL, tree-search, and game-solving baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing libraries lack GPU-optimized, unified implementations of adversarial imperfect information games, and several game mechanics/difficulties remain unstudied in RL, limiting both simulation throughput and the diversity of research challenges in game-theoretic RL.
AI.method: The authors build BluffJAX in JAX with canonical implementations designed for high simulation throughputs and parallelization on GPU accelerators. The suite spans well-studied benchmarks (Texas Hold'Em Poker, Kuhn Poker) and previously unstudied games (Bluff, Stud Poker, Kemps). They benchmark environment throughput and memory usage in single- and multi-GPU settings, and benchmark reinforcement learning, tree search, and game-solving algorithms in JAX to establish baselines.
AI.result: The environments scale up to hundreds of millions of samples per second in single- and multi-GPU settings, with accompanying memory usage measurements. Baseline results are provided for RL, tree search, and game-solving algorithms in JAX, enabling future comparisons and motivating BluffJAX over related GPU- and CPU-based libraries.
AI.conclusion: BluffJAX offers a diverse, high-throughput GPU-parallel suite of imperfect information games with baselines, intended to introduce new challenges and foster novel research directions in game-theoretic methods for RL.

title: AutodidactWAM: Cross-Modal Self-Distillation from Generated Video to Robot Actions
summary: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.

AI.tldr: Adapting a world-action model to a new humanoid reveals a video-action asymmetry: generated video looks plausible but co-generated actions are mis-targeted. AutodidactWAM recovers actions from the generated video via a teleoperation-free hand-pose estimator plus IK, then self-distills with DPO+SFT+DTW, boosting closed-loop success from ~7-17% to 42-90% across pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place.
AI.motivation: World-action models (e.g., Cosmos 3) jointly generate future video and robot actions, but LoRA fine-tuning one to a previously unseen robot (Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands) exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted, limiting real-robot utility.
AI.method: AutodidactWAM: a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, operated on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. These recovered actions, paired with the native prediction, serve as preferred targets for fine-tuning only action-related layers, with the generated video teacher-forced. Supervised relabeling is compared against a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO; the best hybrid objective combines preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW). One-time embodiment adaptation enables self-distillation without additional task-specific teleoperation.
AI.result: Native action succeeds ~17%, 10%, 7% (pre-grasp, grasp, pick-and-place), worse on held-out objects. Recovered-action gate reaches ~75%, 47%, 42%. DPO+SFT+DTW best: on Oreo (training object) 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Video-action asymmetry in WAMs can be corrected by recovering actions from generated video and self-distilling into action layers. Gains stem from the combination of training objectives (DPO+SFT+DTW) rather than the contrastive objective alone, since Flow-DPO with perfect preference accuracy still fails. Once embodiment adaptation is done, no additional task-specific teleoperation is required.

title: On the Boundary of Admission Gates: An Injected-Truth Study of Falsification-First Selection in Quantitative Strategy Research
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code and data to reproduce every result: https://github.com/simplify23/quant-trading-agent
summary: Strategy research conflates two problems: finding a profitable rule, and establishing that the finding is not search luck. The latter calls for admission gates -- statistical criteria that must be satisfied before a conclusion is adopted -- yet whether gates work, and at what cost, remains untested. We introduce an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control that adopts at the same rate as the gate; only if the gate beats this control does it carry information rather than merely raise a threshold. Across synthetic and real-calibrated panels, gates eliminate false discoveries in the weak-signal regime but cut adoption to 1--7%, and add nothing when signals are strong. Most importantly, criteria computed on absolute rather than excess returns silently reject every candidate, including true signals. Keywords: multiple testing, backtest overfitting, strategy admission, injected-truth validation, excess returns, false discovery rate

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether statistical admission gates for trading strategies genuinely filter search luck, using an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control. Gates eliminate false discoveries only in weak-signal regimes at severe adoption costs, and absolute-return criteria reject all candidates including true signals.
AI.motivation: Strategy research conflates two distinct problems: identifying a profitable rule and demonstrating that the finding is not merely the product of search luck (multiple testing/backtest overfitting). Admission gates—statistical criteria required before adopting a conclusion—are widely proposed to address the latter, but their actual effectiveness and cost have never been empirically tested.
AI.method: The authors introduce an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control. The control adopts candidates at the same rate as the gate under test; a gate only carries genuine information—rather than merely raising the adoption threshold—if it outperforms this rate-matched control. Evaluation spans synthetic and real-calibrated panels, and the analysis contrasts criteria computed on absolute versus excess returns.
AI.result: Across synthetic and real-calibrated panels, gates eliminate false discoveries in the weak-signal regime but reduce adoption to 1–7%; they add nothing when signals are strong. Critically, criteria computed on absolute rather than excess returns silently reject every candidate, including true signals.
AI.conclusion: Whether an admission gate works cannot be inferred from its rejection behavior alone; it must be benchmarked against a rate-matched random-admission control. Gates offer limited value—effective only in weak-signal regimes and at high adoption cost—and return-measurement choices (absolute vs. excess returns) can silently invalidate the entire gating procedure.

title: iGPC: Generative Motion Priors for Object-Aware Humanoid Interaction
summary: Humanoid robots operating in unstructured environments must combine robust whole-body control with the ability to perceive and physically interact with surrounding objects. While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for natural and versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains challenging. To address this bottleneck, we propose a framework that extends the recently proposed Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction. First, we adapt GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information. These experts leverage the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors, including reaching toward objects, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. Second, we introduce a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from the experts using onboard sensory observations. To bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, we propose two complementary training objectives that enable effective adaptation of the pretrained motion prior during distillation. Notably, our experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction, using interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance and privileged states, then distilling these skills into a perception-driven student policy with onboard sensing via two complementary training objectives.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots in unstructured environments need both robust whole-body control and the ability to perceive and physically interact with objects. Although large-scale human motion data offers strong priors for natural, versatile humanoid control, transferring these priors to perception-driven object interaction remains difficult.
AI.method: The framework first adapts GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information, leveraging the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors such as reaching toward objects, grasping supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. It then introduces a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from experts using onboard sensory observations. Two complementary training objectives bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, enabling adaptation of the motion prior during distillation.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks show that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interaction in contact-rich real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale generative human motion priors can be effectively transferred to perception-driven humanoid object interaction, yielding deployable policies for contact-rich real-world settings.

title: AgentMemGate: Addressing Speculation Contamination in Conversational Assistant Memory
comment: Accepted at the PALM Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 15 pages, 4 figures
summary: Conversational AI assistants with long-term memory extract facts from user messages into a store consulted in later conversations. A stated plan can enter that store as fact: a user who might move to Seattle may be recorded as already living there. We call this speculation contamination. Final-state memory benchmarks miss this error because they do not probe intermediate state and include few unresolved speculations. We present AgentMemGate, a write-time gate for profile-store memory that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other. Speculations remain outside memory, with conditions governing later promotion or deletion. We also contribute a dataset of multi-session conversations in which plans are confirmed, abandoned, or left unresolved. On our 147-conversation held-out set, Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination relative to the identical ungated pipeline (87.5% to zero for the most exposed extraction style) and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the harder held-out set, gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% and task accuracy rises by 9 to 13 percentage points. Our analysis identifies field matching as the main remaining bottleneck: realistic speculations often match no profile field and never reach the gate. We release our datasets, prompts, and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "speculation contamination"—long-term memory systems recording unconfirmed user plans as established facts—and proposes AgentMemGate, a write-time gating mechanism that classifies extracted statements and prevents speculations from entering profile memory.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI assistants with long-term memory extract facts from user messages into a store consulted in later conversations. A stated plan can erroneously enter that store as fact—e.g., a user who might move to Seattle may be recorded as already living there. Final-state memory benchmarks miss this error because they do not probe intermediate state and include few unresolved speculations.
AI.method: The authors present AgentMemGate, a write-time gate for profile-store memory that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other. Speculations remain outside memory, carrying conditions that govern later promotion or deletion. They also contribute a dataset of multi-session conversations in which plans are confirmed, abandoned, or left unresolved.
AI.result: On a 147-conversation held-out set, Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination relative to the identical ungated pipeline (87.5% to zero for the most exposed extraction style) and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the harder held-out set, gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% and task accuracy rises by 9 to 13 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: AgentMemGate effectively eliminates speculation contamination in profile-store memory, substantially improving task accuracy. Analysis identifies field matching as the main remaining bottleneck: realistic speculations often match no profile field and never reach the gate. Datasets, prompts, and evaluation code are released.

title: Beyond Waypoint Regression: Query-Based Cost Learning over Reachable Ego Futures for End-to-End Driving
comment: Accepted in the 18th Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV 2026)
summary: End-to-end planners based on waypoint regression achieve strong open-loop accuracy, but they primarily learn to mimic expert geometry and remain difficult to adapt to deployment-time safety constraints. We propose a query-based cost-learning framework that estimates bounded costs for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries, rather than dense BEV cells or a small regressed trajectory set. Compact joint scene tokens capture coherent multimodal agent futures, while contingency-aware cost aggregation and cost-guided intra-cluster MPPI mixing convert the learned cost topology into feasible ego plans. On nuScenes, our method improves over prior cost-estimation planners such as ST-P3 and NMP, outperforms most regression baselines in collision rate, while remaining competitive in L2, and retaining an interpretable cost interface. On real-world driving logs, the proposed planner reduces collision rates compared with SparseDrive and Alpamayo without fine-tuning, while maintaining a diverse set of candidate trajectories.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a query-based cost-learning planner that estimates bounded costs for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries, using joint scene tokens for multimodal agent futures and contingency-aware aggregation with cost-guided MPPI mixing to convert learned cost topology into feasible ego plans.
AI.motivation: End-to-end waypoint-regression planners achieve strong open-loop accuracy but mainly mimic expert geometry and are hard to adapt to deployment-time safety constraints. Prior cost-estimation planners (e.g., ST-P3, NMP) are limited by dense BEV cells or small regressed trajectory sets.
AI.method: A query-based cost-learning framework estimating bounded costs for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries instead of dense BEV cells or a small regressed set. It uses compact joint scene tokens to capture coherent multimodal agent futures, plus contingency-aware cost aggregation and cost-guided intra-cluster MPPI mixing to turn the learned cost topology into feasible ego plans.
AI.result: On nuScenes, it improves over prior cost-estimation planners ST-P3 and NMP, outperforms most regression baselines in collision rate while staying competitive in L2, and retains an interpretable cost interface. On real-world driving logs, it reduces collision rates vs. SparseDrive and Alpamayo without fine-tuning while maintaining diverse candidate trajectories.
AI.conclusion: A query-based, bounded cost-learning planner with joint scene tokens and MPPI-based cost-guided mixing yields safer, interpretable planning that generalizes to real-world logs without fine-tuning, offering a practical cost interface for deployment-time safety constraints.

title: Evidence Before Sampling: Interpretable Implicit Negative Candidate Discovery for Recommendation
summary: Recommender systems learn from observed user-item interactions, but explicit negative feedback is often unavailable. Since deep learning models require negative signals for training, negative sampling methods typically treat selected unobserved interactions as negatives. However, a missing interaction does not explain why a user is uninterested in an item or whether there is sufficient evidence to label it negative. This is especially important in business recommendation, where negative signals should be interpretable and aligned with business objectives. We formulate implicit negative candidate discovery to identify unobserved interactions supported by observed customer behavior. We encode these patterns as symbolic rules, score them based on support, informativeness, and product relevance, and rank the retained rules by evidence. An LLM then interprets the retained rules using business objectives and domain knowledge; the interpretations are combined with the statistical evidence in the final report. We evaluate our method in an industrial B2B setting and across five public recommendation datasets. Candidate-quality evaluations in the industrial setting and three public datasets show higher precision than the evaluated baselines, while symbolic selection improves downstream test PR-AUC by 12.5% over random selection with four negatives per positive example in the industrial task. Our results show that negative candidate validity can be evaluated separately from downstream recommendation performance. This distinction enables evidence-based, business-aligned, and explainable negative selection, improving both interpretability and model training in sparse, skewed, real-world recommendation settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes discovering implicit negative candidates for recommender systems by mining observable customer behavior into symbolic rules, then having an LLM interpret them against business objectives, yielding more precise, explainable negatives than standard unobserved-interaction sampling.
AI.motivation: Explicit negative feedback is usually unavailable, so negative sampling labels unobserved interactions as negatives by default. But a missing interaction does not reveal why a user is uninterested nor whether there is enough evidence to call it negative. This matters especially in business recommendation, where negative signals must be interpretable and aligned with business goals.
AI.method: The authors formulate implicit negative candidate discovery to find unobserved interactions backed by observed customer behavior. They encode these behavioral patterns as symbolic rules, score them by support, informativeness, and product relevance, and rank retained rules by evidence. An LLM then interprets the retained rules using business objectives and domain knowledge, and these interpretations are combined with the statistical evidence in a final report.
AI.result: Evaluated in an industrial B2B setting and on five public recommendation datasets. Candidate-quality evaluations in the industrial setting and three public datasets show higher precision than the evaluated baselines. Symbolic selection improves downstream test PR-AUC by 12.5% over random selection with four negatives per positive example in the industrial task.
AI.conclusion: Negative candidate validity can be evaluated separately from downstream recommendation performance. This separation enables evidence-based, business-aligned, and explainable negative selection, improving both interpretability and model training in sparse, skewed, real-world recommendation settings.

title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.

AI.tldr: VLA-ACL learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy via action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model frozen, enabling large token reduction with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models suffer high computational costs from processing long token sequences at each control step, hindering real-time deployment. Visual patches dominate the input and are highly redundant, so visual token pruning is a direct remedy. Existing methods either use indirect training-free heuristics (attention scores, motion thresholds) or need costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model.
AI.method: VLA-ACL learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision with the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions from pruned visual contexts to stay consistent with the full-context teacher, using ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision, thereby tying token selection directly to its effect on downstream control output.
AI.result: On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup.
AI.conclusion: VLA-ACL establishes a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrates the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection.

title: PERSIST: Who-What-When Memory Across Sessions for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue
summary: Modern voice assistants may be shared by multiple users and should be able to answer questions about earlier conversations such as "When did I originally plan to leave?" or adapt their behavior to individual users based on past interactions. This requires more than retrieving a topically similar passage: the assistant must identify the current speaker, recover the relevant past state, and distinguish it from later revisions. We present PERSIST, a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When. PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism that combines semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time full-duplex interaction, PERSIST further reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone, avoiding query-audio re-encoding and reducing retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms. We also introduce SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking. On SpokenTrace, PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% with BGE-large to 82.10%.

AI.tldr: PERSIST is a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that models Who, What, and When, enabling low-latency retrieval and improved end-to-end task accuracy on the new SpokenTrace benchmark.
AI.motivation: Shared voice assistants need to answer questions about earlier conversations and personalize to individual users based on past interactions. This goes beyond topical passage retrieval: the assistant must identify the current speaker, recover the relevant past state, and distinguish it from later revisions.
AI.method: PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism combining semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time full-duplex interaction, it reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone to avoid query-audio re-encoding.
AI.result: Retrieval latency is reduced from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms. On the SpokenTrace benchmark, PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% (BGE-large) to 82.10%.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling Who, What, and When in a persistent memory system enables accurate, low-latency memory retrieval for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue. SpokenTrace provides a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking.

title: ViDAL: A Visual Dynamics-Grounded Action Latent Space for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task $π_{0.5}$ policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.

AI.tldr: ViDAL introduces a visual-dynamics-grounded continuous action latent space for VLA models by aligning an Action VAE latent with future scene dynamics, yielding strong gains on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real robot platforms.
AI.motivation: Existing action representations in VLA models (raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents) primarily model action trajectories and largely ignore the visual dynamics those actions induce in the scene. This limits how well action representations capture the consequences of actions.
AI.method: ViDAL learns a continuous action latent space with an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) that reconstructs action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. The resulting Action VAE acts as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and optionally enables future-video prediction.
AI.result: ViDAL reaches 98.1% average success on LIBERO. It improves a multi-task π0.5 policy on RoboTwin 2.0 across 50 dual-arm tasks from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random). On real hardware, it yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX platforms.
AI.conclusion: Grounding continuous action latents in future visual dynamics provides an effective, architecture-agnostic action representation for robot policy learning, improving both simulated and real-world VLA policy performance.

title: How Well Do LLMs Reason with Noisy Evidence? An Active Visual Reasoning Benchmark
summary: Real-world reasoning rarely reduces to static question answering: agents must actively gather information from tools and sensors that are often noisy and unreliable. Yet most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume that environmental feedback is trustworthy, or introduce noise without exposing an explicit, calibrated uncertainty signal, leaving open how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. We introduce VisualNoiseQA, a novel benchmark for active reasoning under noisy visual feedback. A text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, we draw multiple samples and expose an empirical uncertainty signal via self-consistency, enabling the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. Our construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, we retain only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable. We evaluate multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. VisualNoiseQA thus provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning.

AI.tldr: VisualNoiseQA is a new benchmark where a text-only LLM solves VQA tasks by repeatedly querying a noisy, off-the-shelf VLM as a stochastic visual sensor, using self-consistency across samples as an uncertainty signal to guide active reasoning.
AI.motivation: Real-world reasoning requires agents to gather information from noisy, unreliable tools and sensors, yet existing active reasoning benchmarks assume trustworthy feedback or add noise without providing a calibrated uncertainty signal. This leaves unclear how LLMs should reason when evidence itself is uncertain.
AI.method: A text-only LLM iteratively queries a fixed off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, multiple samples are drawn and an empirical uncertainty signal is exposed via self-consistency, letting the reasoner probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. The construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable are retained.
AI.result: The benchmark contains 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning, and is used to evaluate multiple LLM reasoners.
AI.conclusion: VisualNoiseQA offers a controlled playground for studying how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals to achieve robust reasoning under noisy visual feedback.

title: Nested Power Models for Multirotor Propulsion: From Aerodynamic Drag to Electrical Losses
summary: Speed-only aerodynamic power models for multirotor propulsion cannot represent acceleration-dependent effects. This work develops a nested sequence of propulsion-power models that starts from aerodynamic power dissipation and progressively introduces a reversible kinetic-energy rate, torque-dependent electromechanical dissipation, and lumped speed-proportional dissipation. The models are identified using one subset of experiments and validated using the other on a motor-drive-propeller unit. Independent estimates of rotational inertia and aerodynamic drag complement predictive validation by assessing whether the models correctly attribute the measured power to reversible kinetic-energy exchange and irreversible dissipation and, within the latter, to aerodynamic and electromechanical losses. The results show that the reversible kinetic-energy rate is necessary but insufficient for accurate dynamic power prediction. Dissipation proportional to the squared motor torque provides the main additional improvement, while speed-proportional dissipation further prevents irreversible losses from being attributed to reversible kinetic-energy exchange. The resulting methodology provides a reusable and experimentally verifiable basis for developing and selecting dynamic propulsion-power models for multirotor systems.

AI.tldr: This work develops a nested sequence of multirotor propulsion-power models—progressively adding reversible kinetic-energy rate, torque-dependent electromechanical dissipation, and speed-proportional dissipation—and validates them experimentally, showing that reversible kinetic-energy and torque-squared dissipation terms are essential for accurate dynamic power prediction.
AI.motivation: Conventional speed-only aerodynamic power models for multirotor propulsion cannot capture acceleration-dependent effects, limiting their accuracy under dynamic flight conditions. There is a need for power models that correctly separate reversible kinetic-energy exchange from irreversible dissipation during transients.
AI.method: A nested sequence of propulsion-power models is constructed, starting from aerodynamic power dissipation and progressively adding: (1) a reversible kinetic-energy rate, (2) torque-dependent electromechanical dissipation, and (3) lumped speed-proportional dissipation. The models are identified on one experimental subset and validated on another using a motor-drive-propeller unit. Independent estimates of rotational inertia and aerodynamic drag are used to check whether the models properly attribute measured power to reversible kinetic-energy exchange versus irreversible aerodynamic and electromechanical losses.
AI.result: The reversible kinetic-energy rate is necessary but insufficient for accurate dynamic power prediction. Dissipation proportional to the squared motor torque delivers the main additional improvement. Speed-proportional dissipation further prevents irreversible losses from being misattributed to reversible kinetic-energy exchange.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nested modeling framework offers a reusable, experimentally verifiable basis for developing and selecting dynamic propulsion-power models for multirotor systems, with clear physical interpretability of each added term.

title: ST-Bench: A Spatial-Temporal Benchmark for Multi-Agent System Generation on Scientific Research Tasks
summary: The rapid progress of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) has shown that they largely outperform single agents on coding, math, and QA tasks, where executable tests provide a binary success signal. Whether this advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis remains untested. We introduce ST-Bench, a benchmark designed to answer two questions: whether MAS outperform single agents on complex scientific data analysis tasks, and if so, by how much and at what additional cost. ST-Bench contains 100 data science tasks adapted from published Earth science studies across hydrology, agriculture, and wetland methane research, expanded into 2,067 queries grounded in additional published studies and validated by domain experts. Using ST-Bench, we evaluate five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols, against single-agent baselines on the same GPT-5 backbone. Nine of the ten MAS configurations exceed the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. This gain is primarily attributable to coverage: trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries, while the quality of those metrics, conditional on producing realistic output, is comparable to that of the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration requires approximately four times the single-agent inference time, whereas a more economical workflow captures the majority of the benefit at less than twice the cost. MAS specialization confers measurable benefit on scientific data analysis, but the benefit is conditional rather than universal.

AI.tldr: ST-Bench, a 100-task Earth science benchmark expanded to 2,067 expert-validated queries, shows that LLM-based multi-agent systems (9 of 10 configurations) outperform the cheapest single-agent baseline on scientific data analysis, with the best reaching ~3x the composite score, driven mainly by higher coverage rather than higher per-output quality, at roughly 4x inference time.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) largely outperform single agents on coding, math, and QA tasks, but those domains provide executable tests yielding a binary success signal. It remains untested whether this MAS advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis, which lacks such clean success signals; the paper asks whether MAS outperform single agents on complex scientific data analysis and, if so, by how much and at what additional cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce ST-Bench, comprising 100 data science tasks adapted from published Earth science studies in hydrology, agriculture, and wetland methane research, expanded into 2,067 queries grounded in additional published studies and validated by domain experts. Using ST-Bench, they evaluate five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols against single-agent baselines, all on the same GPT-5 backbone, comparing composite scores and inference cost.
AI.result: Nine of the ten MAS configurations exceed the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. The gain is primarily attributable to coverage: trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries, while metric quality conditional on producing realistic output is comparable to the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration needs approximately 4x the single-agent inference time, whereas a more economical workflow captures most of the benefit at less than twice the cost.
AI.conclusion: MAS specialization confers a measurable benefit on scientific data analysis, but the benefit is conditional rather than universal, and it is mainly a coverage effect achieved at additional inference cost.

title: Compact Robot Policies Need Fine-Grained Visual Representations
summary: Multi-task manipulation policies differ in architecture, scale, and pretrained priors all at once, so published comparisons cannot attribute performance to any single component. We argue that most of it comes from the visual representation, and that parameter scale and generative priors are largely incidental. To test this, we build CoRP (Compressed Representation Policy), a deliberately compact policy (48.9M parameters, no vision-language model and no video-generative prior) that factorizes into a representation extractor and a flow-matching action generator. It reaches 97.0% on LIBERO and 75.78%/73.36% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Randomized, matching systems 40.9-163.6x larger. Holding the action generator fixed, we then vary one extractor property at a time. Pretrained initialization is decisive: a random ViT-S/14 drops to 78.1% and an ImageNet ResNet-34 to 74.5% on LIBERO. Pretraining alone is not enough, as freezing the encoder costs 19.8 points. Compression matters as much: resampling each view to 48 tokens beats passing all patch tokens (97.0% vs 83.2%), and a variational information bottleneck over those tokens is worse than a hard token budget, cutting LIBERO-Goal from 95.8% to 33.0% by suppressing the instruction-dependent token selection the policy relies on. Language conditioning contributes only where the observation leaves the goal ambiguous (LIBERO-Goal: 9.2% to 95.8%), while on RoboTwin 2.0, where observations are unambiguous, removing it slightly improves success. Therefore, we argue that a compact policy works when its representation is pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed. Project page: https://corp-policy.github.io/

AI.tldr: A compact 48.9M-parameter manipulation policy (no VLM, no video-generative prior) matches systems 40.9–163.6x larger, and controlled ablations show performance is driven mainly by the visual representation (pretrained, task-adapted, compressed) rather than scale or generative priors.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-task manipulation policies vary simultaneously in architecture, parameter scale, and pretrained priors, so published comparisons cannot attribute performance gains to any single component. The authors hypothesize that visual representation dominates, while scale and generative priors are largely incidental.
AI.method: They build CoRP (Compressed Representation Policy), a compact policy (48.9M parameters, no VLM, no video-generative prior) factorized into a representation extractor and a flow-matching action generator. With the action generator held fixed, they ablate one extractor property at a time: pretrained initialization vs. random ViT-S/14 and ImageNet ResNet-34, frozen vs. fine-tuned encoder, token compression (48 resampled tokens vs. all patch tokens), a variational information bottleneck vs. a hard token budget, and presence/absence of language conditioning.
AI.result: CoRP reaches 97.0% on LIBERO and 75.78%/73.36% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Randomized. Random ViT-S/14 drops to 78.1% and ImageNet ResNet-34 to 74.5% on LIBERO; freezing the encoder costs 19.8 points. Resampling each view to 48 tokens beats all patch tokens (97.0% vs 83.2%). A variational information bottleneck underperforms a hard token budget, cutting LIBERO-Goal from 95.8% to 33.0%. Language conditioning matters only when the observation is goal-ambiguous (LIBERO-Goal: 9.2% to 95.8%) and slightly hurts on RoboTwin 2.0.
AI.conclusion: Most of multi-task manipulation performance stems from the visual representation, not scale or generative priors. A compact policy succeeds when its representation is pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed, challenging the assumption that large models and generative priors are necessary.

title: OTel: Open Telco AI Datasets, Benchmarks, and Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026, ED Track, Spotlight
summary: We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource that releases derived telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, together with 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines spanning 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. Each baseline starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

AI.tldr: OTel is an open telecom AI resource releasing derived datasets and 30 post-trained baselines (10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, 17 LLMs) for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, achieving 93.1% NDCG@10, 0.947 MRR@10, and 87.8% correctness.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to fill the gap in unified, open, and reproducible telecom AI resources by providing documented data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, and trained models across multiple model families in one place, building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks.
AI.method: Each of the 30 baselines starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. The resource spans 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models.
AI.result: OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. As of May 3, 2026, released models have been downloaded over 16 million times, with 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide.
AI.conclusion: OTel is released as a reproducible starting point, inviting the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

title: VOMMI: Collecting and Leveraging Portable Demonstrations for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations can help alleviate data scarcity for embodied intelligence, but obtaining reliable, low-cost, and robot-free motion supervision from RGB observations remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on teleoperation or specialized devices equipped with additional sensing hardware, while directly using estimated visual odometry (VO) trajectories can introduce inconsistencies due to accumulated drift and imperfect motion supervision. We present the Visual-Odometry-Conditioned Mobile Manipulation Interface (VOMMI), a portable demonstration collection and learning framework that connects portable RGB demonstrations to vision-language-action (VLA) post-training through offline trajectory reconstruction and online visual-motion conditioning. VOMMI synchronizes body and hand views to capture navigation context and local object interactions without requiring human-robot kinematic correspondence calibration. R2-VO refines offline demonstration trajectories using sparse geometric anchors and produces causal local-motion tokens over multiple prediction horizons for online policy conditioning. An action-group residual adapter incorporates these tokens only into the base branch. Experiments use a 500-trajectory portable for each task, with 75 trajectories held out for RGB-VO evaluation, and 200 robot demonstrations as references. Our policy, post-trained only on portable demonstrations, achieves 18.2% lower base-velocity error than a policy trained with robot-collected demonstrations, while maintaining comparable end-effector translation accuracy. Offline reconstruction reduces absolute trajectory errors for the body and hand streams by 24.6% on average relative to the best evaluated baseline for each stream. The complete system improves the mean success rate by 8.3 percentage points over OpenPI 0.5 across three real-robot tasks.

AI.tldr: VOMMI is a portable RGB demonstration collection and learning framework that bridges portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations to VLA post-training via offline trajectory reconstruction (R2-VO) and online visual-motion conditioning, achieving lower base-velocity error and higher success rates than baselines without robot-collected data.
AI.motivation: Portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations can alleviate data scarcity for embodied intelligence, but obtaining reliable, low-cost, robot-free motion supervision from RGB observations is difficult. Existing methods rely on teleoperation or specialized sensing hardware, and using estimated visual odometry (VO) trajectories directly introduces inconsistencies from accumulated drift and imperfect motion supervision.
AI.method: VOMMI synchronizes body and hand views to capture navigation context and local object interactions without requiring human-robot kinematic correspondence calibration. R2-VO refines offline demonstration trajectories using sparse geometric anchors and produces causal local-motion tokens over multiple prediction horizons for online policy conditioning. An action-group residual adapter incorporates these tokens only into the base branch.
AI.result: Using 500 portable trajectories per task (75 held out for RGB-VO evaluation) and 200 robot demonstrations as references, the policy post-trained only on portable demonstrations achieves 18.2% lower base-velocity error than a policy trained with robot-collected demonstrations, while maintaining comparable end-effector translation accuracy. Offline reconstruction reduces absolute trajectory errors for body and hand streams by 24.6% on average versus the best evaluated baseline per stream. The full system improves mean success rate by 8.3 percentage points over OpenPI 0.5 across three real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: VOMMI enables robot-free, low-cost portable demonstration collection and learning for mobile manipulation, connecting RGB demonstrations to VLA post-training through offline trajectory reconstruction and online visual-motion conditioning, yielding improved base-velocity accuracy and task success without relying on robot-collected data.

title: Quantization Effects on Tool-Failure Recovery Vary Across Prompts and Evaluation Designs
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Small Language Models for Agentic Systems (SLM-Agents). 7 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, plus appendix
summary: Post-training quantization reduces the cost of deploying language-model agents, but its effect on recovery from temporary tool failures can depend on how recovery is evaluated. We compare 8-bit and 4-bit variants of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on twenty deterministic tool-use tasks and five prompts. The 8-bit-4-bit recovery comparison changes direction across prompts and evaluation targets. On tasks that both variants complete without faults under the same prompt, the difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points for Llama and from -50.0 to +35.0 points for Qwen. Full-pipeline point estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, whereas the Qwen comparison changes direction across prompts. The evaluation target can also reverse the result. For Llama under one prompt, scoring each variant only on its own clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points; scoring the same tasks for both variants gives no difference, while scoring the full pipeline favors 8-bit by 28.3 points. Executor leniency is a third such choice. Rescoring the same logs with strict output parsing, which 8-bit Llama violates far more often than 4-bit Llama under that prompt, turns that +28.3 into -15.0 while leaving Qwen essentially unchanged. These findings show that one prompt, one screened task set, and one scoring policy do not establish a stable conclusion about quantized-agent robustness. Evaluations should compare variants on matched tasks, report full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, state the scoring policy, and quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites.

AI.tldr: Quantization-recovery comparisons between 8-bit and 4-bit LLM agents are unstable: results reverse depending on prompt, task screening, scoring target, and parser leniency, so robustness conclusions require matched tasks, full-pipeline reporting, explicit scoring policy, and task-level uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization lowers deployment cost for language-model agents, but practitioners need to know whether quantization harms an agent's ability to recover from temporary tool failures. The paper argues that the apparent answer depends heavily on evaluation design choices, which are often left implicit, making single-setting conclusions unreliable.
AI.method: Compare 8-bit and 4-bit quantized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 20 deterministic tool-use tasks with five prompts. Vary three evaluation levers: prompt choice, task screening (matched vs. clean-passing-only sets), and scoring target (full-pipeline vs. own-clean-passing tasks), plus executor leniency via strict vs. lenient output parsing while rescoring identical logs.
AI.result: Recovery differences flip sign across prompts and targets. On tasks both variants cleanly pass, gaps span 0 to +20.2 pp (Llama) and -50.0 to +35.0 pp (Qwen). Full-pipeline estimates favor 8-bit Llama across all prompts, while Qwen flips by prompt. One Llama prompt yields 4-bit +17.5 pp under own-clean scoring, zero under matched scoring, and 8-bit +28.3 pp for full pipeline. Strict parsing converts that +28.3 to -15.0 for Llama, with Qwen roughly unchanged.
AI.conclusion: A single prompt, screened task set, or scoring policy cannot establish quantized-agent robustness. Evaluations should compare variants on matched tasks, report full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, state the scoring policy explicitly, and quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than across injected fault sites.

title: UWB Meets Crazyflow: Simulating Degraded Feedback at Scale for Aerial Robotics
comment: Accepted to 1st Workshop on Robot Meets GNSS and Ranging for Seamless Autonomy @ ICRA 2026
summary: In this work, we introduce Crazyflow, an accurate, differentiable simulator built on JAX. By leveraging jit compilation via XLA, Crazyflow unifies physics and control into a single differentiable computation graph, enabling massive parallelization on accelerated hardware without sacrificing modeling accuracy. This architecture achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing baselines, capable of training deployable reinforcement learning agents in seconds. To highlight its highly modular design, we demonstrate how easily Crazyflow can be extended by integrating a complete, high-fidelity Ultra-Wideband (UWB) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) simulation pipeline coupled with a full-state Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). This capability allows for massive parallel controller evaluation under realistic, degraded state feedback with minimal impact on GPU throughput. By combining speed, accuracy, and extensibility, Crazyflow serves as a foundational tool for the next generation of aerial robotics research.

AI.tldr: Crazyflow is an accurate, differentiable JAX-based simulator that unifies physics and control in a single XLA-jit computation graph, achieving order-of-magnitude speedups, training deployable RL agents in seconds, and easily extending to UWB/IMU simulation with a full-state EKF.
AI.motivation: Existing simulators struggle to combine high modeling accuracy with the massive parallelization needed for fast reinforcement learning training and parallel controller evaluation. The authors aim to provide a foundational tool for next-generation aerial robotics research that delivers speed, accuracy, and extensibility simultaneously.
AI.method: Built on JAX, Crazyflow uses jit compilation via XLA to unify physics and control into a single differentiable computation graph, enabling massive parallelization on accelerated hardware while preserving modeling accuracy. Its highly modular design is demonstrated by integrating a complete, high-fidelity Ultra-Wideband (UWB) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) simulation pipeline coupled with a full-state Extended Kalman Filter (EKF).
AI.result: Crazyflow achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing baselines and can train deployable reinforcement learning agents in seconds. The UWB/IMU plus EKF extension enables massive parallel controller evaluation under realistic, degraded state feedback with minimal impact on GPU throughput.
AI.conclusion: By combining speed, accuracy, and extensibility, Crazyflow serves as a foundational tool for the next generation of aerial robotics research.

title: Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference: What It Costs, What It Buys, and When You Can Tell
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. Accepted as a poster at the Machine Learning for Systems Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents bounds the active KV cache per call rather than total evidence, which matters when KV-cache memory binds. Many such systems add a persistent tier storing and recalling reasoning traces, usually validated by an ablation reporting an accuracy gain. We measure both on one three-tier agent architecture. Decomposition delivers: peak KV working set of 14.3 MiB per query against 35.5 and 35.3 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. The persistent tier does not: across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm it costs +0.368 MiB [+0.167, +0.590] of peak cache and produces no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]). We argue the null is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. Reaching it took four measurement corrections -- three inflating the apparent benefit, the fourth making an effect that size look resolvable -- none visible in the results table. We give the conditions an agent-memory ablation must satisfy and detection procedures that need no knowledge of the specific defect.

AI.tldr: The paper measures a three-tier cooperating-agent architecture for long-context inference, showing that decomposition substantially reduces peak KV-cache memory, whereas the persistent reasoning-trace tier adds cache cost with no detectable accuracy benefit; the null is argued to be structural, and the measurement process required four corrections.
AI.motivation: When KV-cache memory is the binding constraint, decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents bounds the active cache per call rather than total evidence. Many such systems add a persistent tier that stores and recalls reasoning traces, typically justified by an ablation showing an accuracy gain. The paper questions whether that reported benefit is real and whether the underlying evaluation can resolve it.
AI.method: The authors measure both effects on one three-tier agent architecture, comparing peak KV working set against single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. They ablate the persistent tier across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm, reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals, and they apply four measurement corrections, three of which inflated the apparent benefit and one of which made an effect of that size appear resolvable.
AI.result: Decomposition reduces peak KV working set to 14.3 MiB per query versus 35.5 MiB (single-pass) and 35.3 MiB (retrieval-augmented). The persistent tier costs +0.368 MiB [+0.167, +0.590] of peak cache and yields no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]).
AI.conclusion: The authors argue the null effect is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. None of the measurement defects were visible in the results table. The paper specifies conditions an agent-memory ablation must satisfy and detection procedures that require no knowledge of the specific defect.

authors: A. H. T. E. De Silva
title: HexaGripper: A Single-Actuator, Winch-Deployed Gripper for Autonomous Aerial Parcel Collection
summary: Autonomous aerial parcel collection remains constrained by package-transfer operations that require manual loading, landing, or dedicated ground infrastructure. This letter presents HexaGripper, a single-actuator, winch-deployed six-plate gripper for autonomous collection of cuboid parcels. The proposed mechanism provides synchronized grasping with a wide capture region and tolerance to positional misalignment during pickup. The system integrates vision-based alignment, range sensing, winch deployment, and state-based control to enable autonomous collection while maintaining UAV separation from the pickup surface. Experimental evaluation covered static grasping, capture-workspace assessment, and end-to-end outdoor aerial collection. Static experiments achieved 100% pickup success (15/15 trials) across three parcel geometries, while workspace experiments achieved successful pickup at all 28 tested positions up to a 150 mm radial offset. End-to-end outdoor aerial collection achieved an 80% success rate (4/5 trials). These results demonstrate the feasibility of mechanically synchronized, winch-deployed grasping for landing-free autonomous aerial parcel collection.

AI.tldr: HexaGripper is a single-actuator, winch-deployed six-plate gripper that enables autonomous, landing-free aerial collection of cuboid parcels, achieving 100% static pickup and 80% outdoor success.
AI.motivation: Autonomous aerial parcel collection is limited by package-transfer operations that require manual loading, landing, or dedicated ground infrastructure, which restricts true autonomy.
AI.method: A single-actuator, winch-deployed six-plate gripper providing mechanically synchronized grasping with a wide capture region and tolerance to positional misalignment. The system integrates vision-based alignment, range sensing, winch deployment, and state-based control to enable autonomous collection while keeping the UAV separated from the pickup surface.
AI.result: Static grasping achieved 100% pickup success (15/15 trials) across three parcel geometries. Capture-workspace experiments succeeded at all 28 tested positions up to a 150 mm radial offset. End-to-end outdoor aerial collection achieved an 80% success rate (4/5 trials).
AI.conclusion: Mechanically synchronized, winch-deployed grasping is feasible for landing-free autonomous aerial parcel collection.

title: Attacca: Goal-Directed Control under State Continuity for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
summary: A central capability of embodied agents is to accomplish complex objectives through sequences of interdependent tasks. Yet existing visual goal-conditioned policies underlying these agents are typically evaluated on isolated interactions where the target is already visible, and thus do not capture the conditions that arise during continuous long-horizon task execution. In such settings, each task begins from the state left by the previous one: the agent may end at a different position and orientation, the world may have been modified, and the next interaction target may lie outside the current field of view. As a result, agents relying on such policies may struggle to proceed to the next task when they cannot ground their target in the current observation. To address this challenge, we propose Attacca, a new approach that trains visual goal-conditioned policies on complete search-to-interact trajectories using goal images decoupled from the execution environment. Attacca uses context-decoupled goal sampling to pair each demonstration with a class-compatible masked goal image from another world, removing direct scene and pose correspondence. It learns dense current-view grounding through a target-mask prediction head, providing auxiliary supervision beyond action imitation. We further introduce behavioral-phase conditioning that teaches the policy to distinguish Search, Approach, and Interact stages and adapt its control as execution progresses. We evaluate Attacca on multiple short- and long-horizon embodied tasks in Minecraft. Our method achieves 39.0-47.5% clean success, improving over the strongest baseline by 1.7-2.4x. On long-horizon tasks, it attains 54%, 30%, and 28% completion, yielding up to a 7x improvement.

AI.tldr: Attacca trains visual goal-conditioned policies on full search-to-interact trajectories using context-decoupled goal images, target-mask prediction, and behavioral-phase conditioning, improving success on short- and long-horizon Minecraft tasks by 1.7-7x.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents must complete long-horizon sequences of interdependent tasks, but existing visual goal-conditioned policies are evaluated on isolated interactions where the target is already visible. During continuous execution, each task starts from the prior task's state (changed pose, modified world, target possibly out of view), so agents fail to ground targets in the current observation and cannot proceed.
AI.method: Attacca is trained on complete search-to-interact trajectories with goal images decoupled from the execution environment.
