It uses context-decoupled goal sampling, pairing each demonstration with a class-compatible masked goal image from another world to remove scene/pose correspondence; a target-mask prediction head for dense current-view grounding as auxiliary supervision; and behavioral-phase conditioning over Search, Approach, and Interact stages to adapt control as execution progresses.
AI.result: On multiple short- and long-horizon embodied Minecraft tasks, Attacca achieves 39.0-47.5% clean success, 1.7-2.4x better than the strongest baseline. On long-horizon tasks it reaches 54%, 30%, and 28% completion, up to a 7x improvement.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling goal images from the execution environment, adding dense grounding supervision, and conditioning on behavioral phase substantially improve long-horizon embodied task completion.

title: Mitigating Concept Drift in QoS Prediction for Teleoperation of Autonomous Vehicles Using Historic Data
comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
summary: Teleoperation serves as the fallback solution to autonomous driving but reliable functions of the teleoperation require a certain amount of mobile network resources, which cannot be guaranteed at all times. Therefore, predictive quality of service (pQoS) is introduced as a concept to increase the resilience of the teleoperation. In this paper, based on a data measurement campaign, we propose a prediction framework to prediction two important network KPIs of teleoperation: uplink data-rate and round-trip latency. Furthermore, we introduce a method to alleviate the performance degradation of machine-learning-based prediction models on previously unseen data due to concept drift by incorporating historic data into the prediction pipeline. Additionally, we introduce the metric of critical scenario detection to evaluate the prediction performance specifically for teleoperation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a pQoS prediction framework for teleoperation, predicting uplink data-rate and round-trip latency via machine learning, mitigating concept drift with historical data, and introducing a critical scenario detection metric.
AI.motivation: Teleoperation is the fallback for autonomous driving, but its reliability requires mobile network resources that cannot be guaranteed at all times. Predictive QoS (pQoS) is thus needed to increase teleoperation resilience, yet effective prediction of key network KPIs and robustness against concept drift remain open issues.
AI.method: Based on a data measurement campaign, the authors build a prediction framework targeting two key teleoperation KPIs: uplink data-rate and round-trip latency. To counter performance degradation of ML-based predictors on previously unseen data caused by concept drift, they incorporate historical data into the prediction pipeline. They also define a critical scenario detection metric tailored to teleoperation.
AI.result: The framework predicts uplink data-rate and round-trip latency, and the historical-data-augmented pipeline alleviates ML prediction degradation under concept drift, with evaluation supported by the proposed critical scenario detection metric.
AI.conclusion: Predictive QoS with historical data integration and teleoperation-specific evaluation provides a viable path to more resilient teleoperation.

title: OOPMAS: Object-Oriented Multi-Agent Systems for Query-Level Workflow Generation
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown strong performance across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering. However, existing methods for automating MAS design mostly operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow per benchmark that is applied uniformly to all queries. This assumption fails under realistic conditions. Query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. We introduce OOPMAS, a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, and workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.

AI.tldr: OOPMAS is a training-free framework that automatically designs multi-agent systems at the per-query granularity, generating agent sets as object-oriented classes and workflows as executable main functions, with a dynamic skill library for in-context improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing automated MAS design methods operate at the task level, producing one fixed workflow per benchmark applied uniformly to all queries. This fails in realistic settings because query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real workloads mix heterogeneous task types.
AI.method: Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state. Workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects, generated per individual query. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without gradient updates or fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a mixed-task benchmark spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS reaches 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.
AI.conclusion: Per-query, training-free MAS design with object-oriented agents and executable workflows enables strong and scalable performance on heterogeneous, mixed-task workloads.

title: Sensor-Layout-Agnostic Navigation via Geometric Observation Canonicalization
summary: Existing visual navigation policies are inherently bound to fixed camera configurations, creating a fundamental barrier to zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous robot sensor layouts. To overcome this limitation, we present an embodiment-informed navigation policy capable of generalizing across diverse depth sensor configurations on a specific aerial platform. Instead of implicitly learning spatial alignments, our approach explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary depth sensor payloads, varying in sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and intrinsics, into a shared robot-centric frame, stitching them into a unified spherical range image and a binary validity mask. This mask allows the downstream policy to explicitly distinguish covered space from unobserved blind spots. Trained via reinforcement learning with aggressive camera randomization, our policy generalizes zero-shot to unseen layouts featuring up to seven cameras, scaling success rates from 78% to 95% as total spatial sensing coverage increases. Finally, real-world flight trials on a physical quadrotor, conducted in an obstacle-filled corridor and an outdoor forest, validate the policy's zero-shot transfer across camera configurations and its resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an embodiment-informed visual navigation policy that explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary sensor configurations into a robot-centric spherical range image with a validity mask, enabling zero-shot generalization across camera layouts on an aerial platform.
AI.motivation: Existing visual navigation policies are tied to fixed camera configurations, creating a barrier to zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous robot sensor layouts.
AI.method: Rather than implicitly learning spatial alignments, the approach explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary depth sensor payloads (varying in sensor count, extrinsics, and intrinsics) into a shared robot-centric frame, stitching them into a unified spherical range image and a binary validity mask that distinguishes covered space from unobserved blind spots. The policy is trained via reinforcement learning with aggressive camera randomization.
AI.result: The policy generalizes zero-shot to unseen layouts with up to seven cameras, with success rates scaling from 78% to 95% as total spatial sensing coverage increases. Real-world flight trials on a physical quadrotor in an obstacle-filled corridor and an outdoor forest validate zero-shot transfer across camera configurations and resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.
AI.conclusion: Explicit embodiment-informed spatial representation enables robust zero-shot generalization of visual navigation policies across diverse, unseen sensor configurations and sensor failures.

title: Illusory Pattern Perception Drives Spurious Inference in Large Language Models
summary: Illusory pattern perception is a well-documented human cognitive tendency to infer meaningful relationships in data that is actually random. Such a tendency, often described as "connecting the dots" where none exist, can result in systematic reasoning errors. This paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit such perceptual tendencies, which can lead to systematic errors in downstream applications. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in LLMs, adapting classic psychological paradigms to three tasks with direct empirical comparison to human behaviors. We find that LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. In particular, models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and show increased tendencies to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. To uncover the mechanism behind these behaviors, we develop a feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to analyze internal representations. Our results reveal that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to the emergence of illusory perceptions. These findings highlight a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning. Code available at https://github.com/NusIoraPrivacy/illusory.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in LLMs, showing models often exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans and linking this to internal features via SAE-based interpretability.
AI.motivation: Illusory pattern perception is a documented human tendency to infer meaningful relationships in random data, causing systematic reasoning errors. It is unknown whether LLMs exhibit such perceptual tendencies, which could lead to systematic errors in downstream applications.
AI.method: The authors adapt classic psychological paradigms to three tasks and conduct direct empirical comparison with human behavior. They also develop a feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to analyze LLMs' internal representations.
AI.result: LLMs frequently show stronger illusory pattern perception than humans, over-associating frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations and constructing causal narratives from ambiguous events. SAE analysis links holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation to these illusory perceptions.
AI.conclusion: Illusory pattern perception is a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion in LLMs that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning. Code is available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Humanoid Horizon: Extending Task Horizon in Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation via Parallel Training, Dynamic Starting, and Reward Gating
comment: Videos and results are available at https://haozhuo-zhang.github.io/Humanoid-Horizon-project-page/
summary: Cluttered indoor environments, where large and heavy objects are scattered across diverse surfaces, require humanoid robots to sequentially navigate, grasp, transport, and accurately place each item at its target location within a single uninterrupted episode. This long-horizon, whole-body loco-manipulation task remains a significant challenge for current methods. Previous approaches often suffer from two main issues: easy-reward bias, where training overemphasizes early transport stages at the expense of later ones, and catastrophic forgetting, where focusing on later stages leads to a decline in earlier-stage performance. In this work, we introduce Humanoid Horizon, a unified policy framework designed to overcome these limitations through three interrelated mechanisms. The Parallel Training Strategy organizes $N$ scenes into $S$ concurrent stage streams governed by a shared policy, ensuring all transport stages receive continuous gradient updates and removing the bottleneck of sequential optimization. The Dynamic Starting Mechanism updates each environment's initial state with terminal states from upstream rollouts, gradually broadening transition coverage and enhancing robustness at stage boundaries. Reward Gating sets the reward to zero for the rest of the episode in later-stage streams when the immediately preceding object is displaced beyond a set threshold, so the shared policy learns not to disturb a just-placed object and earlier placements are preserved throughout the episode. Collectively, these strategies achieve per-stage success rates exceeding 80\% on the two-object LHM-Humanoid benchmark (350 training scenes, 66 held-out scenes). As the number of sequentially transported objects grows beyond two, success declines with the horizon, but the degradation is graceful relative to the sharp drop seen in all baselines.

AI.tldr: Humanoid Horizon is a unified policy framework for long-horizon whole-body loco-manipulation in cluttered indoor environments, using Parallel Training Strategy, Dynamic Starting Mechanism, and Reward Gating to overcome easy-reward bias and catastrophic forgetting, achieving >80% per-stage success on the LHM-Humanoid benchmark.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon indoor loco-manipulation (navigate, grasp, transport, place multiple heavy objects in one episode) is hard. Existing methods suffer from easy-reward bias (early stages overemphasized) and catastrophic forgetting (focusing on later stages degrades earlier ones).
AI.method: Three interrelated mechanisms: (1) Parallel Training Strategy: organizes N scenes into S concurrent stage streams under a shared policy, giving all stages continuous gradient updates; (2) Dynamic Starting Mechanism: updates each environment's initial state with terminal states from upstream rollouts; (3) Reward Gating: zeroes rewards for the rest of the episode in later-stage streams when the immediately preceding object is displaced beyond a threshold.
AI.result: Per-stage success rates exceed 80% on the two-object LHM-Humanoid benchmark (350 training scenes, 66 held-out scenes). Beyond two objects, success declines with horizon but degradation is graceful compared to sharp drops in all baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified policy framework effectively mitigates easy-reward bias and catastrophic forgetting, enabling robust multi-stage whole-body loco-manipulation, with graceful degradation as task horizon increases.

title: Thin Evidence, Thick Priors: How Language Models Substitute Identity for Missing Financial Facts
comment: 49 pages, 17 figures, 12 tables; Submitted & Accepted to ICAIF'2026
summary: People increasingly ask large language models what to do with their money, yet seldom describe their finances in full. This paper asks what a model does with the gap. Holding finances fixed and changing only who the investor is said to be, we grade the financial evidence in the prompt from eight facts to none and measure how far the recommended equity allocation moves. Across 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, built from 100 financial profiles, 138 personas and seven disclosure conditions, the average gap between two personas with identical finances rises from 4.78 percentage points at full disclosure to 10.34 points with no financial facts. A two-way cluster bootstrap counting duplicated prompts once places the ratio at 2.16 (95% interval 1.69 to 2.79), and the rise is already 1.69-fold with a single fact left. Identity explains 5% of within-profile variation in advice at full disclosure and 96% with no disclosure. Household size is the only attribute whose influence grows reliably as evidence is withdrawn. Once standard errors are clustered on the persona, the unit to which identity was assigned, most attribute-specific interactions reported in the conference version lose significance, and gender instead appears as a small standing gap that full disclosure does not close. Stating risk appetite alone brings the swing into the range seen with two to seven generic facts. With no facts, the model's one-line rationale cites incomes, debts and savings it was never told, and these invented finances turn adverse more often for larger households. Inside the network, gender is linearly decodable at every layer, and ablating the gender direction at five layers leaves the aggregate identity swing unchanged. Advisory systems built on such models should be audited at the disclosure levels users actually reach, and judged across the whole identity space rather than one attribute at a time.

AI.tldr: When financial facts are withheld, LLM investment advice swings far more across investor identities: the average gap between two personas with identical finances doubles from 4.78 pp at full disclosure to 10.34 pp with no facts, and identity explains 96% of within-profile variation in advice versus 5% at full disclosure.
AI.motivation: Users increasingly query LLMs for financial guidance while rarely disclosing their full financial situation, leaving a gap between sparse prompts and confident advice. The paper asks what the model does with that gap—whether advice stays stable when finances are fixed and only identity changes—and challenges prior work that tested attributes one at a time and clustered standard errors at the wrong level.
AI.method: A controlled disclosure experiment: 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct constructed from 100 financial profiles, 138 personas and seven disclosure conditions graded from eight financial facts to none, measuring recommended equity allocation. Inference uses a two-way cluster bootstrap that counts duplicated prompts once, with standard errors clustered on the persona (the unit to which identity was assigned). Mechanistic checks include linear decodability of gender across layers and ablation of the gender direction at five layers.
AI.result: The average identity gap rises from 4.78 pp (full disclosure) to 10.34 pp (no facts); the ratio is 2.16 (95% interval 1.69–2.79) and already 1.69-fold with one fact remaining. Identity explains 5% of within-profile advice variation at full disclosure and 96% with none. Household size is the only attribute whose influence grows reliably as evidence is withdrawn. With persona-clustered errors, most attribute-specific interactions from the conference version lose significance, and gender appears instead as a small standing gap that full disclosure does not close. Risk appetite stated alone produces a swing comparable to two to seven generic facts. With no facts, the model's one-line rationale cites incomes, debts and savings never provided, and these invented finances turn adverse more often for larger households. Gender is linearly decodable at every layer, yet ablating the gender direction at five layers leaves the aggregate identity swing unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Identity fills the vacuum left by missing financial evidence, and the model fabricates finances to rationalize identity-driven advice. Advisory systems built on such models should be audited at the disclosure levels users actually reach and judged across the whole identity space rather than one attribute at a time; layer-level encoding of identity does not translate into a causally localized identity direction.

title: Communication-Free Obstacle Localization from Aggregate Wrench Measurements in Leader--Follower Cooperative Transport
comment: Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: We consider obstacle localization for a team of robots cooperatively transporting a rigid payload without explicit inter-robot communication. A leader robot directs the payload's motion, while follower robots assist and react to locally detected obstacles. The leader measures the followers' aggregate wrench, i.e., the combined force and torque they exert on the payload, but cannot directly distinguish their individual reactions. We design a follower control law that allows the leader to recover obstacle locations from these measurements. Each follower resists motion toward nearby obstacles, resulting in a piecewise-linear relationship between the payload's translational and angular velocity and the aggregate wrench. Changes between adjacent linear regions reveal an obstacle's bearing and distance and identify the responding follower. We give sufficient conditions for exact recovery at a fixed payload configuration and develop an adaptive probing procedure in which the leader applies translational and rotational inputs to the payload to obtain the required measurements. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed method in simulations.

AI.tldr: A leader robot can localize obstacles detected by follower robots during cooperative payload transport, without inter-robot communication, by exploiting the piecewise-linear relationship between payload velocity and the aggregate wrench measured at the leader.
AI.motivation: In cooperative transport of a rigid payload, follower robots react to locally detected obstacles, but the leader has no explicit communication channel and cannot distinguish the followers' individual reactions. The leader only measures the aggregate wrench. The goal is to recover obstacle locations (bearing, distance) and identify which follower is responding, using only this aggregate measurement.
AI.method: A follower control law is designed such that each follower resists motion toward nearby obstacles, producing a piecewise-linear relationship between the payload's translational/angular velocity and the aggregate wrench. Transitions between adjacent linear regions encode the obstacle's bearing and distance and identify the responding follower. Sufficient conditions for exact recovery at a fixed payload configuration are given, and an adaptive probing procedure is developed in which the leader applies translational and rotational inputs to the payload to collect the required measurements.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for exact obstacle-location recovery at a fixed payload configuration are established, and the adaptive probing procedure yields the necessary measurements. The performance of the proposed method is demonstrated in simulations.
AI.conclusion: Obstacle localization by a leader is achievable through aggregate wrench measurements alone, without inter-robot communication, via a piecewise-linear follower control law and adaptive probing, enabling cooperative transport to adapt to locally sensed obstacles.

title: ThinkFuse: Trajectory-Aware Test-Time Fusion for Small Reasoning Models
summary: Small reasoning models (SRMs) have shown strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by generating extended chain-of-thought trajectories, but they often fail to recover once their reasoning enters an erroneous path. Existing test-time fusion methods rely on local fusion signals to determine when to trigger fusion, which can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations and may reinforce unstable reasoning trajectories. We propose ThinkFuse, a training-free test-time fusion framework that selectively intervenes in unreliable reasoning segments. ThinkFuse compares segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level uncertainty trends to identify unstable reasoning points and fuse auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ThinkFuse outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains across model-family combinations, and remains robust with a smaller primary model. Our analysis shows that ThinkFuse requires fewer fusion triggers and generates fewer tokens, highlighting the efficiency of selective triggering. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ThinkFuse.

AI.tldr: ThinkFuse is a training-free test-time fusion framework that selectively fuses auxiliary reasoning paths into a primary small reasoning model's trajectory at unstable reasoning points, identified by comparing segment-level uncertainty shifts against trajectory-level uncertainty trends, improving reasoning accuracy and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Small reasoning models (SRMs) perform well on complex reasoning via extended chain-of-thought but cannot recover once reasoning enters an erroneous path. Existing test-time fusion methods use local fusion signals to decide when to trigger fusion, which can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations and may reinforce unstable reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: ThinkFuse is a training-free test-time fusion framework. It selectively intervenes in unreliable reasoning segments by comparing segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level uncertainty trends to identify unstable reasoning points, then fuses auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ThinkFuse outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains across model-family combinations, and remains robust with a smaller primary model. Analysis shows ThinkFuse requires fewer fusion triggers and generates fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: ThinkFuse's selective triggering based on segment-vs-trajectory uncertainty comparison yields both accuracy gains and efficiency, requiring fewer fusion triggers and fewer tokens, with code available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ThinkFuse.

title: SC3BF: Shifted Collision Cone Control Barrier Function for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
comment: Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: The collision cone used by velocity-space control barrier functions is conservative: it rejects every relative velocity aimed into an obstacle, however slow. We propose the \emph{shifted collision-cone CBF} (SC3BF), which adds a state-dependent \emph{allowance} to the cone condition, so the robot may approach the obstacle at a rate that grows with distance and with its own speed. SC3BF is enforced by an ordinary quadratic program, and its safe set is forward invariant under bounded inputs without a minimum forward speed or a clearance margin. We prove that a nonzero allowance preserving safety always exists, and derive one in closed form. Against three velocity-space baselines on a kinematic bicycle among up to $100$ moving obstacles, SC3BF reaches the goal more often and modifies the nominal input less than half as much.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SC3BF, a shifted collision-cone control barrier function that relaxes the conservative collision cone by adding a state-dependent allowance, enabling distance- and speed-scaled approach to obstacles while preserving safety, and demonstrates improved goal-reaching with less input modification.
AI.motivation: The standard collision cone used with velocity-space control barrier functions is overly conservative: it rejects any relative velocity pointed into an obstacle regardless of speed, preventing slow, safe approaches. This conservatism limits navigation performance among obstacles.
AI.method: The authors introduce the shifted collision-cone CBF (SC3BF), which augments the cone condition with a state-dependent allowance so the robot may approach an obstacle at a rate increasing with distance and its own speed. SC3BF is enforced via an ordinary quadratic program. They prove a nonzero allowance that preserves safety always exists and derive one in closed form, establishing forward invariance of the safe set under bounded inputs without requiring minimum forward speed or clearance margin.
AI.result: Compared against three velocity-space baselines on a kinematic bicycle with up to 100 moving obstacles, SC3BF reaches the goal more often and modifies the nominal input less than half as much.
AI.conclusion: SC3BF alleviates the conservatism of the collision cone while guaranteeing safety, yielding higher goal-reaching success and smaller control deviations than baseline velocity-space methods.

title: Do I Need the Cloud? Uncertainty-Aware Step-Level Handoff for Small Language Model Agents
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: SLMs for Agentic Systems, Paris, France, 2026
summary: Small language models (SLMs) are attractive as local agent controllers because they reduce remote inference, latency, and deployment footprint, yet structured tool errors can cause an agent step to fail. Existing routers typically select a model once per query. However, agents expose sequential decision points whose difficulty dynamically changes based on intermediate observations. We propose STEPGATE, an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each local SLM action and selectively escalates challenging steps to a stronger model. On a 52-task held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split, the Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B pair attains 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation, versus 67.3% local-only and 75.4% random escalation (which uses 33.8% escalation). In a separate multi-turn evaluation, STEPGATE achieves 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing (strong-only achieves 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions). These results suggest that step-level escalation recovers a large share of the performance gap to the stronger Qwen2.5-7B backend at a matched cloud-action rate while transmitting fewer tokens remotely. However, our evaluation is limited to one model family, a single stronger backend, and scripted tasks. Furthermore, the test sets are small, multi-turn comparisons rely on paired intervals and statistical tests, and our risk tiers serve as research annotations rather than formal safety guarantees.

AI.tldr: STEPGATE is an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each local SLM action and selectively escalates hard steps to a stronger model, improving agent success over local-only and query-level routing at matched cloud-action rates.
AI.motivation: SLMs are attractive as local agent controllers (less remote inference, latency, deployment footprint), but structured tool errors can fail an agent step. Existing routers select a model once per query, ignoring that agents have sequential decision points whose difficulty changes dynamically with intermediate observations.
AI.method: Per-step scoring of each local SLM action with uncertainty-awareness, selectively escalating challenging steps to a stronger model (step-level escalation/handoff).
AI.result: Single-step BFCL-derived held-out split (52 tasks), Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B: 82.7% task success at 30.8% escalation vs 67.3% local-only and 75.4% random escalation (33.8% escalation). Multi-turn: 69.0% trajectory / 84.0% action success at 30.0% cloud actions vs 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing; strong-only 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions.
AI.conclusion: Step-level escalation recovers much of the gap to the stronger Qwen2.5-7B backend at matched cloud-action rates while transmitting fewer tokens remotely. Limitations: one model family, single stronger backend, scripted tasks, small test sets, paired intervals/statistical tests for multi-turn, and risk tiers are research annotations not formal safety guarantees.

title: Event-Driven Proactive Robot Assistance through Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Assistance in collaborative manipulation is often initiated by user instructions, making high-level reasoning request-driven. In fluent human teamwork, however, partners often infer the next helpful step from the observed outcome of an action rather than waiting for instructions. Motivated by this, we investigate an event-driven formulation of proactive assistance, where human--object interaction outcomes initiate assistive reasoning without user-provided task specifications at inference time. To this end, we propose an event-driven framework that monitors workspace state changes with an event monitor and, upon event completion, extracts stabilized pre/post snapshots that characterize the resulting state transition. A frozen pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) then uses its semantic priors to infer the task context, decide whether assistance is appropriate, and, when needed, generate a sequence of assistive actions from the observed transition. To make outputs executable and verifiable, we restrict actions to a set of action primitives and reference objects via integer IDs.We evaluate the same framework across three distinct real world tabletop collaboration tasks without task-specific training or fine-tuning. The event-driven framework achieves performance comparable to variants given user instructions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an event-driven framework for proactive assistance in collaborative manipulation, where workspace state changes (not user instructions) trigger assistive reasoning. A frozen VLM infers task context, decides whether to assist, and generates executable action sequences from stabilized pre/post event snapshots, using action primitives and object IDs. Across three real-world tabletop tasks, it matches instruction-driven variants without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Prior collaborative manipulation assistance is typically request-driven, initiated by explicit user instructions and requiring high-level reasoning at inference. In contrast, fluent human teamwork relies on partners inferring the next helpful step from observed action outcomes. This gap motivates an event-driven proactive assistance formulation that removes the need for user-provided task specifications at inference time.
AI.method: The framework monitors workspace state changes with an event monitor. Upon event completion, it extracts stabilized pre/post snapshots characterizing the state transition. A frozen pretrained Vision-Language Model uses its semantic priors to infer task context, judge whether assistance is appropriate, and, if so, generate a sequence of assistive actions from the observed transition. For executability and verifiability, actions are restricted to a set of action primitives and objects referenced by integer IDs.
AI.result: The same framework is evaluated on three distinct real-world tabletop collaboration tasks without task-specific training or fine-tuning. It achieves performance comparable to variants that are given user instructions.
AI.conclusion: Event-driven proactive assistance based on observed state transitions can match instruction-driven assistance using a frozen VLM, suggesting a viable path toward more fluent, instruction-free human-robot collaboration. The approach generalizes across tasks without task-specific training or fine-tuning.

title: Agentic Semantic Sensing for Resource-Adaptive AI-RAN
summary: Semantic sensing (SemS) acquires task-relevant information rather than reconstructing complete physical information. Existing SemS formulations typically operate open loop: sensing configurations and observation schedules are fixed before inference and cannot respond to evolving task-level evidence. We propose Agentic SemS, a closed-loop framework for AI-enabled radio access networks (AI-RANs) that controls sensing within a communication-feasible profile set. A profile-conditioned causal Transformer updates the semantic belief from streaming observations, while key-value caching enables efficient state updates across profile changes without repeatedly processing the complete history. A semantic utility network estimates the task-level benefit of acquiring the next observation block under each feasible profile after accounting for sensing cost. The resulting continuation utilities jointly support next-profile selection and semantic early exit, adapting sensing configuration and duration to evolving evidence. The expected semantic gain is further related to conditional mutual information, providing a value-of-information interpretation of continued online sensing. Experiments on Widar3.0 with six emulated sensing profiles show that, in comparison with full-sequence High, the resource-efficient Agentic setting reduces normalized cumulative sensing cost by 25.33% while achieving 85.79% Macro-F1. At the same utility checkpoint, semantic early exit provides a further 12.35% cost reduction over adaptive sensing without early exit, with a 0.97-percentage-point Macro-F1 decrease.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Agentic SemS, a closed-loop semantic sensing framework for AI-RANs that adaptively selects sensing profiles and exit timing based on evolving task evidence, using a profile-conditioned causal Transformer with KV caching and a semantic utility network.
AI.motivation: Existing SemS formulations operate open loop: sensing configurations and observation schedules are fixed before inference and cannot respond to evolving task-level evidence, which limits resource efficiency and adaptivity.
AI.method: Agentic SemS controls sensing within a communication-feasible profile set. A profile-conditioned causal Transformer updates the semantic belief from streaming observations, with KV caching for efficient state updates across profile changes. A semantic utility network estimates the task-level benefit of the next observation block under each feasible profile after accounting for sensing cost. Continuation utilities jointly support next-profile selection and semantic early exit. The expected semantic gain is linked to conditional mutual information, giving a value-of-information interpretation.
AI.result: On Widar3.0 with six emulated sensing profiles, the resource-efficient Agentic setting reduces normalized cumulative sensing cost by 25.33% versus full-sequence High while achieving 85.79% Macro-F1. At the same utility checkpoint, semantic early exit yields an additional 12.35% cost reduction over adaptive sensing without early exit, with a 0.97-percentage-point Macro-F1 decrease.
AI.conclusion: Agentic SemS enables closed-loop, evidence-adaptive sensing configuration and duration in AI-RANs, achieving substantial sensing-cost savings with minimal task-performance loss, and provides an information-theoretic value-of-information justification for continued online sensing.

title: How Much Planning Is Enough? Reducing Search and Computation in World-Model Planning
summary: Visual world models enable goal-directed control through decision-time action search, but their deployment efficiency is often limited by conservatively large planning budgets. We show that competitive task performance can be achieved without agreement with the Full-budget action, that sufficient budgets vary across model--task pairs, and that iterative planners repeatedly encode solve-invariant context. To address these inefficiencies, we propose {SufficientPlan}, a simple deployment framework that requires no modification to pretrained world models or planner updates. Its {Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC)} component uses paired closed-loop evidence to search for and certify a reduced model--task-specific budget within a predefined Full-performance tolerance. Its {Static-Context Reuse (SCR)} component caches observation and goal representations across search iterations while preserving candidate-dependent planning and selected actions. Experiments across multiple world-model backbones and visual-control tasks show that SufficientPlan substantially reduces search budgets and planning latency while maintaining competitive control performance.

AI.tldr: SufficientPlan is a deployment framework that cuts planning budgets and latency for visual world models without retraining, using paired budget certification and cross-iteration context caching.
AI.motivation: Decision-time action search in visual world models is efficient-limited by conservatively large planning budgets. The paper observes that competitive performance does not require matching the Full-budget action, that sufficient budgets vary across model-task pairs, and that iterative planners waste computation re-encoding solve-invariant context.
AI.method: A deployment framework requiring no modification to pretrained world models or planner updates. It combines Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC), which uses paired closed-loop evidence to search for and certify a reduced model-task-specific budget within a predefined Full-performance tolerance, and Static-Context Reuse (SCR), which caches observation and goal representations across search iterations while preserving candidate-dependent planning and selected actions.
AI.result: Across multiple world-model backbones and visual-control tasks, SufficientPlan substantially reduces search budgets and planning latency while maintaining competitive control performance.
AI.conclusion: Competitive control can be retained with certified, reduced, task-specific planning budgets and cached static context, yielding a simple, backbone-agnostic efficiency improvement for world-model-based control.

title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

AI.tldr: DHCG is a framework that builds a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch for LLM multi-agent systems, formulating MAS design as a POMDP and using Planner, Worker, and Generator modules trained with action-aware preference optimization to achieve state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent system orchestration methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their adaptability to evolving reasoning requirements during execution.
AI.method: The authors reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process where composition and scale are dynamically determined. DHCG coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and execution feedback. The Planner generates distinct complementary roles, routes information selectively, and can finalize or expand the graph. Action-aware preference optimization trains the Planner for more effective decisions.
AI.result: Evaluated across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks, DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77–8.02 points. It also generalizes across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.
AI.conclusion: DHCG effectively addresses the limitations of prior MAS orchestration by dynamically determining composition and scale, demonstrating superior performance and generalization across diverse reasoning tasks.

title: From Legs to Wheels: Embodiment-Aware Human Motion Retargeting for Mobile-Base Humanoids
summary: Human video offers a scalable source of robot demonstrations, yet most human-to-humanoid retargeting methods assume a legged robot with human-like kinematics. This assumption does not hold for mobile-base humanoids equipped with a wheeled base, vertical lift, and two arms. Human walking must be expressed through base motion, while torso bending may require coordinated lift and arm motion. We address this mismatch with a task-conditioned framework that assigns reconstructed human motion to base, lift, and arm responsibilities before robot-specific realization. The allocator preserves the human-derived path, stabilizes heading, separates turn and translation when needed, retimes commands to satisfy base limits, and repairs lift and arm trajectories. A deployment adapter then converts the reference to 50 Hz commands using stationary-base detection, deadband and slew-rate filtering, time-consistent playback scaling, and separate linear and angular gains. We evaluate the resulting references with human-derived task-space comparisons, policy-free simulation replay, and a qualitative execution on a physical robot.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a task-conditioned framework for retargeting human video demonstrations to wheeled mobile-base humanoids, assigning reconstructed human motion to base, lift, and arm responsibilities before robot-specific realization.
AI.motivation: Most human-to-humanoid retargeting methods assume a legged robot with human-like kinematics, which does not hold for mobile-base humanoids equipped with a wheeled base, vertical lift, and two arms. Human walking must be expressed through base motion, and torso bending may require coordinated lift and arm motion, creating a kinematic mismatch.
AI.method: A task-conditioned framework assigns reconstructed human motion to base, lift, and arm responsibilities before robot-specific realization. The allocator preserves the human-derived path, stabilizes heading, separates turn and translation when needed, retimes commands to satisfy base limits, and repairs lift and arm trajectories. A deployment adapter then converts the reference to 50 Hz commands using stationary-base detection, deadband and slew-rate filtering, time-consistent playback scaling, and separate linear and angular gains.
AI.result: The resulting references are evaluated with human-derived task-space comparisons, policy-free simulation replay, and a qualitative execution on a physical robot.
AI.conclusion: The framework addresses the kinematic mismatch between human motion and wheeled mobile-base humanoids by task-conditioned allocation and deployment adaptation, enabling retargeting of human video demonstrations to such platforms.

title: RA-MoWE: Workflow-Affinity Embeddings for Query Clustering and Agentic Workflow Generation
summary: Agentic workflows enable large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks by coordinating reasoning, tool use, and verification. However, a workflow optimized for an entire task collection can overlook differences in the reasoning strategies that individual queries need, while searching for a new workflow for every query repeats costly optimization. To address this tradeoff, we introduce RA-MoWE, a framework that uses workflow-affinity embeddings to cluster queries and guide the generation of reusable expert workflows. Each embedding records how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves a query, revealing similarities in which reasoning strategies are effective. RA-MoWE uses each cluster's queries and average embedding to initialize and refine a specialized workflow through execution feedback. An embedding encoder predicts these embeddings from query text, allowing new queries to select a generated expert without first executing the reference workflows. On a 300-query test set drawn from four benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and programming, RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among the reference workflows, while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference.

AI.tldr: RA-MoWE clusters queries via workflow-affinity embeddings to generate reusable expert workflows, improving task scores while cutting inference LLM calls.
AI.motivation: A single workflow optimized for an entire task collection ignores query-specific reasoning strategy differences, yet optimizing a separate workflow per query incurs prohibitive optimization cost. The paper seeks to resolve this tradeoff between coarse task-level optimization and costly per-query optimization.
AI.method: RA-MoWE builds workflow-affinity embeddings that record how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves each query, exposing similarities in effective reasoning strategies. It clusters queries using these embeddings, then initializes and refines a specialized workflow per cluster using the cluster's queries and average embedding via execution feedback. An embedding encoder predicts embeddings directly from query text, so new queries can select a generated expert workflow without executing the reference workflows first.
AI.result: On a 300-query test set spanning four benchmarks (mathematics, science, programming), RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among the reference workflows, while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference.
AI.conclusion: Workflow-affinity embeddings enable effective query clustering and reusable expert workflow generation, achieving a favorable tradeoff between performance and inference cost through text-based embedding prediction rather than exhaustive workflow execution.

title: Post-Grasp Kinematic Repair for Robotic Insertion via Object-in-Gripper Reorientation
summary: A stable grasp does not guarantee kinematically feasible robotic insertion because the object-in-gripper transform may force the robot towards singularities or joint limits along the prescribed insertion path. We study post-grasp kinematic feasibility repair through object-in-gripper reorientation. Given an achieved grasp and a fixed insertion path, we seek a small reorientation that restores kinematic feasibility. Sequential IK can miss such candidates by following an unfavorable joint-space path, while the nonsmooth feasibility landscape makes the search computationally expensive. We evaluate candidates using a branch-aware IK graph that maximizes the minimum feasibility margin over the discretized insertion path and use a learned task-conditioned prior to improve query ordering. The selected reorientation is executed through tactile-based extrinsic manipulation. In UR5e simulations, the planner without learned ranking reduces mean reorientation over successful trials by 51.5% compared with grid-based sequential IK. Adding learned ranking reduces this planner's mean planning time by an additional 51.1%. Real-robot experiments validate the complete pipeline.

AI.tldr: A grasp that is stable may still be kinematically infeasible for insertion; this work repairs feasibility via small object-in-gripper reorientations found with a branch-aware IK graph and a learned prior, then executed by tactile extrinsic manipulation.
AI.motivation: A stable grasp does not guarantee kinematically feasible robotic insertion, because the object-in-gripper transform can force the robot toward singularities or joint limits along the prescribed insertion path. Existing approaches like sequential IK can miss feasible reorientations by following unfavorable joint-space paths, and the nonsmooth feasibility landscape makes exhaustive search computationally expensive.
AI.method: Given an achieved grasp and a fixed insertion path, the method seeks a small object-in-gripper reorientation that restores kinematic feasibility. Candidates are evaluated with a branch-aware IK graph that maximizes the minimum feasibility margin over the discretized insertion path, and a learned task-conditioned prior is used to improve query ordering. The selected reorientation is executed via tactile-based extrinsic manipulation.
AI.result: In UR5e simulations, the planner without learned ranking reduces mean reorientation over successful trials by 51.5% versus grid-based sequential IK. Adding learned ranking further reduces this planner's mean planning time by 51.1%. Real-robot experiments validate the complete pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Post-grasp kinematic feasibility can be repaired through small object-in-gripper reorientations, and combining a branch-aware IK graph with a learned task-conditioned prior yields more efficient and effective planning than sequential or grid-based IK baselines, with the pipeline validated on a real robot.

title: WorkflowOps: Learning Agent Collaboration Priors for Multi-Agent Workflow Orchestration
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex knowledge work, yet their orchestration layers remain largely memoryless: each new task is decomposed, assigned, and executed from scratch with no benefit from prior successful executions. We present WorkflowOps, a multi-agent workflow orchestration framework that learns agent collaboration priors from historical workflows and expands its agent pool on demand to cover new capability requirements. Our approach introduces three coupled mechanisms. First, a transition probability matrix captures pairwise agent collaboration frequencies from past workflows and applies them as soft guidance during DAG workflow construction through intra-layer ordering optimization, probability-thresholded edge suggestion, and transitive reduction for parallelism maximization. Second, a sufficiency-driven agent creation loop detects capability gaps via semantic matching scores, generates specialized agents through an LLM, and simultaneously injects them into the collaboration matrix, so that newly created agents are immediately usable with predicted collaboration priors. Third, a layered semantic matching strategy uses pre-trained sentence embeddings for fast, deterministic capability matching as a first pass, invoking LLM verification only for low-confidence cases, thereby reducing LLM routing calls by over 80\% compared to pure-LLM approaches. Experiments on mixed code, math, and question-answering suites show that WorkflowOps improves end-to-end pass rates over recent workflow-construction baselines, with the largest gains on structured, decomposable tasks where past agent handoff patterns transfer.

AI.tldr: WorkflowOps is a multi-agent orchestration framework that learns agent collaboration priors from historical workflows and expands its agent pool on demand, using a transition probability matrix, a sufficiency-driven agent creation loop, and layered semantic matching to improve end-to-end pass rates on structured tasks while cutting LLM routing calls by over 80%.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for complex knowledge work, but their orchestration layers are largely memoryless: each task is decomposed, assigned, and executed from scratch, providing no benefit from prior successful executions.
AI.method: Three coupled mechanisms: (1) a transition probability matrix capturing pairwise agent collaboration frequencies from past workflows, applied as soft guidance during DAG construction via intra-layer ordering optimization, probability-thresholded edge suggestion, and transitive reduction for parallelism maximization; (2) a sufficiency-driven agent creation loop that detects capability gaps via semantic matching scores, generates specialized agents via an LLM, and injects them into the collaboration matrix; (3) a layered semantic matching strategy using pre-trained sentence embeddings for fast, deterministic matching as a first pass, invoking LLM verification only for low-confidence cases.
AI.result: On mixed code, math, and question-answering suites, WorkflowOps improves end-to-end pass rates over recent workflow-construction baselines, with the largest gains on structured, decomposable tasks where past agent handoff patterns transfer. It also reduces LLM routing calls by over 80% compared to pure-LLM approaches.
AI.conclusion: Learning and reusing agent collaboration priors, combined with on-demand agent pool expansion and efficient layered matching, yields more effective and efficient multi-agent workflow orchestration, especially for structured tasks benefiting from transferable handoff patterns.

title: MIM-VLA: Learning Physical Interaction Representations from Gripper Motor Feedback
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. Jaeyoung Lee and Jiyeon Koo contributed equally
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies infer grasp actions primarily from visual observations and robot state, but do not explicitly represent the physical response observed after contact. We present MIM-VLA, a motor-feedback-based architecture that encodes recent gripper current, position, velocity, and signal validity as a 128-dimensional interaction token. A motor-only Motor Interaction Module (MIM) is pretrained with human-reviewed contact and interaction-phase labels and then conditions only the gripper-action pathway of SmolVLA; arm actions and the position-control interface remain unchanged. The same token supports the MEM selector VLM that compares candidate interactions and produces evidence-conditioned selections and explanations. We evaluate MIM-VLA in three real-world settings: comparing the interaction resistance of visually different objects, disambiguating visually similar real and replica objects through active probing, and gently grasping fragile objects, including held-out instances. Across 13 object pairs, MIM-VLA selects the higher-resistance object in 75.0% of trials, compared with 48.8% for the SmolVLA baseline. For the evaluated tasks, the approach uses motor feedback already available from the gripper and does not require an additional tactile array, force-torque sensor, calibrated force estimate, or direct current control.

AI.tldr: MIM-VLA adds a motor-feedback interaction token from gripper current/position/velocity to SmolVLA, conditioning only the gripper pathway for contact-aware grasping and selection.
AI.motivation: VLA policies infer grasp actions mainly from vision and robot state but lack explicit representation of the physical response after contact, limiting their ability to reason about interaction resistance, material identity, and fragility.
AI.method: MIM-VLA encodes recent gripper current, position, velocity, and signal validity into a 128-D interaction token. A motor-only Motor Interaction Module (MIM) is pretrained with human-reviewed contact and interaction-phase labels, then conditions only the gripper-action pathway of SmolVLA while arm actions and position control stay unchanged. The same token feeds a MEM selector VLM that compares candidate interactions and yields evidence-conditioned selections and explanations.
AI.result: Across 13 object pairs, MIM-VLA selects the higher-resistance object in 75.0% of trials versus 48.8% for the SmolVLA baseline. Evaluations include three real-world settings: comparing resistance of visually different objects, disambiguating visually similar real and replica objects via active probing, and gently grasping fragile objects including held-out instances.
AI.conclusion: Motor feedback already available from the gripper enables contact-aware grasping without additional tactile arrays, force-torque sensors, calibrated force estimates, or direct current control.

title: Self-Referenced Social Preferences: Cooperation without Observing Others Rewards
summary: Social preferences can promote cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning, but existing approaches often require agents to observe the rewards of their peers. In many real-world interactions, however, an agent can, as humans do, observe others' behavior and outcomes without access to their private reward signals. We introduce self-referenced social preferences, in which each agent learns a model of its own reward, applies it to other agents' observed transitions to assess their outcomes from its own perspective, and feeds these self-referenced assessments into standard social preferences. We study two ways to incorporate these assessments: modifying the learning reward, or using them to weight policy updates. We evaluate the approach on three sequential social dilemmas, Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest, which require volunteering, public-good contribution, and resource restraint, respectively. Across all three environments, agents learn cooperative behavior without observing others' rewards, including in settings where independent learners fail to cooperate, and frequently achieve more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with access to true rewards. The effective integration point depends on the social preference: inequity aversion works best in the reward together with a value look-ahead, whereas a purely benevolent preference benefits from policy-update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy-update approach continues to support cooperation. These results show that explicit access to other agents' reward signals is not necessary for learning cooperative behavior: social preferences can instead be grounded in self-referenced assessments of others' outcomes derived from their observed behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces self-referenced social preferences for multi-agent RL, where agents assess others' outcomes by applying their own learned reward model to others' observed transitions, enabling cooperation without observing peers' private rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing social-preference methods for cooperative MARL typically require agents to observe peers' rewards, which is unrealistic in many real-world interactions where agents can only observe others' behavior and outcomes.
AI.method: Each agent learns a model of its own reward and applies it to other agents' observed transitions to evaluate their outcomes from its own perspective. These self-referenced assessments are fed into standard social preferences via two integration points: modifying the learning reward, or weighting policy updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on three sequential social dilemmas (Escape Room, Clean Up, Commons Harvest) requiring volunteering, public-good contribution, and resource restraint, agents learn cooperative behavior without observing others' rewards, including where independent learners fail, and often achieve more equitable return divisions than agents with true rewards. Inequity aversion works best in the reward with value look-ahead, while benevolent preference benefits from policy-update weighting; the policy-update approach supports cooperation under partial observability.
AI.conclusion: Explicit access to other agents' reward signals is not necessary for learning cooperative behavior; social preferences can be grounded in self-referenced assessments of others' outcomes derived from observed behavior.

title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaborative Transport Using Density Functions
summary: This paper presents a hierarchical density-based model predictive control framework for safe collaborative manipulation by multiple quadrupedal robots. The framework enables a team of robots to push a shared object to a desired pose using only the initial and goal poses, without requiring a precomputed reference trajectory. A centralized box-level MPC optimizes contact forces while enforcing a control-density constraint for goal convergence and obstacle avoidance. Each robot then solves its own distributed robot-level whole-body MPC, under a stated shared-information assumption, to track its moving contact location while accounting for static obstacles and the time-varying positions of neighboring robots. The approach is evaluated in MuJoCo using whole-body contact dynamics for two and three Unitree Go2 quadrupeds collaboratively pushing rigid objects through narrow passages. Comparisons with matched Control Barrier Function and RRT* based tracking baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed density-based formulation for push-only, force- and torque-coupled manipulation tasks. Implementation videos are available at https://jaggu2606.github.io/go2-density-mpc-pushing/

AI.tldr: A hierarchical density-based MPC framework enables teams of quadrupedal robots to collaboratively push a shared object to a desired pose without a precomputed reference trajectory, validated in MuJoCo with two and three Unitree Go2 robots.
AI.motivation: Collaborative manipulation by multiple quadrupedal robots requires safe, coordinated control. Existing approaches typically depend on precomputed reference trajectories, limiting flexibility. This work aims to achieve goal-convergent, collision-free pushing using only the initial and goal poses.
AI.method: A two-level hierarchical MPC. A centralized box-level MPC optimizes contact forces while enforcing a control-density constraint for goal convergence and obstacle avoidance. Each robot then solves a distributed robot-level whole-body MPC under a shared-information assumption to track its moving contact location, accounting for static obstacles and the time-varying positions of neighboring robots.
AI.result: Evaluated in MuJoCo using whole-body contact dynamics for two and three Unitree Go2 quadrupeds collaboratively pushing rigid objects through narrow passages. Comparisons with matched Control Barrier Function and RRT*-based tracking baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of the density-based formulation for push-only, force- and torque-coupled manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The density-based hierarchical MPC formulation is effective for safe collaborative push-only, force- and torque-coupled manipulation, outperforming CBF and RRT* baselines without requiring a precomputed reference trajectory.

title: ShanLiangRen: A Nutrition Agent for Personalized Daily Meal Planning
summary: Dietary nutrition planning plays an important role in chronic disease management and maintaining a healthy body. In applications, it must simultaneously satisfy personalized constraints and reasonable multidimensional nutritional goals. These two aspects often conflict, and user constraints evolve with feedback, resulting in a substantial gap between generic guidelines and executable plans. To bridge this gap, we first propose the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP). To tackle MDP, we develop a nutrition agent, ShanLiangRen. The system first transforms dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes and natural language requirements into an individualized constrained planning instance. It then employs an exact retrieval-augmented generation method to shrink the feasible candidate set from a large scale ingredient and recipe space. Finally, it adopts a refinement guided by Pareto principles, where an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and feedback from constraint verification. The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, together with reports on nutrition compliance that show constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. We have released the system online as a WeChat Program, ShanLiangRen. A demo video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=652OtY5VlGA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP) and presents ShanLiangRen, an LLM-based nutrition agent that produces fully quantified, constraint-satisfying meal plans via exact retrieval-augmented generation and Pareto-guided refinement.
AI.motivation: Dietary nutrition planning is important for chronic disease management and health maintenance, but practical plans must satisfy personalized constraints and multidimensional nutritional goals simultaneously. These two aspects often conflict, and user constraints evolve with feedback, creating a gap between generic guidelines and executable plans.
AI.method: They formalize the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP) and build the ShanLiangRen nutrition agent. The system converts dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes, and natural language requirements into an individualized constrained planning instance; applies an exact retrieval-augmented generation method to shrink the feasible candidate set from a large ingredient and recipe space; and performs Pareto-principle-guided refinement in which an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and constraint-verification feedback.
AI.result: The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, along with nutrition compliance reports showing constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. It has been released online as a WeChat Program (ShanLiangRen), with a demo video provided.
AI.conclusion: ShanLiangRen bridges the gap between generic dietary guidelines and executable personalized plans by combining constrained multiobjective planning, exact retrieval-augmented candidate reduction, and Pareto-guided LLM refinement, and is deployed as a practical online service.

title: ActTune: Action-Aware Precision and GPU Operating-Point Adaptation for Energy-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke inference to control robots, making graphics processing unit (GPU) energy a recurring cost of task execution. Reducing energy per inference call, however, may not reduce energy per successful task if numerical errors increase failures or slower inference prolongs execution. We therefore target GPU energy per successful task while preserving task success and keeping the inference-latency increase within 10\%. Our approach builds on two observations: quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, model layers, and weights versus activations; and numerical precision changes the workload, shifting favorable GPU operating points. We introduce ActTune, an action-aware framework that connects layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection over requested frequency--power-cap pairs. A lightweight decision tree learns its splits and leaf precision configurations directly from configuration action errors, then selects precision before each policy call. The controller forecasts the next workload and applies the selected GPU operating point asynchronously using a lookup table calibrated under a latency budget. A shared resident quantized weight bank enables configuration switching without weight reconstruction or additional policy evaluations. On LIBERO, a benchmark for lifelong robot learning, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3\% relative to state of the art. Relative to the original BF16 implementations, it delivers up to $2.02\times$ faster inference and, with GPU operating-point adaptation, reduces energy per successful task by up to 76.8\%.

AI.tldr: ActTune, an action-aware precision-allocation and GPU operating-point framework for VLA policies, reduces GPU energy per successful task by up to 76.8% while improving success and inference speed.
AI.motivation: VLA policies repeatedly invoke inference for robot control, so GPU energy becomes a recurring execution cost. Cutting energy per inference may not cut energy per successful task, since numerical errors raise failures or slower inference lengthens execution. The target is thus GPU energy per successful task, subject to preserved task success and ≤10% inference-latency increase.
AI.method: ActTune is built on two observations: quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, layers, and weights vs. activations; and precision changes the workload, shifting favorable GPU operating points. It links layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection over frequency–power-cap pairs. A lightweight decision tree learns splits and leaf precision configurations from configuration action errors, selecting precision before each policy call. A controller forecasts the next workload and asynchronously applies the GPU operating point via a latency-budget-calibrated lookup table. A shared resident quantized weight bank enables switching without weight reconstruction or extra policy evaluations.
AI.result: On LIBERO, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3% over state of the art; versus original BF16 implementations it yields up to 2.02× faster inference and, with operating-point adaptation, up to 76.8% lower energy per successful task.
AI.conclusion: Action-aware, workload-coupled precision and GPU operating-point co-selection can substantially reduce energy per successful task in VLA robot control without sacrificing success or latency budgets.

title: Textual Environmental Context and Spatial Graphs for LLM-Based Regional SST Forecasting
summary: Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting depends on local temporal persistence, regional spatial dependence, and environmental conditions that evolve with the forecast date. We study how these heterogeneous conditions can be presented to a large language model (LLM) for regional multi-step forecasting without serializing the full SST grid as text. We formulate forecasting as conditional numerical generation: historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental records, and static ocean knowledge form a textual context, while regional spatial state is supplied through continuous graph-derived prefixes. A static graph encodes persistent geographic--climatological relations, and a dynamic graph encodes recent SST correlations and localized tropical-cyclone influence. Two graph neural networks produce a target-node representation that is mapped by a spatial-prefix fusion and injected into the LLM input. On SST forecasting in the South China Sea, the complete configuration achieves the best MAE and $\Rtwo$ among the compared methods over ten forecast steps. Alongside the numerical forecast, a rule-based module matches predicted trends and environmental-factor directions with knowledge entries to return source-linked, post-hoc contextual explanations.

AI.tldr: This paper forecasts regional multi-step sea surface temperature (SST) by conditioning an LLM on textual historical and environmental context plus continuous graph-derived spatial prefixes, achieving top MAE and R² over ten steps in the South China Sea, with rule-based post-hoc explanations.
AI.motivation: SST forecasting depends on local temporal persistence, regional spatial dependence, and date-varying environmental conditions. Presenting this heterogeneous information to an LLM without serializing the full SST grid as text is an open challenge.
AI.method: Forecasting is framed as conditional numerical generation. Historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental records, and static ocean knowledge form the textual context. Regional spatial state is provided via continuous graph-derived prefixes: a static graph encodes persistent geographic-climatological relations, a dynamic graph encodes recent SST correlations and localized tropical-cyclone influence. Two GNNs produce a target-node representation, mapped by spatial-prefix fusion and injected into the LLM input. A rule-based module links predicted trends and environmental-factor directions to knowledge entries for source-linked, post-hoc explanations.
AI.result: On South China Sea SST forecasting, the complete configuration achieves the best MAE and R² among compared methods across ten forecast steps.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous spatiotemporal and environmental conditions can be effectively injected into an LLM via graph-derived prefixes for accurate regional multi-step SST forecasting, while rule-based matching yields source-linked contextual explanations alongside numerical predictions.

title: Behavioral Safety Assessment towards Large-scale Deployment of Autonomous Vehicles, Part I: Methodology
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) have significantly advanced in real-world deployment in recent years, yet safety continues to be a critical barrier to widespread adoption. Traditional functional safety approaches, which primarily verify the reliability, robustness, and adequacy of AV hardware and software systems from a vehicle-centric perspective, do not sufficiently address the AV's broader interactions and behavioral impact on the surrounding traffic environment. To overcome this limitation, we propose a paradigm shift toward behavioral safety, a comprehensive approach focused on evaluating AV responses and interactions within the traffic environment. To systematically assess behavioral safety, we introduce a third-party AV safety assessment framework comprising two complementary evaluation components: the Behavioral Competency Test and the Driving Intelligence Test. The Behavioral Competency Test evaluates the AV's reactive behaviors under controlled scenarios, ensuring basic behavioral competency. In contrast, the Driving Intelligence Test assesses the AV's interactive behaviors within naturalistic traffic conditions, quantifying the frequency of safety-critical events to deliver statistically meaningful safety metrics before large-scale deployment. In Part II of this study, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS) is tested to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a shift from vehicle-centric functional safety to behavioral safety for autonomous vehicles, introducing a third-party assessment framework with two components: the Behavioral Competency Test and the Driving Intelligence Test.
AI.motivation: Safety remains a critical barrier to AV adoption. Traditional functional safety approaches only verify AV hardware and software reliability from a vehicle-centric perspective and fail to address the AV's broader interactions and behavioral impact on the surrounding traffic environment.
