AI.method: The authors introduce a third-party AV safety assessment framework centered on behavioral safety, consisting of two complementary evaluation components. The Behavioral Competency Test evaluates reactive behaviors under controlled scenarios to ensure basic competency. The Driving Intelligence Test assesses interactive behaviors in naturalistic traffic conditions and quantifies the frequency of safety-critical events.
AI.result: The framework provides statistically meaningful safety metrics prior to large-scale deployment. In Part II of the study, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS) is tested to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed behavioral safety paradigm and third-party assessment framework offer a more comprehensive way to evaluate AV safety by capturing interactions with the traffic environment, complementing traditional functional safety approaches.

title: Isotropic Yet Undecodable: The Sequential Content-Sufficiency Gap in Latent-Predictive Text Representations
summary: We study sequential content sufficiency by investigating whether a representation retains the ordered target information available in its input. An information-theoretic decomposition separates input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. We construct recoverable views where perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity coexist with zero target information, and establish limits imposed by deterministic canonical anchors. Token log-loss provides a one-sided information-loss bound; a fixed-penalty ridge analysis shows why rank alone cannot determine prediction risk. These results motivate CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization. On 40,000 validation sequences, latent-agreement (PL0) and token-grounded (PL2) have nearly identical pooled ranks but reach 13.5% and 98.8% positional Recall@1, respectively, under strong natural corruption when the correct target length is provided. On 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with a trained MatchaTTS readout yields 21.54% word error rate (WER) on corrupted text, versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93%. These results show that geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access in the text settings studied here.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "sequential content sufficiency"—whether a representation retains ordered target information from its input—via an information-theoretic decomposition into input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. It introduces CANOPE, an ordered-latent-canvas framework, and empirically shows that geometric regularity (latent agreement) does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or downstream utility, whereas token-grounded supervision does.
AI.motivation: Representations are often judged by geometric properties (agreement with a latent target, isotropic Gaussianity, or rank quality). The authors argue such geometric regularity can coexist with zero target information, so these proxies are insufficient for assessing whether a representation actually preserves ordered target content or enables effective downstream access.
AI.method: An information-theoretic decomposition separates input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. The authors construct recoverable views in which perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity hold alongside zero target information, and establish limits imposed by deterministic canonical anchors. Token log-loss is used as a one-sided information-loss bound, and a fixed-penalty ridge analysis shows rank alone cannot determine prediction risk. These motivate CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization.
AI.result: On 40,000 validation sequences with strong natural corruption and correct target length, latent-agreement (PL0) and token-grounded (PL2) show nearly identical pooled ranks yet reach 13.5% and 98.8% positional Recall@1, respectively. On 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with a trained MatchaTTS readout attains 21.54% WER on corrupted text versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93%.
AI.conclusion: Geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access; token-grounded supervision is necessary. The findings caution against using latent agreement or rank as sufficient proxies for content sufficiency and support token-grounded objectives like CANOPE.

title: Behavioral Safety Assessment towards Large-scale Deployment of Autonomous Vehicles, Part II: Assessment Results
summary: Third-party evaluations of autonomous vehicle (AV) safety can play a vital role in improving public acceptance, building consumer confidence, and establishing effective safety standards. In Part I of this study, we propose a dedicated third-party testing initiative for systematically evaluating AV behavioral safety. In this paper, we validate our proposed framework using Autoware.Universe, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS), tested both in simulated environments and on the physical test track at the University of Michigan's Mcity Testing Facility. The results indicate that Autoware.Universe possesses 6 out of 14 behavioral competencies and exhibited a crash rate of 3.01x10^-3 crashes per mile, approximately 1,000 times higher than the average human driver crash rate. During the tests, we also uncovered a number of unknown unsafe scenarios for Autoware.Universe. These findings underscore the necessity of behavioral safety evaluations for improving AV safety performance prior to widespread public deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper validates a proposed third-party AV behavioral safety testing framework using Autoware.Universe (open-source L4 ADS) in simulation and at Mcity, finding it met 6 of 14 behavioral competencies with a crash rate ~1,000x higher than human drivers.
AI.motivation: Third-party evaluations of autonomous vehicle safety are seen as key to improving public acceptance, building consumer confidence, and establishing effective safety standards, motivating a dedicated, systematic behavioral safety testing initiative.
AI.method: The authors apply their proposed third-party testing framework (from Part I) to validate it, evaluating Autoware.Universe, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System, through both simulated environments and physical test-track trials at the University of Michigan's Mcity Testing Facility.
AI.result: Autoware.Universe demonstrated 6 of 14 behavioral competencies and exhibited a crash rate of 3.01x10^-3 crashes per mile, approximately 1,000 times higher than the average human driver crash rate. The tests also revealed several previously unknown unsafe scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the necessity of behavioral safety evaluations for improving AV safety performance prior to widespread public deployment.

title: Continuous Memory Machines
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)
summary: Recurrent neural networks typically compress information into a single vector-valued recurrent state, forcing short-term computation and long-term retention to share the same representation. Past extensions alleviate this bottleneck by increasing the memory capacity or separating timescales, but lack the combination of rapid neuron-level processing and longer-term retention found in biology. To that end, we introduce the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent architecture with matrix-valued short- and long-term memory states serving distinct functional roles. Building on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), the CMM's short-term memory tracks recent neural activity, with uniquely parameterized neuron-level models learning to use these activity patterns for computation. A persistent long-term memory stores information for later use, with a Transformer jointly updating both memory stores, providing an expressive bidirectional read--write mechanism such that each store can reorganize its own contents and both read from and write to the other. Across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, the CMM outperforms a broad suite of baselines, exhibiting stronger generalization than prior memory-augmented networks while preserving the CTM's interpretable attention patterns. Code is available at https://github.com/SakanaAI/continuous-memory-machines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent architecture with matrix-valued short- and long-term memory states that combines rapid neuron-level processing with longer-term retention, outperforming baselines across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard recurrent neural networks compress information into a single vector-valued recurrent state, forcing short-term computation and long-term retention to share the same representation. Prior approaches increase memory capacity or separate timescales, but fail to combine rapid neuron-level processing with long-term retention as seen in biology.
AI.method: Building on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), the CMM maintains matrix-valued short- and long-term memory states with distinct functional roles. The short-term memory tracks recent neural activity, with uniquely parameterized neuron-level models learning to use these activity patterns for computation, while the persistent long-term memory stores information for later use. A Transformer jointly updates both memory stores, providing an expressive bidirectional read-write mechanism where each store can reorganize its contents and both read from and write to the other.
AI.result: Across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, the CMM outperforms a broad suite of baselines, exhibiting stronger generalization than prior memory-augmented networks while preserving the CTM's interpretable attention patterns.
AI.conclusion: The CMM successfully integrates rapid neuron-level processing and longer-term retention through dual matrix-valued memory states with bidirectional read-write coupling, offering superior generalization over existing memory-augmented networks. Code is available at https://github.com/SakanaAI/continuous-memory-machines.

title: A Belief-State World Model for Catheter Navigation under Sparse Fluoroscopy: A Planar Proof of Concept
comment: Presented at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026) Workshop on Surgical Digital Twins (SurgTwin). 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Endovascular catheter navigation relies on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to ionizing radiation throughout the procedure. We investigate whether a physics-based world model can sustain the navigation task between deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions, and whether the model can signal when its internal state estimate is no longer reliable. We formulate sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process where a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over the device state, reduced in this implementation to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. We evaluate this formulation in a deliberately simplified setting: a synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections, without clinical or animal data. In this setting, the belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with a root mean square error of 1.30 mm while acquiring observations at one fifteenth of the continuous rate (0.97 mm at every frame, 1.51 mm at one thirtieth), reported 90 percent credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with an AUROC of 0.68. These results constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness; their purpose is to establish that calibrated belief, rather than point-estimate accuracy alone, is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.

AI.tldr: A physics-based belief-state world model (Cosserat rod dynamics + particle filter + sparse X-ray observations) can sustain endovascular catheter navigation under sparse fluoroscopy while providing calibrated uncertainty and contact-risk signals, demonstrated as a proof of concept in a simplified synthetic phantom.
AI.motivation: Endovascular catheter navigation depends on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to sustained ionizing radiation. The authors ask whether a physics-based world model can (1) bridge deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions to maintain the navigation task, and (2) signal when its internal state estimate has become unreliable—i.e., whether calibrated belief, not just point-estimate accuracy, is the key property required.
AI.method: Sparse-fluoroscopy navigation is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process: a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over device state—reduced here to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. Evaluation is restricted to a deliberately simplified synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections; no clinical or animal data are used.
AI.result: The belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with 1.30 mm RMSE while acquiring observations at 1/15 of the continuous rate (0.97 mm per-frame; 1.51 mm at 1/30). Reported 90% credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with AUROC 0.68.
AI.conclusion: The findings constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness. Their purpose is to establish that a calibrated belief—rather than point-estimate accuracy alone—is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.

title: SIGMA: Self-Improving Alignment Generalization from a Model Spec
summary: LLM agents are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks and of recursively improving themselves on easy-to-verify objectives such as software engineering and mathematics. Since alignment is much harder to verify, this creates a growing risk of capabilities increasing without appropriate safety alignment, especially as capabilities expand to auto-research and cybersecurity. Existing approaches focus on capability self-improvement using verifiable feedback or on alignment training with supervision from stronger models or curated data, creating an external supervision bottleneck for alignment. We ask whether current models can improve their own safety alignment, and propose SIGMA, a data generation and training pipeline enabling alignment self-improvement that generalizes to out-of-distribution settings. Given only a "Model Spec" stating the model's desired behavior, SIGMA leverages a model's reasoning capabilities to strengthen its own safety reasoning. SIGMA first performs spec-guided task synthesis, using the candidate model as a task designer agent to generate diverse alignment dilemma scenarios and convert them into training tasks that stress-test its understanding of the Model Spec. Next, SIGMA conducts self-judged alignment training through supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning with the model itself as the reward model. Despite training only on single-turn chat data, SIGMA improves safety alignment in multi-turn agentic environments (AgentHarm harmfulness decreases from 22.6 to 14.8; Agentic Misalignment decreases from 79.1 to 3.8), outperforms Deliberative Alignment and Constitutional AI baselines, and retains general capability. Analyses show that a Model Spec balancing harmlessness and helpfulness, test-time reasoning for safety deliberation, and high-quality rubrics from SIGMA's task designer agent are crucial for effective self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SIGMA, a data generation and training pipeline that enables LLM agents to self-improve their safety alignment using only a Model Spec, generalizing to out-of-distribution agentic settings.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can recursively self-improve on easily verifiable objectives (e.g., software engineering, mathematics), but alignment is much harder to verify, creating a growing risk of capabilities outpacing safety alignment. Existing methods either focus on capability self-improvement via verifiable feedback or rely on alignment training with external supervision (stronger models or curated data), which imposes an external supervision bottleneck for alignment. The authors ask whether models can improve their own safety alignment.
AI.method: SIGMA leverages a model's reasoning capabilities to strengthen its own safety reasoning, given only a "Model Spec" stating desired behavior. It first performs spec-guided task synthesis, using the candidate model as a task designer agent to generate diverse alignment dilemma scenarios and convert them into training tasks that stress-test its understanding of the Model Spec. It then conducts self-judged alignment training via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, with the model itself serving as the reward model.
AI.result: Despite training only on single-turn chat data, SIGMA improves safety alignment in multi-turn agentic environments: AgentHarm harmfulness drops from 22.6 to 14.8, and Agentic Misalignment drops from 79.1 to 3.8. It outperforms Deliberative Alignment and Constitutional AI baselines while retaining general capability. Analyses show that a Model Spec balancing harmlessness and helpfulness, test-time reasoning for safety deliberation, and high-quality rubrics from the task designer agent are crucial for effective self-improvement.
AI.conclusion: Current models can improve their own safety alignment via SIGMA without external supervision, and this self-improvement generalizes to out-of-distribution, multi-turn agentic settings while preserving general capabilities.

title: No Need to Stop the Fleet: Localized Anomaly Isolation via Dead Zones in AGV Fleets
summary: Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) fleets in production and logistics environments rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies such as malfunctions, hazards, or contaminated areas. While safe, this approach halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. This paper proposes dead zones --- a formally defined localized isolation approach that serves as an additional fail-operational mechanism for situations where a full system-wide halt is not strictly needed. Rather than shutting down the entire fleet, a dead zone isolates the anomalous area, allowing unaffected robots to continue operating normally. We introduce two operational strategies: basic dead zone handling, in which affected robots enter a dead zone and stop, and dead zone handling with escaping, in which robots that are sufficiently far from a dead zone reroute around it. For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories we prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation is kept between robots. Experimental evaluation confirms the theoretical guarantees and characterizes the throughput tradeoffs between all three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "dead zones," a formally defined localized isolation mechanism for AGV fleets that replaces (or supplements) the system-wide emergency stop, allowing unaffected robots to keep operating while isolating an anomalous area, with provable collision-freedom and bounded delay for escaping robots.
AI.motivation: AGV fleets currently rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies (malfunctions, hazards, contaminated areas). Although safe, this halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. A mechanism is needed that is fail-operational and localizes the disruption rather than stopping everything.
AI.method: The authors propose dead zones, a formally defined localized isolation approach serving as an additional fail-operational mechanism when a full halt is not strictly required. They define two operational strategies: (1) basic dead zone handling, where affected robots enter the dead zone and stop; and (2) dead zone handling with escaping, where robots sufficiently far from the dead zone reroute around it. For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories, they prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation between robots is maintained. An experimental evaluation validates the theory and characterizes throughput tradeoffs.
AI.result: The theoretical guarantees are confirmed experimentally, and the evaluation characterizes the throughput tradeoffs among the three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.
AI.conclusion: Dead zones provide a locally scoped, fail-operational alternative to whole-fleet emergency stops, with formal collision-freedom and bounded-delay guarantees for escaping robots, and measurable throughput advantages over full stops in partially affected environments.

title: Confidence Reasoning Graphs: Structured Confidence Estimation for LLM Agents
summary: When using an LLM agent in a consequential domain, making an informed decision about whether to trust its output or intervene requires calibrated confidence in the agent's success. Confidence estimation for agents is difficult because evidence about success is distributed across heterogeneous, interdependent steps of an agent's trajectory. Practical agentic deployments introduce further challenges: frontier LLMs often provide limited access to internal signals, agent roll-outs are costly, and training data may be unavailable or quickly become outdated. To address these challenges, we introduce Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time framework that estimates the probability an agent accomplished its task from a single trajectory, without privileged model access or training data. Rather than compressing an execution into a single holistic judgment, a CRG begins with the claim that the agent accomplished its task, decomposes it into contextualized sub-claims grounded in trajectory evidence, estimates confidence for each terminal claim, and finally aggregates these into an overall confidence estimate. Across three agentic benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs yield better-calibrated confidence and stronger risk-aware decision making than verbalized, sampling-based, and white-box surrogate baselines. We further find that calibration error alone can be misleading: a white-box surrogate baseline appears well calibrated while providing near-chance discrimination. Ablations attribute CRG's improvements to claim-level confidence estimation and aggregation rather than graph construction alone. Finally, a CRG exposes the claims and trajectory evidence underlying each confidence estimate, enabling it to be audited at decision time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time method that estimates the probability an LLM agent succeeded at its task from a single trajectory, without privileged model access or training data, by decomposing the success claim into evidence-grounded sub-claims and aggregating their confidences.
AI.motivation: In consequential domains, deciding whether to trust or intervene on an LLM agent's output requires calibrated confidence in its success. This is hard because evidence about success is distributed across heterogeneous, interdependent trajectory steps. Practical deployments add further obstacles: frontier LLMs expose limited internal signals, roll-outs are costly, and training data may be unavailable or quickly outdated.
AI.method: CRGs are an inference-time framework that estimates task-success probability from a single trajectory without privileged model access or training data. Starting from the top-level claim that the agent accomplished its task, a CRG decomposes it into contextualized sub-claims grounded in trajectory evidence, estimates confidence for each terminal claim, and aggregates them into an overall confidence estimate.
AI.result: Across three agentic benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs achieve better-calibrated confidence and stronger risk-aware decision making than verbalized, sampling-based, and white-box surrogate baselines. The authors also show calibration error alone can mislead: a white-box surrogate appears well calibrated yet has near-chance discrimination. Ablations credit claim-level confidence estimation and aggregation, not graph construction alone.
AI.conclusion: CRGs provide a practical, training-free, black-box confidence estimator for LLM agents that improves calibration and risk-aware decisions, and by exposing the claims and trajectory evidence behind each estimate, enables auditing at decision time.

title: WareFly-VLA: A Vision-Language-Action Framework for UAV Navigation and Human Tracking in Smart Warehouses
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation and ground-mobile navigation, yet language-conditioned control of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart warehouses remains largely unexplored, hindered by the lack of benchmarks that jointly provide continuous low-level flight actions, fine-grained natural-language target descriptions, and realistic industrial environments. This paper introduces WareFly-VLA, a photorealistic UAV VLA framework and dataset for language-guided human search, localization, and tracking in warehouse environments. It contains 507 human-teleoperated flight episodes and 8,504 high-resolution RGB transitions collected in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each paired with a human-written appearance description of the target worker and a synchronized four-degree-of-freedom control command. Two aerial tasks are covered: target approach and person following, under occlusion, long-range search, altitude variation, and clutter. A unified benchmark of four open-source VLA architectures (SmolVLA, GR00T N1.7, pi_0 and OpenVLA) is established under a leakage-free episode-level protocol at two control rates. The results show that language-conditioned aerial control in warehouses is far from solved: performance drops substantially under strict generalization settings, continuous action modeling consistently outperforms discrete action tokenization, only the forward channel is reliably learnable from a single frame, and current foundation-model interfaces transfer poorly from ground and humanoid embodiments to aerial platforms. The synchronized video, language, action, pose, and difficulty annotations further support world-model research. The dataset, baselines, and evaluation protocol are released to support language-grounded aerial autonomy in smart warehouses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WareFly-VLA, a photorealistic UAV vision-language-action framework and dataset for language-guided human search, localization, and tracking in smart warehouses, along with a unified benchmark of four open-source VLA architectures, revealing that language-conditioned aerial control remains largely unsolved.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned control of UAVs in smart warehouses is largely unexplored, hindered by the lack of benchmarks that jointly provide continuous low-level flight actions, fine-grained natural-language target descriptions, and realistic industrial environments.
AI.method: The authors built WareFly-VLA in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, containing 507 human-teleoperated flight episodes and 8,504 high-resolution RGB transitions, each paired with a human-written appearance description of the target worker and a synchronized four-degree-of-freedom control command, covering two tasks (target approach and person following) under occlusion, long-range search, altitude variation, and clutter. They established a unified benchmark of four open-source VLA architectures (SmolVLA, GR00T N1.7, pi_0, OpenVLA) under a leakage-free episode-level protocol at two control rates.
AI.result: Performance drops substantially under strict generalization settings; continuous action modeling consistently outperforms discrete action tokenization; only the forward channel is reliably learnable from a single frame; and current foundation-model interfaces transfer poorly from ground and humanoid embodiments to aerial platforms.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned aerial control in warehouses is far from solved. The synchronized video, language, action, pose, and difficulty annotations further support world-model research, and the dataset, baselines, and evaluation protocol are released to support language-grounded aerial autonomy in smart warehouses.

title: Can Agents Work for Everyone? Cross-User Reliability for Mobile GUI Agents in Personalized User Interfaces
summary: Mobile GUI agents increasingly operate on interfaces influenced by users' histories and preferences, but their reliability across different users remains underexplored. We introduce PAIR (Personalized Application-state Instantiation and Rendering), a pipeline for constructing user-conditioned application states that enables controlled evaluation of the same task across different users. We further introduce RePAIR (Reinforcement learning with Personalization-Aware Interaction Rewards), a training approach that learns from cross-user differences in subgoal outcomes to improve reliability across user-conditioned mobile environments. Across six agents, we find substantial variation in task success across users and consistently lower subgoal achievement in user-conditioned UI contexts (6.98 to 15.4 pp). This gap further increases for personal targets drawn from each user's own content (8.77 to 22.0 pp). Failures in these contexts frequently involve selecting another item instead of the intended target, particularly before target exposure. Finally, RePAIR improves user-conditioned SAR (+5.87 pp), all-success (+7.50 pp), and overall Task SR (+9.42 pp) over its supervised fine-tuning parent on unseen users, providing initial evidence that explicitly learning from cross-user variation can improve GUI-agent reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAIR, a pipeline for constructing user-conditioned app states to evaluate GUI agents across different users, and RePAIR, a reinforcement learning approach with personalization-aware rewards. Across six agents, task success varies substantially by user and drops in user-conditioned contexts, while RePAIR improves success rates on unseen users.
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents increasingly operate on interfaces shaped by users' histories and preferences, yet their reliability across different users remains underexplored. There is a need for controlled evaluation of the same task across users and for training methods that improve cross-user reliability in personalized mobile environments.
AI.method: The authors propose PAIR (Personalized Application-state Instantiation and Rendering), a pipeline that constructs user-conditioned application states to enable controlled evaluation of the same task across different users. They also propose RePAIR (Reinforcement learning with Personalization-Aware Interaction Rewards), which learns from cross-user differences in subgoal outcomes to improve reliability across user-conditioned mobile environments.
AI.result: Across six agents, substantial variation in task success across users is observed, with consistently lower subgoal achievement in user-conditioned UI contexts (6.98 to 15.4 pp). This gap widens for personal targets drawn from each user's own content (8.77 to 22.0 pp). Failures often involve selecting another item instead of the intended target, particularly before target exposure. RePAIR improves user-conditioned SAR (+5.87 pp), all-success (+7.50 pp), and overall Task SR (+9.42 pp) over its supervised fine-tuning parent on unseen users.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly learning from cross-user variation can improve GUI-agent reliability, providing initial evidence that personalization-aware training addresses performance degradation in user-conditioned mobile environments.

title: Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized Trajectory Optimization
summary: Trajectory optimization (TO) under nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits and collision avoidance constraints is a fundamental problem in robotics, albeit especially challenging due to its highly non-convex nature. For this setting, Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) is an efficient second-order shooting method, yet its local structure renders it vulnerable to suboptimal basins. Sampling-augmented variants mitigate this susceptibility through stochastic exploration, but often sample only around the few trajectories they retain for reoptimization, based solely on their cost which restricts exploration breadth. We introduce Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized DDP (PER-DDP), an entropy-regularized population framework derived from the free-energy/relative-entropy inequality. Our method combines prior-guided sampling that shapes exploration around each retained trajectory, with expanded rollout evaluations that probe these sampling policies beyond the few retained candidates, and Pareto filtering for preserving task-constraint alternatives across iterations. This decouples sampling effort from the optimization population size and broadens exploration without sacrificing the second-order structure that makes DDP effective. Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, PER-DDP achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art sampling-augmented TO methods and finds reliable solutions in environments beyond the reach of all baselines.

AI.tldr: PER-DDP is an entropy-regularized population framework for trajectory optimization that decouples sampling effort from the optimization population size, combining prior-guided sampling, expanded rollout evaluations, and Pareto filtering to achieve broader exploration while retaining DDP's second-order structure.
AI.motivation: Trajectory optimization under nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits, and collision avoidance is highly non-convex. DDP is an efficient second-order shooting method but suffers from local structure that traps it in suboptimal basins. Existing sampling-augmented variants alleviate this via stochastic exploration but sample only around the few retained trajectories, based solely on cost, which limits exploration breadth.
AI.method: PER-DDP (Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized DDP) is an entropy-regularized population framework derived from the free-energy/relative-entropy inequality. It integrates three components: (1) prior-guided sampling that shapes exploration around each retained trajectory, (2) expanded rollout evaluations that probe these sampling policies beyond the few retained candidates, and (3) Pareto filtering that preserves task-constraint alternatives across iterations.
AI.result: Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, PER-DDP achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art sampling-augmented trajectory optimization methods and finds reliable solutions in environments beyond the reach of all baselines.
AI.conclusion: PER-DDP broadens exploration without sacrificing the second-order structure that makes DDP effective, yielding more reliable and higher-success trajectory optimization than existing sampling-augmented baselines.

title: Learning from Revision Consequences: Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation for Self-Improving Agents
summary: As agents continuously improve by generating and revising Skills, the process that discovers and refines those Skills becomes a learnable object in its own right. Task-Skills directly act on task execution, whereas Meta-Skills govern how agents discover and improve future Skills; their value therefore emerges through the subsequent search processes they induce. Existing approaches improve Meta-Skills from observed raw Skill-search trajectories and branch outcomes. However, branch performance entangles the effects of the initial discovery state and the Meta-Skill revision that generated the search process, making it difficult to characterize what a particular revision actually changed, and pushing updates toward revisions that benefit from favorable states rather than those that improve the process. We introduce HMED (Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation), a mechanism for constructing Meta-Experience for self-improving agents. HMED revisits the completed event from which a revision originates and re-executes the incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, so that the changes associated with the revision can be observed under a shared condition. Each comparison is distilled into a Meta-Experience, a structured record that can be reused by future updates, so that even revisions that are not ultimately retained still contribute a learning signal. Across three interactive agent benchmarks and both open-source and closed-source models, HMED consistently improves Skill discovery performance over strong baselines, shifting Meta-Skill learning beyond branch outcomes toward the consequences of changing the improvement process.

AI.tldr: HMED introduces a Meta-Experience distillation mechanism that re-executes incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, enabling controlled comparison of revisions and reusable learning signals beyond raw branch outcomes.
AI.motivation: As agents self-improve by generating and revising Skills, the Skill-discovery process itself becomes learnable. Task-Skills act directly on execution, while Meta-Skills govern how agents discover and improve future Skills, so Meta-Skill value emerges through induced search processes. Existing methods learn Meta-Skills from observed raw Skill-search trajectories and branch outcomes, but branch performance entangles the initial discovery state with the Meta-Skill revision that generated the search, making it hard to isolate what a specific revision changed. This biases updates toward revisions favored by favorable states rather than revisions that genuinely improve the improvement process.
AI.method: HMED (Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation) constructs Meta-Experience for self-improving agents. It revisits the completed event from which a revision originates and re-executes both the incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, allowing the changes associated with a revision to be observed under a shared condition. Each such comparison is distilled into a Meta-Experience, a structured record reusable by future updates.
AI.result: Across three interactive agent benchmarks and both open-source and closed-source models, HMED consistently improves Skill discovery performance over strong baselines. Even revisions that are not ultimately retained contribute a learning signal, shifting Meta-Skill learning beyond branch outcomes toward the consequences of changing the improvement process.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling initial discovery state from revision effects via state-restored re-execution and distilling reusable Meta-Experience, HMED enables more process-centric Meta-Skill learning and yields consistent gains in Skill discovery across diverse benchmarks and models.

title: Micro Neural Policies for Safe Real-Time Robotic Control
summary: In this paper, we investigate the synthesis of Micro Neural Policies (MNP) to enable safe and robust real-time robotic control on computationally constrained embedded devices. We demonstrate that integrating Evolution Strategy (ES) and Statistical Model Checking (SMC)-based verification for policy search can drastically reduce neural network size without compromising safety and robustness. We conduct a large-scale training and evaluation of MNP on Cartpole and Quadrotor control tasks, varying control frequencies and network architectures. After validating these policies in simulation, we evaluate their deployability through zero-shot transfer to physical systems. Our experiments show that MNP can successfully achieve safe sim-to-real transfer without sacrificing control performance. We then show that the policies' memory footprint, ranging from 0.5 to 7.5 kB, allows deployment on microcontrollers, where they achieve real-time inference latency with under 25 ns of jitter while leaving the chip idle for over 97% of the time for additional workloads. This makes them a highly practical solution for severely resource-constrained robotic systems.

AI.tldr: Micro Neural Policies (MNPs) are synthesized by combining Evolution Strategy and Statistical Model Checking verification, yielding tiny (0.5–7.5 kB) verified policies that achieve safe zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and real-time microcontroller inference with <25 ns jitter.
AI.motivation: Safe and robust real-time robotic control typically requires neural networks too large for computationally constrained embedded devices; the paper seeks policies that are simultaneously safe, robust, and deployable on microcontrollers.
AI.method: The authors integrate Evolution Strategy (ES) for policy search with Statistical Model Checking (SMC)-based verification to synthesize Micro Neural Policies. They conduct large-scale training and evaluation on Cartpole and Quadrotor tasks, varying control frequencies and network architectures, validate in simulation, and then perform zero-shot transfer to physical systems.
AI.result: MNP achieved safe sim-to-real transfer without sacrificing control performance. Memory footprint ranged from 0.5 to 7.5 kB, enabling microcontroller deployment with real-time inference latency and under 25 ns of jitter, while leaving the chip idle for over 97% of the time for additional workloads.
AI.conclusion: MNPs are a practical solution for severely resource-constrained robotic systems, delivering verified safety and robustness at minimal computational cost.

title: Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures. Code, policies, evaluation and videos: https://github.com/JordyKieto/puffermoba-dyna
summary: World models are usually judged from the inside: by prediction loss, by the return a policy earns in imagination, or by how convincing their frames look. We judge one from the outside. We learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, every hero acting every tick, games of up to 6,000 ticks), train a policy only inside it with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes, and measure that policy in the real game against the opponent the game ships with. The real game never provides a gradient; it provides the policy's own games as training data for the world model, and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy. Run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop, the policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421 of 600; 95% CI 66.4-73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, up from 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins none as dire, and neither does the shipped opponent when it plays itself. Four findings explain the result. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: every unanchored run collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric tracked the collapse. A world model that is accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy's own games, and Dyna repairs it there, which is worth +9.2 points of real win rate with the policy recipe held fixed. Finally, the policy inherits its world model's fidelity profile mechanic by mechanic: the model represents the macro game but not crowd control, cast timing or lethality, and the policy wins by map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting. We release the world model, the dream-PPO harness, a world-model debugger, the evaluation protocol, and every policy and log.

AI.tldr: The authors learn a structured multi-agent world model of a full ten-hero MOBA, train a policy purely inside 1,400-tick imagined episodes via an asynchronous Dyna loop, and evaluate it in the real game, where it wins 70.2% of games as radiant on held-out seeds while winning 0% as dire.
AI.motivation: World models are typically evaluated from the inside—by prediction loss, in-imagination return, or visual plausibility—which can mask failure modes that only appear when a policy is deployed in the real environment. The paper argues for judging a world model from the outside: by the real-game performance of a policy trained only within it.
AI.method: A structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, all heroes acting every tick, episodes up to 6,000 ticks) is trained on data from the policy's own real games. A policy is trained solely inside the world model using 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes with dream-PPO. The real game supplies no gradients; instead it provides training data for the world model and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy, run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop.
AI.result: The policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421/600; 95% CI 66.4–73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, versus 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins no games as dire, and the shipped opponent also wins none when playing itself. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: unanchored runs collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric reflected it. A world model accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy's own games, and Dyna repairs it there, worth +9.2 points of real win rate with the policy recipe fixed. The policy inherits the world model's fidelity profile: it represents the macro game but not crowd control, cast timing, or lethality, so the policy wins through map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting.
AI.conclusion: Judging world models by real-game outcomes of policies trained within them exposes failure modes invisible to internal metrics. The Dyna loop's online anchoring is essential for correcting the world model on the policy's own distribution, and the resulting policy's capabilities are bounded by the model's mechanic-level fidelity. The authors release the world model, dream-PPO harness, world-model debugger, evaluation protocol, and all policies and logs.

title: Towards Efficient Robotic Manipulation Models with Self-Recursive Pruning
summary: Network pruning can reduce parameter redundancy in robotic policies. However, generic pruning criteria are tailored for image recognition tasks and commonly designed to preserve weight magnitude, local reconstruction, or language-model likelihood rather than closed-loop action behavior. Directly applying these pruning algorithms to robotic tasks yields unsatisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose Loss-Conditioned Activation-Moment (LCAM) pruning, a training-free method for unstructured pruning of pre-trained robotic manipulation policies. Specifically, we first rank connections using row-normalized weight contribution, activation moments measured on calibration demonstrations, and the sensitivity of output directions to the action-prediction loss. We further design a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure: importance is recalibrated after each nested coarse pruning stage, while held-out offline action distortion guides fine-grained budget allocation after a sparsity knee. Our algorithm is free from costly recovery training and simulator rollouts after pruning. Experiments on three LIBERO suites with competitive robotic policies, together with evaluations on OpenVLA, show that LCAM attains competitive performance across a broad range of pruning ratios. Notably, on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, our LCAM achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning, retaining over 90% of the dense policy's success rate. Promising results on real-world robotic ping pong further demonstrate the effectiveness of our pruning algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LCAM, a training-free unstructured pruning method for pre-trained robotic manipulation policies, using loss-conditioned activation moments and a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure. It achieves strong performance across pruning ratios, retaining over 90% of dense policy success on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA at 50% sparsity, and validates on real-world ping pong.
AI.motivation: Generic pruning criteria are designed for image recognition, language modeling, or reconstruction, preserving weight magnitude, local reconstruction, or likelihood rather than closed-loop action behavior. Applying these directly to robotic policies yields unsatisfactory performance. This motivates a pruning criterion tailored to action-prediction loss for robotic manipulation policies.
AI.method: LCAM is a training-free unstructured pruning method. It ranks connections using row-normalized weight contribution, activation moments measured on calibration demonstrations, and sensitivity of output directions to the action-prediction loss. It uses a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure: importance is recalibrated after each nested coarse pruning stage, and held-out offline action distortion guides fine-grained budget allocation after a sparsity knee. No costly recovery training or simulator rollouts are needed after pruning.
AI.result: Experiments on three LIBERO suites with competitive robotic policies and on OpenVLA show competitive performance across a broad range of pruning ratios. On LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, LCAM achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning, retaining over 90% of the dense policy's success rate. Real-world robotic ping pong results further demonstrate effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: LCAM offers an effective, training-free pruning approach for robotic manipulation policies that is behavior-aware and avoids recovery training or rollouts, performing competitively across pruning ratios and transferring to real-world tasks.

title: Same Feedback, Different Answer: Measuring Run-to-Run Instability in Frontier-Model Customer Feedback Analysis
summary: AI agents are increasingly being programmed to automate knowledge work over large collections of unstructured data. Such automation requires repeatability: when the underlying evidence is unchanged, the agent's categories, priorities, and counts should not shift materially between runs, even if each individual answer appears plausible. We introduce a repeat-run evaluation framework that aligns semantically equivalent categories and focuses on two operating metrics: theme churn, the normalized change in the returned category set, and volume disagreement, the change in counts for categories that persist. We evaluate three recurring customer-feedback tasks across eight frontier models, corpus sizes from 100 to 5,000 records, multiple prompts, and three execution designs: raw generation, taxonomy-free hierarchical decomposition, and a taxonomy-grounded agent (TGA) using persistent themes, subthemes, and record-level predictions. With Claude Opus 4.8 and the 1,000-record corpus fixed, TGA reduces theme churn by 86--88% relative to both raw generation and hierarchical decomposition, while matched-theme volumes have zero disagreement. The taxonomy-grounded agent is more stable than every raw model in the screen, remains more stable at each corpus size, and keeps this advantage when theme matching is made stricter or looser. Although evaluated on customer feedback, the framework targets repeated synthesis of unstructured corpora more broadly, including financial reports, legal documents, incident records, and scientific literature. Overall, these results show that taxonomy grounding produces more consistent and repeatable outputs for recurring knowledge work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a repeat-run evaluation framework for AI-agent knowledge work, using theme churn and volume disagreement as metrics. A taxonomy-grounded agent (TGA) substantially improves output repeatability over raw generation and hierarchical decomposition across eight frontier models and corpus sizes up to 5,000 records.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly used to automate knowledge work over large unstructured corpora, which demands repeatability: with unchanged evidence, an agent's categories, priorities, and counts should not shift materially between runs, even if each individual answer seems plausible. This repeatability property is largely unmeasured by existing evaluation approaches.
AI.method: A repeat-run evaluation framework that aligns semantically equivalent categories and operationalizes two metrics: theme churn (normalized change in the returned category set) and volume disagreement (change in counts for persisting categories). Three recurring customer-feedback tasks are evaluated across eight frontier models, corpora of 100 to 5,000 records, multiple prompts, and three execution designs: raw generation, taxonomy-free hierarchical decomposition, and a taxonomy-grounded agent (TGA) using persistent themes, subthemes, and record-level predictions.
AI.result: With Claude Opus 4.8 on a fixed 1,000-record corpus, TGA reduces theme churn by 86--88% relative to both raw generation and hierarchical decomposition, with zero volume disagreement on matched themes. TGA is more stable than every raw model in the screen, remains more stable at each corpus size, and preserves its advantage under stricter or looser theme matching.
AI.conclusion: Taxonomy grounding yields more consistent and repeatable outputs for recurring knowledge work. Although evaluated on customer feedback, the framework generalizes to repeated synthesis of other unstructured corpora such as financial reports, legal documents, incident records, and scientific literature.

title: One for All, All for One: Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering via Stochastic Optimal Control
summary: Deep generative models often produce structured outputs composed of interacting components. Modelling these outputs with a single model requires learning both the component distributions and their interactions. We pursue a modular alternative: reuse independently trained component generators and learn only how to coordinate them to produce coherent structured outputs. Our framework, Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering (CMDS), treats frozen pretrained diffusion models as reusable generative primitives and coordinates their reverse processes through a learned control. We formulate coordination as a stochastic optimal control problem, balancing an assembly-level reward that specifies the desired properties of the combined output against deviations from the pretrained dynamics. The learned control amortises this optimisation, allowing reuse across new task instances. Experiments show that CMDS can recover a known target distribution, satisfy different spatial constraints with the same trained control, and recover individual sources from degraded mixtures. Across multi-agent maze navigation, articulated robot planning, and text-conditioned human motion, CMDS turns frozen models into coordinated multi-agent generators.

AI.tldr: CMDS coordinates frozen pretrained diffusion models as reusable generative primitives via a learned stochastic optimal control, enabling coherent structured multi-agent outputs without retraining component models.
AI.motivation: Deep generative models for structured, interacting-component outputs typically need a single model that jointly learns component distributions and their interactions. The paper seeks a modular alternative: reuse independently trained component generators and learn only how to coordinate them into coherent structured outputs.
AI.method: The framework treats frozen pretrained diffusion models as reusable generative primitives and coordinates their reverse processes through a learned control. Coordination is formulated as a stochastic optimal control problem, balancing an assembly-level reward (specifying desired properties of the combined output) against deviations from the pretrained dynamics. The learned control amortises this optimisation, enabling reuse across new task instances.
AI.result: CMDS recovers a known target distribution, satisfies different spatial constraints with the same trained control, and recovers individual sources from degraded mixtures. It also turns frozen models into coordinated multi-agent generators across multi-agent maze navigation, articulated robot planning, and text-conditioned human motion.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating independently trained, frozen diffusion generators through a learned control offers an effective modular route to coherent structured outputs and multi-agent generation, with control reusable across task instances.

title: DAEDALUS: Bootstrapping Agent Memory from Self-Generated Tasks
comment: 9 pages (31 including Appendix), 8 figures (11 including Appendix). We release the code and artifacts, including generation and inference traces, at https://github.com/illuin-tech/daedalus
summary: LLM agents often lack the operational knowledge to act reliably in new environments, as they must discover specific tool behaviors or environment conventions on their own. Without memory of past attempts, they repeat the same mistakes across tasks, leading to more task failures and longer trajectories. To address this, agentic systems typically rely on human-written guidelines or on procedural memory built from training tasks and an oracle verifier, both of which require prior knowledge of the environment. We present DAEDALUS, a method for bootstrapping reusable agent memory from self-generated practice without existing tasks or oracle verifiers. DAEDALUS pairs two agents: an explorer that interacts with the environment to generate challenging yet solvable tasks, and a solver that attempts them. A heuristic is derived from each solver failure and accepted only after the solver repeatedly succeeds with that heuristic in context. These outcomes also provide feedback for the explorer to refine the difficulty of future tasks. Accepted heuristics are then consolidated into a memory bank for test-time use. Across AppWorld, $τ^2$-bench, and AutomationBench, DAEDALUS improves mean success rates by up to 15.9 points and pass^5 by up to 2.2x over a no-memory baseline, and is competitive with methods using training tasks, at a lower inference cost than most. We show that performance gains already emerge with a small exploration budget, and that its heuristics also benefit agents from other model families. Our ablations further reveal that solver traces provide the key information needed to derive effective heuristics, while factorizing early discoveries makes exploration more cost-efficient. Beyond memory construction, we find that the tasks generated by DAEDALUS can serve as a proxy for benchmark tasks when ranking models by performance. Code and artifacts: www.github.com/illuin-tech/daedalus.

AI.tldr: DAEDALUS bootstraps reusable agent memory from self-generated practice tasks without pre-existing tasks or oracle verifiers, improving success rates and pass^5 across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents lack operational knowledge for new environments and repeat mistakes across tasks without memory of past attempts, causing more failures and longer trajectories. Existing solutions rely on human-written guidelines or procedural memory from training tasks and an oracle verifier, both requiring prior environment knowledge.
AI.method: DAEDALUS pairs an explorer agent, which interacts with the environment to generate challenging but solvable tasks, with a solver agent that attempts them. A heuristic is derived from each solver failure and accepted only after the solver repeatedly succeeds with it in context. These outcomes also feed back to the explorer to refine task difficulty. Accepted heuristics are consolidated into a memory bank for test-time use.
AI.result: Across AppWorld, τ²-bench, and AutomationBench, DAEDALUS improves mean success rates by up to 15.9 points and pass^5 by up to 2.2x over a no-memory baseline, competitive with methods using training tasks at lower inference cost than most. Gains emerge with a small exploration budget, and heuristics benefit agents from other model families. Ablations show solver traces provide the key information for deriving effective heuristics, while factorizing early discoveries makes exploration more cost-efficient. Generated tasks can also proxy benchmark tasks for ranking models.
AI.conclusion: DAEDALUS enables bootstrapping reusable agent memory from self-generated practice without existing tasks or oracle verifiers, matching training-task-based methods at lower cost, and its generated tasks can serve as a proxy for benchmark tasks in model ranking.

title: A Swarm-Coordinated Multi-Robot System for Early Stress Detection in Agricultural Rows Using Multimodal Leaf Sensing
summary: Early stress detection in crops is a necessity today to improve efficiency and reduce waste of time, money, and effort. However, most modern techniques, such as hyperspectral imaging and AI-based systems, are too costly and complex for medium and small-scale farmers to implement. This paper showcases CropSentry, a low-cost, ground-based multi-robot system that uses multimodal leaf sensing to continuously monitor crop health by tracking stress levels. The system comprises two autonomous bots that continuously detect leaf color and environmental data row by row. The observations are spatially mapped and sent over to the master bot, which uses color-coded row segments to generate a real-time web-based dashboard displaying crop health. After 63 observations were collected during the experiments, the results showed an overall crop health classification accuracy of 84.12%, with 82.60% for healthy plants, 88% for nutrient-deficient plants, and 80% for diseased plants. Also, 100% wireless communication success rate across 10 slave observations was achieved. Close-range leaf inspection across multiple bots can detect early stress in crops while remaining affordable, accessible, and scalable. It provides farmers with timely information to improve resource utilization and crop management.

AI.tldr: CropSentry is a low-cost, ground-based multi-robot system that performs multimodal leaf sensing to continuously monitor crop health and detect early stress, achieving 84.12% overall classification accuracy and real-time dashboard visualization.
AI.motivation: Early stress detection in crops is essential to improve efficiency and reduce waste of time, money, and effort, yet most modern techniques such as hyperspectral imaging and AI-based systems are too costly and complex for medium and small-scale farmers to implement.
AI.method: The system comprises two autonomous bots that continuously detect leaf color and environmental data row by row. Observations are spatially mapped and transmitted to a master bot, which uses color-coded row segments to generate a real-time web-based dashboard displaying crop health.
AI.result: After 63 observations, the system achieved an overall crop health classification accuracy of 84.12%, with 82.60% for healthy plants, 88% for nutrient-deficient plants, and 80% for diseased plants. A 100% wireless communication success rate was achieved across 10 slave observations.
AI.conclusion: Close-range leaf inspection across multiple bots can detect early stress in crops while remaining affordable, accessible, and scalable, providing farmers with timely information to improve resource utilization and crop management.

title: SpeedrunBench: Challenging LLM Agents with Video Game Speedrunning
summary: Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents' capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that SPEEDRUNBENCH is a useful testbed for studying agents' strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark of 9 video games that tests whether frontier LLM agents can form novel strategies beyond human-developed solutions, using speedrunning as the testbed. Agents must iteratively improve strategies, reflect on performance, and reason over long horizons to beat their own and others' records; frontier agents approach human world records on simple platformers but lag on longer, more complex games.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents tackle increasingly complex tasks with known human solutions, a key open question is whether they can go beyond what humans have already solved. Human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems lacking context or training data, making the ability to form sophisticated strategies paramount. Speedrunning provides a communal practice where practitioners uncover unorthodox play styles requiring deep mastery of game mechanics, making it a suitable domain to study strategy formation.
AI.method: The authors introduce SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark evaluating frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit gained knowledge, and reason across a long horizon of actions to become faster than themselves and everyone else.
AI.result: Frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games but remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets.
AI.conclusion: SPEEDRUNBENCH is a useful testbed for studying agents' strategy formation capabilities and serves as a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, since there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.

title: Feeling Through the Load: Compliant Quadruped Locomotion under Payload Interactions
summary: Quadruped robots are increasingly expected to carry objects while moving through human environments. But what happens when a person interacts directly with the payload rather than with the robot? If the payload is unrestrained, the robot must distinguish intentional external interactions from ordinary payload motion, while still keeping the load balanced and maintaining stable locomotion. How can a quadruped infer and compliantly respond to such interactions using only onboard measurements? In this work, we develop a force-aware locomotion framework that treats payload interactions as commands that shape the motion of the combined robot-payload system. Our approach separates the learning of force-aware locomotion and force estimation on an unrestrained payload. We combine a compliant load-carrying policy with a causal force estimator, trained through estimator-in-the-loop data aggregation and finetuning, to predict interactions from onboard robot measurements. Our simulations and real-world experiments show that the resulting controller can maintain stable payload-carrying locomotion, yield compliantly to external interactions, and use the inferred force to support human-guided changes in the robot's trajectory.

AI.tldr: A force-aware locomotion framework for quadruped robots carrying unrestrained payloads, enabling the robot to infer and compliantly respond to human interactions applied directly to the payload using only onboard measurements.
AI.motivation: Quadruped robots are increasingly expected to carry objects while navigating human environments. A key challenge arises when a person interacts directly with the payload rather than the robot itself. If the payload is unrestrained, the robot must distinguish intentional external interactions from ordinary payload motion while keeping the load balanced and locomotion stable. The paper asks how a quadruped can infer and compliantly respond to such interactions using only onboard measurements.
AI.method: The authors develop a force-aware locomotion framework that treats payload interactions as commands shaping the motion of the combined robot-payload system. The approach separates learning of force-aware locomotion from force estimation on an unrestrained payload. It combines a compliant load-carrying policy with a causal force estimator, trained via estimator-in-the-loop data aggregation and finetuning, to predict interactions from onboard robot measurements.
AI.result: Simulations and real-world experiments show that the resulting controller maintains stable payload-carrying locomotion, yields compliantly to external interactions, and uses the inferred force to support human-guided changes in the robot's trajectory.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling force-aware locomotion learning from force estimation and coupling them through a compliant policy and a causal estimator trained with estimator-in-the-loop aggregation and finetuning, the framework enables quadrupeds to carry unrestrained payloads while inferring and compliantly responding to direct human interactions, facilitating human-guided trajectory changes.

title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce prospective learning, which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to $24.2$ pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when $37$--$98\%$ of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In the 2B setting, where $98\%$ of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at $0.0\%$ success, while adding SRD reaches $60.6\%$ under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces prospective learning and its instantiation Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), which distills post-hoc hindsight from completed trajectories into trajectory-blind foresight predictions, complementing RLVR especially when reward contrast is scarce.
AI.motivation: RLVR converts agent experience into learning signals via scalar outcome rewards, but in group-relative objectives the signal vanishes when all rollouts receive identical rewards (reward-uniform groups), even though trajectories still contain useful information about task requirements and failure modes. The authors ask whether hindsight can teach the agent what it could have anticipated before acting.
AI.method: Prospective learning supervises foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view using post-hoc experience. SRD instantiates this by distilling privileged hindsight from a completed trajectory into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy; foresight serves only as a training target and is not generated at inference.
AI.result: Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is strongest when reward contrast is scarce; 37–98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales. In the 2B setting, with 98% all-failure groups, RLVR ends at 0.0% success while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction, providing learning signal even when reward-based contrast is absent.

title: RIWANav: Recursive World-Action Models with Self-Improvement for Urban Navigation
summary: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.

AI.tldr: RIWANAV is a post-training framework that jointly adapts a world model and a policy for long-horizon urban navigation via task-specific recursive self-improvement, outperforming baselines and prior methods.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors compound over time. Imitation learning rarely learns from failures, and physical trial-and-error RL is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback, but a frozen world model becomes less reliable as the policy evolves.
AI.method: RIWANAV casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates: (1) the world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, supplying comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO); (2) the improved policy builds a grounded self-curriculum by selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs based on behavioral novelty and prediction error; the refined world model then feeds the next policy update, closing the RSI loop.
AI.result: RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, and real-world trials demonstrate its practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model, showing that co-adapting both components yields effective and practically applicable long-horizon urban navigation.

title: POLAR: Ontology-Guided Risk Prevention for Tool-Calling LLM Agents
summary: LLM tool-use agents operate in dynamic environments where many actions carry operational risk. However, most safety mechanisms react only after errors manifest. Existing pre-emptive approaches either fine-tune the agent on chain-of-thought deliberation or compile natural-language guardrails into runtime checks, but they do so without exposing a structural, auditable verdict. We propose POLAR, a guardrail framework for small tool-calling agents that assesses reversibility through a structured two-layer ontology. POLAR assigns each action a graded reversibility score by deriving a candidate inverse sequence; calls failing a threshold are pruned before execution. Evaluated on $τ^2$-bench across six agent models, POLAR improves mean task reward by 0.11 to 0.18 points on airline for four of six agents, but only eight of eighteen model--domain cells improve overall; retail and stronger agents often regress. POLAR provides an auditable structural check and characterizes its task-utility trade-offs. Reward is not a direct measure of prevented harm.

AI.tldr: POLAR is a guardrail framework for small tool-calling LLM agents that scores each action's reversibility via a two-layer ontology and prunes irreversible actions before execution, yielding an auditable structural verdict; it improves task reward on some airline tasks but shows inconsistent gains across models and domains.
AI.motivation: LLM tool-use agents act in dynamic environments where many actions carry operational risk, yet most safety mechanisms only react after errors occur. Existing pre-emptive approaches fine-tune agents on chain-of-thought deliberation or compile natural-language guardrails into runtime checks, but neither exposes a structural, auditable verdict. This motivates a guardrail that provides explicit, inspectable pre-execution assessment.
AI.method: POLAR assesses reversibility through a structured two-layer ontology. For each action, it derives a candidate inverse sequence and assigns a graded reversibility score; actions failing a threshold are pruned before execution. Evaluation is conducted on τ²-bench across six agent models.
AI.result: POLAR improves mean task reward by 0.11 to 0.18 points on the airline domain for four of six agents, but only eight of eighteen model–domain cells improve overall; retail tasks and stronger agents often regress.
