The framework provides an auditable structural check and characterizes its task-utility trade-offs, though reward is not a direct measure of prevented harm.
AI.conclusion: POLAR offers an auditable, structural pre-emptive guardrail based on reversibility, but its benefits are inconsistent across models and domains, revealing a trade-off between safety checking and task utility. The authors caution that reward gains are not equivalent to reduced harm.

title: HygieneRoboBench: Benchmarking Hygiene-Aware Planning for Household Robots
summary: Contact with contaminated objects can spread hazards through a household robot's grippers, tools, and shared surfaces, while new contacts can make an existing plan unsafe. Existing benchmarks do not jointly assess how planners identify hygiene risks from contact history and plan safe continuations after new contact events. Planners must do so within time and resource limits while respecting user priorities. We introduce HygieneRoboBench, with 624 instances across 134 task families, to evaluate safe resolution of household tasks from a given execution history. Tasks capture contamination through two grippers and shared objects, treatment costs, and user priorities. We combine controlled history, profile, and event comparisons with independent plan evaluation. These assess safe resolution, cost efficiency under user priorities, and responses to contact events. Evaluation of LLM-based and symbolic planners shows that safely completing a task does not guarantee the lowest execution costs under the user's priorities. To address this problem, we introduce Hygiene-NSP. It combines LLM-based grounding, contact-history reconstruction, and CP-SAT to jointly plan hygiene treatment and task execution under user priorities. Hygiene-NSP achieves safe resolution and optimal safe resolution rates of 94.4% and 90.4%, respectively. Both rates are higher than those of the evaluated baseline planners on the full dataset. Project page: https://euron-zc.github.io/HygieneRoboBench/.

AI.tldr: HygieneRoboBench evaluates how planners resolve hygiene risks from contact history and plan safe continuations after new contact events; Hygiene-NSP combines LLM grounding, contact-history reconstruction, and CP-SAT to jointly plan treatment and execution.
AI.motivation: Contaminated objects can spread hazards via a household robot's grippers, tools, and shared surfaces, and new contacts can render an existing plan unsafe. Existing benchmarks do not jointly assess how planners identify hygiene risks from contact history and plan safe continuations after new contact events, under time/resource limits and user priorities.
AI.method: HygieneRoboBench comprises 624 instances across 134 task families, modeling contamination through two grippers and shared objects, treatment costs, and user priorities. It uses controlled history, profile, and event comparisons with independent plan evaluation. Hygiene-NSP combines LLM-based grounding, contact-history reconstruction, and CP-SAT to jointly plan hygiene treatment and task execution under user priorities.
AI.result: Evaluated LLM-based and symbolic planners show that safely completing a task does not guarantee the lowest execution costs under user priorities. Hygiene-NSP achieves 94.4% safe resolution and 90.4% optimal safe resolution, both higher than baseline planners on the full dataset.
AI.conclusion: Hygiene-NSP demonstrates the value of jointly planning hygiene treatment and task execution, outperforming evaluated LLM-based and symbolic baselines in safe and optimal safe resolution.

title: Natural Language Questions as an Interface for Knowledge Graphs: QRAKEN Graph Distillation and Semantic Self-Healing
summary: Natural-language access to RDF knowledge graphs is a core Semantic Web ambition. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced Text-to-SPARQL, yet on unfamiliar graphs they often generate valid queries that misrepresent the populated data model. QRAKEN is a training-free, ontology-agnostic neurosymbolic pipeline grounding generation in empirical graph evidence rather than schema expectations. An offline distiller produces TTQL, a compact description of populated multi-hop patterns, conditional frequencies and path-conditioned literal examples, plus a class-property co-occurrence matrix. Online, TTQL guides the LLM, while deterministic syntax, vocabulary and data-model checks provide diagnostics for iterative refinement. On CK25 (First International Text2SPARQL Challenge), under matched-condition recomputation on a QLever snapshot, QRAKEN achieves strict F1 of 0.643 $\pm$ 0.026 with GPT-4.1 mini and 0.652 $\pm$ 0.012 with GPT-5.4: relative gains of 30% and 32% over the strongest recomputed participant, outperforming systems using the same base model family. Ablations identify TTQL patterns as the dominant driver (+0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline); the refinement loop provides a cheap safety net, rejecting triple patterns unsupported by the co-occurrence matrix. Compared with auto-derived SHACL, TTQL yields 64% higher strict F1, supporting the value of empirical patterns beyond schema exposure. With two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models at zero marginal cost, the same pipeline matches the strongest recomputed participant, and TTQL advantages over shape-only and SHACL baselines persist. Results on a single, relatively small benchmark provide an initial empirical signal; monolithic TTQL injection on very open cross-domain graphs remains the main limitation.

AI.tldr: QRAKEN is a training-free, ontology-agnostic neurosymbolic pipeline for Text-to-SPARQL that grounds LLM generation in empirical graph evidence (TTQL) instead of schema expectations, achieving 30-32% relative strict-F1 gains on CK25.
AI.motivation: Natural-language access to RDF knowledge graphs is a core Semantic Web ambition. Although LLMs have advanced Text-to-SPARQL, on unfamiliar graphs they often generate syntactically valid queries that misrepresent the populated data model, because they rely on schema expectations rather than the actual populated graph.
AI.method: QRAKEN is training-free and ontology-agnostic. An offline distiller builds TTQL: a compact description of populated multi-hop patterns, conditional frequencies, path-conditioned literal examples, plus a class-property co-occurrence matrix. Online, TTQL guides the LLM, while deterministic syntax, vocabulary, and data-model checks provide diagnostics for iterative refinement, rejecting triple patterns unsupported by the co-occurrence matrix.
AI.result: On CK25 (First International Text2SPARQL Challenge), under matched-condition recomputation on a QLever snapshot, QRAKEN reaches strict F1 of 0.643 ± 0.026 with GPT-4.1 mini and 0.652 ± 0.012 with GPT-5.4 — relative gains of 30% and 32% over the strongest recomputed participant, outperforming systems using the same base model family. Ablations show TTQL patterns are the dominant driver (+0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline); the refinement loop acts as a cheap safety net. TTQL yields 64% higher strict F1 than auto-derived SHACL. With two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models at zero marginal cost, the pipeline matches the strongest recomputed participant, and TTQL advantages persist.
AI.conclusion: Grounding generation in empirical populated-graph evidence (TTQL) outperforms schema exposure, supporting the value of empirical patterns beyond schema-based approaches. The main limitation is that results come from a single, relatively small benchmark, and monolithic TTQL injection on very open cross-domain graphs remains problematic.

title: Fast Non-Parametric Heteroscedastic Imitation Learning With Geometric Priors
summary: When learning probabilistic policies from human demonstrations, data-efficient learning and fast adaptations to new scenarios are key requirements. One popular way to achieve intuitive and reliable adaptations is through non-parametric, typically kernel-based, methods. However, existing solutions either fail to account for the geometry of manifolds common in robotics, limiting data efficiency, or, when geometry-aware, provide unreliable uncertainty estimates or require retraining to adapt. We propose a non-parametric approach leveraging geometric priors in scenarios of data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties for probabilistic modeling. We utilize the method to formulate policies based on time or robot state, where non-separable diagonal kernels allow capturing uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for same-sized in- and outputs. Fast updates, requiring less than 3 ms for a trajectory involving both position and orientation are possible through an optimized formulation. Our approach supports both manifold-valued input and manifold-valued output with large orientation changes. Using task parameterization, adaptation to different object poses is easily possible. We evaluate the approach on a set of toy examples and on real robot manipulation tasks both in autonomous execution and in shared control scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a non-parametric, geometry-aware probabilistic policy learning method using non-separable diagonal kernels to handle manifold-valued inputs/outputs under data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainty, enabling fast (<3 ms) adaptation via task parameterization.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic policy learning from human demonstrations requires both data efficiency and fast adaptation to new scenarios. Existing non-parametric (kernel-based) methods either ignore the geometry of manifolds common in robotics—limiting data efficiency—or, when geometry-aware, yield unreliable uncertainty estimates or need retraining to adapt.
AI.method: A non-parametric approach that leverages geometric priors for probabilistic modeling under data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties. Policies are formulated over time or robot state, using non-separable diagonal kernels that capture uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for equal-sized inputs and outputs. An optimized formulation enables fast updates (<3 ms per trajectory including position and orientation). The method supports both manifold-valued inputs and manifold-valued outputs with large orientation changes, and task parameterization allows adaptation to different object poses.
AI.result: Evaluated on toy examples and real robot manipulation tasks, in both autonomous execution and shared control scenarios; updates take less than 3 ms for a trajectory involving both position and orientation.
AI.conclusion: The geometry-aware non-parametric formulation achieves data-efficient, fast-adapting probabilistic policies with reliable uncertainty handling for manifold-valued robotic data, validated across toy and real-world manipulation settings.

title: Beyond Corrected Memory: Execution Consistency in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Shared memory coordinates agents' actions, but correct records do not establish that those actions satisfy task requirements. Memory governance and failure diagnosis regulate or inspect recorded information; they do not by themselves establish whether it is sufficient to judge task duties. We define execution consistency through duties governing state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, with explicit evidence conditions for judging fulfillment. Our core claim is that identical retained records can correspond to compliant and violating executions under the same task rule. Controlled removal of evidence such as receipt, action dependence, or response validity leaves 82.4% of opposite-label pairs indistinguishable; restoration separates 97.9% of the merged pairs. Natural-log annotations identify the defined violations in actual executions. However, existing logs do not always explicitly represent the execution relationships needed for these judgments. To assess the definition's practical value, we use CAVERT, a framework for consistency diagnosis and recovery, to extract supported relationships from logs and apply these criteria. It consistently outperforms contract-prompted LLM and rule-based baselines in diagnosis across all 12 benchmark-executor settings. Under the same gate and executor limits, it also outperforms rule-guided recovery in all four evaluated environments. These findings identify execution evidence that agent-memory and execution interfaces should preserve for reliable judgment.

AI.tldr: The paper defines execution consistency for multi-agent systems via duties on state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, showing identical records can hide compliant vs. violating executions, and introduces CAVERT to recover the evidence needed for reliable diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Shared memory coordinates agents but correct records do not guarantee task fulfillment. Memory governance and failure diagnosis regulate or inspect recorded information yet do not establish whether it suffices to judge task duties.
AI.method: Define execution consistency through duties governing state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, with explicit evidence conditions. Test this via controlled removal of evidence (receipt, action dependence, response validity) and natural-log annotation. Propose CAVERT, a framework for consistency diagnosis and recovery that extracts supported relationships from logs.
AI.result: 82.4% of opposite-label pairs become indistinguishable under evidence removal; restoration separates 97.9% of merged pairs. Natural-log annotations identify defined violations in actual executions. CAVERT outperforms contract-prompted LLM and rule-based baselines across all 12 benchmark-executor settings, and outperforms rule-guided recovery in all four environments.
AI.conclusion: Execution evidence—such as receipt, action dependence, and response validity—must be preserved by agent-memory and execution interfaces to enable reliable judgment of task compliance.

title: Magnet-Aware Control of Legged Robots
summary: Autonomous robots can increase uptime and reduce human exposure in Big Science facilities, but strong magnetic fields needed for their operation corrupt sensors and induce pose-dependent mechanical wrenches that destabilize robots and challenge conventional reactive controllers. This paper presents a control framework for modeling, estimating, and dynamically compensating for spatially varying magnetic wrenches acting on legged robots to improve robustness in these fields. We introduce a custom physics plugin for the MuJoCo simulator to model magnetic forces on rigid-body elements, alongside an inverse field-estimation framework to infer the latent magnetic field directly from quadruped dynamic responses and any number of sensor readings. Furthermore, we develop a Magnet-Aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Whole-Body Control (WBC) architecture that predicts and counteracts magnetic perturbations during locomotion to increase the range of magnetic fields in which the robot can operate. The effectiveness of the framework is validated through both simulation and physical hardware experiments. We show our method increases the the maximum rejectable disturbances from magnetic field in the force space by a factor of 2.5 and and between 1.6-2 times in torque space compared to a non-compensated system. Within the proposed magnetic field, this constitutes an increase in the area in which the robot can operate by 29,34% of which 10,84% would have previously caused an immediate collapse to non-compensated controllers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a control framework that models, estimates, and dynamically compensates for spatially varying magnetic wrenches on legged robots, enabling them to operate more robustly in strong magnetic fields typical of Big Science facilities.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots can boost uptime and reduce human exposure in Big Science facilities, but the strong magnetic fields required for operation corrupt sensors and induce pose-dependent mechanical wrenches that destabilize robots and defeat conventional reactive controllers. There is a need for a control approach that explicitly accounts for magnetic disturbances to maintain robot stability and expand the operable range within such fields.
AI.method: The authors introduce a custom physics plugin for the MuJoCo simulator to model magnetic forces on rigid-body elements, and an inverse field-estimation framework that infers the latent magnetic field from quadruped dynamic responses and arbitrary sensor readings. Building on these, they develop a Magnet-Aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Whole-Body Control (WBC) architecture that predicts and counteracts magnetic perturbations during locomotion.
AI.result: Validated in both simulation and physical hardware experiments, the method increases the maximum rejectable magnetic-field disturbance by a factor of 2.5 in force space and between 1.6–2 times in torque space compared to a non-compensated system. Within the proposed field, this corresponds to a 29.34% increase in the operational area, of which 10.84% would previously have caused immediate collapse under non-compensated controllers.
AI.conclusion: A magnet-aware MPC/WBC framework with a MuJoCo magnetic physics plugin and inverse field estimation substantially improves legged-robot robustness and operating range in strong magnetic fields, demonstrating the value of explicitly modeling and compensating magnetic wrenches.

title: DSV-Mem: Evaluating Multimodal Memory in Professional Workflows for MLLM Agents
summary: Conversational MLLM agents are increasingly expected to assist in professional workflows, from AI research and engineering design to product management and business operations. Yet this capability remains underexplored: existing benchmarks largely focus on informal, everyday interactions and personal-life scenarios featuring photographic natural images, isolated static artifacts, and recall-oriented questions. In contrast, professional scenarios often involve structured, information-heavy artifacts that undergo frequent revisions and authority updates, and compositional queries requiring reconciliation of many artifact versions while tracking state precisely. To address these challenges, we introduce DSV-Mem, a benchmark for evaluating Dense Stateful Visual Memory. DSV-Mem comprises expert-reviewed scenarios and 1,000 questions across five user-oriented categories (Current State, Past State, Derived State, Change History, and Conflict/Refusal). A Hartley-inspired criterion favors questions with broader visual-evidence inspection demands. We also introduce a generation harness that produces evaluation suites by decoupling state-transition synthesis from conversation filling. Evaluation over 27 configurations spanning frontier and open-weight models and memory management methods reveals that the strongest baseline scores below 45% on DSV-Mem. Analysis surfaces findings: 1) multimodality and information density both contribute to difficulty, but state evolution, particularly the number of governing updates, is the dominant tested factor. Raw conversation/haystack length, OCR, and arithmetic are not the primary bottlenecks; 2) models often fail to verify user premises against prior state updates before answering; 3) increased reasoning effort and memory management methods yield limited gains, whereas state-aware designs prove more effective. The benchmark and code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DSV-Mem, a benchmark for Dense Stateful Visual Memory in professional conversational MLLM agents, comprising 1,000 expert-reviewed questions across five categories. Evaluations show top baselines score below 45%, with state evolution (number of governing updates) as the dominant difficulty factor, and state-aware designs proving more effective than reasoning effort or generic memory management.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for conversational MLLM agents focus on informal, everyday interactions and personal-life scenarios, featuring photographic natural images, isolated static artifacts, and recall-oriented questions. Professional workflows, by contrast, involve structured, information-heavy artifacts that undergo frequent revisions and authority updates, plus compositional queries requiring reconciliation of many artifact versions while tracking state precisely. This capability remains underexplored and inadequately benchmarked.
AI.method: The authors propose DSV-Mem, a benchmark for evaluating Dense Stateful Visual Memory. It comprises expert-reviewed scenarios and 1,000 questions across five user-oriented categories (Current State, Past State, Derived State, Change History, and Conflict/Refusal). A Hartley-inspired criterion selects questions with broader visual-evidence inspection demands. A generation harness produces evaluation suites by decoupling state-transition synthesis from conversation filling. Evaluation covers 27 configurations spanning frontier and open-weight models and memory management methods.
AI.result: The strongest baseline scores below 45% on DSV-Mem. Key findings: (1) both multimodality and information density contribute to difficulty, but state evolution—particularly the number of governing updates—is the dominant tested factor; raw conversation/haystack length, OCR, and arithmetic are not primary bottlenecks. (2) Models often fail to verify user premises against prior state updates before answering. (3) Increased reasoning effort and memory management methods yield limited gains, whereas state-aware designs prove more effective.
AI.conclusion: Professional conversational MLLM agents face substantial gaps in dense stateful visual memory, which DSV-Mem exposes and quantifies. The dominant difficulty driver is state evolution rather than modality, length, or perceptual/symbolic operations. The authors argue for state-aware model and method designs over scaling reasoning effort or generic memory management. The benchmark and code will be publicly released.

title: NMPP: Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning for Agile UAV Flight in Cluttered Environments
summary: Flying a quadrotor through a cluttered environment requires not only planning a collision-free reference trajectory based on perceived obstacles, but the reference also needs to be dynamically feasible and within the actuation limits of the vehicle, so that the controller can track it precisely. Existing methods either optimize a smooth polynomial inside a convex corridor, which limits agility, or treat obstacles as soft costs traded against tracking performance. We propose a Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning (NMPP) that imposes perceived obstacles as hard geometric constraints and hands a full-state reference to an obstacle-blind SE(3) controller. Our planner achieves a 58-67 % lower position RMSE than a linear Model Predictive Control trajectory planner and a 41-70 % lower RMSE than a polynomial trajectory planner. It also completes all forest flights with up to 9.5 m/s speed without collisions, and achieves 86 % flight success rate under a more aggressive speed profile where a state-of-the-art planner has only 26 % success rate. The real-world deployment showed reliable execution flying up to 5.5 m/s in an unknown cluttered environment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning (NMPP) that treats perceived obstacles as hard geometric constraints and outputs a full-state reference for an obstacle-blind SE(3) controller, achieving substantially lower tracking RMSE and higher success rates than linear MPC and polynomial planners in cluttered flight.
AI.motivation: Flying quadrotors through cluttered environments requires a reference trajectory that is simultaneously collision-free, dynamically feasible, and within actuation limits so the controller can track it precisely. Existing approaches fall short: convex-corridor polynomial optimization limits agility, while soft-cost obstacle formulations trade off safety against tracking performance.
AI.method: A Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning (NMPP) framework that encodes perceived obstacles as hard geometric constraints and provides a full-state reference to a separate obstacle-blind SE(3) controller.
AI.result: 58-67% lower position RMSE than a linear MPC trajectory planner and 41-70% lower RMSE than a polynomial trajectory planner. All forest flights completed without collisions at speeds up to 9.5 m/s, and 86% flight success rate under a more aggressive speed profile where a state-of-the-art planner achieves only 26%. Real-world deployment flew reliably up to 5.5 m/s in an unknown cluttered environment.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing obstacles as hard constraints within a nonlinear model predictive planner, paired with an obstacle-blind SE(3) controller, improves tracking accuracy, agility, and flight success in cluttered and unknown environments compared with state-of-the-art planning baselines.

title: ChartBmkAgent: Harness-Governed Multi-Agent Construction of Chart QA Benchmarks from Sparse Error-Taxonomy Specifications
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance rapidly, while conventional benchmark development lags behind, delaying investigation of newly observed capability gaps. Such investigation requires an expressive task format and an on-demand construction process: information-rich charts make chart question answering (Chart QA) suitable for probing coupled perception and reasoning. Automated Chart QA construction is intended to shorten the benchmark-development cycle by turning identified gaps into targeted samples on demand. Current methods, however, commonly separate target guidance from scratch generation: target-guided systems often require prepared data, charts, or templates, while scratch-generation systems primarily ensure artifact validity, without explicitly controlling whether newly synthesized requirements and content remain aligned with an externally specified diagnostic target. We introduce ChartBmkAgent, which turns an identified capability gap into targeted diagnostic evidence by constructing complete Chart QA samples from sparse error-taxonomy specifications. Throughout construction, a central harness governs specialized agents, requires stage-specific evidence of alignment with the original error category, and records the basis for each acceptance decision. On 300 taxonomy-wide samples, MLLM accuracies ranged from 32.7% to 84.3% with distinct category profiles, showing that generated samples reveal capability differences. Across three source-model comparisons, targeted follow-ups scored 50.0% versus 82.2% on matched controls ($p=8.96\times10^{-6}$); all six cross-model comparisons had the same direction, demonstrating targeted validation and diagnostic-data generation. Multiple evaluator models assessed whether each sample tested its specified error category; 86.4% met this criterion, providing empirical evidence of target preservation.

AI.tldr: ChartBmkAgent constructs complete Chart QA diagnostic samples on demand from sparse error-taxonomy specifications, using a central harness to supervise agents and enforce stage-wise target-alignment evidence, thereby revealing and validating MLLM capability gaps.
AI.motivation: MLLM capability advances outpace benchmark development, delaying investigation of newly observed capability gaps. On-demand benchmark construction is needed, and Chart QA is a suitable format because charts couple perception and reasoning. Existing automated construction methods decouple target guidance from scratch generation: target-guided systems need prepared data/templates, while scratch-generation systems verify artifact validity but not alignment with an externally specified diagnostic target.
AI.method: ChartBmkAgent converts an identified capability gap into targeted diagnostic evidence by building full Chart QA samples from sparse error-taxonomy specs. A central harness governs specialized agents, requires stage-specific evidence of alignment with the original error category, and records the basis for each acceptance decision.
AI.result: On 300 taxonomy-wide samples, MLLM accuracies ranged 32.7%–84.3% with distinct category profiles. Across three source-model comparisons, targeted follow-ups scored 50.0% vs. 82.2% on matched controls (p=8.96e-6); all six cross-model comparisons shared the same direction. 86.4% of samples were judged by multiple evaluator models to test their specified error category.
AI.conclusion: ChartBmkAgent enables targeted validation and diagnostic-data generation, preserving diagnostic targets while producing samples that expose genuine capability differences across MLLMs.

title: EgoLAP: Learning from Egocentric Human Data through Language-Action Reasoning
summary: Egocentric human data offer a path to scaling robot learning beyond costly robot demonstrations, yet the embodiment gap makes raw human trajectories a poor supervisory target for control. Our key insight is that, although low-level actions are embodiment-specific, their underlying motion intent can capture task-relevant structure that transfers across humans and robots. We introduce EgoLAP, a VLA pre-training framework that jointly learns from human and robot trajectories through a shared language-based action chain-of-thought. EgoLAP expresses motion intent as structured, temporally abstracted language actions and pairs them with motion-level reasoning grounded in scene geometry, physics, and object affordances. Across extensive real-world and simulated experiments, EgoLAP transfers human experience to robot control more effectively than alternative action representations and reaches 80.1% mean real-world task progress, a 2.3x performance gain over alternative action representations. Motion-level reasoning also outperforms a composite reasoning format that combines subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning.

AI.tldr: EgoLAP is a VLA pre-training framework that bridges the human-robot embodiment gap by representing motion intent as a shared, language-based action chain-of-thought, enabling effective transfer of egocentric human data to robot control.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human data can scale robot learning beyond costly robot demonstrations, but the embodiment gap makes raw human trajectories poor supervisory targets for control. Low-level actions are embodiment-specific, yet their underlying motion intent may capture task-relevant structure that transfers across humans and robots.
AI.method: EgoLAP jointly learns from human and robot trajectories through a shared language-based action chain-of-thought. It expresses motion intent as structured, temporally abstracted language actions and pairs them with motion-level reasoning grounded in scene geometry, physics, and object affordances.
AI.result: Across extensive real-world and simulated experiments, EgoLAP transfers human experience to robot control more effectively than alternative action representations, reaching 80.1% mean real-world task progress (a 2.3x gain over alternative action representations). Motion-level reasoning also outperforms a composite reasoning format combining subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Representing motion intent as a shared language-based action chain-of-thought is an effective abstraction for transferring egocentric human data to robot control, outperforming alternative action representations and reasoning formats.

title: Test-Time Agent Evolution for Long-Horizon Legal Reasoning
summary: Legal intelligence aims to support reliable decision-making across long-horizon legal processes involving evolving case states and multiple roles. However, real-world legal deployment exhibits substantial case heterogeneity in facts, evidence, and procedural contexts, exposing the limitations of static agent strategies. Moreover, legal reasoning is inherently interdependent across roles and procedural stages, making global reliability fundamentally different from isolated role competence. To address these challenges, we study training-free test-time agent adaptation, where agents continuously exploit deployment-time signals from preceding cases and ongoing interactions without updating model parameters. We propose \method, which introduces \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} to retrieve reusable experience from previous cases, adapt it to the current factual and procedural context, and consolidate accumulated experience for subsequent decision-making. Further, \emph{Rubric-Aligned Collaboration} verifies and revises role-specific actions according to behavioral and procedural requirements, enabling coordinated decision-making across roles and stages. Extensive experiments on J1-EVAL and LegalWorld across five backbone models demonstrate consistent improvements over representative reasoning and agent baselines with reasonable interaction and computational costs. Ablation and case studies further show that the two components provide complementary benefits in experience adaptation and cross-role coordination, improving the reliability and efficiency of long-horizon legal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free test-time agent adaptation method for legal intelligence, combining Test-Time Memory Evolution (retrieving and adapting prior-case experience) with Rubric-Aligned Collaboration (verifying and revising role-specific actions), achieving consistent gains on J1-EVAL and LegalWorld across five backbone models.
AI.motivation: Legal intelligence requires reliable decision-making over long-horizon processes with evolving case states and multiple roles. Real-world legal deployment faces substantial case heterogeneity in facts, evidence, and procedural contexts, exposing the limits of static agent strategies. Because legal reasoning is interdependent across roles and stages, global reliability cannot be reduced to isolated role competence. This motivates training-free test-time adaptation that exploits deployment-time signals without parameter updates.
AI.method: The proposed method is training-free test-time agent adaptation with two components. (1) Test-Time Memory Evolution: retrieves reusable experience from previous cases, adapts it to the current factual and procedural context, and consolidates accumulated experience for subsequent decisions. (2) Rubric-Aligned Collaboration: verifies and revises role-specific actions against behavioral and procedural requirements to enable coordinated decision-making across roles and stages.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on J1-EVAL and LegalWorld across five backbone models show consistent improvements over representative reasoning and agent baselines, with reasonable interaction and computational costs. Ablation studies and case analyses indicate the two components yield complementary benefits in experience adaptation and cross-role coordination, improving reliability and efficiency of long-horizon legal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Training-free test-time adaptation via memory evolution and rubric-aligned collaboration effectively addresses case heterogeneity and cross-role interdependence in legal reasoning, improving global reliability and efficiency without model parameter updates. The two components are complementary, validating the design for long-horizon legal decision-making.

title: Towards an Extensible Benchmark for Spoken Dialogue with Social Robots
comment: Accepted to and presented at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Human-Robot Dialogue
summary: Language models provide a plug-and-play interface between humans and robots, but important challenges remain when speech, dialogue, fast interaction, and collaboration are required. We propose a benchmark for the community to use as a way to explore common spoken dialogue artifacts between robots and humans, including requests for clarification, interruptions, embodied signals (e.g., head nods or facial cues), and time constraints. We also explain our vision to extend the benchmark for other aspects of human-robot interaction that are important to the larger research community. To facilitate the benchmark, we further propose using \textit{Retico}, a real-time communication framework that fulfills important technical requirements to enable robots to have spoken dialogue capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a benchmark for spoken dialogue between humans and robots, covering clarification requests, interruptions, embodied signals, and time constraints, and introduces Retico, a real-time communication framework enabling robots' spoken dialogue capabilities.
AI.motivation: Language models offer a plug-and-play interface between humans and robots, yet significant challenges persist when speech, dialogue, fast interaction, and collaboration are required. There is a need for a shared means to explore common spoken dialogue phenomena in human-robot interaction.
AI.method: The authors propose a benchmark for the community to explore common spoken dialogue artifacts between robots and humans, including requests for clarification, interruptions, embodied signals such as head nods or facial cues, and time constraints. They further propose using Retico, a real-time communication framework that meets important technical requirements for enabling robots' spoken dialogue capabilities. They also outline a vision for extending the benchmark to other aspects of human-robot interaction relevant to the broader research community.
AI.result: The paper presents the benchmark design and the Retico framework as an enabling infrastructure, along with a stated plan to extend the benchmark to additional aspects of human-robot interaction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and the Retico real-time communication framework aim to advance spoken dialogue capabilities in human-robot interaction and can be extended to address broader aspects of the field.

title: Partially Observable Zero-shot coordination by Predicting Intention of Partner
summary: Zero-shot coordination in embodied settings requires acting while the partner is intermittently out of view, leaving existing methods with ambiguous partner representations and uncertainty over hidden partner states. We propose Predicting Intention of Partner (PIP) to jointly address these challenges. PIP uses a Joint-view VAE to distill richer training-time evidence from the union of both agents' local observations into a partner representation available from local observations alone. Partner-state Belief networks further infer the partner's hidden location and behavioral tendencies from the ego agent's interaction history. We evaluate PIP in Burrito-PO, Overcooked-PO, and a Melting Pot substrate, together with a human evaluation in Burrito-PO. PIP attains the highest mean performance among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. Human evaluation and diagnostic analyses further support coordination with unseen partners and the contributions of both components under partner occlusion.

AI.tldr: PIP tackles zero-shot coordination in embodied settings with intermittent partner visibility by combining a Joint-view VAE for richer partner representation and Partner-state Belief networks for inferring hidden partner states, achieving top mean performance across three benchmarks plus human evaluation.
AI.motivation: In embodied zero-shot coordination, agents must act while the partner is intermittently out of view, which causes existing methods to rely on ambiguous partner representations and leaves hidden partner states uncertain. These two challenges are typically not addressed jointly.
AI.method: PIP predicts the partner's intention via two components: (1) a Joint-view VAE that distills richer training-time evidence from the union of both agents' local observations into a partner representation obtainable from the ego agent's local observations alone; (2) Partner-state Belief networks that infer the partner's hidden location and behavioral tendencies from the ego agent's interaction history.
AI.result: Evaluated in Burrito-PO, Overcooked-PO, and a Melting Pot substrate, plus a human evaluation in Burrito-PO. PIP achieves the highest mean performance among compared methods across all three benchmarks. Human evaluation and diagnostic analyses support coordination with unseen partners and confirm the contributions of both components under partner occlusion.
AI.conclusion: PIP jointly addresses ambiguous partner representation and hidden-state uncertainty, enabling effective zero-shot coordination under intermittent partner visibility, as validated by benchmark and human evaluations.

title: PhoneBot: A Low-Cost Open Humanoid Robot Platform Reusing Smartphones
summary: The adoption of humanoid robots in education and research remains limited by high hardware costs, complex sensing systems, and substantial computational requirements. This paper presents PhoneBot, a low-cost, open-source humanoid robot platform that repurposes commodity smartphones as its primary sensing and computing unit. By using a smartphone's integrated inertial measurement unit (IMU), camera, wireless connectivity, and onboard processing capabilities, PhoneBot reduces hardware costs and simplifies the system architecture. The robot combines a modular lower-body structure driven by 13 low-cost actuators with a torso-mounted smartphone that supports perception, control computation, and user interaction. We describe the mechanical design, software architecture, and real-time communication framework that support stable locomotion and capabilities including vision-based human following, conversational interaction, filming, and mobile telepresence. Experimental evaluations demonstrate reliable walking, perception-driven interaction, and straightforward deployment using off-the-shelf consumer smartphones. With fully open-source hardware and software designs, PhoneBot provides an affordable, reproducible platform for education, research, and rapid prototyping. More details are available at https://phonebot.dev.

AI.tldr: PhoneBot is a low-cost, open-source humanoid robot that uses a commodity smartphone as its primary sensing and computing unit, reducing hardware cost and complexity while supporting stable walking and perception-driven interaction.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots in education and research are limited by high hardware costs, complex sensing systems, and substantial computational requirements. The paper aims to lower these barriers by repurposing a commodity smartphone's IMU, camera, wireless connectivity, and onboard processing as the robot's core sensing and computing unit.
AI.method: The platform combines a modular lower-body structure driven by 13 low-cost actuators with a torso-mounted smartphone handling perception, control computation, and user interaction. The authors detail the mechanical design, software architecture, and real-time communication framework enabling stable locomotion, along with a fully open-source hardware and software design.
AI.result: Experimental evaluations demonstrate reliable walking, perception-driven interaction, and straightforward deployment on off-the-shelf consumer smartphones. Capabilities include vision-based human following, conversational interaction, filming, and mobile telepresence.
AI.conclusion: PhoneBot provides an affordable, reproducible platform for education, research, and rapid prototyping.

title: Which alloy composition,what process parameters? Inferring the recipe from optimized metallic microstructure and texture
summary: The mechanical properties of a metallic alloy are set by its microstructure and texture: the size and shape of its grains and the orientation of their crystals. That structure is in turn set by a recipe, the alloy composition together with the processing parameters. Alloy development runs this chain forwards, tuning the structure until a target property is met. Running it backwards, from an optimized structure to the recipe that would produce it, still relies on expert knowledge. We ask whether this backwards step can be learned. On an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, each with optical micrographs and an X-ray texture measurement, we compare three descriptors of microstructure and texture: conventional grain and texture statistics, a vision embedding from a pretrained image encoder, and a graph neural network on the grain network. Each is paired with prediction heads for two tasks: the alloy composition given the process (Task A), and the process parameters given the composition (Task B). Under 5-fold cross-validation, the conventional descriptors identify the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions, against 17% for always guessing the most common alloy, while the learned embeddings stay below 30%. The process parameters are recoverable but noisier: compared with using the composition alone, the microstructure roughly halves the temperature error. Because only a few alloys were cast and only a few press settings were used, both answers are discrete, and heads that pick from these known options, while respecting their order, worked better than heads that predict a free value.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the "inverse" step of alloy development—recovering the recipe (composition or process parameters) from the resulting microstructure and texture—can be learned, comparing three microstructure descriptors on a dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions.
AI.motivation: Alloy development conventionally runs forward: recipe (composition + process) determines microstructure/texture, which determines mechanical properties. The reverse step—from an optimized structure back to the recipe that produces it—still relies on expert knowledge and has not been systematically learned. The authors ask whether this backwards mapping can be learned from data.
AI.method: On an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, each with optical micrographs and X-ray texture measurements, the authors compare three microstructure/texture descriptors: (1) conventional grain and texture statistics, (2) a vision embedding from a pretrained image encoder, and (3) a graph neural network on the grain network. Each descriptor is paired with prediction heads for two tasks: Task A predicts alloy composition given the process, and Task B predicts process parameters given the composition. Evaluation uses 5-fold cross-validation, with discrete/order-aware heads compared against free-value regression heads.
AI.result: Under 5-fold cross-validation, conventional descriptors identify the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions, versus 17% for always guessing the most common alloy, while learned embeddings stay below 30%. Process parameters are recoverable but noisier: compared with using composition alone, microstructure roughly halves the temperature error. Heads that pick from the known discrete options while respecting their order outperformed heads predicting free values.
AI.conclusion: The backwards step from structure to recipe is partially learnable. Conventional grain and texture statistics outperform learned embeddings for identifying alloy composition, and microstructure information substantially improves process parameter recovery (notably halving temperature error). Because the dataset contains few alloys and press settings, both targets are discrete, and discrete, order-aware prediction heads are preferable to free-value regression.

title: LBA-CBF: Rapidly Adaptive Safety Filters via Parallel Dynamics Inference
summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) certify commands through an assumed dynamics model, so an abrupt, unmeasured regime change can undermine the certificate exactly when safety matters most. We present Look-Back Adaptive Control Barrier Functions (LBA-CBF), which rank a finite bank of candidate dynamics by recent prediction error over a short look-back window and enforce the high-order CBF condition against every model within a tolerance of the best, spanning best-fit adaptation to full-bank robust filtering. The dynamics may depend nonlinearly on the unknown parameters, and no switching model or continuously parameterized estimator is required. We prove that any feasible filtered input satisfies the true CBF condition whenever a safety-representative candidate is retained. In quadrotor simulation with abrupt wind reversals and an unknown payload, LBA-CBF is safe and reaches the goal from all random initial conditions, matching an oracle, while adaptive and robust baselines achieve 0-88% success. Banks of up to 250,000 models run inside the control loop, and Crazyflie 2.1 and F1TENTH experiments demonstrate adaptation to wind, payload release, and varying tire-road friction. Code, videos, and project details are available at: https://lla-control.github.io

AI.tldr: LBA-CBF ranks a bank of candidate dynamics by recent prediction error and enforces a high-order CBF condition against every model within tolerance of the best, achieving certified safety under abrupt unmeasured regime changes without a switching model or continuous estimator.
AI.motivation: Standard CBFs certify commands using an assumed dynamics model, so an abrupt, unmeasured regime change (e.g., sudden wind reversal or payload shift) can invalidate the certificate exactly when safety is critical. Existing adaptive and robust baselines either lack responsiveness or are overly conservative, yielding low success rates (0-88%).
AI.method: The authors propose Look-Back Adaptive CBF (LBA-CBF). It maintains a finite bank of candidate dynamics, ranks them by recent prediction error over a short look-back window, and enforces the high-order CBF condition against every model within a tolerance of the best-fitting one. This spans a spectrum from best-fit adaptation to full-bank robust filtering. Dynamics may depend nonlinearly on unknown parameters, and no switching model or continuously parameterized estimator is needed.
AI.result: They prove that any feasible filtered input satisfies the true CBF condition whenever a safety-representative candidate is retained. In quadrotor simulation with abrupt wind reversals and unknown payload, LBA-CBF is safe and reaches the goal from all random initial conditions, matching an oracle, while adaptive and robust baselines achieve only 0-88% success. Banks of up to 250,000 models run inside the control loop. Crazyflie 2.1 and F1TENTH experiments demonstrate adaptation to wind, payload release, and varying tire-road friction.
AI.conclusion: LBA-CBF provides a practical, provably safe control framework that handles abrupt, unmeasured regime changes by combining look-back model ranking with robust filtering over a large candidate bank, validated in simulation and hardware (Crazyflie 2.1, F1TENTH). Code, videos, and project details are available at https://lla-control.github.io.

title: LFHE: Local-First Heuristic Evolution for Bounded Local Topology Search in Decentralized Learning with Non-IID Data
summary: Decentralized learning is highly sensitive to communication topology under non-IID data. Adaptive peer-selection methods can exploit local model information, but broader peer discovery may require increasingly large control state, whereas direct spectral optimization typically relies on graph-wide information. We study the intermediate setting of bounded local topology search and propose Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a representation-driven rewiring framework whose candidate discovery and scoring use only ego-neighborhood and friend-of-a-friend (FoF) information. The structural score admits an exact interpretation through graph Dirichlet energy: its sum across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy, which under standard linear consensus dynamics governs the instantaneous dissipation of representation disagreement. LFHE combines this state-dependent structural signal with early exploration and degree control, while algebraic connectivity remains an offline graph diagnostic. Under bounded sparse degree, its FoF candidate state remains local rather than expanding toward population-wide peer tracking. Across four image, speech, and text benchmarks, LFHE achieves competitive decentralized learning performance. Matched-protocol controls identify the structural term as the principal empirical topology-selection signal, while comparison with broader peer discovery exposes a trade-off between predictive performance and discovery-state locality. Together, these results motivate state-aware bounded local topology search between pairwise peer selection and globally informed topology optimization.

AI.tldr: LFHE is a local, representation-driven rewiring framework for decentralized learning that selects peers using only ego-neighborhood and friend-of-friend information, with a structural score exactly linked to graph Dirichlet energy.
AI.motivation: Decentralized learning is highly sensitive to communication topology under non-IID data. Adaptive peer-selection methods exploit local model information but broad peer discovery requires large control state, while spectral optimization needs graph-wide information. This leaves an unexplored intermediate regime of bounded local topology search.
AI.method: The paper proposes Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a representation-driven rewiring framework whose candidate discovery and scoring use only ego-neighborhood and friend-of-friend (FoF) information. The structural score is exactly interpreted via graph Dirichlet energy: summing it across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy, governing instantaneous dissipation of representation disagreement under linear consensus dynamics. LFHE combines this state-dependent structural signal with early exploration and degree control; algebraic connectivity serves only as an offline diagnostic.
AI.result: Under bounded sparse degree, FoF candidate state stays local rather than scaling to population-wide peer tracking. Across four image, speech, and text benchmarks, LFHE achieves competitive decentralized learning performance. Matched-protocol controls identify the structural term as the principal topology-selection signal, and comparison with broader peer discovery reveals a trade-off between predictive performance and discovery-state locality.
AI.conclusion: These results motivate state-aware, bounded local topology search as a middle ground between pairwise peer selection and globally informed topology optimization.

title: DepthWorld: 3D World Model for Robot Manipulation
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: https://www.jaibardhan.com/depthworld. 32 pages including supplementary material, 15 figures, 7 tables
summary: World models offer a data-driven alternative to traditional simulators for robotics, with applications spanning policy evaluation, improvement, and planning. All of these uses depend on faithful 3D geometry, yet current video-based world models are trained on RGB alone and produce rollouts that look correct frame-by-frame but do not compose into a consistent 3D world. Closing this gap requires progress on two fronts: large-scale 3D supervision for manipulation, and an architecture that can absorb it without disturbing strong pretrained video priors. We introduce a calibration pipeline that combines learned stereo depth with a joint factor graph, pooling all episodes collected from the same physical robot to recover its shared kinematic parameters alongside per-scene extrinsics. Applied to the DROID dataset, this yields DROID-3D, a calibrated 3D dataset providing dense metric depth and recalibrated multi-view extrinsics (achieving <0.7 px reprojection error on 90% of episodes for external cameras). We then train DepthWorld, a Stable Video Diffusion-based world model that jointly predicts multi-view RGB and depth via spatial latent tiling, leaving the pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) unchanged. Depth supervision improves RGB prediction itself by +1.48 dB PSNR over an identical RGB-only baseline at equal training budget, while simultaneously yielding accurate metric depth for downstream geometric reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DROID-3D, a calibrated 3D dataset built via a joint factor-graph pipeline combining learned stereo depth with shared kinematic parameters, and DepthWorld, an SVD-based world model predicting multi-view RGB and depth via spatial latent tiling, improving RGB fidelity while yielding accurate metric depth.
AI.motivation: Video-based world models for robotics are trained on RGB alone, producing rollouts that look plausible frame-by-frame but fail to compose into a consistent 3D world. Faithful 3D geometry is required for policy evaluation, improvement, and planning. Closing this gap needs both large-scale 3D supervision for manipulation and an architecture that absorbs it without disturbing strong pretrained video priors.
AI.method: A calibration pipeline combines learned stereo depth with a joint factor graph, pooling all episodes from the same physical robot to recover shared kinematic parameters alongside per-scene extrinsics. Applied to DROID, it yields DROID-3D with dense metric depth and recalibrated multi-view extrinsics. DepthWorld, based on Stable Video Diffusion, jointly predicts multi-view RGB and depth via spatial latent tiling while leaving the pretrained VAE unchanged.
AI.result: DROID-3D achieves <0.7 px reprojection error on 90% of episodes for external cameras. Depth supervision improves RGB prediction by +1.48 dB PSNR over an identical RGB-only baseline at equal training budget, while simultaneously producing accurate metric depth.
AI.conclusion: Depth supervision is a beneficial training signal even for RGB prediction, and coupling calibrated large-scale 3D data with a VAE-preserving multi-view architecture enables geometrically consistent world models for downstream robotic geometric reasoning.

title: Mathematical Proof Assistants for Teaching Logic: The LogiKEy Methodology
summary: We report on an approach to teaching logic to mixed groups of computer science, mathematics, and philosophy students, based on the logico-pluralistic LogiKEy methodology, used for more than a decade in courses, summer schools, and tutorials. LogiKEy uses classical higher-order logic (HOL) as a universal metalogic in which object logics, classical and non-classical alike, are encoded by defining their semantics; through these semantical embeddings a single proof assistant (e.g. Isabelle/HOL), with its automated theorem provers and (counter-)model finders, becomes one environment in which students learn, experiment with, and compare logics. After making the pedagogical case for proof assistants in the logic classroom, we present a graded sequence of classroom examples, each transition motivated by a limitation of the preceding representation, by a need for more explicit modelling resources, or by a new application. A liars-and-truth-tellers puzzle leads from propositional to modal logic; the Wise Men puzzle leads on to dynamic epistemic logic; Boolos's curious inference illustrates what a higher-order meta-logic buys, even for automated proof search; Chisholm's paradox takes the sequence into deontic logic, and from standard to dyadic deontic logic; and Gödel's ontological argument brings it to a research-level metaphysical argument. We then rebut the objection that embedding everything in classical HOL is monism rather than pluralism, reflect on three years of teaching such a course, and sketch the portability of the approach beyond Isabelle.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pedagogical approach to teaching logic to mixed computer science, mathematics, and philosophy students using the logico-pluralistic LogiKEy methodology, which employs classical higher-order logic (HOL) as a universal metalogic for encoding and comparing diverse object logics within a single proof assistant like Isabelle/HOL.
AI.motivation: Teaching logic to interdisciplinary groups poses challenges because students come from computer science, mathematics, and philosophy with different backgrounds and needs. The paper argues for using proof assistants in the logic classroom to provide a unified, pluralistic learning environment.
AI.method: The LogiKEy methodology encodes object logics (classical and non-classical) by defining their semantics in classical HOL, allowing a single proof assistant with automated theorem provers and model finders to serve as one environment. A graded sequence of classroom examples is presented, each transition motivated by limitations or new applications, ranging from propositional to modal, dynamic epistemic, higher-order, deontic, and metaphysical logics.
AI.result: The graded examples include a liars-and-truth-tellers puzzle (propositional to modal logic), the Wise Men puzzle (dynamic epistemic logic), Boolos's curious inference (higher-order meta-logic), Chisholm's paradox (deontic to dyadic deontic logic), and Gödel's ontological argument (research-level metaphysical argument). The paper also rebuts the monism objection, reflects on three years of teaching, and sketches portability beyond Isabelle.
AI.conclusion: Embedding logics in classical HOL constitutes pluralism rather than monism, and the LogiKEy approach offers a portable, effective pedagogical framework for teaching logic to mixed disciplinary groups.

title: PEARS: Physical-Prior-Guided Efficient Adaptation via Failure Reasoning and Diffusion Steering for Tactile Manipulation
summary: Pretrained robotic policies can suffer substantial performance degradation under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions encountered during deployment, motivating post-training through real-world interaction. However, reinforcement-learning (RL)-based post-training typically requires substantial environment interactions, a burden that is especially significant in manipulation, where each trial can be slow, costly, or destructive. Therefore, we present PEARS, a physics-prior-guided hybrid RL framework for sample-efficient online adaptation of pretrained policies with tactile feedback. After each episode, its physics-guided force reasoning (PFR) module uses physical priors encoded in a vision-language model (VLM) to diagnose failures from the visual outcome and tactile interaction history and update task-appropriate contact-force bounds. A high-frequency hybrid force-position controller then enforces these bounds during contact. Complementarily, tactile-conditioned diffusion steering reinforcement learning adjusts the latent noise of the frozen flow-matching policy to correct errors in free-space motion and contact timing without updating the base model. In simulation, PEARS improves success rates by 12.4-37.4 percentage points over the strongest per-task baselines. PEARS also reduces the number of interaction episodes required for a certain success threshold by up to 53.2% relative to the fastest baseline. In real-world experiments, PEARS achieves success rates of 95% on Whiteboard Erasing and 90% on Pipette Liquid Aspiration. These results show that combining the PFR module with policy steering can accelerate adaptation while reducing costly interactions. The project website is available at https://song-kun.github.io/pears.

AI.tldr: PEARS is a physics-prior-guided hybrid RL framework for sample-efficient online adaptation of pretrained robotic policies with tactile feedback, combining VLM-based force reasoning with tactile-conditioned diffusion steering.
AI.motivation: Pretrained robotic policies degrade substantially under out-of-distribution (OOD) deployment conditions, motivating post-training via real-world interaction. However, RL-based post-training demands extensive environment interactions, which is especially burdensome in manipulation where each trial is slow, costly, or destructive. This calls for a sample-efficient adaptation method.
AI.method: PEARS integrates two components: (1) a physics-guided force reasoning (PFR) module that, after each episode, leverages physical priors encoded in a vision-language model (VLM) to diagnose failures from visual outcomes and tactile interaction history, updating task-appropriate contact-force bounds; and (2) a high-frequency hybrid force-position controller that enforces these bounds during contact. Complementarily, tactile-conditioned diffusion steering RL adjusts the latent noise of a frozen flow-matching policy to correct errors in free-space motion and contact timing without updating the base model.
AI.result: In simulation, PEARS improves success rates by 12.4-37.4 percentage points over the strongest per-task baselines, and reduces interaction episodes needed to reach a given success threshold by up to 53.2% versus the fastest baseline. In real-world experiments, PEARS achieves 95% success on Whiteboard Erasing and 90% on Pipette Liquid Aspiration.
AI.conclusion: Combining the PFR module with policy steering enables accelerated adaptation while reducing costly interactions, demonstrating the effectiveness of physics-prior-guided hybrid RL with tactile feedback for sample-efficient online adaptation of pretrained policies.

title: Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?
summary: Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents to adapt to unfamiliar and dynmaic environments. Evaluating this ability is therefore important for understanding how effectively agents acquire and use new knowledge. Existing benchmarks have sought to evaluate this ability, but they primarily evaluate tasks whose rules are provided in the instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it difficult to distinguish learning from interactions from reasoning with existing knowledge. To address this, we introduce Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games, whose rules are novel or counterintuitive, requiring agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than rely solely on pretrained knowledge. These games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, enabling controlled evaluation of learning across repeated attempts. We also vary game instances to test whether agents can apply what they have learned to new situations. Therefore, we evaluate how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect agents' learning ability, revealing three findings: (1) Experience retention: Retaining complete records of actions and feedback can support more effective learning than summarizing these experiences into rules or strategies. (2) Human agent gap: Top-performing human players achieve higher peak scores than the evaluated agents. Human explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less. (3) Harness matters: With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost. Together, these findings provide insights into how LLM agents learn from experience and suggest directions for future work to improve their learning ability. Project website: https://liushiliushi.github.io/learn2play-bench-website/

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Learn2Play Bench, a suite of text-based games with novel/counterintuitive rules that force LLM agents to learn from interaction rather than pretrained knowledge, and use it to study how backbones, self-evolution methods, and harnesses affect learning from experience.
AI.motivation: Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents in unfamiliar, dynamic environments, but existing benchmarks use tasks whose rules are given in instructions or already familiar to pretrained models. This makes it hard to separate genuine learning from interaction versus reasoning with existing knowledge, so a benchmark with truly novel rules is needed.
AI.method: They build Learn2Play Bench, a set of newly designed text-based games with novel or counterintuitive rules requiring knowledge acquisition through interaction. The games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring for controlled evaluation across repeated attempts, and game instances are varied to test transfer of learned knowledge. They then evaluate backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses under this setup.
AI.result: Three findings emerge: (1) Experience retention—keeping complete records of actions and feedback supports better learning than summarizing experience into rules or strategies. (2) Human-agent gap—top human players reach higher peak scores, explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less. (3) Harness matters—with a fixed backbone, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides insights into how LLM agents learn from experience and points to future directions for improving their learning ability.

title: QF3: Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients
summary: Flow policies have become a standard policy class for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations, but reinforcement learning is still critical for improving pre-trained flow policies or learning them from scratch through interaction. We introduce QF3 (Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients), an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy with flow matching plus the critic's action gradient, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow's output. To keep updates where the critic and this prediction are reliable, QF3 applies the critic gradient only to action dimensions that stay near the replay action. To our knowledge, QF3 is the first off-policy flow RL method to train humanoid locomotion policies from scratch and transfer them zero-shot to hardware. Paired with a high-throughput off-policy training recipe, it trains humanoid locomotion and motion-tracking policies with a 10x wall-clock speedup over FPO++, a recent on-policy flow RL method. We further apply QF3 to fine-tune pretrained flow-based manipulation policies on both ABC-Sim and Robomimic tasks. These results suggest that QF3 can both learn robot policies from scratch and refine those acquired from demonstrations. Website: https://qf3-rl.github.io/

AI.tldr: QF3 is an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains flow policies by combining flow matching with filtered critic action gradients, enabling from-scratch humanoid locomotion learning with zero-shot hardware transfer and efficient fine-tuning of pretrained flow policies.
AI.motivation: Flow policies are a standard class for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations, but reinforcement learning remains necessary to improve pretrained flow policies or learn them from scratch via interaction. Existing on-policy flow RL methods are inefficient, and off-policy flow RL had not been shown to train humanoid locomotion from scratch.
AI.method: QF3 is an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy using flow matching plus the critic's action gradient, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow's output. To keep updates where the critic and this prediction are reliable, it applies the critic gradient only to action dimensions that remain near the replay action (filtered Q-gradients). It is paired with a high-throughput off-policy training recipe.
AI.result: QF3 is the first off-policy flow RL method to train humanoid locomotion policies from scratch and transfer them zero-shot to hardware. It trains humanoid locomotion and motion-tracking policies with a 10x wall-clock speedup over FPO++, a recent on-policy flow RL method. It also fine-tunes pretrained flow-based manipulation policies on ABC-Sim and Robomimic tasks.
AI.conclusion: QF3 can both learn robot policies from scratch and refine those acquired from demonstrations, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining flow matching with filtered critic gradients in an off-policy RL framework.

title: Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN): Resource-Aware Hybrid Vision-Language Fusion via Trainable Entanglement
summary: Multimodal vision-language systems typically fuse image and text embeddings through classical operators such as concatenation, attention, bilinear pooling, or tensor interactions. We propose Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN), a hybrid quantum-classical framework that introduces parameterized entanglement as a structured inductive bias for multimodal fusion. Pretrained visual and textual features are projected into compact latent spaces, encoded as angle-parameterized quantum states, processed through intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling circuits, and measured to produce fused representations for retrieval. Under matched parameter budgets and identical frozen CLIP backbones, QEMFN outperforms classical fusion baselines on COCO-5k and Flickr30k, including multilayer perceptron, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, compact transformer, and a dequantized paired-topology analogue. An ablation suite isolates the quantum module's contribution from the surrounding classical projections, and quantum-centric analyses report Meyer-Wallach entangling capability, expressibility, gradient variance against barren-plateau bounds, and entropy-performance correlation under controls for training progress alongside an intervention study on the entangling component. QEMFN is executed under shot-based estimation, a noise-modeled fake backend, and a real superconducting device with zero-noise extrapolation. This work does not claim quantum computational advantage; the contribution is the framework together with a controlled empirical and quantum-centric evaluation that positions trainable entanglement as an interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanism at scales accessible on contemporary devices.

AI.tldr: QEMFN is a hybrid quantum-classical multimodal fusion framework that replaces classical fusion operators with trainable entanglement circuits, outperforming classical baselines on COCO-5k and Flickr30k under matched budgets and validated on simulated and real quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Classical multimodal fusion relies on concatenation, attention, bilinear pooling, or tensor interactions. The work explores whether parameterized quantum entanglement can serve as a structured inductive bias for fusing image and text embeddings, aiming to position trainable entanglement as an interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanism rather than claiming quantum advantage.
AI.method: Pretrained visual and textual features are projected into compact latent spaces and encoded as angle-parameterized quantum states. These are processed by intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling circuits, then measured to yield fused representations for retrieval. Evaluation uses identical frozen CLIP backbones and matched parameter budgets, with a dequantized paired-topology analogue as a control, plus ablation to isolate the quantum module's contribution.
AI.result: QEMFN outperforms classical fusion baselines (MLP, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, compact transformer, and the dequantized analogue) on COCO-5k and Flickr30k. Quantum-centric analyses report Meyer-Wallach entangling capability, expressibility, gradient variance against barren-plateau bounds, and entropy-performance correlation. Execution spans shot-based estimation, a noise-modeled fake backend, and a real superconducting device with zero-noise extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: No quantum computational advantage is claimed. The contribution is the QEMFN framework plus a controlled empirical and quantum-centric evaluation, demonstrating that trainable entanglement can serve as an interpretable, hardware-executable multimodal fusion mechanism at scales feasible on contemporary quantum devices.

title: Confidence-Ordering Reversal under Contextual Priors in Neural Decoding
summary: Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding by reshaping candidate scores. However, confidence is read from the same reshaped scores, so the errors a prior leaves behind can become more confident with no change in accuracy to reveal it. We study how a prior shapes confidence in speech retrieval on MEG-MASC and MOUS using local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined by additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. Among initially incorrect predictions, we find a confidence-ordering reversal: a larger margin makes a repair more likely when the correct candidate starts near the top of the local ranking, but less likely when it starts lower. On MEG-MASC, pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, yet AUROC separating repairs from residual errors falls from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. Errors starting beyond rank 20, inside the reversed region, make up 46.6% of all post-fusion errors. We propose a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, limiting its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. A causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted. Under a word-level LM prior, it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence. Reading local and prior scores separately improves selective decoding: the decoder answers on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7%, while 92% of output sets still contain the correct candidate. Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores. Project website: https://confidencereversal.github.io/; Code: https://github.com/AmadeusFake/NeuDecodingConfReversal

AI.tldr: Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding accuracy but corrupt confidence estimation: errors the prior fails to fix can look more confident. The paper identifies a "confidence-ordering reversal" where larger top-two margins indicate repairs at shallow initial ranks but residual errors at deeper ranks. A score-level account explains this via initial deficit and incorrect-candidate margins, verified by causal fusion-weight intervention. Reading local and prior scores separately improves selective decoding coverage from 56.7% to 74.5% at 92% correctness.
AI.motivation: Contextual priors reshape candidate scores to improve neural-to-language decoding, but confidence is read from these same reshaped scores. Consequently, residual errors left by the prior can become more confident without any accuracy change to signal the problem, making confidence unreliable after fusion.
AI.method: The study analyzes speech retrieval on MEG-MASC and MOUS using local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined via additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. It examines AUROC for correctness and for separating repairs from residual errors across initial ranks, and performs a causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight to test predictions.
AI.result: Among initially incorrect predictions, a confidence-ordering reversal appears: a larger margin predicts repair when the correct candidate starts near the top of the local ranking, but residual error when it starts lower. On MEG-MASC, pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, but repair-vs-residual-error AUROC falls from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. Errors starting beyond rank 20, in the reversed region, comprise 46.6% of all post-fusion errors. The fusion-weight intervention moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted, and under a word-level LM prior it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks. Reading local and prior scores separately raises decoder coverage from 56.7% to 74.5% while 92% of output sets still contain the correct candidate.
