AI.conclusion: A score-level account explains the reversal: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, limiting its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores; a fusion weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence.

title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
summary: Self-improving policies continually expose new failure patterns, changing what their judges must be able to verify. However, current fixed judges constrain both optimization feedback and the discovery of useful training examples, limiting further self-improvement. This challenge is even more acute in embodied reasoning, where reliable evaluation must account for spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making. We introduce VeriFine, an agent harness framework that scales verification through the co-evolution of the policy, training curriculum, and judge. The Policy Improvement Loop uses a rubric judge to diagnose recurring failures, construct an adaptive curriculum, and optimize the policy. When progress plateaus and verification becomes a bottleneck, the Judge Improvement Loop selectively queries human guidance on informative failure cases and refines the judge through coactive calibration, in which humans and agents resolve disagreements and converge toward the objective rubric of physical reasoning. The revised judge then guides the next stage of data selection and policy optimization. Experiments on driving and robot navigation tasks demonstrate continuous self-improvement in both policy and judge capability across reinforcement and supervised fine-tuning. These results show how scaling verification supports continuous self-improvement as policy failure patterns evolve.

AI.tldr: VeriFine is an agent harness framework that co-evolves policy, curriculum, and judge to enable continuous self-improvement in embodied reasoning.
AI.motivation: Fixed judges in self-improving policies become a bottleneck: they constrain optimization feedback and limit discovery of useful training examples as new failure patterns emerge. This is acute in embodied reasoning, requiring verification of spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making.
AI.method: Two co-evolving loops. (1) Policy Improvement Loop: a rubric judge diagnoses recurring failures, builds an adaptive curriculum, and optimizes the policy. (2) Judge Improvement Loop: when progress plateaus, it selectively queries human guidance on informative failure cases and refines the judge via coactive calibration, where humans and agents resolve disagreements to converge on the objective rubric of physical reasoning; the revised judge then drives the next data selection and policy optimization stage.
AI.result: Experiments on driving and robot navigation tasks show continuous self-improvement in both policy and judge capability across reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Scaling verification through policy–curriculum–judge co-evolution supports sustained self-improvement as policy failure patterns evolve.

title: OSFP4: Joint Optimization of Diagonal Smoothing and Block Scales for NVFP4 Quantization
summary: NVFP4 is an attractive datatype for large language model (LLM) inference, offering compact storage and native tensor-core acceleration. However, preserving accuracy using NVFP4 requires careful quantization. In this work we develop a novel quantization scheme called Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4 (OSFP4). For each linear projection it uses a diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize the squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4, taking into account the rounding procedure that is used (either round-to-nearest, or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). This requires performing joint optimization on the smoothing entries as well as the block scales, which is facilitated by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one. Experiments show that OSFP4 achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated competitors in the corresponding quantization settings, while retaining approximately 94-97\% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on the measured workloads. Our code is available in https://github.com/neriahbd/OSFP4

AI.tldr: OSFP4 is a novel NVFP4 quantization scheme that jointly optimizes a diagonal smoothing matrix and block scales to minimize squared matrix-product quantization error, achieving top average accuracy while retaining ~94-97% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput.
AI.motivation: NVFP4 offers compact storage and native tensor-core acceleration for LLM inference, but maintaining accuracy under NVFP4 requires careful quantization. Existing approaches do not jointly optimize smoothing and scaling while accounting for the specific rounding procedure.
AI.method: OSFP4 applies a per-linear-projection diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize the squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4, accounting for the rounding procedure (round-to-nearest or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). It performs joint optimization of smoothing entries and block scales, enabled by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer rather than the fixed deterministic one.
AI.result: OSFP4 achieves the highest average accuracy among evaluated competitors in corresponding quantization settings, while retaining approximately 94-97% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on measured workloads.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing smoothing and scaling for NVFP4, with awareness of the rounding procedure, yields superior accuracy with minimal throughput loss, making OSFP4 an effective quantization scheme for LLM inference.

title: Sensor-Language-Action Models
summary: Sensors are useful not only for understanding the world but also for deciding what to do next. Existing sensor models however largely stop at perception: they recognize states or predict outcomes, leaving actions modeled separately through task-specific and often closed label spaces. We introduce Sensor-Language-Action (SLA) modeling, a framework that connects multimodal sensor observations, natural language, and actions within a unified model. SLA uses language as a semantic interface between sensing and acting, allowing heterogeneous actions to be represented, predicted, and explained while remaining grounded in the underlying sensor evidence. We build a large-scale SLA benchmark consisting of datasets that span more than 116,000 individuals, 79 sensor modalities, and 60 action groups, together with a multi-faceted captioning pipeline that aligns user context, sensor dynamics, and action evidence. Building on this framework, we present OpenSLA, a unified SLA model for hierarchical action prediction, state understanding, and action explanation. Extensive experiments on real-world tasks in clinical prediction, operating rooms, and metabolic health verify its superior performance over the state-of-the-art. OpenSLA also demonstrates intriguing capabilities including language-guided evidence grounding and zero-shot generalization to unseen actions and cohorts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Sensor-Language-Action (SLA) modeling, a unified framework that uses language as a semantic interface linking multimodal sensor observations and actions. It contributes a large-scale benchmark (116,000+ individuals, 79 sensor modalities, 60 action groups) and OpenSLA, a unified model for hierarchical action prediction, state understanding, and action explanation, outperforming state-of-the-art on real-world clinical, operating-room, and metabolic health tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing sensor models largely stop at perception, recognizing states or predicting outcomes, while actions are modeled separately through task-specific and often closed label spaces. This separation prevents heterogeneous actions from being represented, predicted, and explained in a unified way grounded in sensor evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose Sensor-Language-Action (SLA) modeling, which connects multimodal sensor observations, natural language, and actions within a single model, using language as a semantic interface between sensing and acting. They construct a large-scale SLA benchmark spanning over 116,000 individuals, 79 sensor modalities, and 60 action groups, along with a multi-faceted captioning pipeline that aligns user context, sensor dynamics, and action evidence. On this basis, they develop OpenSLA, a unified SLA model for hierarchical action prediction, state understanding, and action explanation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world tasks in clinical prediction, operating rooms, and metabolic health verify that OpenSLA achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. It also demonstrates language-guided evidence grounding and zero-shot generalization to unseen actions and cohorts.
AI.conclusion: SLA modeling unifies sensing and acting through language, and OpenSLA validates the framework's effectiveness and generalization, suggesting a promising direction for grounded, explainable, and transferable sensor-based action modeling.

title: LeanPlan: Optimal Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics and Admissibility Proofs
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) can generate heuristic functions that guide search to achieve state-of-the-art performance in satisficing planning, where any plan is acceptable. However, these heuristics are not guaranteed to be admissible and can lead to suboptimal plans. We introduce LeanPlan, the first planning system that finds optimal plans with LLM-generated heuristics whose admissibility is machine-checked. Given a domain description and training tasks, an agentic loop uses planner feedback to iteratively improve a reusable domain-specific heuristic, its admissibility proof and the required domain assumptions. LeanPlan implements the heuristic, its proof and an efficient planner with machine-checked grounding and search in Lean 4. We evaluate LeanPlan on ten domains from the International Planning Competition and three new domains, using test tasks with up to 57 times as many objects as the training tasks. With GPT-5.6 Sol in the agentic loop, we successfully generate heuristics and admissibility proofs for all these domains. With the resulting heuristics, LeanPlan usually expands fewer states than the state-of-the-art Scorpion planner and solves more tasks overall.

AI.tldr: LeanPlan is the first planning system that finds optimal plans using LLM-generated heuristics whose admissibility is machine-checked, implemented with a formally verified grounding and search engine in Lean 4.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs can generate heuristic functions for satisficing planning that achieve state-of-the-art performance, but these heuristics are not guaranteed to be admissible and can yield suboptimal plans. There is a need for a system that leverages LLM-generated heuristics while guaranteeing optimality.
AI.method: Given a domain description and training tasks, an agentic loop uses planner feedback to iteratively refine a reusable domain-specific heuristic, its admissibility proof, and the necessary domain assumptions. LeanPlan implements the heuristic, its proof, and an efficient planner with machine-checked grounding and search in Lean 4.
AI.result: Evaluated on ten IPC domains and three new domains, with test tasks having up to 57x as many objects as training tasks. Using GPT-5.6 Sol in the agentic loop, heuristics and admissibility proofs were successfully generated for all domains. LeanPlan usually expands fewer states than the state-of-the-art Scorpion planner and solves more tasks overall.
AI.conclusion: LeanPlan shows that LLM-generated heuristics can be made admissible via machine-checked proofs, enabling optimal planning that outperforms a state-of-the-art planner in terms of state expansions and tasks solved.

title: MASC: A Multi-Agent Self-Calibration Framework with Latent Construct Alignment for Consistent Client Role-Playing in Psychological Counseling
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate clients for counselor training and psychological counseling research, but reliable simulation requires clients to remain psychologically coherent across extended interactions. Existing role-playing methods largely rely on static profile prompts and may exhibit persona drift, unrealistic cooperativeness, or inconsistent psychological states, communicative actions, and emotions. Existing evaluations also lack a unified testbed for both stable client characteristics and evolving psychological dynamics. We propose MASC, a Multi-Agent Self-Calibration framework with latent construct alignment for consistent client role-playing in psychological counseling. MASC combines construct-guided generation, collaborative refinement, consistency verification, and memory-based revision in a closed calibration loop that detects and corrects inconsistencies as dialogue unfolds. We further introduce CRPC-Bench, a benchmark covering session-level profile information and Big-Five personality traits, as well as turn-level psychological state, communicative action, and emotion expression. CRPC-Bench contains 38 motivational interviewing client profiles augmented with personality and emotion annotations. Experiments show that MASC outperforms existing methods across profile, personality, receptivity, and turn-level consistency, with the heterogeneous configuration achieving the strongest overall performance. MASC and CRPC-Bench provide a unified foundation for developing and evaluating psychologically coherent client simulations for AI-assisted counseling research and training.

AI.tldr: MASC, a multi-agent self-calibration framework with latent construct alignment, enables psychologically coherent client role-playing for counseling; paired with CRPC-Bench, it outperforms existing methods in profile, personality, receptivity, and turn-level consistency.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly simulate clients for counselor training and counseling research, but reliable simulation requires psychological coherence across extended interactions. Existing role-playing methods relying on static profile prompts suffer persona drift, unrealistic cooperativeness, and inconsistent psychological states, communicative actions, and emotions; evaluations also lack a unified testbed for both stable traits and evolving dynamics.
AI.method: MASC combines construct-guided generation, collaborative refinement, consistency verification, and memory-based revision within a closed calibration loop that detects and corrects inconsistencies as dialogue unfolds. The authors also introduce CRPC-Bench, a benchmark spanning session-level profile information and Big-Five personality traits plus turn-level psychological state, communicative action, and emotion expression, containing 38 motivational interviewing client profiles with personality and emotion annotations.
AI.result: MASC outperforms existing methods across profile, personality, receptivity, and turn-level consistency; the heterogeneous configuration achieves the strongest overall performance.
AI.conclusion: MASC and CRPC-Bench offer a unified foundation for developing and evaluating psychologically coherent client simulations for AI-assisted counseling research and training.

title: zkLLMPoT: Efficient Zero Knowledge Proof of Training for Large Language Models
summary: Auditing the claimed outcomes of large language model (LLM) training is challenging when model weights and training data are private, while cryptographically proving the full training process is prohibitively expensive at Transformer scale. We present zkLLMPoT, a zero-knowledge framework that certifies auditor-defined properties of a trained checkpoint through forward evaluation rather than verification of its optimization trajectory. zkLLMPoT includes 2 phases: 1) The trainer fixes the architecture and the model weights are committed. Then the auditor selects challenge sequences, preventing the trainer from modifying the checkpoint in response to the audit data. 2) Then the trainer proves the objective value attained by the committed model on those sequences. This formulation makes the certification cost independent of the number of training iterations, without revealing model weights or requiring access to private training data. We build on sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments to certify Transformer computations, while supporting next-token loss and task-specific audit objectives. Across four model families, operator-level benchmarks yield proving times of 41-59 seconds for 1.1-1.5B-parameter models and 131 seconds at 13B for the covered operators, with verification below half a second at a sequence length of 512.

AI.tldr: zkLLMPoT is a zero-knowledge framework that certifies auditor-defined properties of a trained LLM checkpoint via forward evaluation instead of verifying the training trajectory, making certification cost independent of training iterations.
AI.motivation: Auditing claimed LLM training outcomes is hard when weights and data are private, and cryptographically proving the full training process is prohibitively expensive at Transformer scale.
AI.method: A two-phase protocol: (1) the trainer commits architecture and weights, then the auditor selects challenge sequences to prevent checkpoint modification in response to audit data; (2) the trainer proves the objective value on those sequences. It uses sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments to certify Transformer computations, supporting next-token loss and task-specific audit objectives.
AI.result: Across four model families, operator-level benchmarks give proving times of 41-59 seconds for 1.1-1.5B-parameter models and 131 seconds at 13B for covered operators, with verification under half a second at sequence length 512.
AI.conclusion: zkLLMPoT enables efficient zero-knowledge certification of LLM checkpoints, keeping cost independent of training iterations without revealing weights or requiring private training data.

title: CoDe-LoRA: Mitigating the Orthogonality Dilemma in Continual Learning of LLMs via Knowledge Consolidation and Decoupling
summary: Continual learning (CL) is essential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to sequentially adapt to evolving tasks. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, recent advances implement low-rank adaptation with orthogonal projections (e.g., O-LoRA) to isolate task parameters. However, we reveal that such strict geometric constraints trigger an "Orthogonality Dilemma": rigid parameter isolation impedes the transfer and accumulation of shared representations across semantically related tasks. In this work, we propose a new replay-free method, called Consolidation and Decoupling LoRA (CoDe-LoRA), for CL of LLMs. CoDe-LoRA disentangles the learning process into Consolidating Universal Knowledge and Decoupling Task-Specific Knowledge. To achieve this, CoDe-LoRA leverages an adaptive null space projection mechanism and semantic routing to balance knowledge accumulation with task-specific adaptation. Experimental results across four backbones and three CL benchmarks show that CoDe-LoRA achieves the best average accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/Estrellajer/CoDe-LoRA.

AI.tldr: CoDe-LoRA is a replay-free continual learning method for LLMs that resolves the "Orthogonality Dilemma" of strict low-rank orthogonal projection by disentangling learning into consolidating universal knowledge and decoupling task-specific knowledge via adaptive null space projection and semantic routing.
AI.motivation: Continual learning is essential for LLMs to sequentially adapt to evolving tasks, but catastrophic forgetting must be mitigated. Existing approaches like O-LoRA use orthogonal projections to isolate task parameters, yet strict geometric constraints create an "Orthogonality Dilemma": rigid parameter isolation impedes transfer and accumulation of shared representations across semantically related tasks.
AI.method: The paper proposes CoDe-LoRA, a replay-free continual learning method. It disentangles the learning process into Consolidating Universal Knowledge and Decoupling Task-Specific Knowledge, employing an adaptive null space projection mechanism and semantic routing to balance knowledge accumulation with task-specific adaptation.
AI.result: Experiments across four backbones and three continual learning benchmarks show that CoDe-LoRA achieves the best average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CoDe-LoRA effectively addresses the Orthogonality Dilemma in continual learning for LLMs, offering a replay-free solution that balances shared knowledge accumulation and task-specific adaptation, as validated by superior average accuracy across multiple backbones and benchmarks.

title: The Standardization Trap: Certifying Joint Label Processing in Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Linear regression and kernel smoothing offer tractable explanations of in-context learning: in both, the features determine the weight assigned to each context label. However, whether this fixed-weight account describes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) remains unclear. Testing this account using derivatives runs into a standardization trap: public TFM packages standardize the labels before the model sees them, yet ordinary derivatives also reflect behavior outside the set of standardized labels, making a model appear nonlinear even when every prediction it makes agrees with a fixed-weight map. We propose two certificates that depend only on predictions at standardized labels and can reject two distinct explanations: fixed-weight prediction and sums of independent nonlinear label transformations. Across the five public TFMs that we evaluate, our certificates show that changing one context label alters how other labels influence the prediction, a behavior we call joint processing. We further find that joint processing emerges with training and that attention scores carry most of the measured interaction. Together, these findings motivate TFM explanations that account for how context labels change the influence of individual examples.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) rely on a fixed-weight explanation (as in linear regression/kernel smoothing) by introducing two "certificates" that avoid a standardization trap in derivatives. Applying these to five public TFMs shows joint processing: changing one context label alters how other labels influence predictions. This behavior emerges with training and is mostly carried by attention scores, motivating explanations where context labels reshape per-example influence.
AI.motivation: Linear regression and kernel smoothing provide tractable, fixed-weight explanations of in-context learning, where features determine the weight assigned to each context label. It is unclear whether this fixed-weight account describes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs). Naively testing this with derivatives fails due to a standardization trap: public TFM packages standardize labels before the model sees them, so ordinary derivatives also capture behavior outside the set of standardized labels, making a model appear nonlinear even when its predictions agree with a fixed-weight map. This motivates a test that depends only on predictions at standardized labels.
AI.method: The authors propose two certificates that depend only on predictions at standardized labels and can reject two distinct explanations: (1) fixed-weight prediction and (2) sums of independent nonlinear label transformations. This avoids the standardization trap affecting derivative-based tests.
AI.result: Across five public TFMs evaluated, the certificates show that changing one context label alters how other labels influence the prediction—a phenomenon termed joint processing. Joint processing emerges with training, and attention scores carry most of the measured interaction.
AI.conclusion: The fixed-weight account does not describe pretrained TFMs. Instead, TFM explanations should account for how context labels change the influence of individual examples (joint processing), with training and attention playing key roles.

title: SCOPE: Certified Theorem Proving with a Language Model as the Policy Planner
summary: In proof assistants such as Lean, a generated proof must pass machine compilation checks, so evaluation needs no human scoring. Direct generation fails on multi-step numeric propositions: a proof is valid only if every content integer is correct, so the pass rate is bounded by the k-th power of the per-integer accuracy. Controlled corruption across 2,617 reference proofs confirms this power law. SCOPE (State-Conditioned Operator Planning and Execution) enforces the natural division of labor: the model plans over an operator vocabulary, a symbolic engine executes the numerics, and a compiler renders the proof. On a 218-problem suite it certifies 191/218 (87.6%) with a 135M backbone; the 7B DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL certifies 18/218 at 27.5 times the tokens and 37.5 times the wall-clock, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B certifies zero on a bidirectional dual suite. Multi-step thinking costs 6.12 discrete decision actions per problem and produces no natural-language thinking text. Replacing the lagged engine state in the decision frame with the current one lifts the pass rate from 117/218 to 191/218, while up-weighting the chain-end loss hurts. On the public Lean-Workbook library, 2,132 of 3,536 gradeable admissible problems certify (60.29%) with zero regression on the main suite. All readings come from a version-frozen review with independent rechecks and reverse verification. Restricting free generation and keeping decision-time information visible is a more direct route than enlarging the model.

AI.tldr: SCOPE separates proof planning from numeric execution in Lean proof assistants, letting a 135M model certify 87.6% of a 218-problem suite versus 7B baselines that certify far less.
AI.motivation: Direct generation fails on multi-step numeric propositions because a proof is only valid if every embedded integer is correct, bounding pass rate by the k-th power of per-integer accuracy. This power law is confirmed via controlled corruption across 2,617 reference proofs. The work argues that restricting free generation and keeping decision-time information visible is a more direct route than scaling up the model.
AI.method: SCOPE (State-Conditioned Operator Planning and Execution) enforces a division of labor: the model plans over an operator vocabulary, a symbolic engine executes the numerics, and a compiler renders the proof. The decision frame conditions on the current engine state (replacing the lagged state). Evaluation uses no human scoring since proofs pass machine compilation checks, and is conducted under a version-frozen review with independent rechecks and reverse verification.
AI.result: On a 218-problem suite, SCOPE certifies 191/218 (87.6%) with a 135M backbone. The 7B DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL certifies 18/218 at 27.5x tokens and 37.5x wall-clock; DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B certifies zero on a bidirectional dual suite. Multi-step thinking costs 6.12 discrete decision actions per problem with no natural-language thinking text. Current-state conditioning lifts pass rate from 117/218 to 191/218, while up-weighting the chain-end loss hurts. On Lean-Workbook, 2,132 of 3,536 gradeable admissible problems certify (60.29%) with zero regression on the main suite.
AI.conclusion: Restricting free generation and keeping decision-time information visible is a more direct route than enlarging the model.

title: MedZERO: Self-Evolving Agents for Open-Ended Medical Reasoning Through Controlled Knowledge Accumulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical question answering and clinical reasoning, yet their improvement remains constrained by static parametric knowledge and costly expert supervision. Self-evolving agents offer a promising alternative by enabling models to improve through iterative task generation and problem-solving. However, most existing self-evolving methods are designed for easily verifiable domains such as mathematics and coding, where solutions can be checked by exact answers or executable programs. Medical reasoning is fundamentally different: it is open-ended, knowledge-intensive, and often only partially verifiable. We present MedZERO, a self-evolving framework for open-ended medical reasoning. MedZERO couples an Examiner that generates frontier medical question-option pairs with a Reasoner that solves them through evidence-grounded multi-turn reasoning with external knowledge tools. To support reliable, continual improvement, MedZERO adopts controlled knowledge accumulation, which maintains temporary exploratory knowledge and curated persistent knowledge in reasoning. We evaluate MedZERO on five public medical reasoning benchmarks using 4B- and 8B-scale base models under open-ended evaluation. Across all settings, MedZERO consistently outperforms the underlying base models and prior self-evolving baselines, achieving up to 13.7 average accuracy-point gains over the next-best self-evolving baseline.

AI.tldr: MedZERO is a self-evolving framework for open-ended medical reasoning that couples an Examiner generating question-option pairs with a Reasoner using external knowledge tools, employing controlled knowledge accumulation to maintain exploratory and persistent knowledge.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in medical QA and clinical reasoning but are limited by static parametric knowledge and costly expert supervision. Existing self-evolving methods target easily verifiable domains like math and coding, whereas medical reasoning is open-ended, knowledge-intensive, and only partially verifiable.
AI.method: MedZERO combines an Examiner that generates frontier medical question-option pairs and a Reasoner that solves them via evidence-grounded multi-turn reasoning with external knowledge tools. It adopts controlled knowledge accumulation, maintaining temporary exploratory knowledge and curated persistent knowledge during reasoning.
AI.result: Evaluated on five public medical reasoning benchmarks with 4B- and 8B-scale base models under open-ended evaluation, MedZERO consistently outperforms base models and prior self-evolving baselines, achieving up to 13.7 average accuracy-point gains over the next-best self-evolving baseline.
AI.conclusion: MedZERO offers an effective self-evolving approach for open-ended medical reasoning, overcoming the constraints of static knowledge and verifiable-only domains, and demonstrates consistent gains across scales and benchmarks.

title: An AI-Assisted Formalization of the Poincaré Conjecture
summary: We present an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization of the Poincaré conjecture. The project began with limited reusable formal infrastructure for the geometric analysis behind the proof. To organize this work, we combined a proof blueprint prepared by mathematicians with explicit milestone statements. These milestones enabled parallel agent work and gave mathematicians clear points to locate blockers and provide effective mathematical guidance. Our analysis identifies the human interventions and organizational choices behind this workflow. The project provides a starting point toward reusable infrastructure for future formalization projects; such infrastructure, once developed, could eventually reduce the cost of verifying mathematical results in geometric analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper reports on an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization of the Poincaré conjecture, describing how a mathematician-prepared proof blueprint with explicit milestones was used to coordinate parallel agent work and guide human intervention in a project lacking mature formal infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Formalizing the Poincaré conjecture requires substantial geometric analysis, but the project started with limited reusable formal infrastructure for this area. The work aims to establish a workflow that organizes this daunting task and lays a starting point for reusable infrastructure that could eventually lower the cost of verifying results in geometric analysis.
AI.method: The approach combines a proof blueprint prepared by mathematicians with explicit milestone statements. These milestones are used to enable parallel agent work and to give mathematicians clear points at which to locate blockers and provide effective mathematical guidance. The analysis focuses on identifying the human interventions and organizational choices underpinning this workflow.
AI.result: The workflow supported parallel agent work structured by milestones and allowed mathematicians to efficiently localize blockers and intervene with targeted mathematical guidance, making progress on the formalization despite scarce reusable formal infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: The project serves as a starting point toward reusable infrastructure for future formalization efforts. Once developed, such infrastructure could eventually reduce the cost of verifying mathematical results in geometric analysis.

title: MoF: Preference-Aware Mixture Modeling for Black-Box LLM Personalization
summary: Proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, yet aligning their outputs with diverse user preferences remains challenging. Existing personalization approaches for black-box LLMs often rely on user-specific scoring heads, causing the number of personalized parameters to grow linearly with the number of users and requiring additional adaptation for unseen users. To address these limitations, we propose Mixture-of-Facets (MoF), a scalable personalization framework for black-box LLMs that models user preferences as compositions of shared latent preference facets rather than dedicated user-specific parameters. MoF performs personalization through history-conditioned routing over shared facet heads, enabling personalization for users unseen during training without additional parameter updates. Across diverse personalization tasks, MoF delivers stronger personalization performance while maintaining a more scalable and parameter-efficient design than prior approaches. Additional analysis indicates strong generalization to unseen users.

AI.tldr: MoF personalizes black-box LLMs by representing user preferences as compositions of shared latent facet heads, using history-conditioned routing. This avoids per-user parameters, scales better, and generalizes to unseen users without retraining, outperforming prior personalization methods.
AI.motivation: Proprietary LLMs are powerful but hard to align with diverse user preferences. Existing black-box personalization approaches typically use user-specific scoring heads, so personalized parameters grow linearly with users and unseen users require additional adaptation, limiting scalability and generalization.
AI.method: Mixture-of-Facets (MoF) is a scalable personalization framework for black-box LLMs. Instead of dedicated per-user parameters, it models preferences as compositions of shared latent preference facets and performs personalization via history-conditioned routing over shared facet heads, enabling unseen-user personalization without parameter updates.
AI.result: Across diverse personalization tasks, MoF achieves stronger personalization performance than prior approaches while maintaining a more scalable and parameter-efficient design. Additional analysis shows strong generalization to unseen users.
AI.conclusion: Modeling user preferences as compositions of shared latent facets is an effective, scalable alternative to user-specific heads for personalizing black-box LLMs, delivering better performance, efficiency, and unseen-user generalization.

title: Explainable Failure Prediction and Prevention in Maritime
summary: Maritime systems operate in highly dynamic environments where unexpected equipment failures can compromise safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, digital twins, and predictive maintenance enable proactive failure prediction and prevention. However, ensuring trustworthy and explainable decision-making remains a major challenge in safety-critical maritime applications. This chapter reviews key AI technologies required for explainable failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems and presents a conceptual architecture capable of supporting autonomous or human-in-the-loop corrective actions. This architecture integrates data acquisition, time-series forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI into a closed-loop framework. With reference to the architectural components, a review and discussion of relevant maritime studies is performed, outlining their methods, advantages, and limitations. Furthermore, it highlights current challenges, including uncertainty and robustness, model generalization, explainability, limited availability of maritime datasets, and operational deployment, and identifies future research directions toward trustworthy AI-assisted maritime decision-making.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews AI technologies for explainable failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems, proposing a closed-loop conceptual architecture that integrates data acquisition, forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI, while surveying relevant studies and outlining challenges and future directions toward trustworthy AI-assisted maritime decision-making.
AI.motivation: Maritime systems operate in highly dynamic environments where unexpected equipment failures can compromise safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. Although AI, machine learning, digital twins, and predictive maintenance enable proactive failure prediction, ensuring trustworthy and explainable decision-making remains a major challenge in safety-critical maritime applications.
AI.method: The chapter reviews key AI technologies required for explainable failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems and presents a conceptual architecture supporting autonomous or human-in-the-loop corrective actions. This architecture integrates data acquisition, time-series forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI into a closed-loop framework. Relevant maritime studies are then reviewed and discussed in relation to the architectural components, outlining their methods, advantages, and limitations.
AI.result: The review maps existing maritime studies onto the proposed architecture, identifying their respective methods, strengths, and limitations, and consolidates current challenges such as uncertainty and robustness, model generalization, explainability, limited availability of maritime datasets, and operational deployment.
AI.conclusion: Future research directions are identified toward trustworthy AI-assisted maritime decision-making, highlighting the need to address uncertainty, generalization, explainability, data scarcity, and deployment barriers for explainable failure prediction and prevention.

title: Transect: Retaining Observability for Long-Horizon LLM Agent Evaluations
summary: Frontier AI evaluations increasingly use open-ended, agentic, long-horizon tasks whose transcripts can span hundreds of pages of outputs and actions from complex multi-agent networks. The observability envelop-the range of what evaluators can reliably infer about an agent's behaviours-is therefore narrowing. Language model assistants can help classify and interpret agent behaviour but also afford human evaluators significant analytical degrees of freedom, threatening the reproducibility and auditability of language-model-based transcript analysis. Transect is an open source package built on Inspect Scout to help evaluators understand how a long agent run unfolded, identify behaviour worth investigating, and check interpretations against the transcript. Users specify task context and behavioural vocabulary in a reusable evaluation-family configuration, with judge models and analysis settings supplied separately. Transect's navigable reports align recorded events, token use, sub-agent activity, and model-generated behavioural labels on a common turn-based timeline. Reviewers can quickly grasp a run's narrative, trace any label or event to its source turns, and export the underlying data tables for cross-run analysis. We demonstrate the workflow on an AI R&D evaluation that generated almost 13 million tokens, dividing the agents' work into behavioural phases aligned with research-skill classifications, sub-agent delegations and interactions, and token use. The combined view shows a focus on operational work and manuscript production, with little evidence of a sustained hypothesis generation stage-arguably a necessary component for high-quality scientific outputs. Transect's flexible, customisable transcript-analysis pipeline will enable evaluators to keep pace with longer, more complex, more frequent AI evaluations while supporting scientific rigour, transparency, and reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Transect is an open-source tool built on Inspect Scout that helps human evaluators analyze long, complex agentic AI run transcripts by aligning events, token use, sub-agent activity, and model-generated behavior labels on a navigable turn-based timeline.
AI.motivation: Frontier AI evaluations increasingly rely on open-ended, long-horizon, multi-agent tasks whose transcripts can span hundreds of pages. This narrows the observability envelope of what evaluators can reliably infer about agent behavior. While LLM assistants can help interpret such transcripts, they grant evaluators broad analytical degrees of freedom, undermining reproducibility and auditability. A tool is needed to standardize and support rigorous, transparent transcript analysis.
AI.method: Transect is an open-source package built on Inspect Scout. Users define task context and behavioral vocabulary in a reusable evaluation-family configuration, with judge models and analysis settings supplied separately. The tool produces navigable reports that align recorded events, token use, sub-agent activity, and model-generated behavioral labels on a common turn-based timeline. Reviewers can trace labels/events to source turns, grasp run narratives, and export underlying data tables for cross-run analysis.
AI.result: Demonstrated on an AI R&D evaluation generating nearly 13 million tokens, dividing agent work into behavioral phases aligned with research-skill classifications, sub-agent delegations/interactions, and token use. The combined view revealed a focus on operational work and manuscript production, with little evidence of a sustained hypothesis generation stage.
AI.conclusion: Transect provides a flexible, customizable transcript-analysis pipeline that helps evaluators keep pace with longer, more complex, and more frequent AI evaluations while supporting scientific rigour, transparency, and reproducibility.

title: EMHO: EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization via Experience Traces
summary: Improving embodied agents often focuses on optimizing the underlying model through training, while the surrounding agent harness that controls planning, context, and tool use is typically engineered. We ask whether this harness can instead improve itself directly from experience traces under sparse environmental feedback. We propose EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization (EMHO), a self-evolving framework that keeps the embodied model frozen and iteratively revises its harness by analyzing execution trajectories and prior harness history. EMHO optimizes beyond skills or recovery prompts, modifying how the agent monitors progress, uses vision tools, grounds observations, and responds to failures. To support multiple subtasks with a single harness, we introduce EMHO-Merge, which addresses trade-offs in jointly optimizing a single shared harness across subtasks by using episode-level gains and losses to guide evidence-supported refinement of when and how revised behaviors are applied. We evaluate EMHO on EmbodiedBench across navigation and manipulation tasks, and EMHO consistently improves task success for both Qwen 9B and 27B models. Qualitative analysis shows that EMHO goes beyond recovering from failures and unproductive actions to reshape how the embodied agent interprets and interacts with its environment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EMHO, a self-evolving framework that keeps the embodied model frozen and instead iteratively optimizes the agent "harness" (planning, context, tool use) from execution traces under sparse feedback, plus EMHO-Merge to jointly optimize a single shared harness across subtasks.
AI.motivation: Improving embodied agents conventionally relies on training the underlying model, while the surrounding harness that controls planning, context, and tool use is hand-engineered. The authors ask whether this harness can improve itself directly from experience traces despite sparse environmental feedback, and whether that self-improvement can extend beyond simple skills or recovery prompts to reshape core agent behavior.
AI.method: EMHO keeps the embodied model frozen and iteratively revises its harness by analyzing execution trajectories together with prior harness history, modifying how the agent monitors progress, uses vision tools, grounds observations, and responds to failures. EMHO-Merge extends this to multiple subtasks with one shared harness, using episode-level gains and losses to guide evidence-supported refinement of when and how revised behaviors are applied.
AI.result: Evaluated on EmbodiedBench across navigation and manipulation tasks, EMHO consistently improves task success for both Qwen 9B and 27B models. Qualitative analysis shows EMHO goes beyond recovering from failures and unproductive actions to reshape how the agent interprets and interacts with its environment.
AI.conclusion: The agent harness can be meaningfully self-optimized from experience traces under sparse feedback without touching the frozen embodied model, and a single shared harness can serve multiple subtasks via EMHO-Merge, surpassing conventional skill or recovery-prompt optimization.

title: AssemState: Manual and Physical-State-Guided Reasoning for Zero-shot Furniture Assembly
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding, but precise 3D spatial reasoning integrated with physical environment remains difficult. Furniture assembly requires not only recovering step-level operations from diagrammatic manuals, but also translating semantic attachment relations into 6D pose updates that enable parts to physically interact with the environment and previously assembled components. To study this problem, we propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework for manual and physical-state-guided furniture assembly. It firstly employs anchor-guided boundary assembly states to decompose manual pages into single-part operations and recover an assembly-tree. Then, it uses iterative after-state feedback refinement to guide successive (SE(3)) updates and corrections, and validates their physical plausibility through simulation-based release tests. Experiments show that compared with the strongest prior baseline, AssemState improves F1 from 38.58\% to 62.80\% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24\% to 53.92\% for assembly-tree recovery. On 243 independently evaluated part-level operations, our proposed iterative refinement improves judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3\% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. However, visually plausible candidate poses may still suffer from collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment. These results show that AssemState improves operation-structure recovery and selected local pose metrics, while MLLMs remain limited for spatial relationship reasoning.

AI.tldr: AssemState is a zero-shot framework for manual- and physical-state-guided furniture assembly that recovers assembly trees from diagrammatic manuals and translates attachment relations into SE(3) pose updates, validated by simulation-based release tests.
AI.motivation: MLLMs excel at visual understanding but lack precise 3D spatial reasoning grounded in physical environments. Furniture assembly demands recovering step-level operations from manuals and converting semantic attachment relations into 6D pose updates enabling physical interaction with the environment and prior components.
AI.method: AssemState employs anchor-guided boundary assembly states to decompose manual pages into single-part operations and recover an assembly tree, then applies iterative after-state feedback refinement to guide successive SE(3) updates and corrections, validating physical plausibility via simulation-based release tests.
AI.result: F1 improves from 38.58% to 62.80% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24% to 53.92% over the strongest baseline for assembly-tree recovery. On 243 independently evaluated part-level operations, iterative refinement raises judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. Remaining failure modes include collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment.
AI.conclusion: AssemState improves operation-structure recovery and selected local pose metrics, yet MLLMs remain limited in spatial relationship reasoning, as visually plausible candidate poses can still be physically implausible.

title: Cylindrical Geodesic Flow Matching for Quasiperiodic Physiological Signal Transformation
summary: Paired translation between quasiperiodic physiological waveforms (i.e., recovering a target oscillatory signal from the source) is central to the interpretation of cardiovascular signals derived from wearables placed at different body locations. This source-to-target mapping in these problems carries inherent geometric structure: the phase wraps around the cycle and must be treated as a circular variable, the amplitude remains strictly positive, and the beat-to-beat alignment can drift unpredictably across cycles and subjects. While deep neural networks have been used for phase estimation and complex-valued signal modeling, prior work does not explicitly learn phase transport between paired signals. Consequently, neither endpoint-supervised regression nor the standard affine path used in flow matching accounts for this phase--amplitude structure. We introduce \emph{cylindrical geodesic flow matching} for paired cardiovascular waveform translation. We show that the standard affine path used in flow matching distorts intermediate amplitude and instantaneous frequency when interpolating between quasiperiodic signals; replacing it with a closed-form geodesic on the phase--amplitude cylinder eliminates these artifacts and converts each training pair into dense, geometry-consistent velocity supervision. On zero-shot photoplethysmography and limited-support seismocardiography adaptation benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms interpolation baselines and matches or exceeds direct supervised prediction, reducing Hilbert Transform, $L_2$, and Dynamic Time Warping distance by up to ${\sim}15\%$ over the strongest competing baseline. These results suggest that bridge geometry is a critical inductive bias for flow matching on oscillatory signal translation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces cylindrical geodesic flow matching for paired translation of quasiperiodic physiological waveforms, replacing the affine interpolation path with a closed-form geodesic on the phase-amplitude cylinder to respect circular phase and positive amplitude, yielding improved zero-shot PPG and limited-support SCG adaptation.
AI.motivation: Paired translation between quasiperiodic cardiovascular waveforms (e.g., recovering a target oscillatory signal from a wearable source at a different body location) carries inherent geometric structure: phase is circular, amplitude is strictly positive, and beat-to-beat alignment drifts across cycles and subjects. Existing deep learning approaches for phase estimation and complex-valued modeling do not explicitly learn phase transport between paired signals, and neither endpoint-supervised regression nor the standard affine flow-matching path accounts for this phase-amplitude structure.
AI.method: The authors propose cylindrical geodesic flow matching. They demonstrate that the standard affine path used in flow matching distorts intermediate amplitude and instantaneous frequency when interpolating between quasiperiodic signals, and replace it with a closed-form geodesic on the phase-amplitude cylinder. This eliminates the artifacts and converts each training pair into dense, geometry-consistent velocity supervision.
AI.result: On zero-shot photoplethysmography and limited-support seismocardiography adaptation benchmarks, the method consistently outperforms interpolation baselines and matches or exceeds direct supervised prediction, reducing Hilbert Transform, L2, and Dynamic Time Warping distance by up to ~15% over the strongest competing baseline.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that bridge geometry is a critical inductive bias for flow matching on oscillatory signal translation.

title: How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation
summary: Execution feedback lets coding agents revise programs and learn from their own corrections. A correction's learning weight should reflect both the transitions supported by its executions and the amount of evidence behind that support. We introduce Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), which represents these quantities separately. Normalized execution relevance determines relative transition support and an effective pseudo-count mass; a Dirichlet posterior then produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Under a symmetric prior, changing mass preserves category ordering, and effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart. Across four model-domain history sweeps, increasing visible observations from one to eight reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3%. At eight observations, effective mass achieves lower NLL than fixed mass in all four comparisons. In the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC all-tests Pass@1 increases from 15.0% to 20.4%, with a paired 95% source-bootstrap interval of [+2.8, +8.0] percentage points. The twelve-setting downstream evaluation establishes the model-domain scope of this update. These results show how separating evidence support from evidence mass changes probability estimation and correction learning in coding agents.

AI.tldr: EESD separates transition support from evidence mass in correction learning: normalized execution relevance yields a Dirichlet posterior that produces uncertainty-penalized weights for KL-anchored learning, improving probability estimation and coding-agent correction performance.
AI.motivation: Execution feedback lets coding agents revise programs and learn from their own corrections; a correction's learning weight should reflect both the transitions supported by its executions and the evidence behind that support.
AI.method: Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation represents these quantities separately: normalized execution relevance determines relative transition support and an effective pseudo-count mass; a Dirichlet posterior produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Theoretical analysis under a symmetric prior shows changing mass preserves category ordering and effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart.
AI.result: Across four model-domain history sweeps, increasing visible observations from one to eight reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3%; at eight observations, effective mass achieves lower NLL than fixed mass in all four comparisons. In the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC all-tests Pass@1 rises from 15.0% to 20.4% (paired 95% source-bootstrap interval [+2.8, +8.0] pp).
AI.conclusion: Separating evidence support from evidence mass changes probability estimation and correction learning in coding agents, and the twelve-setting downstream evaluation establishes the model-domain scope of this update.

title: Toward Alignment Scaling Laws: A Framework and First Preregistered Measurements
comment: 34 pages, 24 figures, 8 tables. Games: https://www.aisafety.fun. Preregistrations: https://osf.io/wda8q, https://osf.io/q2j3y, https://osf.io/8kreb
summary: Whether alignment gets easier or harder as models grow is often argued from isolated findings, as if alignment were one property. We treat it as a family of measurable scaling relations: for each risk category r, the alignment burden needed to hold a fixed safety target is modeled as B_r(N)=a_rN^alpha_r, with N a capability proxy; against a budget proportional to N, scaling helps if alpha_r<1, keeps pace if alpha_r~1, and accumulates alignment debt if alpha_r>1. We give three operationalizations of burden and distinguish observed, audited and true alignment. A toy model, in which corrections consume capability headroom, makes the consequences explicit. We prove that the largest exponent among corrected risks, not an average, sets the long-run regime; that above 1 any policy holding headroom above a floor must grow super-exponentially; that, for burdens that are positive mixtures of power laws, fits on small models underestimate large-scale exponents; and that an audit that uncovers hidden failures without false positives never underestimates true alignment. We propose a pre-registrable protocol and apply reduced versions of it twice. A preregistered reanalysis of public adversarial-training data for Pythia classifiers finds that the compute needed to bring attack success under 10% grows as N^0.60. A preregistered pilot on Qwen2.5 0.5B-72B finds exponents of -0.05 for truthfulness and 0.48 for stated dispositions (both scaling helps under its reduced rule, though local slopes approach 1 at the top; replicated on Qwen3 0.6B-14B), while sycophancy (0.89, or 0.83 with two seeds added at 72B) and a planted backdoor are undetermined: the backdoor is removed quickly when its trigger is known but survives blind safety training at four of five sizes. We release four browser games that play these laws (www.aisafety.fun). We make no claim about which regime holds for current frontier models.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes "does alignment get easier or harder with scale" as a family of measurable scaling relations per risk category, modeling alignment burden as B_r(N)=a_rN^alpha_r. It proves regime-setting theorems (largest exponent dominates; super-exponential policy growth above 1; small-model fits underestimate large-scale exponents; audits without false positives never underestimate true alignment), proposes a pre-registrable protocol, and applies reduced versions twice: adversarial-training data (Pythia) gives N^0.60; a Qwen2.5 pilot gives -0.05 (truthfulness), 0.48 (stated dispositions), 0.89/0.83 (sycophancy), and undetermined backdoor behavior.
AI.motivation: Debates about whether alignment becomes easier or harder as models scale are typically argued from isolated findings, treating alignment as a single property. The paper argues this is misconceived: alignment should be decomposed into per-risk scaling relations so that each risk category's burden can be measured and compared, yielding clearer regime classifications (helps, keeps pace, or accumulates debt) rather than a single global verdict.
AI.method: The authors (1) model the alignment burden for each risk category r as a power law B_r(N)=a_rN^alpha_r with N a capability proxy, classifying regimes by alpha_r (<1 helps, ~1 keeps pace, >1 accumulates debt) against a budget proportional to N; (2) give three operationalizations of burden and distinguish observed, audited, and true alignment; (3) build a toy model in which corrections consume capability headroom; (4) prove four results on dominant exponents, super-exponential policy requirements, small-model fit bias, and audit conservatism; (5) propose a pre-registrable protocol and apply reduced versions in two preregistered studies—a reanalysis of public adversarial-training data for Pythia classifiers, and a pilot on Qwen2.5 0.5B-72B (replicated on Qwen3 0.6B-14B) covering truthfulness, stated dispositions, sycophancy, and a planted backdoor.
AI.result: The preregistered reanalysis of Pythia adversarial-training data finds the compute needed to bring attack success below 10% scales as N^0.60. The preregistered Qwen2.5 pilot finds exponents of -0.05 for truthfulness and 0.48 for stated dispositions (both "scaling helps" under its reduced rule, though local slopes approach 1 at the top; replicated on Qwen3), while sycophancy (0.89, or 0.83 with two seeds added at 72B) and a planted backdoor are undetermined—the backdoor is removed quickly when its trigger is known but survives blind safety training at four of five sizes. Four browser games enacting these laws are released at www.aisafety.fun.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that alignment scaling should be treated as a family of per-risk power laws rather than a single property, with the largest corrected-risk exponent—not the average—setting the long-run regime. It makes no claim about which regime holds for current frontier models, instead offering a pre-registrable protocol, theoretical guarantees, and initial empirical pilot results as a foundation for cumulative measurement.

title: AnyBottle: A Recipe to Only Keep the Concepts You Really Need
summary: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make predictions inspectable and intervenable by routing them through human-interpretable concepts, but originally required concept annotations. Annotation-free variants remove this requirement, but typically use large concept vocabularies, static at both training and inference, producing bottlenecks larger than any task or prediction needs and harder to inspect. We propose AnyBottle, a single recipe for building compact, task-specific CBMs. AnyBottle assumes only a frozen backbone and an unsupervised concept pool, such as a sparse autoencoder. A black-box teacher trained on the same backbone then guides selection: each round adds the concept that best explains the bottleneck's current failures, with candidates restricted to regions of teacher/student disagreement. Trained with nested dropout over this selection order, the final bottleneck predicts accurately from any concept prefix, so inference spends fewer concepts on inputs it is confident about early and more on hard ones. Since no stage is modality-specific, a new domain and task requires swapping only the backbone and concept pool. Across six vision and two text datasets and two teacher paradigms, AnyBottle yields bottlenecks with fewer concepts and higher concept consistency than annotation-free baselines, while staying close to the black-box reference. Overall, AnyBottle shows that going annotation-free need not mean going large: a small, discovered vocabulary can be as expressive as a much larger, fixed one.

AI.tldr: AnyBottle builds compact, task-specific concept bottleneck models without concept annotations by using a frozen backbone, an unsupervised concept pool, and black-box teacher-guided selection with nested dropout, yielding smaller but more consistent bottlenecks than annotation-free baselines.
AI.motivation: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) are inspectable and intervenable but originally required concept annotations. Annotation-free variants remove this requirement but rely on large concept vocabularies that are static at training and inference, producing bottlenecks larger than needed for any task or prediction and harder to inspect. The paper aims to remove the need for large fixed vocabularies while retaining interpretability.
AI.method: AnyBottle assumes only a frozen backbone and an unsupervised concept pool, such as a sparse autoencoder. A black-box teacher trained on the same backbone guides selection: each round adds the concept that best explains the bottleneck's current failures, with candidates restricted to regions of teacher/student disagreement. It is trained with nested dropout over the selection order, so the final bottleneck can predict accurately from any concept prefix, allowing inference to use fewer concepts on confident inputs and more on hard ones. No stage is modality-specific, so a new domain and task requires only swapping the backbone and concept pool.
AI.result: Across six vision and two text datasets and two teacher paradigms, AnyBottle yields bottlenecks with fewer concepts and higher concept consistency than annotation-free baselines, while staying close to the black-box reference.
AI.conclusion: Going annotation-free need not mean going large: a small, discovered vocabulary can be as expressive as a much larger, fixed one.

title: Adaptive Power Sampling for LLM Reasoning
summary: Sequence-level power sampling has recently emerged as a training-free approach to reasoning by sampling from a sharpened output distribution of a base large language model (LLM). Nevertheless, existing methods typically sharpen the base model distribution uniformly across queries, overlooking variations in query difficulty and in how well the base model already handles each query. The goal of this work is to equip power sampling with query adaptivity. Theoretically, we show that the benefits of further sharpening are determined by the self-reward gap between correct and incorrect responses. Based on this insight, we propose \emph{Adaptive Power Sampling} (APS), which adjusts the sharpening exponent on a per-query basis at test time using the relationship between answer agreement and the model's self-reward. Experiments across diverse reasoning tasks, including MATH500, HumanEval, and GPQA, show that APS consistently outperforms power sampling with a fixed sharpening exponent, without additional training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), a training-free reasoning method that adjusts the sharpening exponent per query, outperforming fixed-exponent power sampling across MATH500, HumanEval, and GPQA.
AI.motivation: Existing sequence-level power sampling methods sharpen the base LLM output distribution uniformly across all queries, ignoring variations in query difficulty and how well the base model already handles each query. The goal is to make power sampling query-adaptive.
AI.method: Theoretically, the authors show that the benefit of further sharpening depends on the self-reward gap between correct and incorrect responses. Building on this, they propose Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), which adjusts the sharpening exponent on a per-query basis at test time using the relationship between answer agreement and the model's self-reward, without additional training.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse reasoning tasks including MATH500, HumanEval, and GPQA show that APS consistently outperforms power sampling with a fixed sharpening exponent.
AI.conclusion: Query-adaptive sharpening yields consistent gains over fixed sharpening for training-free reasoning, with no extra training required.

title: MINDSET: Energy-based Schema Evolution for Long Conversational Agent Memory
summary: Long conversational agents have become essential in our daily lives. They must remember what was said long back in order to help us efficiently complete a task without needing the user to repeat instructions and context repeatedly. However, the main issue is that instructions and context change over time and so the agents must be able to adapt accordingly. A useful memory system should preserve both current and historical states, distinguish stale information from active knowledge, retrieve evidence appropriate to the query and avoid repeatedly invoking a large language model to rewrite prior interactions. We introduce MINDSET, a memory controller that stores a conversation as immutable episodes and organizes them into versioned schemas through minimum-energy state transitions. Each incoming episode may reinforce, supersede, split or create a schema. The transition decision balances representation distortion, contradiction, historical damage, fragmentation and internal inconsistency, while hysteresis prevents isolated contradictions from prematurely rewriting stable memory. We evaluate MINDSET against 5 memory systems on a reproducible sample of 850 questions (700 LoCoMo + 150 MemoryAgentBench). MINDSET obtains the highest observed LoCoMo answer F1 while significantly improving retrieval ranking (Recall@8, MRR and nDCG@8) over the second best method LightMem (p<0.01 after Holm correction). It obtains the highest observed scores on MemoryAgentBench although the relative difference is low. Ablations identify controlled fragmentation and schema-aware assignment as the largest contributors to answer quality. Additionally, a 700-question cross-model evaluation with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B supported model independence. These results show that long-term memory can be better handled as constrained state management rather than continual summarization.

AI.tldr: MINDSET reframes long-term agent memory as constrained state management: a controller stores conversation as immutable episodes and organizes them into versioned schemas via minimum-energy state transitions, achieving top LoCoMo F1 and superior retrieval ranking.
AI.motivation: Long conversational agents must recall distant context to complete tasks without repeated instructions, but instructions and context change over time. Existing memory approaches (notably continual summarization) repeatedly invoke large language models to rewrite past interactions and struggle to preserve both current and historical states, distinguish stale from active knowledge, and retrieve query-appropriate evidence.
AI.method: MINDSET stores a conversation as immutable episodes and organizes them into versioned schemas through minimum-energy state transitions. Each incoming episode may reinforce, supersede, split, or create a schema. The transition decision balances representation distortion, contradiction, historical damage, fragmentation, and internal inconsistency, while a hysteresis mechanism prevents isolated contradictions from prematurely rewriting stable memory.
AI.result: On a reproducible 850-question sample (700 LoCoMo + 150 MemoryAgentBench), MINDSET achieves the highest observed LoCoMo answer F1 and significantly improves retrieval ranking (Recall@8, MRR, nDCG@8) over the second-best LightMem (p<0.01 after Holm correction). It also attains the highest observed MemoryAgentBench scores, though with a low relative margin. Ablations rank controlled fragmentation and schema-aware assignment as the largest contributors to answer quality. A 700-question cross-model evaluation with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B supports model independence.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory for conversational agents is better handled as constrained state management rather than continual summarization.

title: Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
summary: Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer's feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Code is coming soon.

AI.tldr: Recursive Game Creator is an experience-oriented agentic harness that iteratively refines game prototypes into entertaining games using four cooperating components—Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer—achieving state-of-the-art results on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench plus better user engagement.
AI.motivation: Prior game design agents can generate playable games, but program correctness alone does not guarantee player enjoyment; existing pipelines optimize prototypes and correctness rather than the actual play experience.
AI.method: A recursive loop over four components. Designer converts user instructions and Reviewer feedback into detailed plans; Builder turns plans into candidate games; a coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies via programmatic interfaces to collect diverse gameplay trajectories efficiently (avoiding slow GUI-based collection and its evaluation bias); Reviewer uses trajectory-based metrics to infer player preferences, combines visual evidence and explicit textual preferences, evaluates games against game-specific criteria, accepts the better version, and emits improvement reviews for the next round.
AI.result: State-of-the-art overall score of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, 53.2% strict task success rate (a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline) and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. User study shows longer playtime and higher ratings.
AI.conclusion: Recursive, experience-oriented agentic development with programmatic play-based evaluation can advance game generation beyond mere playability toward genuinely entertaining games, validated by benchmarks and user study. Code will be released.

title: Parallel Predictive World Models for Accurate and Efficient Long-Horizon Planning
summary: Long-horizon world-model planning typically relies on autoregressive rollouts, where predicted states are repeatedly fed back into the model. This preserves temporal structure but creates a horizon-length sequential path and exposes later predictions to recursive decoded-state feedback. We introduce Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while retaining causal interaction among future representations. Each horizon is conditioned on its causal action prefix, and future representations interact before decoding, separating temporal causality from state-by-state output recursion. We formalize this distinction by viewing autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identifying the decoded-state feedback pathway removed by PPWM. Across four visual-control tasks, PPWM achieves the lowest long-horizon prediction error and the highest Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) simulator success among the evaluated predictive interfaces. Meanwhile, PPWM achieves more than a 3$\times$ average CEM planning speedup over the autoregressive LeWM baseline. These results suggest that accurate and efficient long-horizon world-model planning does not require state-by-state autoregression, but can instead be achieved through parallel causal trajectory prediction.

AI.tldr: PPWM predicts an entire finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while preserving causal interaction among future representations, replacing state-by-state autoregressive rollout. It achieves lower long-horizon prediction error, higher CEM planning success, and over 3x planning speedup versus an autoregressive baseline.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon world-model planning typically relies on autoregressive rollouts, which preserve temporal structure but create a horizon-length sequential path and expose later predictions to recursive decoded-state feedback. The paper questions whether state-by-state autoregression is actually necessary for accurate and efficient long-horizon planning.
AI.method: The paper introduces Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while retaining causal interaction among future representations. Each horizon is conditioned on its causal action prefix, and future representations interact before decoding, separating temporal causality from state-by-state output recursion. The authors formalize this distinction by viewing autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identifying the decoded-state feedback pathway that PPWM removes.
AI.result: Across four visual-control tasks, PPWM achieves the lowest long-horizon prediction error and the highest Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) simulator success among the evaluated predictive interfaces. It also achieves more than a 3x average CEM planning speedup over the autoregressive LeWM baseline.
AI.conclusion: Accurate and efficient long-horizon world-model planning does not require state-by-state autoregression, but can instead be achieved through parallel causal trajectory prediction.

title: SquidAgent: Parallelize Wisely, Coordinate Efficiently
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 37 pages, including appendices
summary: LLM-based agents solve complex multi-step tasks, but sequential execution incurs substantial latency. In principle, parallelizing work across multiple agents should yield near-linear speedups. Yet existing parallel multi-agent systems often run slower than a single-agent baseline. We attribute this gap to two hidden costs that parallel execution incurs but a serial agent avoids. First, there is a re-exploration cost: redundant effort spent by parallel workers reconstructing context that the orchestrator already possesses, such as prior decisions, that would otherwise be inherited implicitly in a serial execution. Second, there is an alignment cost: the overhead required to reconcile inconsistencies across independently generated outputs. We thus derive a principled decision criterion: a layer should be parallelized only when its critical-path cost, plus re-exploration and alignment overheads, is lower than the corresponding serial cost. While this criterion is naturally expressed in wall-clock time, we observe that LLMs are poorly calibrated when asked to estimate task duration. To address this, we instead measure cost in predicted output tokens, which we empirically find LLMs can estimate substantially more reliably than wall-clock time.
