Building on this token-based criterion, we propose SquidAgent. It estimates all token budgets in a single planning step, forks each worker directly from the orchestrator's session to eliminate re-exploration cost, and replaces post-hoc reconciliation with a pre-generated shared convention block that converts alignment into a bounded upfront cost. A deterministic scheduler then applies the criterion layer by layer. Empirically, SquidAgent achieves a 2.2$\times$ mean throughput improvement and a 2.6$\times$ mean wall-time speedup over Claude Code, and a 2.0$\times$ throughput improvement over the strongest multi-agent baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies re-exploration and alignment as hidden costs that make parallel multi-agent LLM systems slower than serial baselines, and proposes a token-based parallelization criterion plus SquidAgent, which achieves 2.2x throughput and 2.6x wall-time speedup over Claude Code.
AI.motivation: Parallel multi-agent systems should theoretically yield near-linear speedups over sequential LLM agents, but in practice they often run slower than a single-agent baseline. The authors attribute this to two hidden costs—re-exploration (parallel workers redundantly reconstructing context the orchestrator already holds) and alignment (reconciling inconsistencies across independently generated outputs)—that serial execution avoids.
AI.method: The authors derive a principled criterion: parallelize a layer only when its critical-path cost plus re-exploration and alignment overheads is below the serial cost. Since LLMs are poorly calibrated for wall-clock estimation, cost is measured in predicted output tokens. Building on this, SquidAgent estimates all token budgets in one planning step, forks each worker directly from the orchestrator's session to eliminate re-exploration, replaces post-hoc reconciliation with a pre-generated shared convention block to bound alignment cost upfront, and applies the criterion layer by layer via a deterministic scheduler.
AI.result: SquidAgent achieves a 2.2x mean throughput improvement and a 2.6x mean wall-time speedup over Claude Code, and a 2.0x throughput improvement over the strongest multi-agent baseline.
AI.conclusion: Framing parallelization as a cost-benefit decision in predicted output tokens, and eliminating the re-exploration and alignment overheads directly, delivers substantial throughput and latency gains over both single-agent and existing multi-agent systems.

title: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding
summary: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

AI.tldr: ParanoiaEval is the first benchmark for unified evaluation of coding agents' risk-treatment capabilities, grounded in the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework, with 200 evidence-controlled repo-level task pairs and metrics for violations and evidence responsiveness.
AI.motivation: Coding agents increasingly do real-world work autonomously, making it important to judge whether their risk treatments are warranted; existing work evaluates related behaviors from separate perspectives without a systematic unifying framework.
AI.method: Grounded in the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework from software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings, containing 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs each differing only in treatment-defining evidence, plus dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness using a human-calibrated agentic judge.
AI.result: Experiments on 8 representative models plus a post-hoc human study show (I) unnecessary risk treatment in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, varying across configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, and violations harm developer experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; (III) agents show systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings.
AI.conclusion: Risk treatment is an independent capability dimension for coding agents, and knowledge from human risk-management practice can guide its diagnosis and improvement.

title: Coupled but Late: Turn-Taking Between Full-Duplex Speech Models in Unscripted Dialogue
summary: Full-duplex speech models are trained to converse with a person, but they are increasingly made to converse with each other, in self-play data generation, agent societies, and model-based evaluation. In that loop no human absorbs a timing error: each model's turn-taking is the other's input. We ask what timing the loop settles into. Two PersonaPlex-7B instances exchange audio tokens on a shared clock in unscripted conversation, and one floor-transfer rule is applied to them and to Switchboard. Their timing is coupled: re-pairing speakers across conversations destroys it. But the floor changes hands late, at a median of 400-560 ms against 137 ms for humans, and the last 120 ms of the partner's turn, where human projection places a tenth of its transfers, holds 1% of theirs. Delaying one direction of the channel shifts the response one-for-one and leaves the run-up to it empty, consistent with a reactive wait after the perceived end rather than the turn-end projection human timing requires.

AI.tldr: Two PersonaPlex-7B full-duplex speech models conversing with each other settle into coupled but systematically late turn-taking: floor transfers occur at a median of 400-560 ms versus 137 ms for humans, and almost none occur in the partner's final 120 ms, indicating reactive waiting rather than human-like turn-end projection.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex speech models are increasingly made to converse with one another in self-play data generation, agent societies, and model-based evaluation, forming a loop where no human absorbs timing errors and each model's turn-taking becomes the other's input. The paper asks what timing such a loop settles into.
AI.method: Two PersonaPlex-7B instances exchange audio tokens on a shared clock in unscripted conversation. A single floor-transfer rule is applied uniformly to these model-model dialogues and to human Switchboard conversations. The authors test coupling by re-pairing speakers across conversations, and probe the mechanism by delaying one direction of the channel.
AI.result: Timing is coupled, since re-pairing speakers across conversations destroys it. However, the floor changes hands late, at a median of 400-560 ms against 137 ms for humans, and the last 120 ms of the partner's turn, which holds a tenth of human transfers under projection, contains only 1% of the models'. Delaying one direction of the channel shifts the response one-for-one and leaves the run-up to it empty.
AI.conclusion: Model-model turn-taking is consistent with a reactive wait after the perceived end of the partner's turn, rather than the turn-end projection that human timing requires, meaning self-play and agent-society loops do not reproduce human conversational timing.

title: ScienceClaw: Benchmarking Continual Self-Evolution of AI-for-Science Agents Across the Natural and Social Sciences
summary: Large language model agents are accelerating scientific automation, yet verified executions rarely become persistent program-level improvements, and existing evaluations do not examine this process across sequential tasks in both the natural and social sciences. We formalize ScienceClaw as fixed-parameter program self-evolution that unifies task solving, scientific verification, and program updates. ScienceClaw-Eval spans 23 disciplines and measures scientific correctness, evolutionary gain, retention, cross-dataset transfer, and evolution cost through sequential streams and independent reset evaluation. Our framework repairs executable workflows through multi-turn interaction, converts re-execution-verified failure--success trajectories into linked Skill and Operator candidates, and retains an update only when source-task replay reproduces the repair and independent scientific tasks improve. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/ScienceClaw.

AI.tldr: ScienceClaw formalizes scientific program self-evolution as fixed-parameter program updates, unifying task solving, verification, and program updates, with ScienceClaw-Eval benchmarking 23 disciplines on correctness, evolutionary gain, retention, transfer, and cost.
AI.motivation: LLM agents accelerate scientific automation, but verified executions rarely become persistent program-level improvements, and existing evaluations fail to examine this process across sequential tasks in both natural and social sciences.
AI.method: ScienceClaw is formalized as fixed-parameter program self-evolution, unifying task solving, scientific verification, and program updates. The framework repairs executable workflows via multi-turn interaction, converts re-execution-verified failure-success trajectories into linked Skill and Operator candidates, and retains an update only when source-task replay reproduces the repair and independent scientific tasks improve.
AI.result: ScienceClaw-Eval spans 23 disciplines and measures scientific correctness, evolutionary gain, retention, cross-dataset transfer, and evolution cost through sequential streams and independent reset evaluation.
AI.conclusion: ScienceClaw provides a formalized and empirically evaluated framework for persistent program-level self-evolution in scientific LLM agents, addressing gaps in prior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/ScienceClaw.

title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://nanomuse.cn ; Code: https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse
summary: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta's Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor's cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person's accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta's public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone's screen and the computer's. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.

AI.tldr: The report defines the personal agent (one that acts on a person's accounts and devices, remembers across weeks, initiates conversation, and is accountable) via five questions and three horizons. It analyzes Meta's closed Muse agent from public records and its production prompt, then presents nanoMuse, a GPL-3.0 open-source counterpart: one agent per device sharing a single conversation over a user-runnable relay, all actions gated by a Sentinel, memory as user-readable files, and a user-chosen model.
AI.motivation: Assistants of 2011 only answered and waited; agents of 2023 performed a task and stopped. Meta's Muse (September 2026) realized a persistent personal agent, but it is closed, tied to a vendor's cloud and a single country. No open counterpart existed, so the report aims to define the personal agent and provide an open equivalent.
AI.method: The report (1) defines the personal agent through five questions and three horizons; (2) reverse-analyzes Muse from Meta's public record plus a copy of its production prompt, marking each statement by source; (3) designs nanoMuse as the open-source counterpart—per-device agents sharing one relay-hosted conversation, a Sentinel mediating every action, file-based memory with provenance, and interchangeable models; and (4) estimates its size and cost and lays out an open roadmap.
AI.result: Muse is characterized as closed software (not a model) confined to a vendor's cloud and one country, with accounts, devices, persistent memory, and a lasting conversation. nanoMuse is presented as an open (GPL-3.0) equivalent covering every device a person owns with screen/computer control, shared conversation via an anyone-runnable relay, Sentinel-mediated actions, readable memory files, and model choice; size and cost are given as estimates.
AI.conclusion: The roadmap identifies what must be opened: memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the "hands" (device control), and an open model to drive them.

title: WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly advancing scientific and engineering problem solving, with physics simulation emerging as a challenging yet practical testbed for reproducing complex physical phenomena with application in embodied AI, games and films. As the workhorse of such simulation, a solver computes how the state of a dynamic system evolves over time. Building such solvers requires physical understanding to identify appropriate models, mathematical reasoning to formulate the underlying dynamics, and software engineering to implement them as executable code, yet this capability of LLM agents remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce WorldSolver, a benchmark of 168 simulation tasks derived from physical phenomena in 61 classic computer graphics papers, spanning 7 physical domains. Each task contains a code scaffold that provides a fixed simulation environment for the scene, with the solver implementation left for the agent to complete. Specifically, we evaluate them along three dimensions: Execution Checks for successful execution, Visual Fidelity for reproducing the intended dynamic behavior in the rendered simulation, and Physical Plausibility for physics-grounded verification of the generated dynamics. Experiments on frontier agents reveal that producing executable solvers is difficult itself, and satisfying visual and physical correctness is even harder. GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5 perform comparatively better than the other evaluated agents, yet achieve overall scores of only 48.7% and 46.7%, respectively. WorldSolver is an early step toward agentic solver generation, and we hope it helps drive progress toward agents that can faithfully simulate the dynamic physical world. Code is available at https://github.com/sirujiang/WorldSolver.

AI.tldr: WorldSolver is a benchmark of 168 physics simulation tasks sourced from 61 classic computer graphics papers across 7 physical domains, where LLM agents must complete solver code scaffolds. Evaluated on three axes (Execution Checks, Visual Fidelity, Physical Plausibility), frontier agents score poorly, with top performers GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5 reaching only 48.7% and 46.7% overall.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used in scientific and engineering problem solving, and physics simulation is a challenging yet practical testbed for reproducing complex phenomena in embodied AI, games, and film. Building solvers requires physical understanding, mathematical reasoning, and software engineering, but LLM agents' capability for solver generation is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce WorldSolver, a benchmark of 168 simulation tasks derived from physical phenomena in 61 classic computer graphics papers, spanning 7 physical domains. Each task includes a code scaffold providing a fixed simulation environment, with the solver implementation left for the agent. Tasks are evaluated along three dimensions: Execution Checks (successful execution), Visual Fidelity (reproducing intended dynamic behavior in rendered simulation), and Physical Plausibility (physics-grounded verification of generated dynamics).
AI.result: Experiments on frontier agents show that producing executable solvers is difficult in itself, and satisfying visual and physical correctness is even harder. GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5 perform relatively better than other evaluated agents, yet achieve overall scores of only 48.7% and 46.7%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: WorldSolver represents an early step toward agentic solver generation, intended to drive progress toward agents that can faithfully simulate the dynamic physical world. The code is publicly available.

title: Does an Agent's History Tell You When Compaction Will Hurt? A Modest, Bounded Effect on the TRACE Paired-Replay Corpus
comment: Accepted at the IAB Workshop (Interpreting Agent Behavior) at NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 20 pages
summary: Many long-horizon agents compact their context on a global rule, usually a token budget, blind to what the agent was doing. We ask whether the agent's recent behaviour predicts when a compaction will hurt. TRACE's public corpus of 590 harness-triggered AppWorld compaction boundaries replays each boundary from a re-executed prefix state under the pre-compaction context and under the summary, and records the burden of the next actions: calls that error or repeat a call already made. We find that pre-boundary history predicts post-compaction harm only weakly. An internally prespecified contrast by prefix placement is a wide null, and the naive "has-written" label behind it turns out to measure trajectory phase. The best extension-protocol trigger reaches held-out AUROC 0.66 (0.64 on the replicate's own label) against a same-boundary replicate of 0.72; the best frozen, interpretable trigger avoids 21% of harmful (positive-burden) boundaries while keeping 84% of compaction opportunities, and exceeds the random-rule expectation on count but not on burden mass (a post hoc comparison). Whether the best trigger beats a token-budget rule at matched retention cannot be evaluated on the release. We state what corpora should ship to answer it.

AI.tldr: Pre-boundary history weakly predicts post-compaction harm; the best frozen trigger avoids 21% of harmful boundaries while retaining 84% of opportunities, but matched-retention comparison to a token-budget rule remains unanswerable on the release.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents compact context on global rules (e.g., token budgets), blind to the agent's activity, which may cause harm. The paper asks whether recent behaviour predicts when compaction will hurt.
AI.method: Uses TRACE's public corpus of 590 harness-triggered AppWorld compaction boundaries. Each boundary is replayed from a re-executed prefix state under the pre-compaction context and under the summary, recording next-action burden (calls that error or repeat an earlier call). Tests an internally prespecified contrast by prefix placement, a naive "has-written" label, and extension-protocol and frozen interpretable triggers, reporting held-out AUROC.
AI.result: Pre-boundary history predicts post-compaction harm only weakly. The prespecified prefix-placement contrast is a wide null; the "has-written" label actually measures trajectory phase. Best extension-protocol trigger: held-out AUROC 0.66 (0.64 on replicate label) vs. 0.72 for same-boundary replicate. Best frozen interpretable trigger avoids 21% of harmful boundaries while keeping 84% of opportunities, exceeding random-rule expectation on count but not burden mass (post hoc). Matched-retention comparison against a token-budget rule cannot be evaluated on the release.
AI.conclusion: Recent behaviour only weakly forecasts compaction harm; interpretable triggers offer modest benefit over random on count but not burden mass. The release lacks what is needed to test triggers against token-budget rules at matched retention, and the paper states which corpora should ship to answer that question.

title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can solve many narrow tasks, but querying them separately for millions of related instances can be prohibitively expensive. Can LLM agents autonomously create cheaper solutions for such workloads? We call this ability "bottling": the ability to turn general capabilities into task-specific solutions that balance answer quality and amortised cost. We introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark in which agents receive an entire unlabelled workload and must complete it under fixed time, compute and LLM API budgets. Agents choose their own approach, such as training a small model or writing a reusable program. Across ten models and three tasks, we find that strong zero-shot task performance does not reliably translate into strong bottling capabilities. Models with similar zero-shot scores can differ substantially after bottling, and 48 of 60 bottling runs score below the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of their model's zero-shot performance. Moreover, 31 of 60 runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget. Nevertheless, bottling can yield substantial savings: on query-product relevance classification, Opus 5 retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 at roughly 657 times lower reported cost. Bottling is also competitive with Jev, a "system one" model built especially for cheap, repetitive inference: Opus 5 on the same task recovers about 94% of Jev's macro-F1 at a quarter of Jev's projected full-workload cost. BOTTLED provides a basis for evaluating and improving agents' ability to invest limited resources in reusable solutions for large, repetitive workloads.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BOTTLED, a benchmark evaluating whether LLM agents can autonomously "bottle" general capabilities into cheaper task-specific solutions under fixed time, compute, and API budgets, and finds that strong zero-shot performance does not reliably predict bottling ability.
AI.motivation: Querying LLMs separately for millions of related instances is prohibitively expensive. The authors ask whether LLM agents can autonomously create cheaper solutions for such repetitive workloads, an ability they term "bottling." Existing evaluations focus on zero-shot task performance and do not assess agents' capacity to convert general capabilities into reusable, cost-efficient solutions under resource constraints.
AI.method: The authors introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark in which agents receive an entire unlabelled workload and must complete it under fixed time, compute, and LLM API budgets. Agents choose their own approach, such as training a small model or writing a reusable program. Evaluation spans ten models and three tasks, comparing bottling performance against zero-shot baselines and two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget, as well as against Jev, a "system one" model built for cheap, repetitive inference.
AI.result: Strong zero-shot task performance does not reliably translate into strong bottling capabilities. Models with similar zero-shot scores can differ substantially after bottling, and 48 of 60 bottling runs score below the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of their model's zero-shot performance. 31 of 60 runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget. Nonetheless, bottling can yield substantial savings: on query-product relevance classification, Opus 5 retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 at roughly 657 times lower reported cost, and recovers about 94% of Jev's macro-F1 at a quarter of Jev's projected full-workload cost.
AI.conclusion: BOTTLED provides a basis for evaluating and improving agents' ability to invest limited resources in reusable solutions for large, repetitive workloads. Bottling constitutes a distinct capability that is not reliably predicted by zero-shot performance, and it can deliver substantial cost savings, sometimes approaching or competing with purpose-built cheap inference models.

title: Sherpa: Teaching LLMs to Teach Adaptively
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures. Code and model are available at https://github.com/SALT-NLP/Sherpa
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable problem solvers, but being able to solve a problem is not the same as being able to teach it. Existing approaches to training LLMs as teachers rely on demonstrations, preference data, or predefined pedagogical criteria that specify what good teaching looks like. However, these signals are often not grounded in individual student learning outcomes, where effective teaching strategies can vary substantially across learners. To address this, we introduce Sherpa, a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that instantiates multiple student archetypes with LLMs conditioned on distinct learning preferences and trains a teacher model to adapt its instruction by directly maximizing their learning outcomes. Teacher LLMs trained with Sherpa improve instructed students' performance across all archetypes by an average of 20.5 percentage points. Under MathTutorBench's evaluation, Sherpa raises the overall pedagogy score from 52.5% to 79.2%, indicating better teaching responses. Our human studies show that the trained teacher is preferred over the base model in 79.6% of pairwise comparisons. Together, Sherpa trains LLM teachers to adapt to diverse simulated students and become better aligned with human teachers, paving the road towards AI tutors teaching real students.

AI.tldr: Sherpa is a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM teacher to adapt instruction to diverse student archetypes by directly maximizing their learning outcomes.
AI.motivation: LLMs can solve problems but cannot necessarily teach them. Existing teacher-training approaches rely on demonstrations, preference data, or predefined pedagogical criteria, which are not grounded in individual student learning outcomes, even though effective teaching strategies vary substantially across learners.
AI.method: Sherpa instantiates multiple student archetypes as LLMs conditioned on distinct learning preferences, then trains a teacher model via multi-turn reinforcement learning to adapt its instruction by directly maximizing student learning outcomes.
AI.result: Students instructed by Sherpa-trained teachers improved performance across all archetypes by an average of 20.5 percentage points. On MathTutorBench, the overall pedagogy score rose from 52.5% to 79.2%. In human studies, the trained teacher was preferred over the base model in 79.6% of pairwise comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Sherpa trains LLM teachers to adapt to diverse simulated students and to align better with human teachers, advancing toward AI tutors that can teach real students.
